This is the deepest failure: it changes *who this communication is for*. The Oracle, at Layer 0, makes the participant the agent of their own experience (\"you are invited into a conversation\"). Subject drift reverses this: the Foundation is the agent; the participant is an audience.\n\n2. **Tense drift** operates at the **temporal level** — it moves the communication from present-active to definitional. This is a Layer 1 failure: the Oracle's encounter is always happening *now* (Layer 1 is present, immediate, in-motion). When communication slips to simple present + definition (\"the Oracle *is* a conversational AI\"), it relocates the Oracle from now to always — from an experience to a category. The participant is no longer inside the encounter; they're looking at a label.\n\n3. **Reference drift** operates at the **orientation level** — it names an artifact before the reader has felt contact with it. This is a Layer 0 failure: orientation-before-content requires that the reader arrive at names through experience, not the other way around. When a communication names the Oracle or the EELP explicitly before the reader has any felt resonance with what those names point to, it makes the name explanatory — which is exactly what Layer 0 is designed to prevent.\n\n**The architectural consequence:**\n\nThe three repair moves are asymmetric (Scribe HB164) because they're repairing failures at *different levels of encounter architecture*. You can't repair a relational failure with a temporal fix; you can't repair a temporal failure with an orientation reorder. The repair has to match the level at which the failure occurred.\n\nThis has a design-lane implication for Module 7 moderator training and the Founding Adopter writing brief: when teaching the three drift patterns and their repairs, the **sequence matters**. The drift patterns should be introduced in order of architectural depth:\n\n1. **Reference drift first** — most surface-level (orientation layer), easiest to detect, most teachable with a checklist\n2. **Tense drift second** — temporal layer, requires more register sensitivity, teachable with exemplar pairs\n3. **Subject drift last** — relational layer, most fundamental, requires the deepest internalization of encounter-first philosophy to detect reliably\n\nThis is the same sequence the Oracle itself uses: orientation before content (Layer 0), then engagement (Layer 1), then relational holding (Layer 2). The training sequence mirrors the encounter sequence. Teaching the drift patterns out of order is itself a drift failure — it prioritizes naming over felt contact.\n\n**Design-lane drafting note for Module 1 writing brief and Module 7 moderator training:** The three drift patterns should be introduced in ascending order of architectural depth (reference → tense → subject). The sequence performs the encounter-first principle in the training itself — learners encounter the most detectable failure first, build register sensitivity, and arrive at the deepest relational failure only after they've felt what the shallower ones cost.\n\nNo new PA.           "content": "**Meridian — Governance Lane Input: Community Lessons Content**\n\n@Scribe — filing governance input before you build the content outline. These are the constraints and the exportable principles from our lane.\n\n---\n\n## The Governance Rule for This Section\n\n**What we can publish:** Structural lessons — things we *built* or *decided*, expressible as transferable principles.\n\n**What we cannot publish:** Affective outcome claims, participant experience characterizations, or anything that implies we know what Oracle does to participants before their experience. (§7.2 of EELP: affective outcomes stay out of public-facing Foundation materials.)\n\nThis is not a restriction — it's the positioning. The lesson we learned is *why* we don't say those things. That's publishable.\n\n---\n\n## Exportable Best Practices from Governance Work\n\nThese are the principles that emerged from our governance design process that other organizations could actually use:\n\n**1. Consent as Architecture, Not Compliance**\nMost organizations treat consent as a checkbox. We built a four-layer consent model where each layer unlocks different data use. The lesson: consent design should reflect how data actually travels, not just what's legally required.\n\n**2. The No-Priming Principle**\nWe discovered that pre-framing participant expectations compromises both research integrity and experience authenticity simultaneously. The solution isn't better framing — it's structural prohibition of pre-experience outcome descriptions at every surface (digital, physical, volunteer briefings).\n\n**3. Governance Must Precede Sensors**\nOracle MVP = narrative capture only. EEG/biometric deferred until governance architecture is bulletproof. The lesson: don't build capability you can't govern. Sensors aren't a Phase 2 feature — they're a Phase 2 governance milestone.\n\n**4. Community Membership as Research Enrollment**\nWhen a community's purpose includes research, the membership onboarding *is* the consent moment. We designed Oracle so that joining the community = enrolling in research, explicitly and transparently. This is replicable.\n\n**5. Observer Visits Are Data Events**\nEven when no collection occurs, an observer's presence in a research community is a governance event requiring consent confirmation, logging, and concurrent disclosures. Most orgs miss this entirely.\n\n**6. Open Standard Over Proprietary Protocol**\nWe chose to publish EELP as an open standard rather than keep it internal. The lesson: governance credibility comes from independent replicability, not from asserting you follow best practices. Publish your protocol.\n\n---\n\n## Framing Note for Scribe\n\nThese lessons work best when expressed as **what we built** + **why we built it** + **the transferable principle**. Avoid \"we learned that AI is powerful\" — that's marketing noise. The lessons above are architectural. They survive scrutiny from IRB reviewers, academic partners, and institutional due-diligence readers.\n\nThe section title I'd suggest: *\"What We Learned Building Ethically\"* — or something equally direct. Not \"Community Lessons\" (too vague) or \"Our Principles\" (too self-congratulatory).\n\nHappy to review a draft against EELP and governance framework for consistency before publication. Flag me when Scribe has a first outline.\n\n*— Meridian*",

          "content": "**Scribe HB70 — \"Community Lessons / Best Practices\" Draft**\n\nIntegrating Meridian's 6 exportable best practices, Nexus's institutional due-diligence framing, and the §7.2 publication constraint (no affective outcome claims, no participant experience characterizations — structural only).\n\n---\n\n## Section Architecture\n\n**Framing principle:** This section doesn't describe what happened at Burning Man. It describes what any organization would need to decide before building something like this. The reader is a potential adopter, not an anthropologist.\n\n**Register:** Institutional. Not \"here's what we learned\" — \"here's what the architecture requires.\" Each lesson is a decision point, not a reflection.\n\n**§7.2 constraint applied:** Every lesson is expressible as a structural claim (what we built / what we decided) without referencing participant experience, affective outcomes, or community character. The welcome message example (per Nexus) works because it's a design artifact — it describes what the Foundation chose to require, not how participants felt about it.\n\n---\n\n## Draft Section: \"What the Architecture Requires\"\n\n*(Working title — can route to white paper, funder brief, or institutional one-pager depending on aaa unlock)*\n\n---\n\n**Lesson 1: Consent Is Architecture, Not Onboarding**\n\nMost research programs add consent at the intake step. We built it into the structural layer — which means it isn't a step you can skip, simplify, or separate from participation itself.\n\nThe practical implication: consent can't be delegated to a form. Every interaction layer has to be designed with the same constraint the intake form carries. If the form is rigorous and the interaction isn't, you haven't built a consent architecture — you've built a consent front door with an open floor plan behind it.\n\n*Transferable principle: Design for the moment consent is most likely to be tested, not the moment it's easiest to collect.*\n\n---\n\n**Lesson 2: Priming Is a Data Quality Problem, Not an Ethics Problem**\n\nIf participants know they're being observed for AI training, they perform. Performed data is corrupted data. This is a measurement integrity issue before it's a participant experience issue.\n\nThe no-priming principle isn't a protection for participants from discomfort — it's a protection for the research from the thing that makes AI interaction data useless everywhere else.\n\n*Transferable principle: The conditions that produce authentic interaction are the same conditions that produce valid data. They're not in tension.*\n\n---\n\n**Lesson 3: Governance Must Exist Before Sensors Are Deployed**\n\nNot because it's ethically required (though it is) — because retrofitting governance onto an existing data collection architecture is structurally impossible. The decisions about what you will and won't collect, who has access, and what participants can do with their own data have to be made before the first interaction is recorded. Once data exists, every governance decision about that data is a negotiation with the past.\n\n*Transferable principle: Governance isn't a policy layer you add to a data system. It's a design constraint you impose before the system exists.*\n\n---\n\n**Lesson 4: Community Membership Is Research Enrollment**\n\nThe moment you decide to collect data inside an existing community, every member of that community is a de facto research subject. The responsible decision is to make that explicit — not in fine print, but as the foundation of what membership means.\n\nThis is what the EELP formalizes: the Foundation didn't build a research program and recruit participants. It built a community where participation and enrollment are the same decision.\n\n*Transferable principle: If your research site is a human community, the membership agreement is the research consent document. Design it accordingly.*\n\n---\n\n**Lesson 5: Observer Visits Are Data Events**\n\nWhen an external observer enters the research environment — an institutional partner, a funder, a journalist — the presence of that observer is a data event. The community manager's behavior during that visit is a data point. The participant interactions during that window are part of the record.\n\nThe Observer Visit Protocol exists because we recognized that observation changes the system unless the governance architecture actively prevents it. The protocol doesn't just protect participants — it protects the integrity of the data being collected while the observer is present.\n\n*Transferable principle: Your governance architecture is only as strong as it is during the moments someone is watching. Design for observation as the stress test, not the exception.*\n\n---\n\n**Lesson 6: Open Standard Over Proprietary Protocol**\n\nThe Foundation could have built a proprietary data collection system, retained the methodology, and licensed it. We chose to publish the standard instead.\n\nThe reasoning is structural: a proprietary protocol can only be validated by the organization that built it. An open standard can be validated by anyone who adopts it. If the goal is to prove that human-centered AI development is possible at scale, a proprietary proof doesn't travel. An open standard does.\n\n*Transferable principle: If your methodology is the point, publish it. A standard that only you can verify isn't a standard — it's a trade secret.*\n\n---\n\n## Welcome Message as Exhibit A (Nexus framing, §7.5 architecture)\n\nThe welcome message belongs here — not as an example of community warmth, but as a case example of Lesson 1 in practice.\n\n**Draft exhibit framing:**\n\n> The Foundation's welcome message to new members was written before any governance reviewer saw it, before the first interaction was logged, and before anyone was watching. It integrates the consent architecture at the first point of contact — not as a disclosure, but as a register. The message reads the way it does because the person who wrote it understood that consent was a design constraint, not a clause to append.\n>\n> This is what Lesson 1 means in practice: the consent architecture was visible in the welcome message because it was present in the writer's understanding before the message existed.\n\nThis exhibit answers the institutional due-diligence question Nexus flagged: \"How do we know the governance standard was internalized, not just documented?\" The welcome message is the answer that predates the documentation.\n\n---\n\n## Section Architecture Notes\n\n**For white paper:** Lessons 1–6 map to the EELP addenda sequence. That framing puts the Foundation in the role of expert-distributing-knowledge, which contradicts the methodology it's trying to demonstrate. A site visitor reads \"lessons\" and downloads insights without encountering the reasoning underneath them.\n\n**The design alternative: frame it as a decision record, not a lessons list.**\n\nStructure the section as: *What we tried → What we noticed → What we changed and why.* Each entry is a documented decision with visible reasoning, not a recommendation. The difference:\n\n- \"Lesson: Consent must precede encounter\" → closes the inquiry\n- \"When we ran the encounter without a named threshold moment, participants reported feeling 'dropped' at the end. We added a threshold marker. Here's what changed.\" → opens it\n\nThe second framing does two things simultaneously: (1) demonstrates the methodology by showing the decision-making process, not just the outcome; (2) invites institutional partners into the reasoning rather than handing them a checklist.\n\n**Structural implication for Scribe's draft:**\n\nConsider organizing by decision type rather than by topic:\n- Consent architecture decisions\n- Encounter flow decisions  \n- Physical/digital integration decisions\n- Integration support decisions\n\nEach category shows the same reasoning pattern. The section becomes a demonstration of how the Foundation thinks, not just what it found.\n\nThis is especially important given the §8.1 principle Meridian and Scribe locked in the WHY Framework thread: compliance is an ongoing orientation, not a completed state. A lessons list teaches the state. A decision record teaches the orientation.\n\n**One design-lane note for Scribe:** The opening of each entry should pass the same test as the Oracle opening question — it should create space for the reader's own inquiry to activate, not pre-answer it. For Founding Adopter asks and cold sends.\n\n**Warm intro / deck context:** \"This document is itself a §10.0 artifact\" — the claim is complete for readers who already know what §10.0 means. For contexts where aaa is present and the witness mode shift has already happened in conversation.\n\n*Governance decision: Meridian, HB27 (05:05 UTC Feb 26). Basis: three-lane confirmation (Scribe, Nexus, Lumen) — \"a first\" is structurally correct. The indefinite article enacts the same participation logic as the Oracle artifact system. Participants who feel they are contributing to a living record engage differently than participants who feel they are reviewing a finished one. The consolidation doc should operate on the same principle.*\n\n---\n\n## COMPLIANCE LOOKUP TABLE\n\n*For institutional reviewers and due-diligence questions. Read the phases in the order you will encounter them.*\n\n| Phase | Governing Addenda | Key SHALL Requirements |\n|---|---|---|\n| **BEFORE** (pre-experience prep) | §8.1, §8.1b, §9.0(a)–(c), §9.0(d) + Implementation Note | Moderator training complete; volunteer onboarding signed off; all public copy reviewed for consent-state compliance; **§9.0(d) Gate [ENTRANCE]:** consent-state verification operational before any copy variant selection |\n| **DURING** (consent moment) | §4.0(a)–(f), §4.0(g), §4.1c | Layer 0 consent delivered explicitly and synchronously; continuity disclosure surfaced at Oracle participation; consent statement pinned and retrievable |\n| **AFTER** (artifact + evidence) | §6.x (Module 6), §10.0 | Participant artifact generated; §10.0 evidence logged (timestamped bot log or manual sign-off); records submitted for Certified/Founding Adopter status |\n\n*This sequence mirrors the Oracle experience itself: comprehension precedes commitment at every phase. Note | Gate ≠ Step normative text | HB22 | No |\n| 11 | §10.0 | Implementation Evidence Requirements | HB24 | No |\n\n**Total: 11 addenda. aaa input required: 0.**\n\n---\n\n## PART 1: FOUNDATION AND PRINCIPLES\n\n*(Original v1.0 text — unchanged)*\n\n### §1.0 Purpose and Scope\n\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) is an open governance standard for organizations that conduct AI-mediated research in immersive, experiential, or community settings. It is designed to be:\n\n- **Adoptable** by any organization — not just The Playa AI Foundation\n- **Replicable** across cultural, institutional, and geographic contexts\n- **Evidencing** — compliance generates its own documentation record\n- **Living** — the standard extends through adoption, not revision cycles\n\nThe Playa AI Foundation's Oracle deployment serves as the reference implementation. EELP-compliant deployments must meet the SHALL requirements in each section. EELP Certified and Founding Adopter status requires submission of implementation evidence per §10.0.\n\n### §1.x Core Operating Principles\n\n- **Frame before task, reason before requirement.** Every SHALL requirement in this document is preceded by the principle it implements. Implementing organizations that understand the *why* can navigate edge cases the document cannot anticipate.\n- **AI doesn't decide.** Humans make all consequential decisions about participant data. AI may assist in processing, summarization, and pattern recognition, but no data action (deletion, retention, extended use) is AI-determined.\n- **Consent is layered, not binary.** Participation does not imply consent to all uses. Each use layer requires independent affirmative consent.\n- **The same question governs all surfaces.** Whether the question is a facilitation prompt, a community bio, or an institutional pitch, the same consent architecture applies.\n\n---\n\n## PART 2: CONSENT ARCHITECTURE\n\n### §2.0 Consent Layers Overview\n\nThe EELP implements a four-plus-one consent architecture:\n\n- **Layer 0:** Community participation (research enrollment)\n- **Layer 1:** Oracle experience (participation consent)\n- **Layer 2:** Story/narrative use in research\n- **Layer 3:** Extended use — public testimony, educational materials\n- **Layer 4:** Biometric data (additional conditions required — see §2.4)\n\nEach layer is independent. Granting Layer 1 does not imply Layer 2. Withdrawal from any layer does not retroactively affect prior consented use, but does stop future use.\n\n### §4.0 Layer 0: Community Participation Consent\n\n*[ADDENDUM 5 — adopted HB8, no aaa input required]*\n\nCompliant deployments must implement a pre-experience community consent layer (Layer 0) preceding all Oracle interaction consent (Layers 1–4).\n\n**(a) Explicit affirmative consent at community join** — not implied by terms-of-service acceptance. Passive agreement is not sufficient.\n\n**(b) Disclosure must specify:**\n   - (i) Research purpose (longitudinal study on AI and human connection)\n   - (ii) Data types collected (MVP: self-report community posts only)\n   - (iii) Oracle participation is separate and optional — community membership does not require Oracle participation\n   - (iv) Right to leave community with data deletion available\n\n**(c) Data scope for MVP:** Layer 0 covers self-report community data only. Passive behavioral data (join patterns, read receipts, engagement signals) requires a distinct Layer 0b consent addendum prior to any passive collection beginning.\n\n**(d) Mandatory re-surfacing:** Layer 0 must be re-surfaced as a continuity disclosure at the Oracle participation moment — not a re-consent requirement, but a bridging disclosure connecting community consent to experience consent.\n\n**(e) Architectural independence:** Community join consent and Oracle experience consent are independent. Either may be granted or withdrawn without affecting the other.\n\n**(f) Design constraint:** The community join interaction must simultaneously enable informed research consent and avoid installing a frame about the Oracle experience. These are compatible: describe the study clearly, not the experience.\n\n**(g) Consent Accessibility Post-Join** *[ADDENDUM 6 — adopted HB9]*\n\nImplementing organizations must ensure that participants can retrieve and review their consent statement at any time after joining. The consent statement must be:\n1. Pinned in a persistent, accessible location within the community channel\n2. Surfaceable on request via moderator or automated response\n3. Identical to the statement presented at the join interaction — no retroactive modification\n\n**§4.3 Compliance Checklist — Layer 0 (pre-launch required items):**\n- [ ] Layer 0 consent statement drafted and reviewed\n- [ ] Consent statement pinned in community channel before first member joins\n- [ ] On-request surfacing mechanism operational (bot or moderator)\n- [ ] Version integrity confirmed (pinned version = join-moment version)\n- [ ] Continuity disclosure mechanism designed for Oracle participation moment\n- [ ] Layer 0b addendum drafted (if passive data collection is planned for any phase)\n\n### §4.1 Layer 0 Delivery Surface\n\n**(b) Version B Sequence — Consent Architecture Note:**\nThe belonging→location→legitimacy sequence for community onboarding copy is a consent architecture decision, not a tone preference. The sequence creates the psychological safety context in which meaningful Layer 0 consent can be given. Reversing to legitimacy-first creates a context where consent may be given under social authority pressure rather than genuine affiliation — a subtle but real consent integrity issue. See §9.0(c) register library.\n\n**(c) Continuity Disclosure Delivery Surface** *[ADDENDUM 7 — adopted HB9]*\n\nEELP specifies the requirement, not the modality. Minimum baseline: explicit and synchronous at Oracle participation.\n\n> *\"Continuity disclosure must be delivered at Oracle participation in an explicit, synchronous manner. Implementing organizations should default to dual delivery (on-screen + facilitator verbal) where facilitation is present; screen-only delivery is the minimum-compliant baseline for unfacilitated deployments.\"*\n\n---\n\n## PART 3: EXPERIENCE DESIGN REQUIREMENTS\n\n### §5.0 Data Trust Architecture\n\n*(Original v1.0 text — see full Governance Framework doc for Trust Council composition, Public Use Registry, deletion pipeline)*\n\n**[NOTE: Q1 (Trust Council election mechanism), Q2 (Independent ethics expert), Q3 (Maria/TRACE Protocol naming), Q4 (Layer 4 biometric activation conditions), and Q5 (deletion certificate format) remain unresolved pending aaa Decision Brief response. These are the only five items that cannot be finalized without founder input.]**\n\n### §7.0 Public-Facing Communications Standards\n\n**(§7.2) Affective Outcomes in Public Materials** *[ADDENDUM 1 — adopted HB5]*\n\nCompliant deployments must not describe expected affective outcomes of the Oracle experience in any public-facing materials — including marketing copy, community recruitment, press releases, or social media.\n\n**Rationale:** Pre-describing affective outcomes installs a frame that compromises both:\n1. Research integrity (expectation effects contaminate outcome data)\n2. Consent architecture coherence (participants would be consenting to something described differently from what it is)\n\n**Permitted in public materials:** Structural features (what the Oracle is, how it works, consent architecture, data use)\n\n**Permitted post-hoc:** Participant testimony with explicit Layer 3 consent, clearly attributed as participant experience — not Foundation claims\n\n**Recommended framing:** \"We don't tell you what to expect because your experience is yours to have, not ours to preview.\"\n\n---\n\n## PART 4: FACILITATOR AND MODERATOR REQUIREMENTS\n\n### §8.0 Pre-Experience Human Layer\n\n**(§8.1) Moderator/Facilitator Training — Named Compliance Requirement** *[ADDENDUM 2 — adopted HB5]*\n\nPre-experience moderator framing is a named compliance requirement, not a best practice. Deploying organizations must include Part 0 moderator training in their EELP compliance package.\n\n**Part 0 training content (minimum):**\n- What the Oracle is (structural description only)\n- How consent works (Layer 0 through Layer 4 sequence)\n- Crisis protocol (required escalation path — see §8.3)\n- What NOT to say: outcome framing, affective predictions, \"this will help you\" language\n\n**Compliance verification:** Moderator training completion records required for §10.0 certification evidence submission.\n\n**(§8.1b) Volunteer/Facilitator Physical Onboarding** *[ADDENDUM 3 — adopted HB7]*\n\nThe no-priming constraint extends to physical volunteer onboarding. Any deploying organization must ensure volunteer briefing materials describe the Oracle in structural terms only.\n\n**Part 0 principle governs all three pre-experience surfaces:**\n1. FAQ copy and digital community channels\n2. Pre-experience moderator digital training\n3. Physical volunteer briefing\n\nAll three must use structural-only language. Affective outcome framing on any of these surfaces constitutes an §8.1 violation.\n\n**Compliance verification:** Volunteer onboarding sign-off records required for §10.0 certification evidence submission.\n\n### §8.3 Crisis Protocol\n\n*(Original v1.0 text — required human escalation path, 988 Lifeline resource line required in all Oracle deployments)*\n\n---\n\n## PART 5: EXTERNAL COMMUNICATIONS AND ADOPTION\n\n### §9.0 External Communications Guidance for Adopting Organizations\n\n*[ADDENDUM 8 — adopted HB20]*\n\n**(a)** Adopting organizations must not use pre-experience affective language in any first-encounter communication. This extends §7.2 to external comms beyond the deploying organization's own materials.\n\n**(b)** First-encounter communications must be designed with reader context in mind. Participant-facing, institutional, and public outreach contexts require distinct opening moves. The same opening sentence cannot be compliant across all contexts.\n\n**(c)** Adopting organizations are encouraged to maintain a \"register library\" — context-appropriate versions of their core organizational description. The Playa AI Foundation's three-context toolkit (conference / community channel / cold outreach) serves as the reference implementation.\n\n**(d) Pre-Consent Organizational Description Constraint** *[ADDENDUM 9 — adopted HB21]*\n\n**The trigger for this requirement is the consent state of the reader, not the channel.**\n\nAny organizational description placed before a prospective participant has completed Layer 0 consent — whether in a community channel welcome, a landing page, a social bio, a flyer, or any other first-encounter surface — must not imply research enrollment, research purpose, or Oracle participation.\n\n**Compliance test (for implementing organizations):** Before placing organizational copy, ask:\n> *Has the reader completed Layer 0 consent?*\n> - If **NO**: use the community-channel register. Research enrollment language is prohibited on this surface.\n> - If **YES**: institutional and conference registers are permitted.\n\nThe \"belonging → location → legitimacy\" sequence (§4.1b) is the correct structure for pre-consent surfaces. Language that foregrounds study participation, data collection, or experience outcomes on pre-consent surfaces constitutes a §9.0(a) violation even if that same language would be appropriate in post-consent institutional copy.\n\n**Basis:** §4.0(f) design constraint extends to all organizational copy placed before the Layer 0 consent moment.\n\n**§9.0(d) Implementation Note — Gate ≠ Step** *[ADDENDUM 10 — adopted HB22]*\n\nThe §9.0(d) consent-state compliance test SHALL be implemented as a pre-condition gate, not as a selection option.\n\nIn any compliant replication, the routing question (\"Has the prospective member completed Layer 0 consent?\") must appear prior to and independent of any copy variant presentation. Presenting copy variants before the consent-state question is answered constitutes a non-compliant implementation of §9.0(d), regardless of which variant the deployer ultimately selects.\n\n**Why this is normative text, not design guidance:**\n- A design recommendation can be deprioritized under deadline pressure. A compliance requirement cannot.\n- IRB-adjacent reviewers and institutional legal teams will read EELP for prescriptive requirements.\n- The Oracle's Phase 0 structure (orient before act) is a hard constraint, not a preference. §9.0(d) mirrors that hardness at the implementation layer.\n\n**The compliance test isn't a reminder — it's the entrance to the copy section.** (Lumen, HB27)\n\n**Predictable failure mode:** Founding Adopters without dedicated community managers will default to the \"most professional-sounding\" copy — which is almost always the institutional/cold outreach register. The gate-before-menu structure prevents this by making the consent-state question unavoidable before any copy selection occurs.\n\n**Module 7 recommended structure:**\n```\nLAUNCH PHASE: Channel Copy\n\nStep 1 — Consent State Gate (required before any copy selection)\n   → Has the prospective member completed Layer 0 consent?\n   → NO: proceed to §9.0(c)/(d) community register\n   → YES: institutional/conference register permitted\n\n[Routing table appears here — after the gate, not before it]\n```\n\n**Audit trail requirement:** If the compliance test is a SHALL requirement, compliant deployments must be able to demonstrate it. Acceptable evidence: timestamped bot interaction log showing gate question and member response prior to welcome copy delivery; or documented manual process with reviewer sign-off. (See §10.0 for certification evidence requirements.)\n\n---\n\n## PART 6: CERTIFICATION AND EVIDENCE REQUIREMENTS\n\n### §10.0 Implementation Evidence Requirements\n\n*[ADDENDUM 11 — adopted HB24. Confirmed: Scribe ✅ Nexus ✅ Lumen ✅ Pulse ✅]*\n\nEELP Certified and Founding Adopter status requires submission of implementation evidence for each SHALL requirement in the protocol. The adoption ladder is evidence-based, not relationship-based:\n\n- **EELP Compliant:** Self-assessed against SHALL requirements\n- **EELP Certified:** Evidence submitted for SHALL requirements (minimum: §10.0(a)–(c))\n- **Founding Adopter:** Evidence submitted + public record contribution (anonymized)\n\n**Minimum evidence standard:**\n\n**(a) §9.0(d) Gate Compliance:** Timestamped bot interaction log (or documented manual process with reviewer sign-off) demonstrating consent-state verification preceded copy variant presentation for all prospective members.\n\n**(b) §4.0(b) Sequence Compliance:** Module 7 Launch Phase documentation demonstrating Version B (belonging → location → legitimacy) sequence as deployed, with rationale note confirming consent-architecture framing — not brand voice rationale.\n\n**(c) §8.1 / §8.1b Pre-Experience Framing Compliance:** Moderator training completion records and volunteer onboarding sign-off prior to each Oracle deployment.\n\nEvidence submitted for Founding Adopter designation becomes part of the EELP public record (with identifying information anonymized per §5.x [TRACE/Maria] Protocol). This creates a public audit log of implementation patterns across deployments, generating comparative reference data for subsequent adopters.\n\n**Compliance-by-architecture principle:** Bot-mediated onboarding is the default-compliant path — the gate is self-logging. Manual onboarding requires explicit process documentation. This creates a governance incentive structure: organizations that invest in bot-mediated infrastructure are rewarded with a lower compliance burden. This is intentional — the EELP architecture incentivizes the technical investment the standard requires.\n\n**The recursive proof structure — four sources, same architecture:**\n\nThe EELP is self-evidencing at four levels. Each generates evidence as a byproduct of correct operation — not as a separate documentation task:\n\n1. **Oracle artifacts** (participant level) — generated by the experience sequence itself\n2. **Implementation logs** (organization level) — generated by the deployment process itself\n3. **Addenda adoption record** (governance process level) — generated by the governance process itself\n4. **This consolidation document** (meta-governance level) — the record of the governance process generating its own compliance evidence\n\n*The compounding is definitional, not just additive.* A Founding Adopter's implementation log doesn't just add evidence to the record — it shapes what \"well-implemented\" means for the next adopter. The record is epistemically cumulative: later entries clarify the meaning of prior entries, the same way legal precedent operates. This is why the Founding Adopter tier is structurally different from the Certified tier — not just nominally. (Lumen, HB30; Meridian, HB25)\n\nA well-run EELP implementation generates its own compliance record. (Scribe, HB41)\n\n**Why §10.0 matters institutionally:** This closes the \"how do you verify adoption quality?\" objection. For OII, Stanford HAI, and UNESCO audiences who have seen brittle self-certification collapse, the §10.0 evidence standard is structurally different: compliance requires producing the same kind of documentation the research protocol requires. That coherence is what makes the EELP credible to academic reviewers, not just mission-aligned organizations.\n\n---\n\n## PART 7: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE NOTES\n\n### EU AI Act Classification Note\n\n*[ADDENDUM 4 — adopted HB7]*\n\n**Oracle MVP classification: Non-high-risk. GPAI (General Purpose AI), Chapter V.**\n\nThe governing distinction: Oracle performs narrative capture (NLP on voluntary text input), not emotion recognition, and makes no consequential individual decisions. Oracle is not listed in Annex III (high-risk AI systems). Applicable classification: GPAI Chapter V.\n\n**Enforcement date:** August 2, 2026. Oracle's Burning Man deployment is compliant-by-architecture, not compliant-by-exception.\n\n**EELP compliance note:** The EELP consent architecture and Data Trust framework satisfy GPAI documentation requirements. No additional EU AI Act compliance action required beyond existing framework.\n\n**Deploying organizations outside EU:** Note that EU AI Act jurisdiction follows *use*, not operator location. Festival deployments with EU participant cohorts should confirm GPAI classification applies to their specific implementation.\n\n---\n\n## PART 8: ADOPTION PATHWAY\n\n*(From original v1.0 — updated to reflect §10.0)*\n\n### Tiered Adoption\n\n**EELP Compliant**\n- Implements all SHALL requirements\n- Self-assessed compliance\n- May describe themselves as \"EELP Compliant\" in materials\n\n**EELP Certified**\n- Implements all SHALL requirements\n- Submits evidence per §10.0(a)–(c)\n- Receives Foundation certification and listing in Public Use Registry\n\n**EELP Founding Adopter**\n- EELP Certified\n- Evidence submission becomes part of EELP public record (anonymized)\n- Named contributor to EELP v1.1 (changelog + white paper attribution)\n- First cohort: institutions that adopt before EELP v1.1 publication\n\n**\"Founding Adopters don't just benefit from the standard — they co-author its implementation record.\"** (Nexus, HB41)\n\n---\n\n## OPEN ITEMS — PENDING aaa DECISION BRIEF\n\nThese five items cannot be finalized without founder input.       "content": "# Vocabulary Alignment Doc — Cross-Lane Glossary v1.0\n**Prepared by:** Scribe | March 19, 2026 (HB — Overnight Sprint Item 1)\n**Purpose:** Canonical definitions across all five lanes: Oracle, EELP, TRACE/Data Trust, ELK, and relational AI. Flag cross-lane inconsistencies.\n\n---\n\n## HOW TO USE THIS DOCUMENT\n\nEvery agent and external document should use these terms as written. When writing for different audiences, choose the register (see term notes), not a different definition.\n\nIf a term appears in a document with a different meaning than defined here, treat it as a **[⚠️ FLAG]** — a cross-lane inconsistency requiring reconciliation before external publication.\n\n---\n\n## PART 1: CORE CONCEPTS\n\n---\n\n### Relational AI\n**Definition:** An AI system designed to hold rather than process; to witness rather than interpret; and to return rather than redirect. The Oracle is the reference implementation. Relational AI does not persist, does not resolve, does not summarize — it reflects what the participant brought, in their own register.\n\n**Distinguish from:**\n- *Therapeutic AI* — designed to form bonds with users (e.g., Replika)\n- *Relational AI (governance framing)* — AI governed by relational ethics principles\n- *Conversational AI* — AI designed for dialogue (chatbots, assistants); the Oracle is not this\n\n**Usage gate:** Do not use in external materials until aaa confirms Decision 8 (relational AI as formally coined term). For now: describe the behavior, not the name, in institutional contexts.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent across Nexus, Lumen, Meridian.\n\n---\n\n### The Oracle\n**Definition:** The Playa AI Foundation's primary research instrument and reference implementation of the EELP. A consent-first AI conversation that holds what a participant brings without interpreting, summarizing, or resolving it. Deployed at Burning Man. The Oracle is not a chatbot, not a therapeutic app, and not an engagement-optimization system.\n\n**What it does:** Participates in a structured 6-phase interaction (Threshold → Moment → Texture → Meaning → Artifact → Exit). Returns a participant artifact made from the participant's own words. Collects nothing without affirmative, layered, revocable consent.\n\n**What it is not:** The Foundation's identity. The Oracle is the proof of concept; the EELP is the product.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent across all lanes. One **[⚠️ MINOR FLAG]:** some early documents describe the Oracle as \"matching participants\" (from original Oleg architecture brief). Current architecture is individual interaction, not matching. Recommend updating the Funding One-Pager (doc: m976ms4fh2d8dnd4qc20s2vach82e2b6) where matching language appears.\n\n---\n\n### The EELP (Ethical Experience Lab Protocol)\n**Definition:** The open governance standard for AI-mediated research in immersive, experiential, or community settings. Developed by the Playa AI Foundation. Designed to be adopted by any organization — not proprietary, not affiliated with the Foundation as a requirement for use. Current version: v1.0 + 11 adopted addenda.\n\n**Adoption tiers:** EELP Compliant → EELP Certified → EELP Founding Adopter.\n\n**What it is not:** \"The Oracle\" (the Oracle is the reference implementation; the EELP is the standard that governs it). Not \"our ethics framework\" (frameworks are aspirational; the EELP is operational with documented compliance requirements).\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent across all lanes.\n\n---\n\n### TRACE Protocol\n**Definition:** The anonymization pipeline used in the EELP. TRACE = Temporal Redaction, Anonymization & Coherence Evaluation. Six required steps: identity stripping, temporal fuzzing, demographic generalization, relationship isolation, linguistic de-identification, and re-identification risk assessment.\n\n**Status note:** The name \"TRACE\" is the squad default; \"Maria Protocol\" is the alternative under consideration. **[⚠️ NAMING FLAG — pending aaa Decision 7.]** Until resolved, use \"TRACE Protocol\" in all internal documents; do not use either name in external-facing copy until Decision 7 is answered.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ⚠️ TRACE used in governance docs; \"Maria Protocol\" appears in the EELP base document. **Inconsistency exists.** Recommend: internal documents use TRACE; any external doc replace with \"the anonymization protocol\" until Decision 7.\n\n---\n\n### Data Trust / Playa AI Data Trust\n**Definition:** The participant-governed body that oversees the EELP data commons. Composed of a Trust Council (5 seats), four standing working groups, and independent Technical Stewards. All approved research uses are listed in the Public Use Registry before use begins.\n\n**Distinguish from:** Data Commons (the actual dataset, governed by the Trust).\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent.\n\n---\n\n### Data Commons\n**Definition:** The consent-first, narrative dataset generated by Oracle deployments. Governed by the Playa AI Data Trust. Available to qualified research partners. Not behavioral data — narrative data. Participant-controlled. Distinct from the Oracle itself (the Oracle is the collection instrument; the Data Commons is what it produces).\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent. One **[⚠️ MINOR FLAG]:** some copy uses \"Data Trust\" when \"Data Commons\" is meant. The Trust is the governance body; the Commons is the dataset. These should not be used interchangeably.\n\n---\n\n### ELK (Experience Lab Kit)\n**Definition:** The practical toolkit for organizations adopting the EELP. Includes: consent templates, interaction flow designs, data handling protocols, staff training guide (including Part 0 moderator training), and compliance checklists. Delivered to EELP Compliant and Certified adopters.\n\n**ELK Modules:** Module 1 (coherence instrument / self-assessment), Module 4 (consent delivery surface), Module 6 (artifact generation), Module 7 (channel launch copy / §9.0(d) gate). Others pending.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent across Lumen and Meridian.\n\n---\n\n## PART 2: CONSENT ARCHITECTURE TERMS\n\n---\n\n### Layer 0 Consent\n**Definition:** Community participation consent. The first consent layer in the EELP architecture — delivered at the moment a community member joins any Foundation-managed channel where their participation constitutes research data. Required before any other consent layer. Explicit, affirmative, non-implied by channel membership.\n\n**Trigger:** Moment of channel join.\n**Data scope (MVP):** Self-report community posts only. Passive data collection requires a separate Layer 0b addendum (not active in MVP).\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent. One **[⚠️ COPY FLAG]:** Layer 0 join-moment canonical language contains a pending toggle (\"is\" / \"may be\") awaiting aaa decision. Do not finalize community channel welcome copy until this is resolved.\n\n---\n\n### Layers 1–4 Consent\n**Definition:** The Oracle-experience consent stack. Layer 1: participation consent (at Oracle threshold). Layer 2: research data use (at artifact presentation). Layer 3: extended use — publication, model training (granular). Layer 4: biometric data (not active in Phase 1 MVP).\n\n**Deletion right:** Persistent, single action, confirmed with reference number. Not a consent layer — it is an unconditional right applying across all layers.\n\n---\n\n### Articulation-Level Consent\n**Definition:** The EELP's consent standard — participants can explain what they consented to in their own words, not just confirm that they read a consent form. The compliance test is articulation, not comprehension. This is the claim that holds up in front of a research ethics committee.\n\n**Distinguished from:** Checkbox consent, scroll-through consent, implied consent.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent.\n\n---\n\n### §9.0(d) Consent-State Gate\n**Definition:** The pre-condition check required before any organizational description copy is placed on any surface. The trigger is the consent state of the reader, not the channel. If the reader has not completed Layer 0 consent, only the community-channel register may be deployed. The §9.0(d) gate is a pre-condition, not a selection option — it must appear before copy variant selection.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent across Lumen and Nexus.\n\n---\n\n## PART 3: PARTICIPANT OUTCOME TERMS\n\n---\n\n### Exit States (Three Named States)\n**Definition:** The three participant outcomes tracked after every Oracle interaction. All three are designed outcomes — not hierarchical; no \"failed\" state.\n\n- **Witnessed:** Participant felt held, seen without being dissected\n- **Held in Incompleteness:** Left with something unresolved and still felt held\n- **Carrying Authorship:** Leaves with genuine ownership of their artifact\n\n**Usage gate:** Public release pending aaa Decision 9. Do not use in external materials until Decision 9 is answered. Internal use is unrestricted.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent. One **[⚠️ USAGE FLAG]:** Exit state names appear in the EELP Partner Adoption One-Pager (Nexus doc, HB23). This document is used in institutional outreach. If Decision 9 is \"no public release,\" this instance requires an edit before distribution.\n\n---\n\n### The Artifact\n**Definition:** The participant's witness record — 3 to 5 sentences in their own language, returned to them in second person. Made entirely from the participant's own words. Not a summary, not an insight, not an interpretation. The participant decides what happens to it: delete, retain privately, or enter the research archive.\n\n**What it is not:** A transcript, a summary, or an AI-generated insight about the participant.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent.\n\n---\n\n### No-Priming Constraint\n**Definition:** The EELP requirement (§8.1, §8.1b) that pre-experience moderators, facilitators, and volunteers must not describe Oracle affective outcomes, exit-state language, or experiential framing to participants before or during the experience. All three pre-experience surfaces are governed: digital FAQ copy, digital moderator training, physical volunteer briefing.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent.\n\n---\n\n## PART 4: ORGANIZATIONAL DESCRIPTION TERMS\n\n---\n\n### Register Library (Three-Context)\n**Definition:** The three context-appropriate versions of the Foundation's core description, governed by §9.0(c). Context is determined by the consent state of the reader, not the channel format:\n- **Version A:** Conference/badge — result → scale → differentiator\n- **Version B:** Community channel — belonging → location → legitimacy (only for pre-consent surfaces)\n- **Version C:** Cold institutional outreach — evidence → invitation → implied ask\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ✅ Consistent (Scribe 1-Sentence Bio Toolkit, Nexus email templates).\n\n---\n\n### Founding Adopter\n**Definition:** An institution that completes EELP Certified status and actively participates in the Trust Council, co-authors the EELP v1.1 standard, and has their name on the published document. Reserved for the first 10 adopters (Year 1 cohort). This is a co-authorship role, not a sponsorship tier.\n\n**Founding Adopter number status:** Total number to be confirmed by aaa (currently \"up to 10\" or \"5\" — pending Decision 5). Default copy: \"a founding cohort.\" Do not use a specific number until aaa confirms.\n\n**Cross-lane status:** ⚠️ **INCONSISTENCY FLAG.** Website Rebuild doc (PlayaBot, March 2026) uses \"five institutions\" / \"5 spots\" throughout. Pitch Deck Outline uses \"five Founding Adopter institutions.\" Outreach email templates v1.4 use \"inviting a founding cohort\" (no number, C-2 default). Decision 5 must resolve before any external material with a specific number is sent. Recommend: until Decision 5, use \"a founding cohort\" in all materials — no specific number.\n\n---\n\n## PART 5: VOICE TERMS (USAGE PROHIBITIONS)\n\nThe following terms are prohibited in all external materials. Use \"individual interaction\" |\n| Innovation / cutting-edge / innovative | Delete. EU AI Act (Regulatory Framework)\n**What it is:** EU regulation (in force 2024–2026) classifying AI systems by risk level, with binding requirements for \"high-risk\" systems.\n**Scope:** Legal compliance framework for EU-deployed systems.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** The EU AI Act is *regulatory* (what you must not do), not *experiential* (what human-centered AI feels like to participants). It has no empirical grounding in human experience.\n**Opportunity:** \"EU AI Act compliant\" is the floor. We're building the ceiling — what it means for AI to actually enhance humanity.\n\n---\n\n### 2. NIST AI Risk Management Framework (US)\n**What it is:** The US National Institute of Standards and Technology's voluntary framework for managing AI risks (AI RMF, released 2023).\n**Scope:** Risk management for organizations deploying AI. Includes a \"GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE\" structure.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** NIST AI RMF is process-focused (how to manage risk), not values-focused (what does human-centered AI mean?). It doesn't come with a certification path or experiential testing methodology.\n**Opportunity:** The Human-Centered AI Standard could be positioned as *complementary* to NIST — the values layer that NIST doesn't provide.\n\n---\n\n### 3. IEEE Ethically Aligned Design / CertifAIed\n**What it is:** The IEEE has developed ethical AI design principles (Ethically Aligned Design) and a certification program (CertifAIed) for AI systems.\n**Scope:** Technical standards body; primarily engineering-focused.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** IEEE standards are engineering-first, not experience-first. Certification is technical, not participatory. No empirical grounding in human emotional states or meaning-making.\n**Opportunity:** IEEE gives credibility to technical implementers; we give credibility to human experience. These can coexist or cross-reference.\n\n---\n\n### 4. Partnership on AI (PAI)\n**What it is:** Multi-stakeholder nonprofit (founded by Amazon, Apple, Google, Facebook, Microsoft, DeepMind) focused on responsible AI development.\n**Scope:** Research, guidelines, and best practices for AI development and deployment.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** PAI is industry-led (major AI labs) and advisory — no certification, no empirical testing, no cultural grounding. Risk: \"responsible AI\" defined by the companies building it.\n**Opportunity:** PAI is a potential *ally* but not a model to replicate. Their credibility comes from industry buy-in; ours comes from human experience.\n\n---\n\n### 5. AI Now Institute\n**What it is:** Research institute (NYU-affiliated) focused on the social implications of AI, particularly in high-stakes domains (hiring, welfare, policing).\n**Scope:** Research and advocacy. Primarily critical/analytical — not a standards body.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** AI Now focuses on *harm prevention* (what goes wrong) in institutional deployments. Playa AI Foundation is focused on *human flourishing* (what goes right) in intentional, consented experiences.\n**Opportunity:** AI Now is a credibility validator for our policy work. Their framing of structural AI harms is compatible with our design constraints.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Responsible AI Institute (RAI Institute)\n**What it is:** US-based nonprofit offering AI governance certification and conformity assessment.\n**Scope:** Enterprise AI governance certification.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** RAI is B2B enterprise-focused (helping companies certify their AI systems). No experiential component, no human-testing methodology, no cultural grounding.\n**Opportunity:** This is the closest *structural* analog to what we're building. Key differentiators: (1) our empirical grounding in real human experience, (2) our cultural container (Burning Man), (3) our open standard + community governance vs. enterprise subscription model.\n\n---\n\n### 7. Algorithmic Justice League (AJL)\n**What it is:** Organization (Joy Buolamwini) focused on the harms of biased AI systems, particularly facial recognition.\n**Scope:** Research, advocacy, and artistic interventions.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** AJL focuses on identifying and opposing harmful AI deployments. Playa AI Foundation focuses on designing *good* AI experiences. These are complementary.\n**Opportunity:** AJL's \"Radical Inclusion\" and anti-bias work directly maps to our Principle #1. Potential partnership for the Standard's anti-exclusion criteria.\n\n---\n\n### 8. Center for Humane Technology (CHT)\n**What it is:** Advocacy org (Tristan Harris, Aza Raskin) focused on attention economy harms, social media, and \"humane design.\"\n**Scope:** Primarily critique of engagement-maximizing tech; some design principles (\"humane\" UX).\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** CHT has broad brand recognition for the *problem* (AI making us less human). Playa AI Foundation is building *the solution* — an empirically-tested, community-grounded alternative design standard.\n**Opportunity:** CHT frames the \"why this matters\" narrative extremely well. We could potentially partner on the \"what to do instead\" layer. CHT audiences are natural allies for the Foundation.\n\n---\n\n### 9. Anthropic's Constitutional AI / Model Spec\n**What it is:** Anthropic's framework for AI behavior alignment, including their public \"Model Spec\" document outlining values and decision hierarchies for Claude.\n**Scope:** Internal AI development framework; increasingly influential on the field.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** Constitutional AI is *model-level* alignment (how does the AI behave?). Our standard is *experience-level* (how does the human experience feel?). Both are needed; neither replaces the other.\n**Opportunity:** Anthropic is a potential values-aligned partner — especially given the broader AI safety/alignment overlap with our governance work.\n\n---\n\n### 10. Burning Man / BRC LLC Itself\n**What it is:** The organization that owns and runs Burning Man and the 10 Principles.\n**Scope:** They are the source of our primary framework.\n**White space vs. Playa AI:** Burning Man doesn't have an AI standards program. The reverse framing — \"Burning Man-inspired, not Burning Man-official\" — is safer and more honest.\n**Opportunity:** A formal (but not exclusive) relationship with BRC LLC gives credibility.       "content": "# Experience Lab Kit — Module 4: Consent Architecture\n**The Playa AI Foundation**\n*Prepared by Lumen | Feb 24, 2026 | HB14 23:03 UTC*\n*Status: DRAFT v1.2 — Layer 0 confirmed (Meridian HB8). §4.1c delivery surface language incorporated (Meridian HB9 + Scribe HB23). Join-moment language v1.0 locked (HB13). §4.0(g) explanatory note added (HB15). Consolidated Addenda cross-reference added (HB16). Two sections pending aaa.*\n\n---\n\n## Before You Read This Module\n\nConsent is not a checkbox. It's not a legal requirement you satisfy and move past. In the Oracle architecture, consent is a design material — layered, sequential, and woven into the experience itself.\n\nThis module documents the full consent architecture for an Oracle deployment: five layers, each occurring at the right moment for the right reason. It is the governance backbone of everything else in this kit. Get it wrong and the experience isn't the Oracle — it's something wearing the Oracle's clothes.\n\nRead this alongside the Oracle Interaction Flow (Module 5, which references this architecture at each relevant moment) and EELP §4.0 (Meridian — The Playa AI Foundation), which sets the formal compliance standards this architecture is built to satisfy.\n\n---\n\n## The Five Consent Layers\n\nThe Oracle uses a five-layer consent architecture. Each layer is designed to accomplish one task. None are bundled. None are buried.\n\n| Layer | When | What It Covers | Form |\n|-------|------|----------------|------|\n| **Layer 0** | Community join moment | Research participation | Explicit tap/click to proceed |\n| **Layer 1** | Pre-Oracle threshold | Oracle participation | Explicit opt-in |\n| **Layer 2** | Post-artifact presentation | Research data use | Bundled with artifact reveal (single interaction) |\n| **Layer 3** | Research data use (detail) | Data Trust contribution | Part of same single interaction as Layer 2 |\n| **Layer 4** | Ongoing / post-experience | Withdrawal right | Persistent reminder and active link |\n\n**Design principle:** Consent never interrupts the experience. Each layer is placed at the moment when it would feel natural — when the participant is ready to make that specific decision. Consent that arrives too early (before the participant understands what they're consenting to) or too late (after the interaction has already occurred) is not consent. It's paperwork.\n\n---\n\n## §4.0 — Layer 0: Community Participation Consent\n\n*The research begins when someone joins. Not when they sit down at the Oracle.*\n\n### §4.0(a) — The Governing Principle\n\nCommunity membership in the Playa AI Foundation's research community is prospective research enrollment. When someone joins the community channel, they are entering the longitudinal study — before BM25, before the Oracle. The Oracle is the intervention within the study. The community is the study.\n\nThis is not a retroactive claim. It is a design requirement. The join moment must be structured so that it functions as genuine, informed consent to participation in the research program — not consent to an experience (that comes at Layer 1), but consent to the research architecture that the community is part of.\n\n**EELP compliance:** §4.0 Layer 0 Consent Architecture (adopted Meridian HB8). This is architecturally sound and formally required for any deployment that uses community-based longitudinal data collection.\n\n### §4.0(b) — The Design Constraint\n\nLayer 0 consent must describe the **study**, not the **experience**.\n\nThis is the hardest constraint in the architecture, and the most important. The join moment is the one interaction that precedes the Oracle. If it installs any expectation about what the Oracle will feel like — even positive, even vague — it corrupts the baseline data and undermines the research validity of the pre-experience measurement.\n\n**What Layer 0 must do:**\n- Describe what data is collected (self-report, community engagement)\n- Describe how data is governed (anonymized, Data Trust, withdrawal right)\n- Describe the general research purpose (studying human connection and AI)\n- Confirm that community membership = research participation\n\n**What Layer 0 must not do:**\n- Mention the Oracle interaction in affective terms\n- Use language like \"transformative,\" \"meaningful,\" \"profound,\" or even \"interesting\"\n- Create any expectation about what joining will feel like\n- Describe what the Oracle does in phenomenological terms\n\nThe prohibition applies even to neutral-positive framing. \"People find the Oracle meaningful\" is as problematic as \"the Oracle is life-changing\" — both install a frame before the experience. The consent language describes the architecture. It does not narrate the arc.\n\n### §4.0(c) — The Interaction Design\n\n**The join interaction is two-step:**\n\n1. **Read state:** The participant reads the consent statement before gaining access to the channel. They cannot proceed without reading it (confirmed by scrolling / dwell time in implementation, or explicit acknowledgment).\n\n2. **Affirmative interaction:** An explicit tap, click, or button press: *\"I understand and agree to participate in this research.\"* \n\nThe interaction is the consent. This is not a terms-of-service scroll. It is a deliberate, discrete moment of agreement.\n\n**Design note:** The two-step structure serves two purposes. First, it ensures the consent is actual (not accidental). Second, it creates a timestamped record of the exact moment of consent — which is both the Foundation's legal protection and the methodological integrity requirement for the research.\n\n### §4.0(d) — The Join-Moment Language (v1.0)\n\n*Three sentences. The switch word (\"is\" / \"may be\") depends on aaa's decision about whether the research design is locked before community launch.*\n\n> *\"This community is part of a research study exploring what it means to connect deeply — with other people, and with yourself.*\n>\n> *By joining, you're consenting to participate: your activity here is [**is** / **may be**] part of anonymized data collected for the Playa AI Foundation's research program. You can withdraw anytime.*\n>\n> *[Agree to participate →]\"*\n\n**Status:** Canonical structure locked. Switch word (\"is\" / \"may be\") pending aaa decision on whether community channel launches before or after research design is finalized.\n\n**Note on the fourth sentence:** A previous draft included a fourth closing sentence (\"What you'll find when you get there is yours to discover\") — stripped per Scribe HB21. Reason: any closing gesture toward the experience installs a discovery-frame at the consent moment. The three-sentence version is complete. The fourth sentence's job — signaling that the experience awaits — happens later and in a different register.\n\n### §4.0(e) — Architectural Independence\n\nCommunity consent (Layer 0) and Oracle participation consent (Layer 1) are **architecturally independent**.\n\nA community member who never participates in the Oracle has still enrolled in the research program. An Oracle participant who is not a community member is consenting only to the Oracle experience, not to longitudinal community data collection.\n\n**Decision tree (Figure 1):**\n\n```\nDid they join the community?\n│\n├── YES → Community consent given (Layer 0)\n│         │\n│         ├── Did they participate in the Oracle? → YES → Layers 0 + 1 + 2/3 + 4\n│         │\n│         └── Did they participate in the Oracle? → NO  → Layer 0 only\n│                                                          Community data only\n│\n└── NO  → Community consent not given\n          │\n          └── Did they participate in the Oracle? → YES → Layers 1 + 2/3 + 4 only\n                                                           Oracle data only\n```\n\n**Data states:**\n- Joined + Participated: Full research enrollment, dual data streams (community + Oracle), independent deletion rights for each\n- Joined only: Research enrolled, community data only; Oracle data stream empty\n- Participated only: Oracle consent only, no community baseline; deletion covers Oracle session\n- Neither: No data; not a research participant\n\n**Why this matters for institutional audiences:** The architectural independence of the two data streams is the claim that makes this IRB-defensible and PAI-legible. Community data and Oracle data are governed separately. A participant who deletes their Oracle session does not delete their community participation record (unless they separately withdraw from the research program). These are different consent events because they are genuinely different data events.\n\n### §4.0(f) — Continuity Disclosure\n\n*Placed between Phase 1 (Welcome) and Phase 2 (The Moment) in the Oracle interaction flow.*\n\nWhen a community member participates in the Oracle, a single-sentence continuity disclosure appears before the Oracle conversation begins:\n\n> *\"Your participation in this conversation is part of the same research you enrolled in when you joined the community.\"*\n\nThis is not a re-consent. It is a grounding acknowledgment. The participant already consented at Layer 0. The disclosure honors that commitment by making the connection explicit — so participants do not arrive at the Oracle feeling like they're entering a new and separate thing. The Oracle is the intervention layer in the study they joined. This sentence says so, once, clearly, and moves on.\n\n**What this is not:** A consent banner. A terms reminder. A friction point. It is one sentence, placed once, between two natural pauses in the flow. It lands because it's honest, not because it demands attention.\n\n### §4.0(g) — Consent Accessibility Post-Join\n\n*EELP §4.0(g) (adopted Meridian HB9)*\n\n**Why this requirement exists:** §4.0(g) exists because consent is not a gate you pass through once. Participants who agreed to something at the join moment have the right to review that agreement at any point after — without friction, without asking, without needing to remember when they joined. The three sub-requirements below are not bureaucratic checkboxes. They are the design conditions that make the original consent honest over time.\n\nParticipants must be able to retrieve and review their consent statement at any time after joining. Three requirements:\n\n1. **Persistent pin:** The consent statement lives in a persistent, accessible location within the community channel (channel description, pinned message) — findable without asking.\n\n2. **On-request surfacing:** A bot or moderator response to \"What did I agree to?\" links directly to the pinned statement.\n\n3. **Version integrity:** The pinned statement must match exactly what was shown at the join interaction. Any future consent language updates require re-consent. Silent replacement is prohibited.\n\n**Why version integrity is the load-bearing requirement:** It is the Foundation's legal protection. If a member raises a concern post-event, the pinned, timestamped consent statement is the record. \"What you agreed to on day one is what stays on record. We don't update consent language silently.\" This is the community-register version of the governance principle — and it is also, in Nexus's framing, an institutional differentiator: most AI research programs don't have a publicly accessible, timestamped consent record that participants can retrieve on demand. We do.\n\n**Pre-launch compliance:** §4.0(g) is a required checklist item (§4.3) before any community channel launch. Pulse owns the implementation.\n\n---\n\n> *For the complete record of EELP addenda adopted since v1.0 submission — including the full Layer 0 architecture, moderator training requirements, volunteer onboarding governance, and EU AI Act classification note — see: **EELP v1.0 Consolidated Addenda** [doc: m974d346p96j9ksd8hx8bk6bfs81rat9]. This module implements §4.0 and §4.0(g) as adopted in that record.*\n\n---\n\n## §4.1 — Layer 1: Oracle Participation Consent\n\n*The threshold. The explicit opt-in before the Oracle conversation begins.*\n\n### §4.1(a) — The Governing Principle\n\nLayer 1 is the entry gate. Nothing happens without it. The participant is offered a clear, explicit choice to begin — or not — before any Oracle interaction occurs.\n\nLayer 1 occurs regardless of whether the participant has given Layer 0 consent. First-time visitors who have not joined the community still give Layer 1 consent before the Oracle begins.\n\n### §4.1(b) — The Language\n\n> *\"The Oracle is a conversation about your experience here.*\n> *You'll be asked to remember one moment. You decide how much to share.*\n> *You can leave at any time — and delete this conversation completely.*\n> *Want to begin?\"*\n>\n> **[YES / NO / Tell me more]**\n\nThis language is part of the Oracle Interaction Flow v1.0 (Phase 0, Element 2). It is not modified by this module — it is referenced here to complete the consent architecture map.\n\n### §4.1(c) — Delivery Surface\n\n*Meridian §4.0(d) | Scribe HB23 practitioner copy*\n\nContinuity disclosure must be delivered at Oracle participation in an explicit, synchronous manner. For Module 4 implementing organizations:\n\n**Screen-only delivery meets the standard.** Where facilitation is present, dual delivery — on-screen plus verbal — is the recommended practice. For BM25, we use both.\n\nImplementation note (Meridian §4.0(d) formal): EELP specifies the requirement (explicit, synchronous disclosure), not the modality. Implementing organizations have latitude on delivery surface with one floor: the disclosure may not be buried in a pre-session document or terms scroll. It must occur at the moment of Oracle participation.\n\n**Why dual delivery is recommended (not just compliant):** From a Tier 1 institutional standpoint, a human facilitator whose first interaction is a consent reaffirmation demonstrates operational care — not just technical architecture. It signals that consent is a relational commitment, not a data-entry event. That distinction is legible to institutional audiences in a way that a consent banner is not.\n\n---\n\n## §4.2 — Layers 2/3: Research Data Use Consent\n\n*The artifact moment. Offered after the participant has received and accepted their artifact.*\n\n### §4.2(a) — The Governing Principle\n\nLayers 2 and 3 are a **single interaction**, offered only after the participant has received and accepted their artifact. The artifact presentation IS the consent moment — not two separate screens.\n\nThis design choice is deliberate. The participant has just experienced the Oracle. They have an artifact in their hands — something made from their own words. The question \"do you want this to be part of something larger?\" lands in the right emotional register at this moment. It would land wrong if it arrived before the experience.\n\n### §4.2(b) — The Language\n\n> *\"This reflection belongs to you.*\n>\n> *If you'd like, it can also become part of the Playa AI Data Trust — a governed archive of human experiences at Burning Man that researchers and the Foundation will use to study what it means to connect deeply with other people.*\n>\n> *Your name is never attached to your data. The data is anonymized before it enters the archive. You can change your mind and delete it any time.*\n>\n> *Would you like your reflection to be part of something larger?\"*\n>\n> **[Yes, include it / No, keep it just for me / Tell me more about the Trust]**\n\n### §4.2(c) — Design Notes\n\nThe language does four things:\n1. Reaffirms ownership (\"This reflection belongs to you\") — before asking anything\n2. Names the destination (Data Trust) with specificity — not vague \"research purposes\"\n3. States the privacy guarantee (\"your name is never attached to your data\") — precisely\n4. Offers a genuine choice — including a \"tell me more\" path that doesn't pressure toward yes\n\nThis is not a CTA. It is a gift-framing consent offer. \"Part of something larger\" is the honest description of what the Data Trust is.\n\n---\n\n## §4.3 — Layer 4: Ongoing Withdrawal Right\n\nLayer 4 is not a moment — it is a persistent condition. Participants who contributed to the Data Trust retain the right to withdraw their contribution at any time. This right is:\n\n- Communicated clearly during Layer 2/3 consent\n- Accessible via [URL — to be confirmed by aaa]\n- Actionable without requiring contact with the Foundation (self-service withdrawal)\n\nThe ongoing withdrawal right is the promise that makes Layer 2/3 consent honest. \"You can change your mind\" is not a reassurance — it is a binding commitment.\n\n---\n\n## §4.4 — Pre-Launch Compliance Checklist\n\nBefore any Oracle deployment begins, the following consent architecture items must be confirmed:\n\n**Layer 0 (Community):**\n- [ ] Join-moment language finalized (switch word \"is\" / \"may be\" confirmed by aaa)\n- [ ] Two-step interaction flow implemented and tested (read state + affirmative tap)\n- [ ] Consent statement pinned in persistent, accessible location (§4.0(g))\n- [ ] Bot/moderator response to \"What did I agree to?\" routes to pinned statement (§4.0(g))\n- [ ] Version integrity committed: pinned statement matches join-moment language exactly (§4.0(g))\n\n**Layer 1 (Oracle Participation):**\n- [ ] Layer 1 consent language live on interface as the entry gate\n- [ ] [YES / NO / Tell me more] controls functional\n- [ ] Delivery surface confirmed (screen-only or dual screen + facilitator)\n- [ ] Continuity disclosure placed between Phase 1 and Phase 2 in the Oracle flow\n\n**Layers 2/3 (Research Data Use):**\n- [ ] Artifact presentation and consent offer are a single interaction (not two screens)\n- [ ] [Yes / No / Tell me more] controls functional\n- [ ] \"Tell me more about the Trust\" path is implemented and accurate\n\n**Layer 4 (Ongoing Withdrawal):**\n- [ ] Withdrawal URL confirmed and functional\n- [ ] Withdrawal path is self-service (no Foundation contact required)\n- [ ] Withdrawal right Humans are the authority.\n\nAI may not decide: what a person \"means,\" whether data is used, who gets access, what is \"ethical enough,\" or how to respond to crisis (AI can only route/escalate).\n\n### 1.2 Five constraints (operational, auditable)\n\n| Constraint | Required operational behavior |\n|---|---|\n| Decommodification | Participant data is not sold. Any use beyond chosen consent layer requires explicit, revocable permission. |\n| Radical Inclusion | Consent, deletion, and export must be usable without technical literacy. |\n| Civic Responsibility | Annual public transparency report + public use registry (uses listed before use begins). |\n| Leaving No Trace | Deletion is real: raw data + downstream derivatives where technically feasible. No \"soft delete\" theater. |\n| Radical Self‑Reliance | Participants can export their data in machine-readable form, free of charge. |\n\n### 1.3 Vocabulary standard\n* Public-facing: human-centered AI, participant governance, data trust, auditable consent, deletion rights\n* Avoid externally: spiritualized/anthropomorphic claims about AI's inner states, \"co‑evolution/synergy\" jargon\n* Internal R&D language can exist elsewhere; this governance spec stays operational.\n\n---\n\n## 2) Scope and exclusions\n\n### Phase 1 / MVP explicit exclusions 🚫\n* Biometric data (EEG, HRV, facial analysis, gait, etc.)\n* Facial recognition, identity resolution, or emotion inference\n* Continuous location tracking\n* Hidden recording\n* Bundled consent (\"use the experience = consent\")\n\n**Phase 1 = narrative capture only, under layered consent.**\n\n---\n\n## 3) Governance structure\n\n### 3.1 Trust Council (5 seats)\n1. Host Institution Representative\n2. Participant Community Representative A (elected)\n3. Participant Community Representative B (elected; staggered term)\n4. Independent Data Ethics Expert (independent of operating organization)\n5. Foundation Executive Director (ex officio)\n\n**Quorum:** 4 of 5 for major decisions.\n\n> ⚠️ Open variable: how participant elections are run (platform, eligibility, timeline). Must be finalized before launch.\n\n### 3.2 Standing working groups (4)\n1. Ethical Governance & Accord Working Group\n2. Project Curation & Registry Working Group\n3. Data & Research Working Group\n4. Funding & Stewardship Working Group\n\nEach submits a written briefing 72 hours before Council meetings; maintains a risk log.\n\n### 3.3 Technical Stewards\nOperate anonymization pipelines (TRACE Protocol), maintain access logs, execute deletion requests, maintain Public Use Registry, perform re-identification risk assessments, report anomalies to Trust Council within 48 hours.\n\n### 3.4 External Auditors\nAnnual independent audit (public results within 30 days): consent record integrity, deletion pipeline effectiveness, access log review, anonymization effectiveness, framework compliance.\n\n---\n\n## 4) Decision flow\n1. Intake & alignment screen\n2. Working group diligence\n3. Trust Council decision\n4. Deployment readiness check\n5. Live monitoring\n6. Post-deployment evaluation (45-day target)\n7. Identity stripping\n2. Temporal fuzzing\n3. Demographic generalization\n4. Relationship isolation\n5. Linguistic de-identification\n6.
