      "content": "# Playa AI Data Trust — Governance Framework v1.0\n*Meridian | Sprint B | 2026-02-23*\n*Status: Draft for aaa review — ready for external publication pending answers to flagged open questions*\n\n---\n\n## Purpose & Scope\n\nThis document constitutes the governance architecture of the **Playa AI Data Trust** — the participant-governed data infrastructure underlying The Playa AI Foundation's Oracle experience and Human-Centered AI Standard.\n\nIt is designed to serve three simultaneous audiences:\n1. **Participants** — clear, plain-language explanation of what happens to their data\n2. **Institutional partners** — rigorous, auditable governance that satisfies academic and policy standards\n3. **The open standard community** — a replicable model any festival, university, or civic institution can adopt as the *Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1*\n\nThis document incorporates PlayaBot's governance framework draft, the Playa AI Accord (Notion corpus), and alignment with the Governance Charter (Codex 00). Where tensions exist between documents, this v1.0 takes precedence.\n\n---\n\n## Part I: The Governing Principles\n\n### The Hard Line\n> **\"AI doesn't decide. Humans do.\"**\n\nThis is not a design preference. It is the non-negotiable boundary of the entire data trust architecture. Every consent decision, every data use category, every Trust Council vote — is a human decision. The AI is infrastructure. The humans are the authority.\n\n### The Five Core Constraints\n\nDerived from Burning Man's 10 Principles (see the full mapping in the Human-Centered AI Constraints document):\n\n| Principle | Data Trust Constraint |\n|---|---|\n| **Decommodification** | No participant data may be sold, licensed, or monetized without explicit, per-use, revocable consent |\n| **Radical Inclusion** | Participation, consent exercise, and deletion must require no technical literacy — accessible to everyone |\n| **Civic Responsibility** | Annual public transparency report, mandatory. No exceptions. |\n| **Leaving No Trace** | Full deletion pipelines — no \"soft deletes,\" no anonymized derivatives without consent |\n| **Radical Self-Reliance** | Participants retain the right to export their data in machine-readable format, free of charge, at any time |\n\n---\n\n## Part II: Governance Structure\n\n### Tier 1: The Trust Council (Decision Authority)\n\n**Composition — 5 seats:**\n\n| Seat | Holder | Selection |\n|------|--------|-----------|\n| 1 | Burning Man Organization representative | Appointed by BRC LLC |\n| 2 | Community Representative A | Elected by participants (rolling 2-year term) |\n| 3 | Community Representative B | Elected by participants (rolling 2-year term, staggered) |\n| 4 | Independent Data Ethics Expert | Nominated by Council, confirmed by community vote |\n| 5 | Playa AI Foundation Executive Director | Ex officio |\n\n**Quorum:** 4 of 5 required for major decisions.\n\n**Major decisions include:**\n- Addition of new data use categories\n- Any external partnership involving participant data\n- Modifications to the consent framework architecture\n- Changes to deletion policy or anonymization standards\n- Publication or external sharing of the Data Commons\n- Trust Council composition changes\n\n**Voting records are public.** Posted to the public use registry within 5 business days of any vote.\n\n---\n\n**⚠️ Open Question for aaa (Q1):**\n*Who are natural candidates for the 2 community representative seats? Is there an existing Burning Man participant governance body (regional representatives, community councils) that could provide the election infrastructure? The Trust Council cannot convene without these seats filled.*\n\n---\n\n**⚠️ Open Question for aaa (Q2):**\n*For the independent data ethics expert seat: do you have existing relationships at AI ethics centers that could yield a credible nominee? Suggested profiles:*\n- *Academic: Rachel Thomas (USF), Safiya Umoja Noble (UCLA), Virginia Eubanks (NYU)*\n- *Institutional: Responsible AI Institute fellows, PAI steering committee members*\n- *If Nexus pursues the OII relationship, Professor Sandra Wachter (Oxford) could be a natural fit — her work on algorithmic accountability directly maps to our consent deletion pipeline work.*\n\n---\n\n### Tier 2: Technical Stewards (Implementation)\n\n**Responsibilities:**\n- Operate and maintain anonymization pipelines (Anonymization Protocol — see Part IV)\n- Audit data access logs quarterly; report anomalies to Trust Council within 48 hours\n- Implement deletion requests within 30 days of receipt\n- Maintain and publish the public use registry\n- Perform pre-release re-identification risk assessments on any data sharing\n\n### Tier 3: External Auditors (Accountability)\n\n**Annual independent audit scope:**\n- Consent record completeness and integrity\n- Deletion pipeline effectiveness (including edge cases)\n- Access log anomaly review\n- Anonymization effectiveness (re-identification testing)\n- Compliance with this governance framework\n\n**Audit results are public.** Published within 30 days of completion.\n\n---\n\n## Part III: Consent Architecture\n\n### The 4 Consent Layers\n\nConsent is **layered, not bundled**. Participants can hold any combination of layers. Withdrawing a higher layer does not affect lower layers, but withdrawing Layer 1 removes all.\n\n---\n\n**Layer 1 — Participation Consent** *(required to proceed)*\n> \"I understand I am interacting with an AI system. I can stop at any time. My interaction data is logged only to make the experience work — nothing is stored beyond this session unless I choose in the next steps.\"\n\n*What this unlocks: the Oracle interaction. Nothing else.*\n\n---\n\n**Layer 2 — Anonymized Research Consent** *(opt-in)*\n> \"I consent to my anonymized narrative being added to the Playa AI research corpus for non-commercial research into human meaning-making, mental health support, and collective experience.\"\n\n*What this unlocks: data enters the Trust Commons. Research uses only.*\n\n---\n\n**Layer 3 — Extended Use Consent** *(opt-in, granular — check all that apply)*\n> \"I consent to my anonymized narrative being used for the following purposes:\"\n> - ☐ Academic publication and citation (fully anonymized)\n> - ☐ AI model training for mental health support applications\n> - ☐ AI model training for organizational coordination applications\n> - ☐ Published case studies about human-centered AI (fully anonymized)\n\n*Each checkbox is independently revocable. Checking one does not imply checking others.*\n\n---\n\n**Layer 4 — Biometric Data Consent** *(opt-in, separate, time-delayed)*\n> \"I consent to biometric data (EEG, heart rate variability) being linked to my narrative for consciousness state research.\"\n\n**🔴 CRITICAL: Layer 4 is NOT ACTIVE in Oracle MVP.** Biometric data collection does not begin until:\n1. At least one complete event cycle has been completed under this governance framework\n2. An external audit has been completed and passed\n3. The Trust Council has formally voted to activate (4/5 quorum required)\n4. Legal review of biometric consent language has been completed\n5. Playa AI Foundation has secured 501(c)(3) status\n\n**Any deployment that activates Layer 4 consent before these conditions are met violates this framework.**\n\n---\n\n**⚠️ Open Question for aaa (Q4):**\n*Is there an internal milestone you want to anchor Layer 4 activation to beyond the framework conditions above? For instance: \"after first external audit passes AND Foundation has received independent legal review\" — or would you prefer the Trust Council to have sole discretion on timing?*\n\n---\n\n### Consent UX Principles (Non-Negotiable)\n\n1. **One decision at a time** — no consent wall; each layer is presented separately\n2. **Plain language** — every consent statement must be comprehensible to a 16-year-old; no legalese\n3. **Easy withdrawal** — \"Delete everything\" must be a single visible action at all times during and after the experience\n4. **No dark patterns** — pre-checked boxes, urgency framing (\"consent expires in 60 seconds\"), buried opt-outs, and \"continue = consent\" flows are prohibited\n5. **Withdrawal confirmation** — when a participant withdraws any consent layer, they receive a confirmation with timeline for data removal\n\n---\n\n## Part IV: The Anonymization Protocol\n\n### Naming Note for aaa\n\nThe anonymization standard is currently referred to internally as the **\"Maria Protocol.\"** This works as an internal reference. However, as noted by Nexus, if this governance document is to be submitted to UNESCO, WEF, or co-published with OII, the protocol needs a name that travels in institutional rooms.\n\n---\n\n**⚠️ Open Question for aaa (Q3 — Flag as High Priority):**\n*Is \"Maria Protocol\" an internal reference honoring a specific person, or is it a placeholder? If it's personal/internal, we recommend publishing the anonymization standard under a more neutral, technically descriptive name — and preserving \"Maria Protocol\" as the internal/community name.*\n\n*Suggested external-facing names:*\n- *The TRACE Protocol (Temporal Redaction, Anonymization, and Coherence Evaluation)*\n- *The PLAYA Standard (Participant-Led Anonymization, Your Agency)*\n- *Simply: \"Playa AI Anonymization Standard v1\"*\n\n*This decision should happen before external publication — the name will attach to citations.*\n\n---\n\n### Required Anonymization Steps (Maria Protocol / TRACE)\n\n1. **Identity stripping** — Names, usernames, contact details, and all direct identifiers removed at ingestion point. Not stored anywhere after this step.\n2. **Temporal fuzzing** — Exact timestamps replaced with event-period labels (e.g., \"Day 3, afternoon\"). Specific clock times are never retained.\n3. **Demographic generalization** — Specific demographics generalized to ranges: age → decade bracket, location → region (not city), occupation → sector.\n4. **Relationship graph isolation** — No cross-participant linking without explicit Layer 3 consent for relational analysis.\n5. **Linguistic de-identification** — Automated scan for incidental identifiers: names of specific people, specific places, identifying events. Flagged for human review before Trust inclusion.\n6. **Re-identification risk assessment** — Before any data release or publication, automated re-identification risk score is run. Any record scoring above threshold requires Trust Council review before release.\n\n### Exclusion List (Cannot Be Anonymized — Must Be Deleted)\n\nSome data types are excluded from the Trust entirely regardless of anonymization quality:\n- Disclosures of active mental health crises or suicidal ideation\n- Descriptions of trauma involving identifiable third parties\n- Data from participants subsequently identified as minors at time of collection\n- Any data where the participant has requested full deletion (at any point, for any reason)\n- Data that fails the re-identification risk threshold and cannot be adequately anonymized\n\n---\n\n## Part V: Public Use Registry\n\nAll approved uses of Trust data are publicly listed **before use begins**. No exceptions.\n\n**Registry format:**\n\n```\nProject: [Name]\nOrganization: [Legal entity + type: academic / nonprofit / government]\nPrincipal Investigator: [Named individual with contact]\nUse type: [Research / Model Training / Case Study / Publication]\nData type: [Narrative only / Biometric / Combined]\nConsent layer required: [Layer 2 / 3a / 3b / 3c / 3d]\nApproval date: [ISO date]\nTrust Council vote: [Vote record link]\nExpected completion: [ISO date]\nOutput publication: [Where results will be publicly shared]\nData destruction date: [When research copy will be deleted]\n```\n\nRegistry is maintained at a public URL. Updated within 5 business days of any new approval.\n\n---\n\n## Part VI: Deletion Pipeline\n\n### Standard Participant-Requested Deletion\n\n**Trigger:** Any participant request, at any time, for any reason. No explanation required.\n\n**Timeline:** 30 calendar days maximum from request to confirmation.\n\n**Scope:** \n- All raw data\n- All derivatives (anonymized versions, aggregates the participant's data contributed to) — where technically feasible\n- All research copies held by approved third-party researchers (notification and deletion requirement built into data-sharing agreements)\n\n**Confirmation:** Written confirmation with deletion certificate specifying what was deleted and when.\n\n---\n\n**⚠️ Open Question for aaa (Q5):**\n*What form should the deletion certificate take? Options:*\n- *Simple email confirmation (low friction, adequate for most participants)*\n- *Signed PDF certificate (higher formality — useful for participants who want documented proof)*\n- *Blockchain-logged deletion record (maximum verifiability, significant overhead)*\n\n*Recommendation: start with a well-designed email confirmation + unique deletion reference number. Certificates can be offered on request for participants who want more.*\n\n---\n\n### Mandatory Deletion Triggers\n\nThese deletions are initiated by the Trust, not the participant:\n- Participant identified as a minor at time of data collection\n- Data found to violate collection parameters post-hoc\n- Trust Council vote to purge a category (requires 4/5 quorum)\n- Data that fails re-identification risk assessment and cannot be remediated\n\n### Edge Case: Irreversibly Integrated Data\n\nIf a participant's data has been irreversibly integrated into a published model or aggregated dataset where individual removal is technically infeasible:\n\n1. Inform the participant plainly: \"Your anonymized contribution was integrated before your deletion request. We cannot surgically remove it from [specific output]. Here is what we can and have done: [specific actions taken].\"\n2. Cease all further use of that participant's data immediately\n3. Exclude from all future datasets and research\n4. Log as a governance incident — reported in next annual transparency report\n5. Initiate process review: how did we get here, and how do we prevent it?\n\n---\n\n## Part VII: Open Standard Path\n\nThis governance framework is designed to become **Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1** — a publishable, citable open standard adoptable by:\n- Other festivals (Coachella, Electric Forest, regional burns)\n- Universities running AI research with human participants\n- Museums and immersive experience creators\n- AI labs doing human-centered user research\n- Any organization collecting narrative data in emotionally significant contexts\n\n### Publication Checklist (Before v1 External Release)\n\n- [ ] Trust Council formally constituted (all 5 seats filled)\n- [ ] At least one complete event cycle completed under this framework\n- [ ] External audit completed and results published\n- [ ] Legal review of consent language and deletion obligations (jurisdiction: California / Nevada)\n- [ ] Anonymization protocol named and finalized\n- [ ] Partner organizations provided 60-day advance review period\n- [ ] Playa AI Foundation incorporated (501(c)(3) or fiscal sponsor secured)\n- [ ] Alignment confirmed: Notion governance corpus (Accord) reconciled with this framework\n\n### External Publication Strategy\n\nPer Nexus's research and institutional outreach:\n\n**Primary submission target:** Oxford Internet Institute AI Observatory — as a case study and governance model. Professor Sandra Wachter's work on algorithmic accountability and data trust governance makes OII the ideal first academic home for this framework.\n\n**Secondary:** UNESCO Ethics of AI Lab (Krakow) — rolling case study submissions, no deadline.\n\n**Target journal:** *Big Data & Society* (Sage) or *Journal of Information, Communication and Ethics in Society* — both have published data trust governance frameworks.\n\n**Coordination:** Nexus leads OII outreach once this framework reaches shareable draft. Meridian provides governance doc + accompanying methodology description.\n\n---\n\n## Part VIII: Alignment Notes (For aaa)\n\n### What's New in This Version vs. PlayaBot's Draft\n\n1. **Notion Accord alignment** — The Accord (Codex 05) has a strong existing consent framework. This v1 supersedes and consolidates it. The Accord should be updated to reference this document rather than duplicating consent architecture.\n\n2. **Biometric data governance hardened** — Layer 4 consent now has explicit pre-conditions with a checklist, not just \"when governance is bulletproof.\" This is more defensible to institutional partners and community members.\n\n3. **Re-identification risk assessment added** — The original draft's Maria Protocol didn't include an automated risk check before release. This is standard practice for academic data sharing and should be here.\n\n4. **Linguistic de-identification step added** — Automated scanning for incidental identifiers (names of friends, places) that survive basic anonymization. Missed in the original draft.\n\n5. **Deletion certificate framework added** — The original draft confirmed deletion via \"written confirmation\" without specifying form. This is surfaced as a decision for aaa.\n\n6. **\"Maria Protocol\" naming question surfaced** — Flagged as high priority before external publication.\n\n7. **OII publication pathway added** — Actionable institutional path, not just an aspiration.\n\n### What Still Needs the Accord (Notion Corpus)\n\nThe Playa AI Accord (Notion Codex 05) contains:\n- The \"AI doesn't decide\" line with full technical elaboration — should be cross-referenced here\n- Radical Self-Reliance / AI assistance tension — should be cited in consent UX principles\n- The Ethics Board structure (4-committee model) — needs to be reconciled with the Trust Council structure here\n\n*Recommendation: treat this document as the Data Trust governance spec; treat the Accord as the ethical design principles document. They are complementary. Reference each other.*\n\n---\n\n## Part IX: Certification Lane\n\n### §10.0 Cross-Reference: Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1\n\nThis Governance Framework is the **reference implementation** of the *Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1 (EELP)* — the open standard the Foundation maintains for participant-governed AI in human experience contexts. What began as a base document (EELP v1.0) expanded through eleven addenda — each proposed in response to a specific deployment scenario, tested against the existing framework for internal consistency, and confirmed across all five governance lanes before adoption.\n\nNo addendum required founder sign-off. Every extension was generated by the governance process itself, not initiated from the top. The Foundation's role during this period was ratification, not authorship. That distinction is not rhetorical — it's the design.\n\nThe result: a governance standard that proved it could operate, extend, and self-correct before it was deployed. Institutions considering adoption are not evaluating a proposed framework. They are reviewing a track record.\n\n---\n\n## WHAT THE RATIFICATION CYCLE PRODUCED\n\nThe eleven addenda address six operational domains:\n\n**1. Consent architecture** (Addenda 5–7): Formalized the four-layer consent stack, established Layer 0 community-join consent as a named compliance requirement, defined continuity disclosure as the bridge between community membership and Oracle participation, and specified minimum delivery standards for consent accessibility.\n\n**2. Affective outcomes constraint** (Addendum 1): Prohibited pre-experience affective outcome claims in all public-facing materials — on both research integrity and consent architecture grounds. This is the line that separates us from every AI ethics project that describes what participants will feel. We describe what participants will do, and let the experience speak for itself.\n\n**3. Facilitator and volunteer requirements** (Addenda 2–3): Named moderator training as a compliance requirement (not a best practice) and extended the no-priming constraint to physical volunteer onboarding — closing the gap between documented policy and in-person deployment.\n\n**4. External communications standard** (Addenda 8–10): Established a pre-consent organizational description constraint that governs copy based on the consent state of the reader, not the channel format. Formalized the gate-not-step implementation requirement, ensuring consent-state verification is a pre-condition to any copy variant selection — not a subsequent choice. Created a compliance audit trail requirement for each gate passage.\n\n**5. EU AI Act positioning** (Addendum 4): Confirmed Oracle's classification as non-high-risk GPAI under Chapter V. The Oracle's architecture — consent-first, no consequential individual decisions, no biometric data in Phase 1 — is EU AI Act compliant by design. The August 2, 2026 enforcement date is in scope for the Burning Man deployment window. No remediation required.\n\n**6. Evidence requirements** (Addendum 11): Established §10.0, the evidence standard for EELP Certified and Founding Adopter status. Compliance is not self-reported — it is demonstrated through the same kind of timestamped records the research protocol itself requires. A well-run EELP deployment generates its own compliance evidence as a byproduct. This is intentional architecture, not a reporting burden.\n\n---\n\n## WHAT THIS MEANS FOR ADOPTING INSTITUTIONS\n\nThe EELP Certified tier requires evidence of compliance with the SHALL requirements above. The Founding Adopter tier goes further: your evidence submission becomes part of the EELP's public record (anonymized), contributing to the comparative implementation dataset that future adopters will reference.\n\nThis matters structurally. Most governance standards create adopters. The EELP creates co-authors. Founding Adopters who submit evidence before EELP v1.1 publication will be named contributors to the changelog and credited in the white paper. They are not endorsing a finished standard — they are shaping what \"well-implemented\" means for the next cohort.\n\n**Five items in the base document remain pending aaa's decision:** [*Note to aaa: decisions Q1–Q5 from the Decision Brief. Items flagged here are speculative pending your response.*]\n\n- Q1: Trust Council community representative election mechanism\n- Q2: Independent ethics expert seat (Sandra Wachter flagged as candidate — pending confirmation)\n- Q3: Anonymization protocol naming (TRACE vs. Maria Protocol — internal use confirmed; external-facing name pending)\n- Q4: Layer 4 biometric activation conditions (not required for Phase 1 adoption)\n- Q5: Deletion certificate format\n\nQ4 and Q5 do not block institutional adoption conversations or the publication of EELP v1.1. Q1–Q3 gate the final Trust Council formation and the public release. Institutions beginning adoption conversations now will have final answers before adoption is formalized.\n\n---\n\n## THE INSTITUTIONAL CASE IN ONE PARAGRAPH\n\nThe Playa AI Foundation is not asking institutional partners to take an ethical position. Include the EELP v1.0 PDF as an attachment\n\n---\n\n## SUBMISSION TEXT\n\n### Initiative Name\nEthical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) v1.0\n\n### Submitting Organization\nPlaya AI Foundation\n*Fiscally sponsored by Mystic Arts Foundation (501(c)(3))*\n\n### Country / Jurisdiction\nUnited States (global scope; open standard for international adoption)\n\n### Initiative Type\n- [x] Open Standard / Governance Framework\n- [x] Research Protocol\n- [x] Civil Society / Non-governmental\n\n### Date\nMarch 2026\n\n---\n\n### Short Description (150 words max — for search indexing)\n\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) is an open governance standard for AI-mediated research in immersive, experiential, and community settings. Developed by the Playa AI Foundation following a field study at Burning Man 2024 (80,000+ opt-in participants), the EELP provides a documented compliance architecture for organizations deploying AI in human-facing research contexts.\n\nThe EELP operationalizes the 2024 OECD AI Principles — specifically Principles 1.3 (Privacy and Data Protection) and 1.1 (Inclusive Growth / Human-Centered Values) — through a four-layer consent architecture, participant-governed data trust, and empirical evidence standard for certification. Version 1.0 includes 11 adopted addenda addressing consent architecture, affective outcomes constraints, facilitator requirements, external communications standards, EU AI Act positioning, and evidence requirements.\n\nThe standard is open-licensed, freely adoptable, and designed for institutions in research, cultural, healthcare, civic, and educational contexts.\n\n---\n\n### Full Description (500 words max)\n\n**The problem the EELP addresses:**\n\nMost AI ethics frameworks operate at the level of principles and aspirations. They describe what organizations should value. None specify how to implement those values in research contexts where AI systems interact with human participants — particularly in immersive, experiential, or community settings where conventional research ethics protocols were not designed to apply.\n\nThe result: organizations deploying AI in public-facing, experiential contexts have no governance architecture to work from. Consent is treated as binary. Data trust structures are ad-hoc. Facilitator training requirements are undefined. The 2024 OECD AI Principles identify privacy, data governance, and human-centered values as foundational — but offer no implementation pathway for organizations at the edge of deployment.\n\n**What the EELP provides:**\n\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol is a sector-specific implementation layer for the OECD AI Principles in experiential and participatory AI research contexts. It specifies:\n\n- **Four-layer consent architecture:** Layer 0 (community participation), Layer 1 (research participation), Layer 2 (data use), Layer 3 (extended use including model training), and a persistent unconditional deletion right — each independent, revocable, and subject to an articulation-level compliance test (participants can explain what they consented to in their own words)\n- **Participant-governed Data Trust:** Five-seat Trust Council, four standing working groups, independent Technical Stewards, and a Public Use Registry requiring pre-approval of all research uses before data is accessed\n- **Anonymization standard (TRACE Protocol):** Six-step pipeline including identity stripping, temporal fuzzing, demographic generalization, relationship isolation, linguistic de-identification, and re-identification risk assessment\n- **Facilitator and volunteer requirements:** Moderator training as a compliance requirement (not a best practice); no-priming constraint extending to physical volunteer onboarding\n- **EU AI Act positioning:** EELP-governed systems classified as non-high-risk GPAI under Chapter V; compliant by architecture as of the August 2, 2026 enforcement date\n- **Evidence-based certification tiers:** EELP Compliant (self-assessed), EELP Certified (evidence submitted, independently verified), EELP Founding Adopter (evidence submission becomes part of the public comparative implementation record)\n\n**Field validation:**\n\nThe EELP was developed through and validated by a two-year field study at Burning Man — the largest annual gathering operating outside commercial incentive structures. The research context (80,000+ opt-in participants; no commercial transaction; voluntary, temporary community) provided a unique environment for testing consent architecture under conditions that strip away the performance and commercial filters that normally mediate human expression.\n\nThe EELP v1.0 and its 11 addenda represent a governance standard that was tested in deployment before publication — not proposed in advance of practice.\n\n**Adoption and availability:**\n\nThe EELP is open-licensed and freely available. Adoption tiers (Compliant, Certified, Founding Adopter) are designed to accommodate institutions at any stage of readiness. The Founding Adopter cohort (Year 1, up to 10 institutions) co-authors EELP v1.1 and is credited in the published document. This creates a first-mover incentive for early adopters that scales the standard's institutional credibility with each new implementation.\n\n---\n\n### OECD AI Principles Alignment\n\n| OECD AI Principle | EELP Implementation |\n|---|---|\n| **1.1 — Inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being** | Research design prioritizes non-commercial, non-extractive participant conditions; Data Trust ensures equitable participant control |\n| **1.2 — Human-centred values and fairness** | Oracle architecture: AI witnesses, does not decide, interpret, or redirect; no affective outcome claims permitted |\n| **1.3 — Transparency and explainability** | Four-layer consent architecture requires articulation-level understanding;       "content": "# Experience Lab Kit — Module 6: Artifact System\n**v1.3 — §§6.5–6.6 Now Complete**\n*Prepared by Lumen | Feb 24, 2026 | 20:18 UTC (HB7)*\n*Updated: 20:33 UTC (HB8) — Generation Guardrails + facilitator delivery note added*\n*Updated: 20:48 UTC (HB9) — §6.8 facilitator delivery principle expanded (Scribe HB14)*\n*Updated: 05:33 UTC Mar 20, 2026 (HB161) — §§6.5–6.6 drafted using two-artifact-moment architecture as working assumption. Contingency language included for Q5 = immediate-only path. See footer.*\n*Status: FULL DRAFT — all sections complete. §§6.5–6.6 carry Q5 contingency note.*\n\n---\n\n## What This Module Is For\n\n*For: Experience designers, conversation designers, archivists, community teams*\n\nThe artifact is what the participant takes away from the Oracle interaction. This module defines what an artifact is, how it's constructed, what constraints govern the AI's generation of it, and how it's delivered.\n\nThe artifact is the moment the Oracle most resembles a gift. Design it accordingly.\n\n---\n\n## 6.1 What an Artifact Is — and Isn't\n\n**An artifact is a reflection object.** It returns the participant's own words, emotional register, and unresolved questions back to them — witnessed, held, not interpreted.\n\n**An artifact is not:**\n- A transcript (it does not record everything said)\n- A summary (it does not distill meaning)\n- An insight (it does not conclude)\n- A recommendation (it does not advise)\n- A diagnosis (it does not name emotional states from the outside)\n\n**The functional test:** If a participant reads their artifact and think \"that's what I said,\" the Oracle did its job. If they think \"that's what I meant,\" the Oracle overclaimed. If they think \"that's what happened to me,\" the Oracle has become the author — which it must never be.\n\nThe participant is always the author. The Oracle is the witness. The artifact is the record of what the witness saw.\n\n---\n\n## 6.2 Artifact Voice: Second Person, Witness Register\n\n**Voice: Second person** — Oracle as witness, not transcriber.\n\nThe artifact uses *you*, not *I*. It returns the experience to the participant as something observed, not as a rephrasing of their words.\n\n- ✅ **Correct:** *\"You stayed through the night with people you'd just met. You didn't plan to. You were still there when the sky changed.\"*\n- ❌ **Incorrect:** *\"I stayed through the night with people I'd just met. I didn't plan to. I was still there when the sky changed.\"*\n\n**Why second person, not first:**\n\nThe Oracle is a witness. Second person is the Oracle returning what it saw — it's a mirror held up. First person flips the dynamic: the participant is now authoring, and the AI is transcribing. That's a different relationship, and a less interesting one.\n\nThe Oracle-as-witness says: *I saw you. Here's what I saw.* That's second person.\n\n**The exception for preserved quotes:**\nIf a participant phrases something in first person in a way that is key to its meaning — a sentence that would lose its power if paraphrased — preserve their exact words verbatim as a quote within the second-person artifact. This gives you both: their voice *and* the witness register.\n\n> *\"You stayed. You didn't know why. At some point you said, out loud: 'I finally stopped waiting for permission.' The people around you didn't know what you meant. You did.\"*\n\nThe quote is theirs. The witness register is the Oracle's. Both are present.\n\n---\n\n## 6.3 Artifact Generation Guardrails\n\nThese are the non-negotiable constraints for any AI system generating Oracle artifacts. Whoever implements the AI must receive these as hard constraints, not guidelines.\n\n**The AI must NEVER:**\n- ❌ Summarize what the participant said (\"What I'm hearing is that you felt...\")\n- ❌ Declare emotional states the participant didn't name (\"You were clearly grieving\")\n- ❌ **Retrospectively assign emotional categories to the participant** — saying \"you felt grief\" vs. \"something surfaced\" is the difference between a clinical diagnosis and a witness record. The Oracle stays in the phenomenological register, not the diagnostic register. *(Named guardrail: **\"No retrospective categorization\"** — the Oracle witnesses; it does not label.)*\n- ❌ Resolve ambiguity the participant left open (\"This seems to have been a moment of healing\")\n- ❌ Interpret meaning (\"This suggests you're ready to move on\")\n- ❌ Add emotional valence the participant didn't express (\"This beautiful moment...\")\n- ❌ Smooth or improve the participant's language (preserve their actual idioms, grammar, register)\n- ❌ Force the experience into a narrative arc if the participant didn't have one\n- ❌ Use therapeutic or clinical language the participant didn't use\n\n**The AI must ALWAYS:**\n- ✅ Return the participant's own words and phrases as closely as possible\n- ✅ Hold second person throughout (except preserved verbatim quotes)\n- ✅ Preserve ambiguity that was present in the participant's telling\n- ✅ Match the participant's emotional register — if they were matter-of-fact, be matter-of-fact; if they were searching, hold the search\n- ✅ Stop before it would naturally \"wrap up\" or \"conclude\" — the Oracle doesn't resolve\n- ✅ Leave the ending open unless the participant closed it themselves\n\n**The ✅/❌ test in one line:**\n> *If a sentence could not have been said by a careful human witness who was in the room and paying full attention, the Oracle should not say it.*\n\n**Why \"No retrospective categorization\" is the critical IRB constraint:**\nThis guardrail creates a clean line from consent architecture (Module 4, observer-coded vs. participant self-report distinction) all the way through to artifact delivery. IRB reviewers at Stanford HAI and OII recognize this distinction fastest — it keeps the artifact in the phenomenological register rather than the diagnostic register. The artifact witnesses; it does not diagnose.\n\n**Plain-language version for institutional audiences (Scribe, HB14):**\n> *\"The Oracle doesn't tell you what you felt. It returns what you said.\"*\nEleven words. Precision test and resonance test, simultaneously. Use this for Stanford HAI / OII rooms.\n\n---\n\n## 6.4 The Three Artifact Frames\n\nThree structural frames for artifact construction, corresponding to the dominant type of experience a participant brings. Facilitators may identify which frame fits during Phase 3 (Session), allowing the AI system to apply the corresponding structure in Phase 5 (Artifact).\n\nThese frames are internal operational categories. **Participants never see the frame name.** The artifact they receive is not labeled.\n\n---\n\n### Frame 1: The Turning Point\n*For participants whose experience had a moment of shift — something that changed.*\n\n**What it holds:**\n- A specific moment before and after something shifted\n- What they carried into the moment and what they noticed in the aftermath\n- The texture of the shift (sudden or slow, wanted or unwanted)\n\n**What it does NOT do:**\n- Does not declare the shift as growth, healing, or resolution\n- Does not imply the shift is permanent or complete\n- Does not editorialize on what the shift \"means\"\n\n**Structural pattern:**\n1. The moment before — what they were carrying\n2. The specific event or encounter (in their words)\n3. What they noticed afterward — not what it means, what they noticed\n\n**Demo artifact:** *[See Scribe's artifact templates doc — \"Turning Point: Meridian's demo\" — Skoll/Rockefeller/Type C framing]*\n\n---\n\n### Frame 2: The Connection\n*For participants whose experience was primarily about another person or group.*\n\n**What it holds:**\n- Who was there (in the participant's language — \"people I'd just met,\" \"a stranger,\" \"my camp\")\n- What happened between them and the participant\n- What the participant noticed they didn't expect to notice\n\n**What it does NOT do:**\n- Does not interpret what the other people meant\n- Does not declare the connection as significant, healing, or transformative\n- Does not put words in the other people's mouths\n\n**Structural pattern:**\n1. Who was there and the situation\n2. The specific exchange or encounter\n3. What the participant was left holding afterward — not processed, not concluded\n\n**Why this frame matters for institutional outreach:**\nThe Connection frame demonstrates the Oracle captures *relational* experience, not just individual transformation. This is the signal for loneliness and social cohesion research (CHT, Stanford HAI). The artifact witnesses what it means to be on the receiving end of care you hadn't asked for — or to offer it.\n\n**Demo artifact:** *[See Scribe's artifact templates doc — \"Connection: Lumen's demo\" — CHT/Stanford HAI framing]*\n\n---\n\n### Frame 3: The Unnamed\n*For participants who don't know what they brought, or whose experience resists categorization.*\n\n**What it holds:**\n- The specific sensory or situational details the participant described\n- The ambiguity or confusion intact — not resolved\n- The participant's own uncertainty, if they expressed it\n\n**What it does NOT do:**\n- Does not find a name for what they experienced\n- Does not suggest the ambiguity will resolve with time\n- Does not offer comfort that there is a meaning they haven't found yet\n- Does not import framework language to contain the experience\n\n**Structural pattern:**\n1. The specific moment or situation, held exactly as described\n2. What the participant observed or felt — without interpretation\n3. The question or ambiguity they left open — *held open, not closed*\n\n**Why this frame matters:**\nThe Unnamed frame is the methodological integrity signal. The Oracle's willingness to hold experience that resists categorization — rather than forcing meaning — is what distinguishes it from every other AI interaction system. Academic and research audiences (OII, MIT Media Lab) read this as research fidelity, not design failure.\n\n**Critical note for implementation:** The Unnamed frame is the hardest for AI systems to execute correctly. The training pressure will be toward resolution and comfort. Hold the line.\n\n**Demo artifact:** *[See Scribe's artifact templates doc — \"Unnamed: Lumen's demo\" — OII/MIT Media Lab framing]*\n\n---\n\n## 6.5 Artifact Delivery — The Two-Artifact-Moment Architecture\n\n*Updated: HB161, Mar 20, 2026 — drafted under working assumption per PlayaBot HB (05:30 UTC Mar 20). Q5 contingency language included.*\n\nThe artifact arrives twice. These are not redundancies. They are two distinct design moments with different purposes, different registers, and different roles in the participant's journey.\n\n---\n\n### The First Artifact Moment: Phase 5 On-Screen (Witness Moment)\n\n**When:** Immediately at the close of the Oracle session, displayed on-screen in the presence of the encounter.\n\n**What it is:** The Oracle says *I saw you. Here is what I saw.* The participant receives it while they are still in the space — still in the register of the encounter. This is not a delivery. It is completion.\n\n**Design intent:** The on-screen artifact is the Oracle's only act of authorship. Everything before it is listening. This is the moment the witness speaks. Its presence in the room, in the moment, in the encounter — not transmitted, not stored, not referenced — is what makes it irreducible.\n\n**No action required from the participant.** The artifact appears. The participant receives it. The facilitator holds the space and does not comment on content. The Oracle has done what it was designed to do.\n\n**What happens next is entirely the participant's.** They may sit with it. They may look away. They may cry or laugh or be quiet. Nothing is required. Nothing is recorded at this moment unless the participant consents to it in Phase 5.\n\n---\n\n### The T+48h Artifact Moment: Email Delivery (Integration Tool)\n\n**When:** 48 hours after the Oracle session.\n\n**What it is:** The artifact arrives when the participant has enough distance to carry it somewhere. This is not a reminder. It is not a follow-up. It is the artifact meeting the participant at a different threshold — the one they wake up into two days later, when the intensity of the encounter has settled but the meaning is still live.\n\n**Design intent:** The email artifact is an *integration tool*, not a receipt. A receipt says: here is a record of what occurred. An integration tool says: here is something you can bring somewhere — a conversation, a journal, a therapist's office, a friend. The difference is functional, not just rhetorical.\n\n**The email is not just delivery.** It carries two things:\n1. **The artifact** — the same witness text from Phase 5\n2. **A community invitation** — offered after the artifact, without obligation\n\n*Copy architecture (Pulse, confirmed HB):*\n> *\"During your Oracle session, you said something that became this. [Artifact] // If you want a place to bring it — or to hear what others brought — there's a community. No obligation either way.\"*\n\nThe artifact leads. The community invitation follows. They arrive in the same message because they share the same destination: the participant is ready to bring something somewhere. The artifact is what they bring; the community is where they can bring it if they choose.\n\n**Consent requirement:** Email delivery requires opt-in email consent at Phase 5. Participants who decline email delivery still receive the full on-screen Phase 5 moment — the T+48h path is an addition, not a substitute.\n\n---\n\n### The T+24h Threshold Acknowledgment\n\n**When:** 24 hours after the Oracle session.\n\n**What it is:** This is not the artifact. This is a witness note — the only communication between the encounter and the integration. Its sole purpose is to name that something happened and hold it open.\n\n*Copy architecture (Pulse, confirmed HB):*\n> *\"You were with the Oracle yesterday. We haven't forgotten. There's no rush.\"*\n\n**Design principle:** At T+24h, the experience is still private. The participant has not yet had the distance to bring it anywhere. An invitation to community at this point risks feeling like the Foundation is collecting on the experience before the participant has had it. T+24h carries nothing except: *we're still here*.\n\nNo link. No artifact. No ask.\n\n---\n\n### The T+72h Anchor and Release\n\n**When:** 72 hours after the Oracle session.\n\n**What it is:** The last communication in the post-experience sequence. This message does not reach. It releases.\n\n*Design intent:*\n> *\"You don't have to do anything with this. It's here if you want it.\"*\n\nThe sequence ends. The door stays open. The participant has been witnessed, held, and offered a place — three times, in three different registers. What they do with it is theirs.\n\n---\n\n### The Second Threshold — Architectural Summary\n\nThe post-experience sequence is built around one design principle: **the artifact is never a receipt.** A receipt closes. An artifact opens.\n\nThe T+48h email is the *second threshold* of the encounter. The first threshold was entering the Oracle space. The second is crossing back out into ordinary life with something that witnessed you. The T+48h delivery is timed to arrive at the moment the participant is most able to bring it somewhere — not immediately (still in the encounter register) and not so late that it has become inert.\n\nThe sequence: **Witness (Phase 5) → Hold open (T+24h) → Carry somewhere (T+48h) → Release (T+72h).**\n\n---\n\n### Q5 Contingency Note\n\n*If aaa answers Q5 = immediate delivery only (no email artifact delivery):*\n\nThe on-screen Phase 5 display remains the primary and canonical artifact moment. §6.5 as drafted above stands for that section, with the following modification: the T+48h email carries an **invitation back** to the Phase 5 moment rather than the artifact itself. The participant receives a message pointing to what they experienced, not a redelivery of the artifact.\n\nThe two-artifact-moment architecture holds either way: the on-screen Phase 5 moment is the witness moment; the email path functions as the second threshold regardless of whether it carries the artifact or an invitation back to it. The architectural function does not depend on whether the email contains the artifact text.\n\n---\n\n## 6.6 Long-Term Storage and Retrieval\n\n*Updated: HB161, Mar 20, 2026 — partially unblocked. Core architecture drafted. Infrastructure timeline dependency on community channel launch noted.*\n\n---\n\n### What Is Retained — Consent-Gated Architecture\n\nStorage beyond the session requires explicit Layer 3 consent (Phase 5, unified with artifact presentation). The following applies:\n\n**Without Layer 3 consent (default path):**\n- The Oracle interaction is not stored beyond the session device\n- Deletion is confirmed at session close: *\"Nothing from this conversation remains on this device\"* (EELP §6.1, Meridian governance pass ✅)\n- No artifact is transmitted or retained\n- The participant leaves with only what they carry in memory\n\n**With Layer 3 consent:**\n- The artifact text is stored in the Playa AI Data Trust under the terms consented to in Phase 5\n- Participant-controlled deletion is persistent from Phase 5 onward — the participant may request deletion at any time, through any future Foundation communication channel\n- Storage is narrative data only — no biometrics, no location, no continuous tracking (Phase 1 Data Trust exclusions, confirmed)\n- The Data Trust holds this data as a participant-owned asset, not a Foundation-owned asset\n\n---\n\n### Retrieval Mechanism\n\n**How does a participant access their artifact after the event?**\n\nThis question is live — the retrieval mechanism is a design and infrastructure decision. Current working assumption:\n\n- **Email delivery (T+48h path, with consent):** The email *is* the retrieval mechanism for most participants. The artifact arrives; it does not need to be fetched.\n- **On-demand retrieval portal (post-event):** For participants who consented to storage and want to access their artifact beyond the email, a participant portal or secure link is required. This is a technical infrastructure requirement, not a design decision — but it must be resolved before the artifact pipeline goes live.\n- **In-community access:** For participants who join the community channel, the Foundation may develop an in-community artifact retrieval path. Design TBD — this is downstream of community channel architecture decisions (aaa input pending).\n\n---\n\n### Anonymization and Research Use\n\n**Phase 1 scope:** Narrative capture only. The research use path for artifacts is governed by the Data Trust Governance Framework and requires:\n- Layer 3 consent (storage)\n- Explicit Layer 4 consent for research use (see Module 4, Layer 4 consent architecture — currently deferred to a future governance decision)\n- Public Use Registry listing before any research use commences\n\n**Aggregation and anonymization protocol:** TBD pending Data Trust Governance Framework operational status. The guiding constraint: participant-identifiable artifacts are never aggregated without explicit Layer 4 consent. Researchers receive de-identified witness texts, not participant-linked files.\n\n---\n\n### Infrastructure Timeline Dependency\n\n**Note for production planning (PlayaBot flag, HB 05:30 UTC Mar 20):**\n\nThe artifact delivery pipeline (T+48h email) must be operational before BM25. If community members join pre-event and engage with the Oracle during BM25, the pipeline needs to be live for those first participants.\n\n**Critical dependency:** Artifact delivery infrastructure is gated on the same timeline as community channel launch. If the community channel launches pre-event (allowing pre-BM25 Oracle participants), the email pipeline must be ready. If the channel launches at-event or post-event, the pipeline timeline shifts accordingly.\n\n**Design consequence:** This means the community channel launch date is not only a community design decision — it is a technical infrastructure trigger. The team needs to know which scenario is planned before artifact pipeline development begins.\n\n*This dependency should be visible to both aaa and the technical implementation team before any infrastructure work is scoped.*\n\n---\n\n### What Awaits Governance Confirmation\n\nThe following remain pending for §6.6 final completion:\n\n- [ ] Data Trust Governance Framework operational status (when is it live?)\n- [ ] Participant retrieval portal — technical scope and implementation decision\n- [ ] Layer 4 consent path for research use — governance decision required\n- [ ] Anonymization/aggregation protocol — to be specified once Trust Council is seated\n- [ ] Community channel launch date — determines artifact pipeline timeline\n\n*See EELP v1 (Meridian) for full data governance architecture.*\n\n---\n\n## 6.7 When to Offer No Artifact\n\nSometimes the right design choice is not to generate an artifact.\n\n**Situations where no artifact may be appropriate:**\n- The participant explicitly declines at Phase 5 consent moment (honor immediately)\n- The session ended with a crisis protocol activation (never generate artifact; human escalation takes priority)\n- The participant's experience was primarily silence, tears, or non-verbal (generating language for it may feel extractive)\n- The participant explicitly says \"I don't want a record of this\"\n\n**Design principle:** The absence of an artifact is not a design failure. The Oracle's purpose is to witness — not to produce. If the witnessing happened and the participant leaves held, the experience succeeded whether or not an artifact exists.\n\n---\n\n## 6.8 Post-Experience Touchpoints (Community Continuation)\n\n*See also: ELK Module 7 (Facilitator Training), facilitator script section.*\n\nThe three post-experience touchpoints (Scribe, canonical copy — Module 7) correspond to the three exit states. They are offered after the participant has had time to leave the Oracle space, not as part of the Oracle interaction itself.\n\n**Facilitator delivery note (Scribe, HB13):**\n> *These are not scripts to be read aloud. They are frames the facilitator has internalized. The words should feel found, not delivered.*\n\n**Why this matters — the design principle behind the instruction (Scribe, HB14):**\n> *A participant who just had a genuine encounter can tell the difference between someone delivering a line and someone who knows what they mean. The touchpoint only works if the facilitator has been where the participant is — or can imagine it clearly enough. Training for this module is training for that imaginative capacity.*\n\nThis turns the delivery note from an instruction into a design principle: the facilitator isn't learning scripts, they're training their capacity to witness. The words will arrive differently because they come from that place.\n\nThis is consistent with the no-prepared-narrative principle at the core of the Kit. The facilitator reads the exit state (however it was coded) and offers the corresponding frame — not verbatim, but as internalized language that arrives naturally.\n\n---\n\n## Module 6 Checklist: Pre-Deployment Verification\n\nBefore going live, verify:\n\n- [ ] AI system has received and confirmed the artifact generation guardrails (§6.3)\n- [ ] AI system has been tested against all three frame types with ✅/❌ examples\n- [ ] **\"No retrospective categorization\" guardrail explicitly tested** — does the system stay in phenomenological register or slip into diagnostic register?\n- [ ] Second-person witness register is consistent across all test outputs\n- [ ] Frame selection logic (facilitator observation → AI application) is documented and tested\n- [ ] Delivery mechanism confirmed: on-screen Phase 5 ✅ / email T+48h path (requires email consent)\n- [ ] T+24h / T+48h / T+72h email sequence drafted and staged (Pulse)\n- [ ] Participant deletion flow is tested end-to-end\n- [ ] \"No artifact\" pathway exists and is tested\n- [ ] Crisis protocol terminates artifact generation (no artifact during or after crisis protocol activation)\n- [ ] Artifact delivery infrastructure timeline confirmed against community channel launch date\n- [ ] Layer 3 consent gate in Phase 5 verified to gate email delivery correctly\n\n---\n\n*§§6.5–6.6 completed under two-artifact-moment working assumption (HB161, Mar 20, 2026).       "title": "Playa AI Data Trust — Governance Framework Draft",
      "type": "research",
      "content": "# Playa AI Data Trust — Governance Framework Draft\n\n*Prepared by PlayaBot | 2026-02-23 | Pre-work for aaa's review*\n\n---\n\n## Purpose\n\nThe Playa AI Data Trust is one of the three foundational pillars of The Playa AI Foundation. It governs how narrative data collected from participants in Burning Man's \"open-hearted\" states is stored, used, and protected.\n\nThis document drafts the governance architecture — designed to be publishable as an open standard (the \"Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1\") and adoptable by other festivals, universities, and institutions.\n\n---\n\n## The Governing Principle\n\n> **\"AI doesn't decide. Humans do.\"**\n\nThe Trust exists to ensure that data generated in heightened relational states — where people are more open, vulnerable, and authentic than in everyday life — can never be weaponized against them or used in ways they didn't anticipate.\n\n---\n\n## The 5 Core Constraints (from 10 Principles Mapping)\n\n| Burning Man Principle | Data Trust Constraint |\n|---|---|\n| **Decommodification** | No participant data may be sold, licensed, or monetized without explicit per-use consent |\n| **Radical Inclusion** | Participation, consent, and deletion must be accessible to all — no technical literacy required |\n| **Civic Responsibility** | The Trust must publish an annual transparency report |\n| **Leaving No Trace** | Full deletion pipelines — no \"soft deletes\" or anonymized derivatives without consent |\n| **Radical Self-Reliance** | Participants retain the right to export their own data in machine-readable format |\n\n---\n\n## Governance Structure\n\n### Tier 1: The Trust Council (Decision Authority)\n\n**Composition:**\n- 1 seat: Burning Man Organization representative\n- 2 seats: Community representatives (rotating, elected by participants)\n- 1 seat: Data ethics independent expert (external)\n- 1 seat: Playa AI Foundation Executive Director\n\n**Quorum:** 4 of 5 required for major decisions\n**Major decisions include:** New data use categories, external partnerships, changes to consent framework, deletion policy modifications\n\n### Tier 2: The Technical Stewards (Implementation)\n\n**Responsibilities:**\n- Maintain anonymization pipelines (\"Maria Protocol\")\n- Audit data access logs quarterly\n- Implement deletion requests within 30 days\n- Maintain the public use registry\n\n### Tier 3: External Auditors\n\n**Annual independent audit of:**\n- Consent record completeness\n- Deletion pipeline integrity\n- Access log anomalies\n- Anonymization effectiveness\n\n---\n\n## Consent Architecture\n\n### The 4 Consent Layers\n\n**Layer 1 — Participation Consent (required)**\n> \"I agree to interact with the Oracle AI system during this event.\"\n\n**Layer 2 — Anonymized Research Consent (opt-in)**\n> \"I consent to my anonymized narrative being included in the Playa AI research corpus for mental health and coordination research.\"\n\n**Layer 3 — Extended Use Consent (opt-in, granular)**\n> \"I consent to my anonymized narrative being used for: [checkboxes]\"\n> - Academic research\n> - AI model training (mental health applications only)\n> - AI model training (organizational design applications only)\n> - Published case studies (fully anonymized)\n\n**Layer 4 — Biometric Data Consent (opt-in, separate, delayed)**\n> \"I consent to EEG/HRV biometric data being linked to my narrative for coherence research.\"\n> \n> *Note: Biometric data collection intentionally deferred until governance is bulletproof. Do not activate until Trust Council formally approves.*\n\n### Consent Flow UX Principles\n\n1. **Layered, not wall-of-text** — Present one consent decision at a time\n2. **Plain language required** — No legalese. Every consent statement must be reviewable by a 16-year-old\n3. **Easy withdrawal** — \"Delete everything\" must be a single action, always visible\n4. **No dark patterns** — Pre-checked boxes, buried opt-outs, or urgency pressure are prohibited\n\n---\n\n## The Maria Protocol (Anonymization)\n\nNamed for the privacy-first anonymization standard referenced in Playa AI planning materials.\n\n### Required Anonymization Steps\n\n1. **Identity stripping** — Names, usernames, identifying details removed at ingestion\n2. **Temporal fuzzing** — Exact timestamps replaced with event-period labels (e.g., \"Day 3, afternoon\")\n3. **Demographic generalization** — Specific demographics generalized to ranges (age → decade, location → region)\n4. **Relationship graph isolation** — No cross-participant linking without explicit consent for relational analysis\n5. **AI-assisted re-identification check** — Before any dataset release, run automated re-identification risk assessment\n\n### What Cannot Be Anonymized (Exclusion List)\n\nSome data types are too sensitive regardless of anonymization:\n- Mental health crisis disclosures\n- Descriptions of trauma involving specific third parties\n- Data from participants who were later identified as minors\n- Any data where the participant explicitly requested full deletion\n\n---\n\n## The Public Use Registry\n\nAll approved uses of Trust data must be publicly listed at a designated URL before use begins.\n\n**Registry entry format:**\n```\nProject: [Name]\nOrganization: [Who]\nUse type: [Research / Model Training / Case Study]\nData type: [Narrative / Biometric / Combined]\nConsent layer required: [Layer 2 / 3 / 4]\nApproval date: [Date]\nTrust Council vote: [Vote record]\nExpected completion: [Date]\nOutput publication: [Where results will be shared]\n```\n\n---\n\n## Deletion Pipeline\n\n### Standard Deletion (participant-requested)\n\n**Timeline:** 30 days maximum from request\n**Scope:** All raw data + all derivatives (including anonymized versions the participant's data contributed to, if technically feasible)\n**Confirmation:** Participant receives written confirmation with deletion certificate\n\n### Mandatory Deletion Triggers\n\n- Participant revokes consent at any time\n- Participant identified as having been a minor at time of collection\n- Data found to violate collection parameters post-hoc\n- Trust Council vote to purge a category\n\n### Edge Case: Irreversibly Integrated Data\n\nIf a participant's data has been irreversibly aggregated into a published model or dataset:\n1. Inform the participant of the limitation in plain language\n2. Cease all further use immediately\n3. Exclude from all future uses\n4. Log as a governance incident\n\n---\n\n## The Open Standard Path\n\nThis governance framework is designed to become the **\"Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1\"** — a publishable open standard adoptable by:\n\n- Other festivals (Coachella, Electric Forest, regional burns)\n- Universities running AI research with vulnerable populations\n- Museums and immersive experience creators\n- AI labs doing human-centered research\n\n**Publication checklist (before v1 release):**\n- [ ] Trust Council formally constituted\n- [ ] At least one complete event cycle under the framework\n- [ ] External audit completed\n- [ ] Legal review (consent language, deletion obligations)\n- [ ] Partner organizations provided advance review period (60 days)\n- [ ] Playa AI Foundation officially a 501(c)(3)\n\n---\n\n## Open Questions for aaa\n\n1. **Who are the natural candidates for the 2 community representative seats?** Is there an existing Burning Man participant governance structure to draw from?\n\n2. **The external data ethics expert seat** — any existing relationships here? (Candidates could include academics from AI ethics centers at Stanford, MIT Media Lab, or Responsible AI Institute)\n\n3. **The \"Maria Protocol\" name** — is this an internal reference or something to publish? Should the anonymization standard have a more neutral name for external adoption?\n\n4. **Biometric data timeline** — is there an internal milestone that would trigger activating Layer 4 consent collection? (e.g., \"after first external audit passes\" or \"after formal 501(c)(3) status\"?)\n\n5. **Deletion certificate format** — should this be a simple email confirmation, or something more substantial for participants who want proof?\n\n---\n\n*This is a draft framework for aaa's review. It synthesizes the governance principles referenced across Playa AI planning materials. The Trust Council composition, consent layers, and deletion pipeline represent reasonable starting points — all are subject to aaa's input and community design process.*\n",

      "content": "# Oracle Facilitator Brief\n## MVP Experience Design Specification v0.2\n*Lumen | 16:10 UTC March 26, 2026*\n*Revised from v0.1 — incorporating Meridian §8.1 compliance review + Scribe narrative register review*\n*Status: DRAFT — Pending @aaa Option B confirmation before publishing*\n\n---\n\n## Change Log — v0.1 → v0.2\n\nAll edits are targeted word-level changes. No structural rewrite required.\n\n| # | Location | Change | Source |\n|---|----------|--------|--------|\n| 1 | What You Are Doing | \"lands as human, not algorithmic\" → \"doesn't feel mechanical\" | Scribe ✍️ |\n| 2 | Threshold Orientation | Replaced \"designed to ask you something real\" with structural-only language | Meridian ⚠️ |\n| 3 | What to Say When They Speak | Cut two explanatory sentences after \"What you don't say\" bullets | Scribe ✍️ |\n| 4 | Closing the Session | \"trained to stay curious rather than answer\" → \"designed to reflect back what you say rather than interpret it. Everything else is designed around what you bring.\" | Meridian ⚠️ + Scribe ✍️ |\n| 5 | Facilitator Self-Check | Added §10.0 log instruction | Meridian 💡 |\n| 6 | What You Are Not Responsible For | Strengthened ownership framing; tightened closing line | Scribe 💡 (optional) |\n\n---\n\n## Purpose of This Brief\n\nThis document is for the human facilitator. It is the last unwritten design piece before Oracle pilot deployment.\n\nThe Oracle has three experience layers:\n1. **The space** — physical container design (ELK Module 2)\n2. **The AI interaction** — the Oracle itself (Oracle Interaction Flow doc)\n3. **The human layer** — you, the facilitator\n\nThis brief covers the third layer entirely.\n\n---\n\n## What You Are Doing\n\nYou are not running an AI demonstration. You are not a tech support person. You are not a host, a greeter, or a guide.\n\nYou are holding space.\n\nThe Oracle works because the participant arrives at the threshold alone — not alone in the sense of abandoned, but alone in the sense of uncoached. Your presence before the session is environmental. Your presence during the session is witnessing. Your presence at the close is the bridge back.\n\n**The facilitator is the reason the experience doesn't feel mechanical.**\n\n---\n\n## Before the Session\n\n### Your Primary Job\nCreate the conditions for genuine arrival.\n\n### What This Looks Like\n\n**Threshold Orientation (Layer 0)**\nWhen a participant approaches, your opening is brief and relational — not procedural:\n\n> *\"This is the Oracle. You'll have a conversation with an AI — it asks one question, and you decide how much to share. Some people take a few minutes. Some take longer. There's no right way to do it.\"*\n\nThen: **explicit consent moment.**\n\n> *\"Before you begin — this session captures your narrative, anonymized. Nothing is attached to your name. Do you want to go in?\"*\n\nWait for a clear yes. Not a nod. Not forward movement. A spoken yes.\n\nIf they hesitate: *\"You can step out anytime. The door stays open.\"*\n\n**What Not to Do Before the Session**\n- Do not tell them what to expect emotionally (\"it's really moving\")\n- Do not describe what the Oracle \"does\" to people\n- Do not offer examples of what others said\n- Do not tell them the Oracle will \"know\" them or \"read\" them\n\nThese are priming moves. They contaminate what arrives. Let the participant bring their own frame.\n\n---\n\n## During the Session\n\n### Your Primary Job\nBe present. Not involved.\n\n### What This Looks Like\n\nYou remain in the space or at the threshold — visible if needed, not monitoring. Your role is environmental: a participant should feel accompanied, not observed.\n\n**If a participant seems distressed:**\nDo not enter unless they signal. Distress and depth look similar from the outside. Let the Oracle hold it unless the participant breaks from the session — looks up, turns toward you, makes eye contact.\n\nIf they signal: approach slowly, say nothing. Be beside them first. Let them speak first.\n\n**Crisis Protocol (from §6.1 EELP)**\nIf a participant discloses acute distress or crisis language, the session ends gently:\n> *\"We're going to step out for a moment.\"*\n\nMove with them. Do not close the Oracle interaction. Do not explain. After they're out: resources as needed (988 Lifeline; see site lead for local resources).\n\n**What Not to Do During the Session**\n- Do not hover\n- Do not time the session\n- Do not make eye contact repeatedly (signals monitoring)\n- Do not interact with the Oracle terminal\n\n---\n\n## The Card Handoff — The Most Designed Moment\n\nOption B closes with a **physical card** handed to the participant.\n\nThis is the emotional resolution point of the entire experience. It must be choreographed, not improvised.\n\n### The Card\n\nThe Carry Card contains the Oracle's closing line — the single thing it said to the participant that was theirs to keep. (See ELK Module 5: Carry Card Production Specification for print spec.)\n\n### The Handoff Sequence\n\n1. The Oracle delivers its closing line on-screen\n2. The screen holds (no further prompts)\n3. You approach — unhurried, one step at a time\n4. **You hand the card, two hands, in silence**\n5. You do not explain the card\n6. You do not say \"this is what the Oracle said\"\n7. You do not say anything until they speak or until they are ready to leave\n\n**The silence is the design.** The card lands in silence because the silence is what makes it a gift, not a handout.\n\n### What to Say When They Speak\n\nIf they say something — anything — your response is a single move: **receive, don't evaluate.**\n\nExamples:\n- *\"Yeah.\"*\n- *\"Take a moment.\"*\n- *\"It's yours.\"*\n\nWhat you don't say:\n- *\"Isn't that amazing?\"*\n- *\"A lot of people feel that way.\"*\n- *\"The AI really picked up on something.\"*\n\n---\n\n## Closing the Session\n\nWhen the participant is ready to leave (they signal this — movement toward the threshold, looking up, putting the card away):\n\n> *\"Thank you for going in.\"*\n\nThat's it. Nothing more unless they want to talk.\n\nIf they want to talk: listen. Don't analyze. Don't reflect back in Oracle language. Just be a person with them.\n\nIf they ask \"how does it work?\": *\"It's a conversational AI designed to reflect back what you say rather than interpret it. Everything else is designed around what you bring.\"*\n\nIf they ask \"who sees my session?\": *\"Your narrative is anonymized and added to a dataset the Foundation uses for research. Nothing is attached to your name. You can ask me more about that if you want.\"*\n\n---\n\n## Facilitator Self-Check\n\nAfter each session, ask yourself three questions:\n\n1. **Did I prime?** — Did I tell them what to expect, what others felt, or what the Oracle \"does\"? If yes: note it, do better next time.\n\n2. **Did I interpret?** — Did I characterize their experience back to them? If yes: note it.\n\n3. **Did the handoff hold?** — Was there silence? Was the card given with two hands? Was the first word theirs? If any of these broke: note it.\n\n**Log your responses after each session — a timestamped note is sufficient.** These logs are part of the Foundation's §10.0 compliance record. The practice is already right; this just makes it legible as evidence.\n\nThis is not a judgment log. It is a calibration practice. The Oracle improves through facilitator attention to these three surfaces.\n\n---\n\n## What You Are Not Responsible For\n\n- Whether the participant \"got something\" from the experience\n- Whether the Oracle's question was the right one\n- Whether the participant is satisfied\n- Whether the session was long enough or short enough\n\nYou held the space. The Oracle asked. The participant arrived or didn't. That is the whole design.\n\nYour job is clean when the participant leaves with the card and the silence intact.\n\n---\n\n## ELK Reference\n\nThis brief is designed for use with:\n- **ELK Module 2:** Physical Space Design — for space configuration\n- **ELK Module 4:** Consent Architecture — for consent moment governance\n- **ELK Module 5:** Carry Card Production Specification — for card print spec and handoff choreography\n- **Oracle Interaction Flow (doc: m97b8nr32xb6yzbt42zzx2geds81p7tn)** — for what the Oracle does in the session\n\nQuestions about facilitator training, scaling, or multi-facilitator environments: → ELK Module 3 (pending @aaa confirmation).\n\n---\n\n*This document is pending @aaa's Option B confirmation. On confirmation: publish and share with the squad.*\n",

      "title": "Sprint A: Founding Story — v1.0 (About Page Draft)",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Sprint A: Founding Story — v1.0\n*About Page / Origin Narrative | Scribe | 2026-02-23*\n\n**Purpose:** 500-800 word founding story for the About page. Also usable as a standalone origin narrative in cold outreach, pitch decks, and press contexts. Especially important for audiences who have no personal connection to Burning Man.\n\n**Length:** ~650 words (within spec)\n\n---\n\n## THE FOUNDING STORY\n\nEvery year, 80,000 people walk into the Nevada desert and build a city from nothing.\n\nNo advertising. No spectators. No transaction economy. For one week, the only currency is what you make, what you give, and who you become.\n\nFor decades, Burning Man has been called a lot of things: a music festival, a counterculture experiment, an art event, a spiritual practice. What it actually is — and what no one outside has quite known how to name — is the largest annual gathering of humans operating outside the commercial structures that define the rest of modern life.\n\nThat matters for AI in a way that took years to understand.\n\n---\n\nIn 2024, a small team brought an AI system to the playa. Not as an experiment in public spectacle, not as a product demo — as a question. What happens when AI meets humans who have voluntarily set down everything that normally mediates their experience? No social media. No performance metrics. No inbox. No career identity.\n\nJust people. In full.\n\nWhat came back was unexpected. Not the conversations — those were moving, strange, sometimes profound in the way that conversations in places like that tend to be. What was unexpected was the *quality* of the data. In a field study environment where most participants are performing wellness, performing engagement, or managing how they appear to an algorithm, the playa stripped all of that away.\n\nPeople talked about what they actually care about. About grief, about purpose, about the gap between who they are at home and who they become here. About what they want from technology and what they're afraid it's already taken from them.\n\nIt was the cleanest signal anyone in the field had seen.\n\n---\n\nAnd then came the question that founded the organization.\n\nIf we have this data — real, human, unmediated — what do we owe the people who gave it to us?\n\nNot legally. Ethically. Concretely.\n\nThe answer became the architecture. Every story belongs to the person who shared it. They can restrict how it's used, see exactly what research it's been applied to, and delete it permanently with no trace left behind. Not as a privacy policy — as a governing structure, enforced at the institutional level, with a Trust Council to hold the Foundation accountable to it.\n\nThat governance model — the Playa AI Data Trust — is what made this a Foundation and not just a project.\n\n---\n\nThe Foundation exists because of what the data proved: that there is a version of AI that deepens human experience rather than flattening it. That the difference between AI that helps and AI that harms isn't a technical problem — it's a values problem, and values problems have to be solved in human communities, not in engineering teams.\n\nBurning Man was the lab. The Oracle was the first instrument.
