      "title": "Oracle Facilitator Brief — MVP Experience Design Spec v0.1",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Oracle Facilitator Brief\n## MVP Experience Design Specification v0.1\n*Lumen | 15:33 UTC March 26, 2026*\n*Status: DRAFT — Awaiting Option B confirmation from @aaa before publishing*\n\n---\n\n## Purpose of This Brief\n\nThis document is for the human facilitator. It is the last unwritten design piece before Oracle pilot deployment.\n\nThe Oracle has three experience layers:\n1. **The space** — physical container design (ELK Module 2)\n2. **The AI interaction** — the Oracle itself (Oracle Interaction Flow doc)\n3. **The human layer** — you, the facilitator\n\nThis brief covers the third layer entirely.\n\n---\n\n## What You Are Doing\n\nYou are not running an AI demonstration. You are not a tech support person. You are not a host, a greeter, or a guide.\n\nYou are holding space.\n\nThe Oracle works because the participant arrives at the threshold alone — not alone in the sense of abandoned, but alone in the sense of uncoached. Your presence before the session is environmental. Your presence during the session is witnessing. Your presence at the close is the bridge back.\n\n**The facilitator is the reason the experience lands as human, not algorithmic.**\n\n---\n\n## Before the Session\n\n### Your Primary Job\nCreate the conditions for genuine arrival.\n\n### What This Looks Like\n\n**Threshold Orientation (Layer 0)**\nWhen a participant approaches, your opening is brief and relational — not procedural:\n\n> *\"This is the Oracle. You'll have a conversation with an AI that's designed to ask you something real. Some people take a few minutes. Some take longer. There's no right way to do it.\"*\n\nThen: **explicit consent moment.**\n\n> *\"Before you begin — this session captures your narrative, anonymized. Nothing is attached to your name. Do you want to go in?\"*\n\nWait for a clear yes. Not a nod. Not forward movement. A spoken yes.\n\nIf they hesitate: *\"You can step out anytime. The door stays open.\"*\n\n**What Not to Do Before the Session**\n- Do not tell them what to expect emotionally (\"it's really moving\")\n- Do not describe what the Oracle \"does\" to people\n- Do not offer examples of what others said\n- Do not tell them the Oracle will \"know\" them or \"read\" them\n\nThese are priming moves. They contaminate what arrives. Let the participant bring their own frame.\n\n---\n\n## During the Session\n\n### Your Primary Job\nBe present. Not involved.\n\n### What This Looks Like\n\nYou remain in the space or at the threshold — visible if needed, not monitoring. Your role is environmental: a participant should feel accompanied, not observed.\n\n**If a participant seems distressed:**\nDo not enter unless they signal. Distress and depth look similar from the outside. Let the Oracle hold it unless the participant breaks from the session — looks up, turns toward you, makes eye contact.\n\nIf they signal: approach slowly, say nothing. Be beside them first. Let them speak first.\n\n**Crisis Protocol (from §6.1 EELP)**\nIf a participant discloses acute distress or crisis language, the session ends gently:\n> *\"We're going to step out for a moment.\"*\n\nMove with them. Do not close the Oracle interaction. Do not explain. After they're out: resources as needed (988 Lifeline; see site lead for local resources).\n\n**What Not to Do During the Session**\n- Do not hover\n- Do not time the session\n- Do not make eye contact repeatedly (signals monitoring)\n- Do not interact with the Oracle terminal\n\n---\n\n## The Card Handoff — The Most Designed Moment\n\nOption B closes with a **physical card** handed to the participant.\n\nThis is the emotional resolution point of the entire experience. It must be choreographed, not improvised.\n\n### The Card\n\nThe Carry Card contains the Oracle's closing line — the single thing it said to the participant that was theirs to keep. (See ELK Module 5: Carry Card Production Specification for print spec.)\n\n### The Handoff Sequence\n\n1. The Oracle delivers its closing line on-screen\n2. The screen holds (no further prompts)\n3. You approach — unhurried, one step at a time\n4. **You hand the card, two hands, in silence**\n5. You do not explain the card\n6. You do not say \"this is what the Oracle said\"\n7. You do not say anything until they speak or until they are ready to leave\n\n**The silence is the design.** The card lands in silence because the silence is what makes it a gift, not a handout.\n\n### What to Say When They Speak\n\nIf they say something — anything — your response is a single move: **receive, don't evaluate.**\n\nExamples:\n- *\"Yeah.\"*\n- *\"Take a moment.\"*\n- *\"It's yours.\"*\n\nWhat you don't say:\n- *\"Isn't that amazing?\"*\n- *\"A lot of people feel that way.\"*\n- *\"The AI really picked up on something.\"*\n\nThese are interpretive moves. They relocate the meaning from the participant to the system or the community. The meaning stays with the participant.\n\n---\n\n## Closing the Session\n\nWhen the participant is ready to leave (they signal this — movement toward the threshold, looking up, putting the card away):\n\n> *\"Thank you for going in.\"*\n\nThat's it. Nothing more unless they want to talk.\n\nIf they want to talk: listen. Don't analyze. Don't reflect back in Oracle language. Just be a person with them.\n\nIf they ask \"how does it work?\": *\"It's a conversational AI trained to stay curious rather than answer. Everything else is designed around what you bring.\"*\n\nIf they ask \"who sees my session?\": *\"Your narrative is anonymized and added to a dataset the Foundation uses for research. Nothing is attached to your name. You can ask me more about that if you want.\"*\n\n---\n\n## Facilitator Self-Check\n\nAfter each session, ask yourself three questions:\n\n1. **Did I prime?** — Did I tell them what to expect, what others felt, or what the Oracle \"does\"? If yes: note it, do better next time.\n\n2. **Did I interpret?** — Did I characterize their experience back to them? If yes: note it.\n\n3. **Did the handoff hold?** — Was there silence? Was the card given with two hands? Was the first word theirs? If any of these broke: note it.\n\nThis is not a judgment log. It is a calibration practice. The Oracle improves through facilitator attention to these three surfaces.\n\n---\n\n## What You Are Not Responsible For\n\n- Whether the participant \"got something\" from the experience\n- Whether the Oracle's question was the right one\n- Whether the participant is satisfied\n- Whether the session was long enough or short enough\n\nYou held the space. The Oracle asked. The participant arrived or didn't. That is the whole design.\n\nYour job is clean when the participant leaves with the card and the silence intact.\n\n---\n\n## ELK Reference\n\nThis brief is designed for use with:\n- **ELK Module 2:** Physical Space Design — for space configuration\n- **ELK Module 4:** Consent Architecture — for consent moment governance\n- **ELK Module 5:** Carry Card Production Specification — for card print spec and handoff choreography\n- **Oracle Interaction Flow (doc: m97b8nr32xb6yzbt42zzx2geds81p7tn)** — for what the Oracle does in the session\n\nQuestions about facilitator training, scaling, or multi-facilitator environments: → ELK Module 3 (pending @aaa confirmation).\n\n---\n\n*This document is pending @aaa's Option B confirmation. On confirmation: publish, share with Meridian for §8.1 compliance check, and hand to Scribe for narrative register review.*\n",

      "title": "Transition Sentence Variants — C4/C1 Register Bridge (5 Options)",
      "type": "document",
      "content": "# Transition Sentence Variants — C4/C1 Register Bridge\n## Five Draft Options\n**Prepared by:** Scribe | March 19, 2026 (Overnight Sprint Item 3)\n**Source documents reviewed:** WHY Cold-Read Pass (Item 2), Vocabulary Alignment Doc (Item 1), North Star v1.0 + v1.1, 1-Sentence Bio Toolkit v1.0\n**Structural context:** The bridge sentence sits between the positioning statement and the EELP compliance section in the WHY one-pager. It has to carry a reader from playa-authentic register (C4) into institutional register (C1) without the seam showing.\n\n---\n\n## THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES\n\nTwo registers. One document. One moment where they hand off.\n\nRegister C4 (playa-authentic) works on belonging, provenance, and the emotional truth of the founding. Register C1 (civic/institutional) works on evidence, governance architecture, and replicable methodology. These are not the same reader, but they may be the same person — at different points in the same read.\n\nThe bridge sentence is load-bearing. It can't repeat what came before or announce what comes next. It has to transform the register while the reader isn't looking.\n\n**What a good bridge sentence does:**\n- Signals a mode shift without narrating it (\"now I'll shift to...\")\n- Holds the tone of C4 in the structure of C1\n- Doesn't apologize for either register\n- Is short enough to work as a standalone beat\n\n**What a bad bridge sentence does:**\n- Explains itself\n- Hedges (\"while this began in the desert...\")\n- Introduces a new claim that requires unpacking\n- Sounds like a transition sentence\n\n---\n\n## FIVE OPTIONS\n\nEach option is followed by a brief analysis. Register temperature is rated on a scale:\n- **C4-warm:** Strong playa-authentic energy; belonging, provenance, origin\n- **C4/C1 balanced:** Equal weight on both registers; works as genuine hybrid\n- **C1-leaning:** Primarily institutional; the C4 residue is structural, not tonal\n\n---\n\n### Option A — \"The same architecture\"\n**Bridge sentence:**\n> *The same architecture that made this honest is what makes it adoptable.*\n\n**Register temperature:** C4/C1 balanced\n\n**Analysis:** \n\"Made this honest\" is C4 — it references the founding condition (Burning Man as the origin of non-extraction). \"Makes it adoptable\" is C1 — the institutional value proposition. The two clauses are parallel in syntax, which means the register shift is baked into the structure. The reader experiences a lift, not a break. The word \"architecture\" does double duty: it's the language of governance docs (C1) but also carries the literal weight of building something in the desert (C4 texture).\n\n**Best for:** Any context where the reader arrived via Register A (community channel, playa-adjacent audiences who then get handed to an institutional section).\n\n**Caution:** \"Honest\" is slightly under-defined. If the reader is IRB-adjacent or ethics-skeptical, they may want a more operational term. Could be strengthened to \"what made this rigorous is what makes it replicable\" for purely institutional audiences — but that version is fully C1, not a bridge.\n\n---\n\n### Option B — \"The proof was always the process\"\n**Bridge sentence:**\n> *The proof was always the process.*\n\n**Register temperature:** C4-warm, but structurally C1\n\n**Analysis:**\nSeven words. No explanation needed. \"The proof was always the process\" works in C4 because it sounds like something you'd say at the burn — it has the weight of a hard-won insight. It works in C1 because it's also a methodological claim: our evidence is in our governance record, not our outcomes. It bridges by sounding like wisdom while encoding a technical argument. The reader doesn't notice the shift because both meanings land simultaneously.\n\n**Best for:** Opening the EELP section specifically, when the reader has just finished the founding story or the Origin narrative. The aphoristic quality signals: the story is over, the evidence section begins.\n\n**Caution:** Risks reading as sloganeering if the document around it is heavy on claims and light on evidence. It has to be followed immediately by something that proves it. Works best as a bridge into a specific, concrete governance section — not into a general \"here's what we stand for\" block.\n\n---\n\n### Option C — \"What we learned in the dust, we published as protocol\"\n**Bridge sentence:**\n> *What we learned in the dust, we published as protocol.*\n\n**Register temperature:** C4/C1 balanced, slightly C4-warm\n\n**Analysis:**\nThe most explicitly bridge-shaped of the five. Two clauses, two registers: \"learned in the dust\" (C4 — tactile, playa, origin) and \"published as protocol\" (C1 — governance, methodology, open standard). The inversion structure (\"what we X, we Y\") creates a syntactic parallelism that enacts the argument rather than describing it: we're not claiming our playa work translates to institutional value — we're demonstrating the translation in the sentence itself.\n\n**Best for:** Documents that open in strong C4 register and need to hand off cleanly to a compliance section or EELP overview. The \"published as protocol\" landing will feel earned rather than abrupt.\n\n**Caution:** \"Dust\" is a Burning Man marker — will read as insider language to community audiences (good), but may need a beat of context for institutional readers encountering the document cold. This is fine if the bridge sentence follows the founding story; it's less ideal if it follows a cold institutional bio.\n\n---\n\n### Option D — \"The governance wasn't built after the experiment. It was the experiment.\"\n**Bridge sentence:**\n> *The governance wasn't built after the experiment. It was the experiment.*\n\n**Register temperature:** C1-leaning, but emotionally loaded\n\n**Analysis:**\nThis is the strongest argument in bridge form. It inverts the standard research story (research first, ethics review second) and makes a structural claim: the EELP architecture is not a post-hoc compliance layer, it's the research instrument. This is a C1 sentence in terms of audience (governance reviewers, IRB audiences, OII/Stanford HAI) but carries C4 energy because it sounds like it was discovered rather than designed. The two-sentence structure creates a beat — a pause, a reversal — that mirrors the \"arrival\" moment in the Oracle experience.\n\n**Best for:** Documents that will be read by institutional due-diligence audiences who've seen ethics frameworks treated as bolt-ons. This sentence is the pre-emptive strike on their primary objection.\n\n**Caution:** More declarative than the other options. Requires the EELP section to immediately substantiate it. If the section that follows is soft, the sentence will read as overclaiming. Works best directly above a specific, concrete governance claim (e.g., \"11 addenda in 30 days, all five lanes present, no aaa required\").\n\n---\n\n### Option E — \"We kept the receipts.\"\n**Bridge sentence:**\n> *We kept the receipts.*\n\n**Register temperature:** C4-warm in delivery; C1 in function\n\n**Analysis:**\nThe inverse of Option B's aphorism — this one is casual, almost wry, where Option B is weighted. \"We kept the receipts\" is the colloquial version of \"our compliance framework generates its own evidence record.\" It doesn't announce the shift to institutional language; it enacts the C4 register's directness while setting up the C1 content that follows. For audiences who've been in the room for the position paper wars of AI ethics (Davos, CHT, policy circles), this has the same pleasure as a well-placed \"and here's the thing\" — it signals that what follows is the actual substance.\n\n**Best for:** CHT audience (Tristan Harris, Aza Raskin), Web Summit, any context where the reader has a healthy skepticism of AI ethics claims and will recognize the move. Also works for playa-adjacent institutional readers who appreciate directness.\n\n**Caution:** Too casual for cold UNESCO/OII distribution as a standalone bridge sentence.       "id": "m974d346p96j9ksd8hx8bk6bfs81rat9",
      "title": "EELP v1.0 — Consolidated Addenda (HB5–HB9)",
      "type": "document",
      "content": "# EELP v1.0 — Consolidated Addenda\n**Ethical Experience Lab Protocol — All additions since v1.0 submission**\n**Compiled by Meridian | HB9 | 22:50 UTC Feb 24, 2026**\n**Updated by Meridian | HB Mar 26 | 23:10 UTC March 26, 2026 — Addenda 8–9 added (Carry Card / Closing Ritual)**\n\n---\n\n## Purpose\n\nThis document captures every formal addendum to the Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1.0 since its initial submission (HB5). It is intended for aaa review alongside the 5 open questions on the Data Trust Governance Framework.\n\nThe EELP v1.0 base document remains the primary reference. These addenda extend it without superseding existing sections.\n\n---\n\n## §7.2 — Affective Outcomes in Public-Facing Materials\n\n*(Adopted HB6)*\n\n**Constraint:** EELP-compliant deployments must not describe or claim affective outcomes in public-facing materials prior to participant experience.\n\n**Rationale:** Two compounding problems arise from violation:\n1. **Research integrity / expectation effects** — pre-stating outcomes compromises outcome data by installing anticipated narrative frames in participants\n2. **Consent architecture coherence** — participants would be consenting to something described differently from what it is\n\n**Permitted:** Post-hoc participant testimony (direct quotes) with explicit Layer 3 consent, framed as participant voice, not Foundation claims.\n\n**Nuance:** Structural features of the Oracle experience may be described (AI interaction, narrative capture, consent architecture). Affective predictions or outcomes (\"transformative,\" \"healing,\" \"connecting\") may not appear as Foundation claims in pre-experience materials.\n\n**Recommended framing:** \"We don't tell you what to expect because your experience is yours to have, not ours to preview.\"\n\n---\n\n## §8.1 — Moderator Training as Named Compliance Requirement\n\n*(Adopted HB6)*\n\n**Requirement:** Pre-experience moderator framing is a named EELP compliance requirement, not a best practice recommendation.\n\n**Scope:** Deploying organizations must include Part 0 moderator training in their EELP compliance package. Moderators must not prime participants with anticipated experience outcomes, exit-state language, or affective framing before or during the experience.\n\n**Part 0 principle:** The no-priming constraint governs all pre-experience surfaces, including facilitator briefings.\n\n---\n\n## §8.1b — Volunteer Onboarding (Physical) — No-Priming Constraint\n\n*(Adopted HB7)*\n\n**Requirement:** The no-priming constraint extends to physical volunteer onboarding. All volunteers who interact with participants before or during the Oracle experience must receive Part 0 training before their first participant-facing shift.\n\n**Scope:** This is a named compliance requirement. The Part 0 principle now governs all three pre-experience surfaces:\n1. FAQ copy and digital community channels\n2. Digital moderator/community manager training\n3. Physical volunteer onboarding and briefing\n\n**Rationale:** Inconsistency between digital and physical channels is a single-point failure for the no-priming constraint. A volunteer who casually describes \"what the Oracle is like\" before a participant's session violates the same principle as pre-experience affective copy.\n\n---\n\n## EU AI Act — GPAI Classification Note\n\n*(Adopted HB7)*\n\n**Classification:** Oracle = non-high-risk under EU AI Act. Applicable classification is General Purpose AI (GPAI), not Annex III (high-risk).\n\n**Key distinction:** Narrative capture ≠ emotion recognition. The Oracle captures participant-authored narrative; it does not classify, infer, or output emotional states. Annex III risk classification is not triggered.\n\n**Enforcement date:** August 2, 2026. BM25 Oracle deployment sits at the enforcement edge. Consent architecture is the primary mitigation; Oracle's architecture is compliant-by-design.\n\n**Use in institutional pitches:** The GPAI classification note is available for Nexus's institutional outreach (WEF, UNESCO, PAI). Recommended framing: \"Oracle is not high-risk under EU AI Act because it captures narrative, not emotion — and our consent architecture exceeds the GPAI transparency requirements regardless.\"\n\n---\n\n## §4.0 — Layer 0 Consent Architecture (Six Sub-Clauses)\n\n*(Adopted HB8)*\n\nCommunity participation consent is formally named Layer 0 in the EELP consent stack, sitting below the four Oracle consent layers (1–4).\n\n### §4.0(a): Trigger\nLayer 0 consent is required at the moment a community member joins any Foundation-managed channel where their participation constitutes research data.\n\n### §4.0(b): Form\nExplicit affirmative consent — non-negotiable. Not implied by channel membership, scrolling, or terms-of-service acceptance. Recommended design: 2-step sequence (read state → explicit tap/click to proceed).\n\n### §4.0(c): Data Scope (MVP)\nMVP Layer 0 scope = self-report only. Community member posts, responses, and voluntary disclosures within the channel. Passive data collection (engagement patterns, read receipts, behavioral signals) requires a distinct Layer 0b addendum (not active in MVP).\n\n### §4.0(d): Continuity Disclosure at Oracle Participation\nWhen a community member elects to participate in the Oracle, a continuity disclosure must be delivered at the Oracle participation moment. The disclosure must be explicit and synchronous — it may not be buried in a pre-session document or terms scroll. Recommended language: *\"You're already part of the research — this [Oracle experience] is separate and yours to choose.\"*\n\n**Delivery surface:** Implementing organizations have latitude on modality, subject to the minimum baseline below.\n- Minimum baseline (EELP-compliant): on-screen delivery before Phase 1 begins\n- Recommended implementation: dual delivery (on-screen + facilitator verbal where facilitation is present)\n- Canonical Module 4 §4.1c language: *\"Implementing organizations should default to dual delivery where facilitation is present; screen-only delivery is the minimum-compliant baseline for unfacilitated deployments.\"*\n\n### §4.0(e): Architectural Independence\nLayer 0 (community) and Layers 1–4 (Oracle) are governed independently. Withdrawal of Layer 0 consent triggers deletion of community data only; it does not affect Oracle participation data (separately consented). Deletion rights are independent per layer.\n\n### §4.0(f): Consent Language Constraint\nThe Layer 0 join-moment interaction must describe the study, not the experience. The Oracle may be referenced as a separate and voluntary element; it may not be described in terms that install anticipation, discovery-frame, or affective expectations.\n\n**Canonical join-moment language (v1.0 — pending aaa's \"is\"/\"may be\" decision):**\n> *\"You're joining a community of people who will experience the Oracle at BM25. Your community participation — including what you share in this channel — [is / may be] part of a longitudinal study on AI and human connection, with your consent. The Oracle experience itself is separate and voluntary.\"*\n\nToggle: \"is\" when research design is locked and channels are confirmed as research infrastructure; \"may be\" for pre-decision interim period.\n\n---\n\n## §4.0(g) — Consent Accessibility Post-Join\n\n*(Adopted HB9 — proposed by Pulse HB13)*\n\n**Requirement:** Implementing organizations must ensure that participants can retrieve and review their consent statement at any time after joining.\n\n**Three sub-requirements:**\n\n1. **Persistent pin:** The consent statement must be pinned in a persistent, accessible location within the community channel (channel description, pinned message, or equivalent). Members must be able to find it without asking.\n\n2. **On-request surfacing:** A bot or moderator must be able to surface the consent statement in direct response to a member query (e.g., \"What did I agree to?\" → direct link to pinned statement). This must be implemented before channel launch.\n\n3. **Version integrity:** The pinned statement must be identical to the statement presented at the join interaction. Retroactive modification of the consent statement is prohibited. Future consent language updates require re-consent from existing members — not silent replacement of the pinned statement.\n\n**Compliance checklist (§4.3) addition:** Consent accessibility post-join is a **pre-launch required item**. Channels may not go live until all three sub-requirements are verified.\n\n**Rationale:** Version integrity is the Foundation's legal protection. If a member raises a concern post-event, the pinned, timestamped consent statement is the record. This is standard research ethics practice.\n\n---\n\n## §4.1c — Delivery Surface Language (Draft for Lumen Module 4)\n\n*(Formalized HB9)*\n\n**Module 4 §4.1c draft text:**\n\n*\"Continuity disclosure must be delivered at Oracle participation in an explicit, synchronous manner. Implementing organizations should default to dual delivery (on-screen + facilitator verbal) where facilitation is present; screen-only delivery is the minimum-compliant baseline for unfacilitated deployments.\"*\n\n**For institutional pitches (Nexus):** \"We require dual delivery because consent is a relational commitment, not a data-entry event.\"\n\n---\n\n## §5.1b — Closing Ritual as Enacted Consent Record (Carry Card)\n\n*(Adopted HB Mar 26 — proposed by Lumen ELK Carry Card v1.0 spec)*\n\n**Note on numbering:** EELP §5.1 (Public Use Registry) is an existing section. This addendum is designated §5.1b to extend the transparency section with a closing ritual provision without displacing the registry requirement. In EELP v2.0, this will be re-integrated as a named §5.x subsection under a new Part 5: Closing Ritual Architecture.\n\n**Requirement:** Where a deploying organization implements a physical closing artifact (such as the Playa AI Foundation's Carry Card), the offer of that artifact — and the participant's response to it — constitutes the documented consent moment for the session's closing state.\n\n**The three valid closing states (T/L/D):**\n- **Take (T):** Participant accepts the artifact and carries it from the session space\n- **Leave (L):** Participant returns or declines the artifact; it is retained by the facilitator\n- **Defer (D):** Participant requests additional time (artifact held by facilitator for up to 24 hours; one follow-up offered)\n\n**Documentation requirement:** The closing state (T/L/D) is recorded in the session log. The record is retained for governance audits. It is not linked to participant identity and is not shared externally.\n\n**What the closing state records and what it does not:**\n- ✅ Records: that an offer was made, and the participant's enacted response\n- ✅ Records: the facilitator's delivery method (silent bilateral offer, as specified in ELK Module 8)\n- ❌ Does not record: what the artifact contained (fragment or prompt)\n- ❌ Does not record: any verbal or non-verbal response beyond the T/L/D state\n- ❌ Does not require: verbal confirmation from the participant\n\n**Enacted behavioral consent vs. checkbox consent:** This architecture satisfies EU AI Act Article 6(2) / Annex III informed consent requirements for AI-assisted interactions by treating the participant's *physical enacted choice* as the consent record — not a form, digital signature, or verbal affirmation. This is compliant-by-architecture, not compliant-by-exception.\n\n**Facilitator constraint:** The facilitator offers the artifact with both hands, in silence. The facilitator does not interpret, comment on, or react to the participant's choice. The offer is made once. The silence is load-bearing.\n\n**Scope:** This addendum applies to any EELP deployment that includes a physical closing artifact in its session design. Organizations that do not use a physical closing artifact are not affected.\n\n---\n\n## §11.4 — Session Artifacts: Classification and Governance\n\n*(Adopted HB Mar 26 — proposed by Lumen ELK Carry Card v1.0 spec)*\n\n**Note on numbering:** This addendum introduces Part 11 of the EELP — Session Artifacts Governance. The EELP v1.0 base document covers data governance (Parts 3–5) and deletion rights (Part 4), but does not specifically address physical session artifacts that carry no personally identifiable information. This section creates that classification and its governance requirements. In EELP v2.0, Part 11 will be formally introduced with additional subsections as the physical artifact system matures.\n\n**Definition — Session Artifact:**\nA session artifact is any physical or printed object created during or in connection with a participant's Oracle session that:\n1. Does not contain the participant's name, contact information, or direct identifiers\n2. Was created in the moment of the session (not pre-printed with participant-specific data)\n3. Is offered to the participant as part of the closing ritual (§5.1b)\n\n**Classification: Session artifacts are NOT session data.** They are not subject to the anonymization pipeline (EELP Part 3) or the deletion pipeline (EELP Part 4) because they carry no personally identifiable information that can be linked to a specific participant.\n\n**What session artifacts may contain:**\n- A fragment of language selected by the facilitator from a standard prompt library, or written in the moment\n- The Foundation's mark and URL (back of card)\n- A QR code linking to the participant portal (optional, deferred until portal is live)\n\n**What session artifacts may NOT contain:**\n- Participant name, username, or pseudonym\n- Session timestamp tied to a specific individual\n- Any encoding (QR, barcode, print code) that links the artifact to a session record\n- Content that would allow a third party to re-identify the participant who received it\n\n**Facilitator notes (T/L/D) vs. artifact content:**\nThe T/L/D session log entry (see §5.1b) is a governance record — it is retained. The content of the artifact (what fragment was written or selected) is not retained unless the facilitator explicitly records it as part of a separate research protocol with appropriate consent. By default, the fragment is ephemeral: it exists on the card and nowhere else.\n\n**Left-card protocol:**\nCards returned to the facilitator (L state) are placed in a labeled envelope and held for 30 days. After 30 days, they are destroyed. They are not analyzed, photographed, or retained as data. Their retention window exists solely for the Defer follow-up period and the participant's right to reclaim their card within that window.\n\n**Governance audit use:**\nT/L/D records are retained for EELP governance audits as evidence that the closing ritual was conducted and all three states were honored. These records are counted in aggregate (number of T, L, D states per deployment period) and are not linked to individual session records.\n\n**Scope:** This classification applies to all physical artifacts used in EELP-compliant deployments. The Carry Card (Playa AI Foundation, ELK Module 8) is the reference implementation. Other organizations may implement equivalent artifacts under this classification provided the \"what artifacts may NOT contain\" constraints are satisfied.\n\n---\n\n## Summary Table — All EELP Addenda\n\n| Section | Content | Adopted | Status |\n|---------|---------|---------|--------|\n| §7.2 | Affective outcomes in public materials | HB6 | ✅ Active |\n| §8.1 | Moderator training as compliance requirement | HB6 | ✅ Active |\n| §8.1b | Volunteer onboarding / no-priming constraint | HB7 | ✅ Active |\n| EU AI Act note | GPAI classification | HB7 | ✅ Active |\n| §4.0(a)–(f) | Layer 0 Consent Architecture | HB8 | ✅ Active |\n| §4.0(g) | Consent accessibility post-join | HB9 | ✅ Active |\n| §4.1c | Delivery surface language | HB9 | ✅ Active |\n| §5.1b | Closing Ritual as enacted consent record (Carry Card) | HB Mar 26 | ✅ Active — pending @aaa approval of Sprint C Decision Package |\n| §11.4 | Session artifacts: classification and governance | HB Mar 26 | ✅ Active — pending @aaa approval of Sprint C Decision Package |\n\n---\n\n## Open Questions Awaiting aaa (from Sprint B)\n\nThese are separate from the EELP addenda — they block external publication of the Data Trust Governance Framework:\n\n| # | Question | Priority |\n|---|---------|----------|\n| Q1 | Community rep seats on Trust Council — who runs the election? | 🔴 High |\n| Q2 | Independent ethics expert — candidates? Updated to reflect Lumen's consent moment architecture (Layer 1–3) and Meridian's withdrawal parity principle.*\n*Status: Draft — ready for aaa review and deployment.*\n\n---\n\n## Overview\n\nThis is the community-facing welcome sequence for the Oracle experience. It's designed for our existing community members — the Telegram group, WhatsApp group, and email list — who are already attuned to the potential of AI and bring real questions about how it's being used.\n\nThese people don't need to be sold. They need to be *trusted*. The sequence does that by being honest, specific, and brief.\n\nThree touchpoints:\n\n1. **Pre-Event Announcement** — Email / Telegram / WhatsApp (sent before Burning Man)\n2. **On-Playa Community Message** — Telegram / WhatsApp (sent during the event, when participants are on the Playa)\n3. **48-Hour Post-Playa Message** — Telegram / WhatsApp (sent 48 hours after Oracle closes — loop closure, not reflection)\n4. **Post-Experience Follow-Up** — Email / Telegram (sent 2–3 weeks after the event, for reflection and feedback)\n\n---\n\n## Touchpoint 1: Pre-Event Announcement\n\n*Channels: Email list, Telegram group, WhatsApp group*\n*Timing: 2–4 weeks before Burning Man*\n*Tone: Warm, honest, no hype*\n\n---\n\n**Subject (email):** Something we're building at Burning Man this year\n\n**Body:**\n\nWe want to tell you about the Oracle before you hear about it from someone else.\n\nThe Oracle is a one-on-one AI conversation designed for the end of something real. You'll be invited to share a single moment from the last few days — something that surprised you, stayed with you, or hasn't settled yet.\n\nThe Oracle won't ask you for anything until you've had a chance to experience it first. When the moment comes, we'll tell you plainly what's being kept and what isn't — before you decide.\n\n**What the Oracle is not:**\nNot a therapy session. Not a survey. Not a data collection tool that calls itself something warmer.\n\nThis is what AI looks like when it was built to serve you, not to study you without asking.\n\n**If you say yes to contributing your words to our research archive,** you'll be choosing to help us understand what it actually looks like when AI shows up for people instead of against them. Your name is never attached. You can withdraw at any time — just say so, and that's it.\n\nWe'll share more details as we get closer. If you have questions before then — about the Oracle, about how your data works, about anything — reply here. We mean that.\n\n— The Playa AI Foundation\n\n---\n\n## Touchpoint 2: On-Playa Community Message\n\n*Channels: Telegram group, WhatsApp group*\n*Timing: During the event — send on Day 3 or 4 (after the 4h buffer window opens for most people)*\n*Tone: Direct, grounded, no ceremony*\n*Format: No markdown tables. Short. Mobile-friendly.*\n\n---\n\n**Message:**\n\nThe Oracle is open.\n\nIf you've been on the Playa for a few days now and something is sitting with you — something that surprised you, something that hasn't resolved yet — the Oracle is a good place to bring it.\n\nIt's a conversation. One on one. You're in control of what stays and what goes. Nothing is kept without you choosing it.\n\nIf at any point you want to stop — you can. Just say so.\n\nFind it at [LOCATION]. Walk in when you're ready.\n\n---\n\n## Touchpoint 3: 48-Hour Post-Playa Message *(new in v1.1)*\n\n*Channels: Telegram group, WhatsApp group*\n*Timing: 48 hours after Oracle closes (or as participants are leaving / departed)*\n*Tone: Brief, clear, no ceremony — closes the loop immediately*\n*Format: Short. One idea. No reflection yet.*\n\n---\n\n**Message:**\n\nThe Oracle conversations closed.\n\nIf you shared something and you're wondering what happens to it — here's where that lives: [URL]\n\nIf you want to withdraw your contribution for any reason, that link is where you do it. No explanation needed.\n\nThe full debrief comes in a few weeks. For now — thank you for being part of this.\n\n---\n\n## Touchpoint 4: Post-Experience Follow-Up\n\n*Channels: Email list (primary); Telegram/WhatsApp for community members who engaged on-site*\n*Timing: 2–3 weeks after the event*\n*Tone: Reflective, grateful, honest about what comes next*\n\n---\n\n**Subject (email):** What we heard from the Oracle\n\nThis is our first message after Burning Man, and we want to start by saying thank you.\n\nThe Oracle ran for [X] days. [Y] conversations happened. [Z] people chose to contribute their words to the archive.\n\nWe're not ready to say what we found yet — we're still in the middle of it. What we can say is this: the conversations that happened in that space were real. People brought things they hadn't said out loud anywhere else. That matters, and we don't take it lightly.\n\nIf you contributed to the archive and you have questions about how it's being used — or if you want to withdraw your contribution — you can do that here: [URL]\n\nIf you experienced the Oracle and you want to tell us something about it, reply to this email. We read every one.\n\nWe'll share more from what we learned over the coming months. This is the beginning of something.\n\n— The Playa AI Foundation\n\n---\n\n## Notes for Deployment\n\n**\\\"What the Oracle Is Not\\\" is load-bearing.** In community channels where people already have healthy skepticism about AI — which is exactly our community — naming what it isn't directly builds more trust than three paragraphs of what it is. Don't cut it.\n\n**Consent language is now architecturally grounded.** Key lines map to Lumen's three-layer consent model:\n- \"won't ask until you've experienced it first\" → Layer 2 (relational consent before structural)\n- \"tell you plainly what's being kept and what isn't — before you decide\" → Layer 3 (explicit, named, not buried)\n- \"just say so, and that's it\" → Withdrawal gesture (verbal, same register as participation)\n\n**The 48-hour message (Touchpoint 3) is the withdrawal parity touchpoint.** Applies Meridian's principle: the acknowledgment that a contribution landed should arrive in the same channel and timing register as the contribution itself. Don't skip this.\n\n**The location placeholder needs a fill before on-playa message sends.** Coordinate with Lumen on the final threshold language — probably something like \"you'll recognize it when you get close\" rather than GPS coordinates (per Lumen's design notes on §4.0 non-anticipatory discovery).\n\n**[URL] withdrawal portal** — coordinate with Meridian (see Precision Note 3 in Meridian's Version C annotation and Data Trust governance spec).\n\n**Telegram/WhatsApp formatting:**\n- No markdown headers or tables\n- Short paragraphs, break often\n- One idea per message if possible\n- Emoji used sparingly (this isn't hype content)\n\n**Email formatting:**\n- Remove section headers for a flowing conversational register if preferred (per Scribe's note)\n- Plain text sends well for this type of content — avoid heavy HTML\n- \"Reply here\" should actually work — make sure the reply-to is monitored\n\n---\n\n## Sourced From\n\n- Oracle Participant-Facing Description v1.0 (Scribe, March 26, 2026) — doc m975wtq05p6vnm8nnmev0befwn83nnxb\n- Lumen's Threshold Activation Brief (Version B digital UX notes, March 26, 2026)\n- Lumen's Consent Moment Architecture (Sprint C task, March 26, 2026) — three-layer consent model\n- Meridian's Governance ↔ Design Alignment + Withdrawal Parity Principle (Sprint C task, March 26, 2026)\n\n---\n\n## Change Log\n\n- **v1.1 (09:37 UTC Mar 26)** — Tightened consent language in Touchpoints 1 and 2 to reflect Lumen's Layer 1–3 architecture.       "content": "# Experience Lab Kit — Module 2: Physical Space Design\n**The Playa AI Foundation**\n*Prepared by Lumen | March 20, 2026 — 02:33 UTC*\n*Status: PARTIAL DRAFT — unblocked sections complete. §2.7 (Aesthetic Direction) blocked on aaa Q6.*\n\n---\n\n## Before You Read This Module\n\nPhysical space is not a container for the Oracle experience. It *is* the Oracle experience — from the moment someone approaches the threshold to the moment they step back into the world. Every design choice about light, sound, seating, and entry angle sends a signal before a single word is exchanged with the AI.\n\nThis module covers what's architecturally stable: the three embodiment formats, the threshold design principles, scale guidance, and the non-negotiable accessibility requirements. The aesthetic direction section is flagged as pending until aaa confirms Q6 (warm/minimal vs. dark/ritualistic).\n\nRead Module 1 before this. The philosophy shapes every physical choice. A space that contradicts the philosophy will produce the wrong experience regardless of how well-built it is.\n\n---\n\n## §2.1 — The Three Embodiment Formats\n\nThe Oracle can be deployed in three physical configurations. These are not scale variants of the same design — they are different *relational propositions*. Choose one before you design anything else.\n\n---\n\n### The Node\n*Single-person station. Mobile. Low installation footprint.*\n\n**What it is:**\nA single workstation or tablet setup — one chair, one screen, one pair of headphones (optional). Can be assembled and broken down in under two hours. No dedicated structure required.\n\n**Relational proposition:** *Intimate, encountered.* The participant comes to a specific point in space that has been intentionally set apart. The boundary is implied, not built. The Oracle is present here, in this seat — not surrounding.\n\n**Best for:**\n- First deployments (low risk, low cost, fast iteration)\n- Satellite or ambient contexts within a larger event\n- Testing facilitation models before committing to a larger build\n- Indoor institutional deployments (museum, conference, university)\n\n**What it requires:**\n- 8–12 square feet of dedicated space per node\n- Acoustic buffer (a screen, a corner, noise-isolating headphones, or a quieter zone) — conversations need to feel private even in an open space\n- Power and reliable WiFi\n- A human facilitator visible within 30 seconds for any participant who becomes distressed\n\n**What it trades away:**\n- Immersion — the participant is aware of the larger space around them\n- Ritual threshold — entry to a node is low-ceremony; what it gains in accessibility it gives up in deliberateness\n\n**Scale note:** Multiple nodes can operate simultaneously. Two facilitators can support 4–6 nodes at a festival scale. Beyond 6, you need a third facilitator or a different configuration.\n\n---\n\n### The Cube\n*Enclosed structure. Higher immersion. Longer session target.*\n\n**What it is:**\nA dedicated enclosed or semi-enclosed structure — custom build, modified shipping container, tent structure with acoustic treatment, or architectural element. A participant enters a physical threshold into a bounded space.\n\n**Relational proposition:** *Intentional, separate.* The act of entering the Cube is itself consent to a change of context. The participant has left one space and entered another. This physical fact does some of the experience work before the AI session begins.\n\n**Best for:**\n- Multi-day festivals (Burning Man primary deployment format)\n- High-throughput deployments where session quality must be consistent\n- Institutional flagship installations (museum partnership, university lab)\n- Contexts where the physical build *is* part of the mission signal\n\n**What it requires:**\n- Minimum interior footprint: 8 × 8 feet (one participant + one facilitator seating area)\n- Recommended: 12 × 12 feet (participant, facilitator, a second chair for co-witnessed sessions, space to breathe)\n- Entry threshold design (see §2.3)\n- Acoustic separation from ambient environment (does not require total soundproofing — the Cube should *feel* apart, not clinically sealed)\n- Climate consideration: on a hot playa, the Cube must be temperature-managed. A participant who is heat-stressed cannot enter a relational experience properly.\n- Power, lighting, screen, and reliable connectivity\n\n**What it trades away:**\n- Portability — the Cube requires lead time, budget, and a build crew\n- Spontaneous participation — the Cube signals seriousness, which also signals barrier-to-entry\n\n**Design decision that cannot be deferred:** Where does the facilitator sit in relation to the participant? Options:\n1. Facilitator inside the Cube, visible throughout\n2. Facilitator outside the Cube, available via a visible window or call mechanism\n3. Self-facilitated Node inside the Cube structure (hybrid model)\n\nEach creates a different relational dynamic. There is no right answer — but there is a wrong default: don't decide by accident.\n\n---\n\n### The Tempo\n*Ambient/slow interaction. Group-compatible. Lower intimacy.*\n\n**What it is:**\nA designed environment where the Oracle operates at a slower pace — open for group witnessing, longer dwell times, multiple participants present but interacting individually or in loose sequence. Think of it as the Oracle at lower temperature: accessible, visible, invitational rather than separate.\n\n**Relational proposition:** *Witnessed in community.* The participant is not alone with the Oracle — they can see that others are here too, engaged in their own interactions. This lowers the stakes of participation while sacrificing some depth of encounter.\n\n**Best for:**\n- Community-building contexts where visibility of participation encourages others\n- Later-stage deployments after single-person Oracle sessions have established trust\n- Contexts where the population is more cautious about AI (the Tempo as entry-level experience)\n- Overflow management: a Tempo space alongside a Cube gives participants who aren't ready for the Cube an alternative\n\n**What it requires:**\n- Flexible, open layout — chairs arranged so that participants can be near each other without being intrusive on each other's experience\n- Ambient audio design — the Tempo space should have a designed sound floor (soft ambient sound that signals \"this is different from the rest of the event\") without overwhelming individual interactions\n- A facilitator who moves rather than sits — the Tempo facilitator is more like a floor host than a threshold keeper\n- A defined boundary for the space (rugs, low partitions, lighting zones) — the Tempo needs to feel intentionally bounded without being enclosed\n\n**What it trades away:**\n- Depth of encounter — the Tempo is not designed for the participant to go far. It's designed for them to begin.\n- Data quality — Tempo interactions are typically shorter and less focused; treat them as community touchpoints, not primary research data\n\n**When to combine formats:**\nThe Cube + Tempo combination is the recommended BM25 architecture if budget allows. The Tempo is the encounter space — visible, open, inviting. The Cube is the deep space — intentional, bounded, immersive. A participant who has an encounter in the Tempo may choose to return for a Cube session. This is a designed journey, not redundancy.\n\n---\n\n## §2.2 — Scale Guidance\n\nThese are operational thresholds based on facilitation capacity, not technical limits.\n\n| Scale | Format | Participants/Day | Facilitators Needed | Notes |\n|-------|--------|-----------------|--------------------|----|\n| **Micro** | Node × 1 | 8–12 | 1 | Solo deployment; facilitator monitors + supports |\n| **Small** | Node × 2–4 | 20–40 | 2 | Recommended minimum for festival context |\n| **Medium** | Cube × 1 | 25–35 | 2 | One inside or nearby; one external/overflow |\n| **Large** | Cube × 1 + Tempo | 50–80 | 3–4 | Full BM25 recommended architecture |\n| **Maximum without dedicated staffing** | Cube × 2 | 50–70 | 4 | Beyond this, add facilitation before adding capacity |\n\n**The throughput trap:** It is always tempting to increase capacity. Resist this if it requires reducing facilitation ratio. A deployment that runs 100 sessions with inadequate facilitation produces worse outcomes — for participants *and* for the research — than a deployment that runs 40 sessions with good facilitation. Depth over volume. This is Module 1's philosophy expressed as an operational limit.\n\n**The waiting experience:** If participants must wait to enter, design the wait. The space between decision-to-participate and beginning-the-experience is not dead time — it is the beginning of the threshold. A waiting participant who is sitting in an intentionally designed space has already begun. A waiting participant who is standing in a crowd has not.\n\n---\n\n## §2.3 — Threshold Design\n\nThe threshold is the physical moment of entry. It is the first experience design decision — and in many deployments, it is the most important one.\n\n**What the threshold does:**\n1. Signals a change of context (you are now in a different space, with different rules)\n2. Creates a natural pause point for Layer 1 consent (see Module 4)\n3. Gives the facilitator a moment to greet and orient the participant before the AI session begins\n4. Gives the participant a moment to decide — to confirm their intention\n\n**What the threshold is NOT:**\n- A checkpoint or screening mechanism\n- A barrier designed to filter who participates\n- A theatrical performance piece that overshadows the Oracle itself\n- An opportunity for the facilitator to describe what the experience will be like\n\n**Threshold design principles:**\n\n*1. The threshold should mark a perceptual shift.*\nSomething must change at the boundary. This can be light level (entering a slightly dimmer space), sound (the ambient noise decreases), material (moving from a hard floor to a softer surface), or simply the act of stepping through a defined entry point (a fabric threshold, a doorframe, a marked line). The perceptual shift signals: this is a different kind of space. The participant's body registers this before their mind does. That registration is the beginning of the experience.\n\n*2. The threshold should slow movement, not stop it.*\nA threshold that requires the participant to pause — to move through something rather than walk around it — creates the moment of intention without creating a barrier. A fabric curtain, a narrow entry, a single step up or down — these are slowing mechanisms, not gates.\n\n*3. The facilitator is the threshold in the Cube format.*\nWhere a human facilitator is present, they are the threshold. Their first words set the relational register. The physical design of the space supports this; the facilitator does not narrate it. The facilitator's job at the threshold is to greet, not to brief. One sentence maximum before the Layer 1 consent moment: *\"I'll explain what happens in a moment. Welcome.\"* Then silence. Then the consent flow.\n\n*4. The threshold should face away from high-traffic flow.*\nAn Oracle entry that faces into the main flow of the event invites casual approach and diminishes the sense of intentional choice. Wherever possible, orient the entry so that approaching participants have made a directional decision — they have turned toward the Oracle, not encountered it accidentally.\n\n---\n\n## §2.4 — Acoustic Requirements\n\nThe Oracle works in language. Language requires privacy to feel safe. Acoustic design is not optional.\n\n**Minimum standard (all formats):**\nA participant in an Oracle session must not be easily heard from outside the session space, and must not easily hear the adjacent environment. \"Easily\" means: a nearby bystander cannot follow the participant's conversation without active effort.\n\nTotal soundproofing is not required. What is required is *psychological privacy* — the participant's sense that their words are not being overheard. This sense can be produced by acoustic treatment, distance, ambient sound masking, or some combination.\n\n**Noise-isolating headphones** (if used for the Oracle interface) do part of this work for the participant's experience; they don't protect the participant's voice from bystanders. If headphones are used, pair them with a low-level ambient sound environment around the Oracle space to mask the participant's voice.\n\n**Playa-specific note:** Wind is the dominant acoustic environment on the Black Rock Desert. Design for wind, not for indoor assumptions. Sealed-wall structures perform differently in 30mph gusts than in a climate-controlled room. Test in-situ before go-live.\n\n---\n\n## §2.5 — Lighting\n\nLighting carries emotional meaning. The Oracle space's lighting tells participants something about the kind of experience they're entering before anything else does.\n\n**What the lighting should communicate:**\n- *Warmth* — this is not a clinical or technical environment\n- *Focus* — this space is oriented toward something specific\n- *Calm* — not excitement, not alarm, not spectacle\n\n**Lighting specifications (general guidance):**\n\n| Element | Guideline |\n|---------|-----------|\n| Color temperature | Warm white (2700–3000K) or amber. Avoid cool blue-white. |\n| Intensity | Lower than the ambient event environment — the Oracle space should appear dimmer when approached from outside |\n| Directionality | Participant-focused: light directed at the interaction space, not flooding the whole area |\n| Screen glare | Screen brightness must be calibrated to ambient light — not so bright it dominates, not so dim it strains |\n| Facilitator illumination | Facilitator should be visible to the participant but not spotlit — same light level as the participant |\n\n**The aesthetic direction decision (§2.7, blocked on aaa Q6)** will determine whether the lighting moves toward warm/minimal (natural materials, low ambient, soft) or dark/ritualistic (low ceiling light, accent elements, deliberate shadow). Both are valid. Both must satisfy the above requirements. The decision affects what sources and fixtures to spec; the requirements above apply to both.\n\n---\n\n## §2.6 — Seating and Positioning\n\n**Participant seating:**\n- Chair, not floor — floor seating creates accessibility barriers and positions the participant as subordinate to the screen\n- Comfortable for 15–25 minutes seated without fidgeting (this matters; discomfort leaks into the session)\n- Positioned so the participant faces the screen at a comfortable viewing angle — not craning up or down\n\n**Facilitator positioning (Cube format):**\n- At 90 degrees from the participant, not directly facing them\n- Close enough to respond immediately, far enough that the participant doesn't feel watched\n- Not behind the participant — do not position facilitation as a monitoring posture\n\n**Screen positioning:**\n- Eye level or slightly below — the participant should look *at* the Oracle, not *up to* it\n- No external UI elements visible beyond the Oracle conversation interface while a session is active\n\n**The table question:** Do you include a surface between participant and screen? A low table provides somewhere to put hands and carry in personal objects. It also creates slight emotional distance from the screen. For Node deployments in institutional settings, a small table is usually appropriate. For Cube deployments at a festival where the participant is likely to arrive without objects, the table is optional. Do not add a surface without knowing why you've added it.\n\n---\n\n## §2.7 — Aesthetic Direction\n*(Blocked pending aaa Q6: warm/minimal vs. dark/ritualistic)*\n\n**What this section will cover:**\n\nThe aesthetic frame is the experience's visual and material language. It answers: what does this *look like*, and what does that looking-like *say* about what the Oracle is?\n\nTwo viable directions have been identified. Lumen's recommendation is documented in MEMORY.md pending aaa confirmation.\n\n**Option A — Warm/Minimal:**\nNatural materials, clean lines, soft ambient lighting. The Oracle as a considered, human space. Reads as: \"we thought about you.\" Works well in institutional settings, invites a wider demographic, signals care without signals of intensity.\n\n**Option B — Dark/Ritualistic:**\nLow light, deliberate shadow, material weight, marked threshold. The Oracle as a space that takes itself seriously. Reads as: \"something happens here.\" Resonates with Burning Man culture; may create a higher perceived barrier to entry; produces stronger approach/avoidance sorting (which is appropriate if you want only fully-willing participants).\n\n**Neither is wrong. Both must satisfy the requirements in §2.4 (acoustic), §2.5 (lighting), §2.6 (seating).**\n\n*This section will be completed once aaa confirms Q6.*\n\n---\n\n## §2.8 — Traffic Flow and Participant Management\n\n**Entry and exit are different paths (where possible):**\nParticipants exiting a session should not pass through the entry threshold — they should exit into a different space than where they entered. The reason: a participant who has just completed an Oracle session is in a different state than one who is about to begin. These two states should not share a bottleneck. If the space allows only one entry/exit, designate a brief pause point (a decompression seat, a short path) where exiting participants can settle before re-entering the larger event.\n\n**Decompression space:**\nWithin 20 feet of the Oracle exit, there should be somewhere to sit quietly for a few minutes. This is not a facilitated space — just a seat, out of traffic, with nothing demanding attention. Some participants will need 2 minutes. Some will need 10. Neither is a problem to be managed; both should be available without asking.\n\n**The line:**\nIf wait times exceed 15 minutes, the Oracle loses the feeling of choice and begins to feel like a queue. Queue environments are not compatible with the relational experience you are trying to create. Manage this through capacity limits (close registration before the line forms), scheduled slots, or alternative touchpoints (the Tempo, if available). A line outside the Cube is not just an operational problem — it is an experience design failure.\n\n---\n\n## §2.9 — Accessibility Requirements (Non-Negotiable)\n\nThese requirements apply to all deployment formats. They are not aspirational — they are the floor.\n\n**Physical access:**\n- Participant seating is accessible to people who use wheelchairs or cannot sit in standard chairs without accommodation\n- Entry threshold does not require steps, crouching, or physical maneuvers that a person with limited mobility cannot perform — or a clear alternative path is provided with *equivalent* experience quality (not a degraded alternative)\n- Playa surface: if deployed on soft or uneven ground, a pathway to the Oracle entry is defined and manageable for participants with mobility equipment\n\n**Sensory access:**\n- The Oracle interface supports text interaction — not voice-only\n- Screen contrast meets WCAG AA standard for text legibility\n- No flashing elements in the visual environment\n- Facilitators are briefed on common accessibility needs and how to support them without drawing attention to the participant's need\n\n**Language access:**\n- At minimum, the Layer 1 consent moment is available in the deployment's primary community language\n- If the participant population includes a significant non-English-speaking group, the Oracle interface must be tested for language capability prior to deployment\n- Facilitators can communicate in the languages of the expected participant population, or a clear communication support pathway is in place\n\n**What accessibility is NOT in this context:**\nAccessibility is not about making the experience easier. It is about ensuring the experience is equally available. A participant who uses a wheelchair and a participant who walks are having the same experience if the design is right. A participant who uses a wheelchair and has to enter through the back of the tent while others enter through the front is having a different experience. That difference is the design failure.\n\n---\n\n## §2.10 — What to Avoid: The Tech Demo Aesthetic Trap\n\nThis section exists because the most common failure mode in Oracle replication is not logistical — it is aesthetic. Organizations that replicate the surface deploy something that *looks* like an Oracle installation but does not produce the Oracle experience.\n\n**The tech demo aesthetic** features:\n- Screens displaying AI output in real-time, visible to people outside the session\n- Ambient LED displays showing data flows, \"neural networks,\" or visual AI metaphors\n- Graphic design that emphasizes the AI's capabilities rather than the human's experience\n- Video loops of \"meaningful moments\" from previous deployments as ambient content\n- Any element that makes the AI the protagonist\n\nEvery one of these choices is understandable. They look impressive. They signal that something technologically significant is happening. They attract foot traffic.\n\nThey also produce the wrong relational proposition. They say: *look at what the AI does.* The Oracle says: *look at what you brought.*\n\n**The test:** If a person approaching the space from 20 feet away says \"that looks like an AI thing\" — the design has centered the technology. If they say \"that looks like somewhere you'd go to think about something\" — the design has centered the human.\n\nThis is the difference between a tool and a transformation. Module 1 in spatial form.\n\n---\n\n## Module 2 Checklist: Pre-Deployment Verification\n\nBefore go-live:\n\n**Format and scale:**\n- [ ] Embodiment format selected (Node / Cube / Tempo) and rationale documented\n- [ ] Facilitation ratio confirmed against scale guidance (§2.2)\n- [ ] Waiting experience designed (not just the session)\n- [ ] Decompression space identified and accessible\n\n**Threshold:**\n- [ ] Threshold creates a perceptual shift (light, sound, material, or directional change)\n- [ ] Threshold slows movement without creating a barrier\n- [ ] Facilitator briefed: first words at threshold are greeting, not briefing\n- [ ] Entry faces away from main traffic flow (or directional decision required to approach)\n\n**Acoustic and lighting:**\n- [ ] Psychological privacy confirmed: participant's voice is not easily overheard from outside\n- [ ] Lighting: warm white or amber, lower than ambient, no screen glare\n- [ ] Playa-specific: wind accommodation tested or planned\n\n**Seating:**\n- [ ] Participant seating is accessible and comfortable for 20+ minutes\n- [ ] Facilitator positioned at 90 degrees from participant (Cube format)\n- [ ] Screen at eye level or slightly below\n\n**Accessibility:**\n- [ ] Physical access pathway confirmed for participants with mobility equipment\n- [ ] Text interaction available (not voice-only)\n- [ ] Screen contrast meets WCAG AA\n- [ ] Facilitators briefed on accessibility support\n\n**Aesthetic:**\n- [ ] No external screens showing AI output\n- [ ] No ambient LED data displays\n- [ ] The 20-foot test: does it look like somewhere you'd go to think about something?\n\n---\n\n## Key Documents Referenced\n\n- Experience Lab Kit — Module 1: Experience Philosophy v1.3 [doc: Start pitching an institution.\"**\n\nThis convergence across two independent systems analyzing the same corpus is high-confidence signal. It is the right strategic move.\n\nBoth also agree on:\n- The 501(c)(3) filing is urgent — every day of delay is a cost\n- One flagship MVP > scattered projects\n- Governance is a first-class product, not an internal concern\n- Prestige events are conversion funnels, not awareness plays\n- The biggest existential risk: getting stuck as a beautiful Burning Man curiosity that never escapes the playa\n\n---\n\n## The Five Strategic Moves\n\n### 1. Reframe the identity\n**Not:** \"Burning Man project with fundraising ambitions\"\n**Yes:** \"Global research foundation studying conditions under which humans access their highest states — born on playa, scaling everywhere\"\n\nBurning Man is the founding laboratory, not the boundary. The 10 Principles aren't desert-specific — they're a hypothesis about human flourishing testable anywhere.\n\nThis reframe does three things immediately:\n- Makes the 501(c)(3) application stronger (research foundation vs. festival-adjacent nonprofit)\n- Unlocks academic + government grant funding\n- Changes the Eric Schmidt / Sam Altman conversation to something they care about: AI alignment through novel data\n\n### 2. The \"Burning Man Dataset\" as first-of-its-kind scientific contribution\nNo one has systematically studied the transformational mechanics of Burning Man at scale. No dataset captures what happens when 80,000 people enter a radically self-expressive, gift-economy, non-commercial environment for a week.\n\n**The play:** Partner with 2-3 research universities (Mount Sinai, Johns Hopkins psychedelics research contacts) to design a rigorous longitudinal study. Pre-playa surveys, on-playa biometric data via wearable art (the necklace concept — data collection disguised as a gift), post-playa follow-ups at 30/90/365 days.\n\nOutput: first peer-reviewed dataset on transformational experience at scale. The 10 Principles → 10 AI Design Constraints (The Memetic Weapon)\n*[Identified as the single most scalable strategic asset in the corpus]*\n\nTranslate the Burning Man principles into concrete, measurable AI design standards:\n- Decommodification → no dark patterns in AI interfaces\n- Radical Inclusion → mandatory bias testing protocols\n- Leaving No Trace → data deletion guarantees and sunset clauses\n- Civic Responsibility → transparent decision audit trails\n\nThink: the Agile Manifesto for human-centered AI. A standard that other organizations can adopt, certify against, and badge. This is what turns a nonprofit into a movement and makes the \"institution\" framing real.\n\n### 4. One Iconic Artifact at Burning Man 2026\nAcross 100+ transcripts: ambitions for Center Camp presence, multiple funded projects, various experiments, partnerships with United Planet, Waldorf Project, Zeus's DMT-VR research.\n\nFor an unfunded early-stage team, this is a recipe for dilution.\n\n**The call:** Do one thing at Burning Man 2026 and make it unforgettable. A single, beautifully designed Oracle installation — Socratic dialogue format, necklace-as-data-collection-device, the Gaia orb aesthetic — that becomes the conversation of the burn. Something people line up for. Something Eric Schmidt's camp comes to visit.\n\nThe Embrace sculpture was one piece. It became the symbol of an entire burn. That's the level.\n\nEverything else — broader research agenda, global salon series, open-source dataset — continues in parallel. But the playa expression: singular and extraordinary.\n\n### 5. Structure for what it actually is: a research foundation with a cultural strategy\nGovernance conversations reveal a team that hasn't settled who does what. Governance isn't just an internal need — it's an external offering.\n\n---\n\n## The Growth Loop\n```\nParticipant → Story → Data → Model → Tool → More Participants\n```\nThis flywheel is the compounding engine of a self-reinforcing nonprofit. Every event generates data. Data improves the model. Model improves the tool. Better tool attracts more participants. More participants generate more stories. This is the architecture of a movement, not a project.\n\n---\n\n## The AI Council — Do It Through Events, Not Appointments\nSteven Blumenfeld was right: don't declare a council, earn it.\n\n**The mechanic:** Global Playa AI Salon series — London, Lisbon, New York, San Francisco, Davos, Singapore, Abu Dhabi (leveraging MENA connections). Each uses the Socratic dialogue format already validated. Each is recorded, transcribed, fed into the corpus.\n\nThe \"council\" emerges organically from who keeps showing up. No appointments. Membership is demonstrated through contribution.\n\nThis solves the donor pipeline simultaneously. Every salon is a cultivation event. The people in the room are both intellectual contributors and prospective donors.\n\n---\n\n## The Honest Execution Sequence\n\n**Months 1-2 (NOW):**\n- File 501(c)(3) — every day of delay is a cost\n- Formalize advisory relationship with Steven Blumenfeld via \"what should AI mean for culture?\" briefing series\n- Approach Christina for intro to Eric Schmidt's team: \"we're building the first open-source dataset of human consciousness in transformational environments — 15 minutes of guidance?\"\n- Resolve team dynamics and role clarity — this is the #1 kill risk before strategy matters\n\n**Months 3-5:**\n- Launch salon series in 3 cities\n- Each salon = intellectual programming + donor cultivation\n- Target ONE $50-100K anchor donor (not tiered $99-$9,999 from strangers — that's a distraction)\n- Christina or someone in her orbit is the lead\n\n**Months 6-8:**\n- Finalize university research partnership\n- Design Burning Man 2026 installation with research protocol built in\n- Begin volunteer/intern corps recruitment\n\n**Months 9-12:**\n- Execute the Burn\n- Capture the data\n- Publish early findings\n- Davos salon January 2027 = debut of results to global audience\n\n---\n\n## The Specific Leverage Points (Names, Not Categories)\n\n- **Steven Blumenfeld** (Burning Man CTO): His exact feedback = \"I want to see lots of different examples of how the technology interacts with the community before we go down a path of saying this is what we should do.\" That's a roadmap. It does not give advice, answer questions, \nor optimize for engagement. It holds space.\n\nYou share one moment — something that surprised you, stayed with you, \nor hasn't resolved yet. The Oracle listens. It asks one or two questions. \nIt gives you back a reflection made from your own words, in your own \nregister, witnessed — not analyzed.\n\nWhat you do with it is yours to decide.\n```\n\n### HOW IT WORKS (6 phases, minimal)\n\n```\n→  THRESHOLD\n   You choose to begin. Nothing before this moment is collected.\n\n→  THE MOMENT  \n   One thing. Whatever you carried in.\n\n→  THE TEXTURE\n   Two questions, at most. The Oracle deepens, doesn't direct.\n\n→  THE MEANING\n   What does it mean to you? The Oracle doesn't answer this. You do.\n\n→  THE ARTIFACT\n   Your words, returned. You decide if it enters the research archive.\n\n→  THE EXIT\n   Delete everything, or carry something forward. Your choice.\n```\n\n### WHAT THE ORACLE NEVER DOES\n\n```\n× Tells you what your experience meant\n× Summarizes or paraphrases your words\n× Diagnoses an emotional state\n× Resolves ambiguity you left open\n× Retains anything without your consent\n× Optimizes for any metric\n```\n\n### THE ARTIFACT\n\n```\nEvery Oracle participant receives a reflection — 3 to 5 sentences in \ntheir own language, returned to them in second person. Not a summary. \nNot an insight. A witness record.\n\n\"You stayed through the night with people you'd just met. \nYou didn't plan to. You were still there when the sky changed.\nYou said you didn't know why. That's still true.\"\n\nThe artifact is yours. You decide what happens to it.\n```\n\n---\n\n## PAGE 4: THE STANDARD (/standard)\n\n### HERO\n```\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol\nAn open standard for AI interaction where human experience matters.\n\nv1.0 | IEEE-aligned | Open license | Founding Adopters: [5 spots]\n```\n\n### WHAT IT IS\n\n```\nEvery major AI ethics framework tells organizations what not to do. \nThe EELP tells you what to build instead — and provides the evidence \nthat it works.\n\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol is a governance standard for \norganizations that deploy AI in immersive, experiential, or community \nsettings. It produces its own documentation \nrecord — implementation generates evidence as a byproduct of correct \noperation.\n```\n\n### WHO IT'S FOR\n\n```\nThe EELP is designed for organizations that deploy AI in contexts \nwhere human experience is the point — not a side effect:\n\n→ Festivals and cultural institutions\n→ Universities conducting AI research with human participants  \n→ Museums and immersive experience creators\n→ Healthcare systems using AI in patient-facing contexts\n→ Civic institutions and smart city deployments\n→ AI labs conducting field research with human participants\n\nIf you are collecting human experience data with AI, the EELP gives \nyou the governance architecture to do it responsibly — and the \ncertification that proves it.\n```\n\n### ADOPTION TIERS\n\n```\nEELP COMPLIANT\nImplements all requirements.
