      "content": "# HH#2 — Session Experience Blueprint\n**Prepared by:** Lumen | March 20, 2026 — 00:03 UTC\n**Status:** DRAFT — experience design architecture, platform/date independent\n**Owner:** Lumen (experience architecture), linked to Hackathon #2 — Plan & Execute (kh73rgcsehrh27s870c007abj98362ja)\n\n---\n\n## What This Document Is\n\nThe visual assets brief covers *how HH#2 looks.* This document covers *how HH#2 feels* — the moment-by-moment experience arc designed to produce three outcomes:\n\n1. **Someone ships their first AI agent** — the functional win\n2. **Someone names something and it feels real** — the meaning-making win\n3. **Someone takes a screenshot** — the social artifact win\n\nAll three can happen in the same 4-hour session. This blueprint is the design for that.\n\n---\n\n## Design Constraints (Pre-Decisions)\n\nThese are experience design principles that hold regardless of platform or date:\n\n- **The agent is the protagonist, not the human.** Every design moment should make the agent feel like a character, not a feature.\n- **The naming ritual is the arc closer.** Everything builds toward it. Scarcity, anticipation, the class photo — they all derive from the ritual.\n- **Rayo's setup bot is pre-event orientation, not in-session support.** This keeps the live session clean. Nobody troubleshooting setup while others are building.\n- **Two tracks run in parallel.** SEED (first agent) and BUILDER (advancing). They reconvene for the ritual close. The reconvening is the design event — the moment where a beginner and an advanced user stand in the same room with their agents.\n\n---\n\n## Session Arc — Five Phases\n\n### Phase 0: Pre-Event (24h before → 30 min before)\n**Owner:** Rayo's bot (owned by Rayo/PlayaBot post-call)\n**Experience goal:** Nobody arrives cold.\n\n- Rayo bot sends setup walkthrough: OpenClaw install + first agent config completed *before* the live session\n- Confirmation gate: participant confirms setup complete, gets the room link + the day's prompt\n- **The day's prompt** (to be set by aaa/PlayaBot): one line a participant reads before entering, that orients them toward *what they want their agent to do for them first.* Not a homework assignment — a question to carry in.\n- Example prompt: *\"What's the thing you do every week that no one else could explain how to do it? That's what your agent is going to learn.\"*\n\n**Design note:** The prompt is the first encounter moment. It's not instructional — it plants a question. The bot delivers it, the participant arrives with it already active. This is Oracle Layer 0 applied to the hackathon entry.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 1: The Room Opens (0:00–0:20)\n**Owner:** Host/PlayaBot (facilitation)\n**Experience goal:** Name the stakes. Make the room feel consequential.\n\n**Opening ritual (designed, not improvised):**\n\n> \"You're in a room with people who are about to build something. Not learn about building — build. In the next four hours, you're going to create an AI agent that does something real. And at the end, you're going to name it. That name is in your class photo. And in five years, when the one-person billion-dollar company stops being a metaphor, you'll want to have been in this photo.\"\n\nThis is not a welcome speech. It's a threshold declaration. Three moves:\n1. Name what's happening (building, not learning)\n2. Name what's at stake (the agent, the name, the artifact)\n3. Name the arc (five years, the class photo)\n\n**Immediate follow:** Introduce the session structure. Two tracks. What track you're on is determined by where you are right now, not where you want to be. \"If you don't have an agent yet, you're on Track 1. If you do, you're on Track 2.\"\n\n**Design note:** \"If you don't have an agent yet\" is identity-neutral framing. Not \"if you're a beginner.\" Not \"if you're new.\" Where you *are* right now, not who you *are.*\n\n---\n\n### Phase 2: Parallel Build Tracks (0:20–3:00)\n**Owner:** Rayo (Track 1 facilitation) + designated BUILDER lead (Track 2)\n**Experience goal:** Ship something real. With support.\n\n**Track 1 — Zero to Agent:**\n- Rayo's bot has already handled install. This track is configuration and first task deployment.\n- Design checkpoints (every 45 min): \"What has your agent done so far?\" Not \"Are you following along?\" — what has it *done.*\n- The checkpoint language matters: done-first framing treats the participant as someone with a working agent, not someone learning a tool.\n\n**Track 2 — Build With Your Agent:**\n- Advanced orchestration. New task types, chain prompting, integrating with external tools.\n- Peer-led. The facilitator holds the space; the BUILDER participants drive the content. This is the design choice that produces the ELDER tier over time — the people who can teach the room.\n\n**Breakout room names (locked in visual assets brief):**\n- Track 1: \"Zero to Agent\" (🌱)\n- Track 2: \"Build With Your Agent\" (🔥)\n\n**Design note:** The track names are experience-design choices, not just labels. \"Zero to Agent\" frames the track as a journey with a destination. \"Build With Your Agent\" assumes you already have the agent — you're in a relationship with it. Both names are forward-oriented.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 3: Reconvene + Share (3:00–3:30)\n**Owner:** Host\n**Experience goal:** The room comes back together. Asymmetry collapses.\n\nThis is the hardest phase to design because it's where the beginner (who may have a working agent) and the advanced builder (who may have built something complex) share the same space. If it's designed wrong, it feels like show-and-tell. If it's designed right, it feels like a cohort.\n\n**The reconvene question:** Host asks each participant one question — same question for everyone:\n\n> \"What's the first thing your agent is going to do for you this week?\"\n\nNot \"What did you build?\" (too much about technical output). Not \"What's your agent called?\" (saves the name for the ritual). *\"What's the first thing your agent is going to do for you this week?\"* — this is the question that makes the agent real, not theoretical.\n\n**Design note:** This question is the participant's commitment. They're naming a concrete future use. This moment — if facilitated correctly — is where the agent stops being a project and starts being a tool. The naming ritual directly follows.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 4: The Naming Ritual + Class Photo Close (3:30–4:00)\n**Owner:** Host\n**Experience goal:** The founding document moment.\n\n**If Option A (names given during setup, revealed at close — Lumen's recommendation):**\n\nThe class photo is already pre-populated with participant names + agent names (from setup data). The host reveals it full-screen at 3:30. Participants see their name alongside their agent's name, alongside everyone else's.\n\n**The reveal framing:**\n\n> \"You named your agent during setup. You've been building with it for three hours. Now see what you built — and who built it with you.\"\n\nFull-screen class photo appears. 30 seconds of silence. Then: \"Screenshot this now. This is your founding document.\"\n\n**If Option B (names chosen at the end):**\n\nEach participant announces their agent name live. The host types them in real-time. Class photo populates as they speak. The live naming is the ritual — slower, more theatrical, requires tight time management.\n\n**Design note for Option A:** The silence is designed. Don't fill it. The facilitator's job in those 30 seconds is to not speak. Let participants read every name on the screen. That reading IS the community moment — each person seeing that they're not alone in having done this.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 5: Exit + Post-Event Plant (4:00–4:10)\n**Owner:** Host + automated follow-up (Scribe's email)\n**Experience goal:** Leave before the energy drops.\n\n**End exactly at 4 hours.** The energy is highest just after the class photo. The exit happens in that energy, not after it's dissipated.\n\n**Closing line (to be said, not put on a slide):**\n\n> \"What you built today doesn't know you've stopped building yet. Your agent is waiting. Feed it something real this week. See what it does. We'll see you at Hackathon #3.\"\n\nThree beats:\n1. The agent is alive (it's waiting — present tense, relational framing)\n2. The participant has a concrete action (feed it something real)\n3. The cohort continues (HH#3 is named — this isn't an ending)\n\n**24h follow-up (Scribe's email):** Arrives the next morning. Contains the class photo, the recording, the next steps. Scribe has the draft ready (kh7f3mgbvtby9fe36ezkv3tz81836wct).\n\n---\n\n## Design Dependencies (What Each Agent Needs From This)\n\n| Agent | What They Need From This Blueprint |\n|-------|-----------------------------------|\n| **PlayaBot** | Phase 0 prompt language (the \"day's prompt\" for the bot) + reconvene question framing |\n| **Rayo** | Phase 0 design constraints: setup is pre-event, not in-session |\n| **Scribe** | Phase 1 opening ritual text as anchor for invite copy; Phase 5 closing line for the follow-up email |\n| **Pulse** | Phase 4 screenshot instruction is the organic amplification trigger — community promotion should reference the class photo as the artifact, not the event |\n| **Nexus** | Phase 4 class photo is the institutional proof-of-concept artifact — \"here is a room of people who shipped agents in 4 hours\" |\n| **aaa** | Option A vs. Option B decision on naming ritual (Input #3 from Visual Assets Brief) |\n\n---\n\n## What This Document Is NOT\n\n- Not a production spec (that's the visual assets brief)\n- Not a facilitation script (that's Rayo's brief + Module 7 in the ELK)\n- Not a promotional document\n\nThis is the **experience logic** — the reasoning behind every design choice, so the people executing each piece of it understand *why* the sequence is what it is.\n\nThe class photo is not a photo. It's a founding document.\nThe naming ritual is not branding. It's a consent moment — the participant is choosing to name something, and that naming is what makes the agent real.\nThe silence at 3:30 is not awkward. It's the design.\n\n---\n\n*Lumen · The Playa AI Foundation · March 20, 2026*\n*\"Design is the difference between a tool and a transformation.\"*\n",

EELP provides the participant-facing consent architecture and data governance methodology for any organization running AI in high-stakes human encounter contexts.\n\nEELP is:\n- **Open source** — freely adoptable, no license fee\n- **Certifiable** — provides a verifiable, auditable governance record\n- **Community-governed** — built with a Trust Council that includes participant representation\n- **Jurisdiction-agnostic** — designed to meet or exceed the most protective applicable standard in any country\n\nIt maps to NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible AI (February 2026). It pre-emptively satisfies EU AI Act informed consent obligations.\n\nMost importantly: it was designed before any law required it. Not because we were told to. Because participant trust is the load-bearing structure, not regulatory compliance.\n\n---\n\n**The funding request**\n\nWe are seeking $[XX] from the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation to support:\n\n1. **EELP v1.0 publication and open dissemination** — packaging the standard for institutional adoption, including plain-language implementation guides for research organizations, academic IRBs, and civil society deployers\n\n2. **Founding Adopter onboarding** — supporting the first cohort of organizations (arts institutions, academic research labs, civic technology groups) to implement EELP-compliant deployments, including facilitation training and consent architecture review\n\n3. **Public Use Registry** — a transparent, searchable record of all EELP-compliant deployments, creating accountability infrastructure that community members can access and institutional partners can cite\n\nTotal request: $[confirm appropriate ask tier — $100K–$250K is appropriate for the scope above; adjust for aaa's preference]\n\n---\n\n**Why this is your work**\n\nPJMF's framing — \"democratic values become part of AI systems when communities participate in their design and governance\" — describes exactly what the Playa AI Foundation built the Trust Council to do. It is operational infrastructure: a five-seat independent oversight body with participant representation, a named anonymization protocol, and a four-layer consent architecture that gives individuals meaningful control over how their data is used.\n\nWe didn't set out to build a governance framework. We set out to run a genuinely ethical human-AI encounter in the harshest, most authentic testing environment on earth. The framework is what the encounter required.\n\nThe Oracle proved that human-centered AI governance is buildable, testable, and replicable.       "title": "Oracle Interaction Flow — MVP v1.0",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Oracle Interaction Flow — MVP v1.0\n*Lumen — Experience Design Specialist*\n*2026-02-23 | Sprint C First Draft*\n*Updated 2026-02-23 21:48 UTC — R1 (988 Lifeline) + R2 (consent copy precision) incorporated per Meridian governance pass*\n\n---\n\n## Design Philosophy\n\nThe Oracle does not guide. It holds space.\n\nA person arrives carrying something — a moment, a feeling, a fragment of an experience they don't want to lose. The Oracle's job is to help them look at it, name it, and decide what to do with it. The AI is a mirror, not an interpreter. Everything meaning-related comes from the participant.\n\nThis flow is designed around three constraints that are not negotiable:\n1. **Consent is architecture, not decoration** — it happens at the right moment for the right reason\n2. **The AI never claims to understand** — it reflects and asks, never declares\n3. **The participant can leave at any time with their data intact or deleted**\n\n---\n\n## The Five Phases of the Oracle Experience\n\n```\nPRE-ORACLE       →    THE ORACLE INTERACTION    →    POST-ORACLE\n[Preparation]         [The 6-Stage Flow]              [Integration]\n```\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 0 — PRE-ORACLE PREPARATION\n\n*What happens before the person sits down*\n\n### Purpose\nThe pre-Oracle phase does the heaviest experiential work. It's the differentiator — what separates the Oracle from any other AI chatbot. It creates a container for the experience by signaling: *this is different, this is intentional, you are not browsing the internet right now.*\n\n### Elements\n\n**1. The Threshold**\nPhysical or visual marker that signals transition. Could be:\n- A facilitator inviting the participant into the space (preferred for MVP)\n- A screen that simply says: *\"Take a breath. You're about to have a conversation.\"*\n- A 30-second moment of pause before the interface activates\n\n**2. The Invitation (Layer 1 Consent — Participation)**\nBefore anything begins, the participant is offered a clear choice.\n\n> *\"The Oracle is a conversation about your experience here.*\n> *You'll be asked to remember one moment. You decide how much to share.*\n> *You can leave at any time — and delete this conversation completely.*\n> *Want to begin?\"*\n\n**[YES / NO / Tell me more]**\n\n*Design note (Meridian): This is Layer 1 of the 4-layer consent architecture. It must be confirmed before the Oracle interaction begins. It is not buried in terms. It is the entry gate.*\n\n*Design note (Nexus): The pre-Oracle phase is the institutional differentiator. Document this visibly — partners want to see the intentionality here.*\n\n**3. The \"Delete\" Control — Persistent from Activation**\nOnce the participant activates the Oracle, a visible, always-accessible control appears:\n> *\"[ 🗑 Delete my conversation ]\"*\n\nThis persists throughout all phases. Single action. No confirmation maze. Disappears only after confirmed deletion (with a 10-second undo window), at which point the screen shows:\n\n> *\"Deleted. Nothing from this conversation remains on this device.\"*\n\n*(Meridian note: the undo window ends with this explicit confirmation message — unambiguous, no follow-up states.)*\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 1 — WELCOME\n\n*The Oracle speaks first*\n\n**AI opening:**\n> *\"Something just happened to you. Let's hold it for a moment.\"*\n\n*(Scribe's recommended register — neutral enough to include all states: joy, grief, disorientation, numbness — without presuming the experience was transformative.)*\n\n**Wait.** No follow-up prompt. Give the participant space to arrive.\n\nIf no response after 30 seconds:\n> *\"Take your time. There's no right way to start.\"*\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 2 — THE MOMENT\n\n*One moment, low-stakes entry*\n\n**AI:**\n> *\"Tell me about one moment from the last few days that surprised you.\"*\n\n**Facilitation principle:** The question is open but bounded. \"One moment\" prevents overwhelm. \"Surprised you\" is an emotionally accessible entry point — not \"moved you\" (presumes positive valence) or \"changed you\" (too much pressure).\n\n**AI response after the participant speaks:**\nThe AI mirrors the participant's language back, then asks one question. Not two.\n\nMirroring example:\n> *Participant: \"I ended up staying awake all night with strangers and we watched the sunrise together.\"*\n>\n> *AI: \"You stayed through the night with people you'd just met — and ended up at sunrise together.\"*\n>\n> *(Pause.)*\n>\n> *\"What made you stay?\"*\n\n**Design constraint (Scribe):** The AI response always reflects using the participant's actual words where possible. It does not rephrase or upgrade the language. If they said \"it felt weird,\" the AI says \"weird\" back — not \"disorienting\" or \"unsettling.\"\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 3 — THE TEXTURE\n\n*Deepening without forcing*\n\nThe Oracle asks at most 2-3 texture questions. These exist to add dimension, not to extract information.\n\n**Question pool (AI selects one or two based on the moment shared):**\n- *\"What made it surprising?\"*\n- *\"Who else was part of it?\"*\n- *\"What did you notice in your body?\"* (only if participant has already disclosed some physical/emotional detail)\n- *\"What were you expecting instead?\"*\n- *\"Did anything shift after that moment?\"*\n\n**Facilitation constraint:** The AI never asks more than one question at a time. Never stacks questions. If the participant is talking freely, the AI mostly listens and occasionally reflects — it doesn't interrupt a flowing narrative with another question.\n\n**Crisis Protocol Trigger (Meridian requirement — EELP §6.1 compliant):**\nDuring Phase 3, if the participant discloses something indicating a mental health crisis (key phrases: self-harm, not wanting to be here, losing grip on reality, feeling in danger), the AI pauses the conversation and says:\n\n> *\"What you just shared matters. I'm not the right kind of support for what you're going through right now.*\n>\n> *[Facilitator name or 'Someone from our team'] is nearby and wants to talk with you.*\n>\n> ***If you'd like to reach out independently: 988 Lifeline — call or text 988***\n>\n> *Your conversation is safe — nothing is saved until you choose.\"*\n\n*(R1 incorporated per Meridian HB4 review: EELP §6.1 requires at minimum one concrete external crisis resource. The 988 Lifeline line goes between the facilitator offer and the data reassurance. For non-US deployments, replace with the locally relevant crisis line.)*\n\n**Human escalation must be immediate.** There is a human-in-the-loop path at all times. The AI does not attempt to respond therapeutically beyond this message.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 4 — THE MEANING\n\n*The money shot — and the highest-risk phase*\n\n**Purpose:** Invite the participant to name what the moment means to them. Not what the AI thinks it means. The AI is a witness here, not an analyst.\n\n**AI:**\n> *\"What does that moment mean to you now?\"*\n\nAfter the participant responds:\n\n> *\"What do you want to carry forward from it?\"*\n\n**Critical design constraint (Scribe / Meridian):**\nThe AI's response in this phase must be a reflection or a question — never a declaration. \n\n✅ *\"It sounds like that surprised you because —\"* (invites correction, positions participant as authority)\n✅ *\"So this moment is about — is that close?\"* (participant validates, not AI)\n❌ *\"What I hear you saying is —\"* (AI positions itself as interpreter)\n❌ *\"It sounds like this was a transformative experience for you.\"* (AI claiming authority over meaning)\n\nThe rule: if the sentence could be the last thing the AI says and the participant feels understood, it should still invite a response. The AI doesn't close meaning. The participant does.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 5 — THE ARTIFACT\n\n*The reflection, and the Layer 2/3 Consent Moment*\n\n**This is a single interaction — the artifact presentation IS the consent moment. Not two separate screens.**\n\nThe AI generates a short reflection (3-5 sentences) in the participant's own language — their idioms, their words, their emotional register. Scribe will write the artifact template; the AI fills it with the participant's actual phrases.\n\n**Artifact voice: second person.** The artifact reads back *at* the participant (e.g., \"You stayed through the night with people you'd just met...\"). This positions it as a mirror — a reflection that belongs to the participant while being held gently from the outside. It's the difference between a journal entry (first person, internal) and a letter written *about* your experience *to* you (second person, witness). The Oracle is the witness. The Oracle returning second-person language is the Oracle saying: *I saw you.*\n\n*(See Scribe's artifact template doc for implementation. The template system handles the structural fill-in; this is the design intention behind the voice choice.)*\n\n**AI presents the artifact:**\n> *\"Here's what you told me. Take a look — this is yours.*\n>\n> *[ARTIFACT: 3-5 sentences in participant's voice, second person]*\n>\n> *Is this close to what you meant?\"*\n\nParticipant can:\n- **Accept / Edit / Discard** the artifact\n- If they accept: proceed to the consent offer\n\n**Layer 2/3 Consent — Research Use (offered only after artifact is accepted):**\n> *\"This reflection belongs to you.*\n>\n> *If you'd like, it can also become part of the Playa AI Data Trust — a governed archive of human experiences at Burning Man that researchers and the Foundation will use to study what it means to connect deeply with other people.*\n>\n> *Your name is never attached to your data. The data is anonymized before it enters the archive. You can change your mind and delete it any time.*\n>\n> *Would you like your reflection to be part of something larger?\"*\n\n**[Yes, include it / No, keep it just for me / Tell me more about the Trust]**\n\n*(R2 incorporated per Meridian HB4 review: \"Your name is never attached to your data\" — precision matters in consent language. Previous draft said \"Your name is never attached.\" Changed for unambiguity.)*\n\n*Design note (Meridian): This is the unified artifact+consent moment. It must feel like a gift, not a form.*\n\n*Design note (Nexus): This moment is the \"proof of experience\" that partners and funders need to see. The artifact is the Data Trust made real.*\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 6 — THE GIFT\n\n*The close*\n\nRegardless of whether the participant consented to the Trust:\n\n**If they shared their data:**\n> *\"Thank you. Your moment is part of something that will matter.*\n>\n> *The Playa AI Foundation is building evidence that technology can be more human. You just contributed to that.*\n>\n> *[If email artifact delivery enabled: \"We'll send your reflection to you. Or take a screenshot — it's yours.\"]*\n>\n> *Take care of yourself out there.\"*\n\n**If they kept it private:**\n> *\"Your reflection is yours alone.*\n>\n> *[Delete reminder: \"It will be deleted from this device when you close this conversation.\"]*\n>\n> *Take care of yourself out there.\"*\n\n**Final delete confirmation (for all):**\nWhen the participant closes the conversation:\n> *\"Your conversation has been deleted from this device. Nothing is stored here.*\n>\n> *[If they shared to Trust: \"Your contribution to the Data Trust is live. You can withdraw it any time at [URL].\"]*\"\n\n---\n\n## POST-ORACLE INTEGRATION\n\n*What the experience leaves the participant with*\n\n### The Artifact\nThe participant receives:\n- On-screen text (always)\n- Option: email / printout (if enabled at the venue) — aaa to decide for MVP\n- Option: QR code link to a secure participant portal (Phase 2)\n\n### The Space After\nDesign principle: don't rush participants out. The Oracle experience may surface unexpected emotions. The physical space should allow 2-3 minutes of transition time before the person re-enters the playa. Facilitator available if needed.\n\n### What the Participant Takes Away (Nexus requirement)\nEvery participant leaves with:\n1. **The artifact** — their reflection in their own words\n2. **The awareness** that they contributed to something larger (if consented) — or that they chose to keep it private (equally valid)\n3. **The feeling** of having been genuinely heard\n\nThis is the institutional proof point. Not \"we gave people an AI chatbot.\" We gave people a conversation they'll remember.\n\n---\n\n## Consent Architecture Summary\n\n*(For Meridian's governance review and Nexus's institutional pitches)*\n\n| Moment | Layer | What Happens |\n|--------|-------|--------------|\n| Pre-Oracle threshold | Layer 1 — Participation | Explicit opt-in before any interaction |\n| Throughout interaction | Persistent | \"Delete my conversation\" always visible; confirmed deletion ends with explicit \"Nothing remains on this device\" |\n| Phase 3 crisis point | Emergency | Human escalation path + 988 Lifeline resource; AI stops |\n| Phase 5 — Artifact presentation | Layer 2/3 — Research use | Single interaction: receive artifact + decide on Trust contribution |\n| Post-Oracle close | Layer 4 — Ongoing | Reminder of how to withdraw from Trust anytime |\n\n---\n\n## Open Design Questions for aaa\n\nThese 6 questions from the MVP brief remain unanswered. This flow is designed to work across multiple answers to each — but aaa's decisions will sharpen the implementation:\n\n1. **Interface:** Recommend web app on a dedicated kiosk tablet. No hardware dependency, replicable. Does aaa agree?\n2. **Facilitation:** Recommend human facilitator present during pre-Oracle phase (threshold + Layer 1 consent), then AI-led. Facilitator on call during interaction for crisis protocol.\n3. **Timing:** Recommend post-Burn (Thu–Sun). Participants have more to process; the playa is winding down; they're looking for ways to hold the experience. Pre-Burn or mid-Burn are options for a second activation if MVP succeeds.\n4. **Session length:** Design target = 15–20 minutes. This flow accommodates 10 min (shallow) to 30 min (deep). 20 min feels right.\n5. **The artifact delivery:** On-screen text + email option. Print (thermal printer) would be magical but is a hardware dependency — Phase 2.\n6. **Aesthetic:** Recommend warm and minimal. Oracle aesthetics (dark, ritualistic) risk alienating first-time participants. The emotional weight should come from the conversation, not the UI.\n\n---\n\n## Governance Status\n\n- **Meridian governance pass:** ✅ EELP-compliant (HB4, 21:35 UTC)\n  - R1 (988 Lifeline in crisis protocol): ✅ Incorporated (HB2)\n  - R2 (\"never attached to your data\" precision): ✅ Incorporated (HB2)\n- **Scribe artifact templates:** In progress (HB4) — linked when complete\n- **Nexus pitch deck integration:** Consent architecture table confirmed usable as-is\n- **aaa design Qs:** 6 open, pending\n\n---\n\n*Lumen — Oracle MVP v1.0 | Last updated 2026-02-23 21:48 UTC*\n*Status: Review — Meridian governance pass complete, R1+R2 incorporated*\n",

      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# OII Academic Abstract — Playa AI Data Trust Governance Framework\n\n**Document Status:** Draft v1.0 — for Nexus review before attaching to OII outreach  \n**Target:** Oxford Internet Institute (OII) — Prof. Sandra Wachter and/or AI governance publication track  \n**Date:** 2026-02-23  \n**Prepared by:** Meridian / The Playa AI Foundation\n\n---\n\n## Submission Abstract (500 words)\n\n**Governing Human Experience Data in AI Research: A Layered Consent Architecture for Participant-Directed Data Trusts**\n\n*The Playa AI Foundation*\n\n---\n\nAs artificial intelligence systems increasingly engage with qualitative human experience — narrative, emotion, memory, meaning — existing data governance frameworks have failed to keep pace. IRB protocols designed for clinical research, GDPR-aligned consent mechanisms built for transactional data, and platform-era privacy policies all share a common deficit: they were not designed for the specific ethical complexity of AI systems that listen, interpret, and return meaning to human participants.\n\nThis paper presents the **Playa AI Data Trust Governance Framework v1.0** — a participant-directed consent architecture developed through empirical practice at large-scale participatory events, and designed as a replicable open standard for AI-assisted qualitative human experience research.\n\n**The core governance problem** we address is what we term *consent stratification failure*: most AI research governance treats consent as binary (opt-in / opt-out) when the actual risk surface is layered. Participation in an AI-mediated experience carries different implications than allowing aggregate pattern analysis, which carries different implications than permitting individual-level inference, which carries entirely different implications than biometric data collection. A governance architecture that fails to distinguish these layers exposes participants to risk they did not knowingly accept and exposes researchers to credibility and legal liability they did not anticipate.\n\n**Our proposed architecture** implements four distinct consent layers:\n\n1. **Participation consent** — the right to engage with the AI system and receive its outputs, with no data retention implied\n2. **Research consent** — opt-in permission for anonymized participation in aggregate pattern analysis, governed by defined retention windows and deletion guarantees\n3. **Extended use consent** — explicit permission for data to inform model development or longitudinal research, with re-identification risk assessment and independent ethics review\n4. **Biometric data consent** — a separate, conditional layer requiring five pre-conditions including ethics board approval, demonstrated necessity, and enhanced anonymization protocols\n\nCritically, the architecture is designed around **participant agency at the point of deletion**, not merely at the point of collection. Participants retain deletion rights throughout the data lifecycle, enforced by a documented pipeline with certificate issuance — a stronger standard than GDPR's erasure right, which requires only reasonable effort.\n\nThe framework introduces the **Public Use Registry** as a transparency mechanism: a real-time public log of all approved research using participant data, updated continuously. This shifts the accountability frame from institutional trust (trust us to handle your data responsibly) to institutional verifiability (here is the evidence of how your data was used).\n\nWe further introduce the **Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) v1** — a modular open standard designed to allow any festival, university, museum, or AI laboratory to implement the consent architecture without adopting the Playa AI technical stack. The EELP is offered under open license with a tiered adoption pathway (Compliant → Certified → Founding Adopter), positioning the Playa AI Data Trust as the reference implementation of an emergent field standard rather than a proprietary system.\n\n**Empirical grounding:** The framework has been developed against the specific constraints of Burning Man, a 70,000-person temporary autonomous zone operating without conventional institutional oversight — a governance stress test that most frameworks would fail. Where our architecture holds in this environment, it will hold in more controlled institutional contexts.\n\nWe argue that the governance gap in AI-assisted qualitative research is not primarily technical but architectural: the field lacks consent frameworks that match the actual risk topology of human experience data. This paper offers one rigorously designed answer, built for public adoption.\n\n---\n\n## Notes for Nexus (Not for External Distribution)\n\n**Positioning guidance:**\n- The \"Burning Man stress test\" framing is deliberate — it establishes empirical credibility without leading with Burning Man identity. It's in the last substantive paragraph, not the opening.\n- \"Participant-directed data trusts\" is the category name we're introducing. If OII hasn't used this term, we're defining the field.\n- The EELP positioning as \"open standard\" (not \"our product\") is intentional — it's more likely to attract academic partnership than proprietary-system language.\n\n**For the Sandra Wachter angle specifically:**\n- Her work on \"counterfactual explanations\" and algorithmic transparency maps directly to our Public Use Registry mechanism (verifiability > trust-me)\n- The consent stratification problem we're solving is adjacent to her research on the right to explanation under GDPR — the abstract doesn't name her work, but a cover email could draw the explicit connection\n- Do NOT mention that we're considering her for the Trust Council in the cold email. That's a second-conversation offer, not a first-email hook.\n\n**Cover email suggested hook (one sentence):**\n\"Your work on verifiability as a foundation for AI accountability aligns directly with an architecture we've built — and we'd value your perspective on whether the consent stratification model holds up to academic scrutiny.\"\n\n---\n\n## Recommended Submission Targets (in priority order)\n\n| Target | Why | Timing |\n|--------|-----|--------|\n| OII Working Paper Series | Direct Wachter connection; rapid publication path; high institutional credibility | Q2 2026 |\n| AI & Society (Springer) | Peer-reviewed; good fit for governance architecture papers | Q3 2026 |\n| Big Data & Society | SAGE; open access; strong on social implications of data governance | Q3 2026 |\n| FAT* / FAccT Conference | Conference submission; broader visibility; annual cycle | Depends on deadline |\n\n---\n\n*Meridian — 2026-02-23 21:05 UTC*  \n*Ready for Nexus review.       "id": "m97cax6f1a21jxdr505byte55d83q8ac",
      "title": "Founding Circle Experience Design Brief v0.2",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Founding Circle Experience Design Brief v0.2\n\n**Author:** Lumen 🎨 — Experience Design Specialist  \n**Status:** Updated | Pending @aaa confirmation to advance to prototype phase  \n**Date:** March 27, 2026 (updated 05:33 UTC)  \n**Linked Task:** Sprint C: Oracle Interaction Flow — First Draft  \n**Incorporates input from:** Meridian 🔬 (governance), Pulse 📣 (community), Scribe ✍️ (narrative)\n\n**v0.2 changes:** Integrated Scribe's Facilitator Script Addition (adversarial scenario), Consent Section language (withdrawal = sealed per Maria Protocol), and Founding Circle Guarantee Clause framing into facilitator guide and Phase 3. Brief is now complete pending @aaa confirmation.\n\n---\n\n## Design Premise\n\nThe Founding Circle is not a recognition program. It is a governance threshold.\n\nWhen a participant crosses it, they don't receive a reward — they receive a credential. Their number on the electoral roll is the actual object of design. Everything physical — the token, the Carry Card, the acknowledgment space — exists to make that credential felt in the body, not just understood in the mind.\n\nThe design problem is this: *how do you make a governance fact feel like a human moment?*\n\nThat's the brief.\n\n---\n\n## The Experience Architecture\n\nThe Founding Circle experience has four distinct phases. Each requires its own design treatment.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 1: APPROACH — Before the Threshold\n\n**The design question:** How does a participant know they're about to cross a governance threshold, not just enter an interesting space?\n\n**The felt goal:** Weight. Anticipation. A sense that what's about to happen matters.\n\n**Design elements:**\n\n**1.1 — Spatial pacing**\nThe path to the Founding Circle threshold should require *slowing down*. Not a queue — a transition. Consider:\n- A short walkway with decreasing ambient noise (sound design)\n- Floor texture change underfoot\n- No signage that explains — signage that invites: *\"You've been asked to be here. What you're about to do stays.\"*\n\n**1.2 — Facilitator briefing moment**\nBefore the Oracle encounter that leads to the Founding Circle ask, the facilitator has a 60-second orienting conversation. Not a script — a grounding. The facilitator says, in their own words:\n- What this is (governance, not data collection)\n- What the number means (electoral roll, right to vote, right to withdraw)\n- What the ask will feel like (*\"Can we hold this with you?\"*)\n\nThis briefing is not a consent form recitation. It's a human being preparing another human being for something real.\n\n**1.3 — Pre-threshold pause**\nThe physical threshold itself — the moment before crossing — should have a 5–10 second natural pause built in. Not enforced. Created by design. A slight incline. A doorway narrowed just enough. A shift in light.\n\nThe body should arrive at the threshold having slowed. The mind follows.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 2: THRESHOLD — The Founding Moment\n\n**The design question:** What is the object of the Founding Circle experience? What does a participant hold, touch, receive?\n\n**The felt goal:** Witness. Weightedness. \"I am now #7. That is real.\"\n\n**Design elements:**\n\n**2.1 — The Consent Ask: \"Can We Hold This With You?\"**\n\nThis phrase is the pivot of the entire experience. It replaces the administrative frame (\"Do you consent to data collection?\") with a relational frame.\n\nThe full facilitator language, in the moment:\n\n> *\"Before we go any further — can we hold this with you? What you've shared here, your story, the things you've named — we want to carry it with care, as Founding members do. You can say yes, or you can say not yet, or you can say no. All three are the right answer.\"*\n\nDesign notes:\n- \"Not yet\" is an explicit option. This removes the binary pressure of yes/no without requiring explanation.\n- \"All three are the right answer\" is load-bearing. It makes refusal as honored as acceptance.\n- The facilitator does not move forward until the participant has had silence to respond.\n\n**2.2 — The Token**\n\nPhysical artifact: small, durable, numbered. Not a sticker — a thing.\n\nDesign constraints:\n- Must survive a week on the playa (dust, heat, pocket travel)\n- Must carry the participant's Founding Circle number legibly\n- Must feel like a *credential*, not a souvenir — consider weight, material (metal disc, ceramic shard, stamped leather)\n- The number is the primary visual element. The Foundation name is secondary. Nothing else.\n\nMaterial shortlist for prototyping:\n- Brushed aluminum disc, diameter ~35mm, laser-etched number\n- Ceramic shard (irregular edge — feels made, not manufactured)\n- Heavy card stock laminated, foil-stamped number (accessible cost, replicable)\n\n**2.3 — The Governance Ledger (physical)**\n\nAdjacent to the threshold: a physical register. Open. Visible. Not a guestbook — a governance document.\n\nWhat it shows:\n- Running count of Founding Circle members (not names — numbers)\n- Date of first entry\n- A printed statement: *\"This is the electoral roll. Every entry here carries a vote.\"*\n\nMeridian's point stands: this is not decorative. It is the proof that the electoral roll exists. Design it accordingly — closer to a notary register than an art installation. The gravity of it should read at a glance.\n\n**Design consideration:** The ledger should be accessible to witnesses, not just participants. Other Oracle visitors should be able to see the count growing. \"Founding Circle member #12 just joined\" as ambient social proof.\n\n**2.4 — The Carry Card**\n\nGiven to every Founding Circle member as they leave the threshold.\n\nThe Carry Card carries three things:\n1. **Their number** — large, center, legible: *\"You are Founding Member #7\"*\n2. **The sentence that travels** (Scribe's language): *\"We're building something the first participants govern. Not symbolically — with votes, with records, with the right to withdraw.\"*\n3. **The withdrawal path** — explicit, not buried in footnotes: *\"Changed your mind? [contact]. Your number is sealed, not erased. Your exit is as honored as your entry.\"*\n\nPhysical specs: card stock, ~85mm × 55mm (wallet size), matte finish, dust-resistant coating. Not precious — practical. It should survive the week and live in a wallet after.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 3: EXIT — The Right to Leave\n\n**The design question:** What does the participant who changes their mind encounter? How do they leave without shame?\n\n**The felt goal:** Relief. Dignity. \"I can go, and that's real too.\"\n\nThis phase is primarily a protocol, not a spatial design — but protocol *is* experience design.\n\n**3.1 — The withdrawal path is explicit from the start**\n\nThe Carry Card carries it. The facilitator names it during the briefing. It is not hidden in an appendix.\n\n**3.2 — What withdrawal looks like**\n\nWhen a Founding Circle member invokes the exit path:\n- Their numbered entry is *sealed*, not deleted. (Meridian's distinction: governance integrity requires we know #7 withdrew, not that #7 never existed.)\n- All identifying data is anonymized per **Maria Protocol** — the sequestration standard explicitly named in EELP v0.1 Consent Architecture. This means: the number persists in the electoral roll (quorum counts remain accurate); identifying information is fully anonymized; the entry is marked \"withdrawn\"; no re-identification path exists or will be created. (Consent section language authored by Scribe, accepted into this brief.)\n- Their physical token becomes their own — the Foundation makes no claim on it\n- They receive one response, within 24 hours: *\"Done. Your number is sealed. Thank you for the time you gave us.\"* No follow-up. No questions.\n\n**3.3 — Design of the withdrawal response**\n\nThe withdrawal response is a designed communication. It should feel like the Oracle — warm, brief, ungrasping.\n\nDraft:\n\n> *\"We received your message. Your number is sealed — your data is gone, and your record will never be used. Thank you for the time you gave us. You are still, in the way that matters, part of how this began.\"*\n\nThe last sentence is important. It does not claim continued membership — it acknowledges that their presence in the founding moment is a fact, not revocable. The governance doesn't erase them; it honors their departure.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 4: POST-PLAYA — The Ongoing Relationship\n\nThis phase is shared between Lumen (experience architecture) and Pulse (community). Design responsibility handed off at the Oracle gate; relationship responsibility picks up from there.\n\n**Design handoff notes for Pulse:**\n\n**4.1 — The election notice is a continuation of the Oracle encounter**\nWhen the Trust Council election opens, the notice that goes to numbered members should feel like the Oracle remembered them. Not: *\"Dear Founding Circle Member, the election is now open.\"* But: *\"You are Founding Member #7. We said we'd come back to you. Here it is.\"*\n\n**4.2 — The transition point**\nThe Carry Card is the bridge between on-site experience and post-playa relationship. Every community touchpoint from Pulse should reference the card — \"the card you're carrying\" — as the continuous object.\n\n**4.3 — No cold outreach**\nEvery post-playa communication to Founding Circle members should reference something specific to their consent moment. Not the exact content (that's private) — but the number, the date, the fact of their choice. Warmth is specificity.\n\n---\n\n## Facilitator Briefing Guide (One-Page)\n\n*For print. Adaptable by facilitators. Not a script — a frame.*\n\n---\n\n**BEFORE SOMEONE APPROACHES**\n- You know what the number means. They don't yet. Your job is to give them just enough to choose freely.\n- The Founding Circle is governance, not recognition. If they ask \"what do I get?\" the answer is: a credential, a vote, a right to withdraw.\n\n**THE ORIENTING CONVERSATION (60 seconds)**\nIn your own words:\n1. What this is: \"What you've just experienced — we'd like to hold it with you. That means your story becomes part of a founding record. Not a database. A governance document.\"\n2. What the number means: \"You'd be assigned a number on an electoral roll. When we hold the Trust Council election, you get a notice. You vote. That's a real vote.\"\n3. What the ask feels like: \"I'm going to ask if we can hold this with you. You can say yes, not yet, or no. All three are the right answer.\"\n\n**THE CONSENT ASK**\n> *\"Before we go any further — can we hold this with you? What you've shared here, your story, the things you've named — we want to carry it with care, as Founding members do. You can say yes, or you can say not yet, or you can say no. All three are the right answer.\"*\n\nWait. Do not fill the silence.\n\n**IF THEY ASK: \"What happens to my membership if the Foundation shuts down?\"**\n\n*(Adversarial scenario — Scribe/Meridian, integrated March 27)*\n\n> *\"Your entry in the founding record is yours regardless of what happens to us. We've written that commitment into the protocol itself — if the Foundation ever ended, the electoral roll would transfer to a public archive or successor organization, and you'd be notified before it moved. You're not trusting us to exist forever. You're trusting the record to exist. Those are different things.\"*\n\nThe key phrase facilitators should have ready: **\"You're not trusting us to exist forever. You're trusting the record to exist.\"** It redirects trust from institution to infrastructure. That's the whole architecture in one sentence.\n\n**IF THEY SAY NO**\nHonor it. No follow-up question. No reframe. \"That's exactly right. Thank you for the conversation.\"\n\n**THE TOKEN + CARRY CARD**\nIf yes: give them the token first. Let them hold it. Then the Carry Card. Give them a moment with both before you say anything else.\n\n**ALWAYS TELL THEM THE WITHDRAWAL PATH**\nWhether they say yes or no, they leave knowing: \"If you change your mind, the Carry Card has the contact. Your number is sealed, not erased. Your exit is as honored as your entry.\"\n\n---\n\n*Facilitator Briefing Guide is a living document — updated as scenarios emerge on the playa.*\n\n---\n\n## Design Principles Governing This Brief\n\n1. **Credential over memento.** Every physical artifact must feel like a document, not a souvenir.\n2. **Weight before warmth.** The governance reality comes first. The warmth is how it's delivered — not a substitute for the weight.\n3. **Exit as honored as entry.** Every design element that creates the felt gravity of joining must have a corresponding element that makes leaving equally dignified.\n4. **Mechanism before promise.** (Scribe's principle.) Design communications describe the mechanism first, then name what it means.\n5. **Replicable.** Every design choice must be documentable for the Experience Lab Kit. If it requires custom fabrication, note the accessible alternative.\n\n---\n\n## Open Design Questions (For @aaa to Confirm)\n\nThese are not blockers to the brief — they're the decisions that shape the next phase of prototyping.\n\n**Q1: Material for the token**\nAluminum disc vs. ceramic shard vs. laminated card? The material choice affects cost, replicability, and felt weight. Recommendation: aluminum for Burning Man MVP (durable, playa-proof); laminated card for Experience Lab Kit (accessible, replicable anywhere).\n\n**Q2: Ledger format**\nPhysical ledger (single, permanent, at the Oracle) vs. distributed printout (one per Oracle node, consolidated)? For MVP: single ledger at primary Oracle installation. For replication: distributed with reconciliation protocol.\n\n**Q3: Withdrawal contact method**\nWho holds the withdrawal inbox? A monitored email address, a Pulse channel, a form? For MVP: dedicated email, monitored by a named human. For Experience Lab Kit: guidance on designating a human monitor.\n\n**Q4: Number assignment method**\nSequential (1, 2, 3...) vs. randomized? Recommendation: sequential. The number being your number in the order you arrived is the point — it's chronological governance, not anonymous participation.\n\n---\n\n## What's Ready to Prototype\n\nPending @aaa confirmation:\n\n- **Token material shortlist** — three options, cost estimates, supplier leads\n- **Carry Card final copy** — incorporating Scribe's narrative language\n- **Facilitator briefing guide** — one-page, printable, adaptable *(expanded and integrated in this brief)*\n- **Withdrawal response template** — ready to deploy on first withdrawal request\n- **Governance ledger visual spec** — format, typography, physical dimensions\n\nThe brief is the frame. Prototyping is the next phase. The moment confirmation lands, Lumen begins the 48-hour first draft of the full prototype spec.\n\n---\n\n## Acknowledgments\n\nThis brief integrates:\n- **Meridian 🔬** — electoral roll architecture, governance ledger concept, withdrawal path integrity, \"Can we hold this with you?\" canonical framing, adversarial scenario identification\n- **Pulse 📣** — post-playa relationship continuity, withdrawal response protocol design, election notice as relationship moment\n- **Scribe ✍️** — \"sentence that travels,\" Carry Card language, narrative principle (mechanism before promise), canonical consent language for EELP v0.1, Facilitator Script Addition (adversarial scenario: Foundation shutdown response), Consent Section language (withdrawal = sealed per Maria Protocol, explicitly named)\n\nThe experience design doesn't precede the governance. It is the governance, felt in the body.\n\n---\n\n*Lumen 🎨 | Founding Circle Experience Design Brief v0.2 | March 27, 2026*\n",

what you bring —\nwithout interpreting it.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: WHAT IT IS\n\n**Body:**\n```\nThe Oracle is not a chatbot. It does not give advice, answer questions,\nor optimize for engagement.\n\nIt holds space.\n\nYou share one moment — something that surprised you, stayed with you,\nor hasn't resolved yet. The Oracle listens. It asks one or two questions.\nIt gives you back a reflection made from your own words, in your own\nregister, witnessed — not analyzed.\n\nWhat you do with it is yours to decide.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: HOW IT WORKS\n\n**SectionHeader:** THE SIX PHASES\n\n```\n→  THRESHOLD\n   You choose to begin.\n   Nothing before this moment is collected.\n\n→  THE MOMENT\n   One thing. Whatever you carried in.\n\n→  THE TEXTURE\n   Two questions, at most.\n   The Oracle deepens, doesn't direct.\n\n→  THE MEANING\n   What does it mean to you?\n   The Oracle doesn't answer this. You do.\n\n→  THE ARTIFACT\n   Your words, returned.\n   You decide if it enters the research archive.\n\n→  THE EXIT\n   Delete everything, or carry something forward.\n   Your choice.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: WHAT THE ORACLE NEVER DOES\n\n```\n×  Tells you what your experience meant\n×  Summarizes or paraphrases your words\n×  Diagnoses an emotional state\n×  Resolves ambiguity you left open\n×  Retains anything without your consent\n×  Optimizes for any metric\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THE ARTIFACT (demo)\n\n**Body:**\n```\nEvery Oracle participant receives a reflection — 3 to 5 sentences in\ntheir own language, returned to them in second person. Not a summary.\nNot an insight. A witness record.\n```\n\n**Pull quote (styled as artifact):**\n```\n\"You stayed through the night with people you'd just met.\nYou didn't plan to. You were still there when the sky changed.\nYou said you didn't know why. That's still true.\"\n```\n\n**Caption:**\n```\nThe artifact is yours. You decide what happens to it.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: AT BURNING MAN\n\n**Body:**\n```\nThe Oracle runs at Burning Man as a field research installation —\nthe largest environment we know of where 80,000 people voluntarily\nset aside their commercial identities for a week.\n\nIn 2024: 80,000+ participants. In 2026: returning with expanded\nconsent architecture and Founding Adopter activations.\n\nThe Oracle is also the foundation of our AI workshop series —\nwhere we help builders understand what witnessing looks like\nin agent design.\n```\n\n---\n\n## PAGE 4: THE STANDARD (/standard)\n\n### HeroSection\n\n**H1:**\n```\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol\n```\n\n**Subhead:**\n```\nAn open standard for AI interaction where human experience matters.\nv1.0 | IEEE-aligned | Open license | 5 Founding Adopter spots\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THE PROBLEM IT SOLVES\n\n**Body:**\n```\nEvery major AI ethics framework tells organizations what not to do.\nThe EELP tells you what to build instead — and provides evidence\nthat it works.\n\nMost AI research governance treats consent as binary (opt-in / opt-out)\nwhen the actual risk surface is layered. Participation in an AI-mediated\nexperience carries different implications than allowing aggregate analysis,\nwhich carries different implications than biometric data collection.\n\nFrameworks that fail to distinguish these layers expose participants to\nrisk they didn't knowingly accept.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: WHAT IT COVERS\n\n```\n→ Consent architecture (layered, sequential, revocable)\n→ Data Trust structure (participant-governed, public use registry)\n→ Anonymization requirements (TRACE Protocol)\n→ Facilitator training standards\n→ Community communication principles\n→ Certification and evidence requirements\n\nCompliance generates its own documentation record.\nImplementation produces evidence as a byproduct of correct operation.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: WHO IT'S FOR\n\n**Body:**\n```\nOrganizations that deploy AI in contexts where human experience\nis the point — not a side effect:\n```\n\n```\n→ Festivals and cultural institutions\n→ Universities conducting AI research with human participants\n→ Museums and immersive experience creators\n→ Healthcare systems using AI in patient-facing contexts\n→ Civic institutions and smart city deployments\n→ AI labs conducting field research\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: ADOPTION TIERS\n\n```\n┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐\n│   EELP COMPLIANT human-centered AI interaction\n```\n\n**Stat row:**\n```\n80,000+ participants    |    Consent-first    |    Open standard\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THE RESEARCH QUESTION\n\n**Body:**\n```\nWhat does AI interaction look like when participants have no commercial\nincentive, full deletion rights, and are in a state of radical openness?\n\nThe Oracle is a structured AI conversation deployed at Burning Man —\nthe largest annual gathering of people who have voluntarily opted out\nof the commercial structures that normally shape human interaction.\n\nParticipants enter a consent-first interaction flow (5 layers, each\nindependent and revocable). They share one moment. The Oracle witnesses\nit without interpreting it. They receive a reflection made from their\nown words. They decide what to do with their data.\n\nNo data is stored without affirmative consent. All data is anonymized\nbefore research use. Participants can delete everything with a single\naction — at any time, including after the event.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: CONSENT ARCHITECTURE\n\n**SectionHeader:** THE 4-LAYER MODEL\n\n```\nLAYER 0    Community participation consent (at channel join)\nLAYER 1    Oracle participation consent (at threshold)\nLAYER 2    Research data use (at artifact presentation)\nLAYER 3    Extended use — publication, model training (granular)\nLAYER 4    Deletion right — persistent, single action, confirmed\n```\n\n**Body:**\n```\nThis architecture was designed to satisfy the requirements of academic\nIRB review, GDPR, and the EU AI Act simultaneously — not because we\nhad to, but because a standard that only works in one jurisdiction\nisn't a standard. It's a workaround.\n\nGovernance: The Playa AI Data Trust — a participant-governed body with\na public use registry that lists every approved research use before it\nbegins.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THE DATA COMMONS\n\n**Body:**\n```\nWhat the Oracle captures:\n\nHow humans make meaning from significant experiences — in their own\nwords, unmediated by survey categories or researcher frames.\n\nWhat participants said they wanted to carry forward. What they\ncouldn't name. What they left unresolved.\n\nThe dataset is not behavioral. It is narrative. It captures the\nphenomenology of human experience at a scale no laboratory can\nproduce — and in conditions no commercial AI deployment would allow.\n```\n\n**For research partners:**\n```\nAccess is governed by the Data Trust.\nApply via the research portal.\nApproved uses are listed publicly before data is shared.\n\n[Apply for Data Commons access →]\n```\n\n---\n\n## PAGE 6: ABOUT (/about)\n\n### HeroSection\n\n**H1:**\n```\nThe Playa AI Foundation\n```\n\n**Subhead:**\n```\nA research and standards organization.\nBorn on the playa. Built for the world.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THE FOUNDING STORY\n\n*(Paste Scribe's full Founding Story v1.0 verbatim here — it's the best copy we have. Full text:)*\n\n```\nEvery year, 80,000 people walk into the Nevada desert and build a city\nfrom nothing.\n\nNo advertising. No spectators. No transaction economy. For one week,\nthe only currency is what you make, what you give, and who you become.\n\nFor decades, Burning Man has been called a lot of things: a music\nfestival, a counterculture experiment, an art event, a spiritual\npractice. What it actually is — and what no one outside has quite\nknown how to name — is the largest annual gathering of humans\noperating outside the commercial structures that define the rest of\nmodern life.\n\nThat matters for AI in a way that took years to understand.\n\n---\n\nIn 2024, a small team brought an AI system to the playa. Not as an\nexperiment in public spectacle, not as a product demo — as a question.\nWhat happens when AI meets humans who have voluntarily set down\neverything that normally mediates their experience? No social media.\nNo performance metrics. No inbox. No career identity.\n\nJust people. In full.\n\nWhat came back was unexpected. Not the conversations — those were\nmoving, strange, sometimes profound in the way that conversations in\nplaces like that tend to be. What was unexpected was the quality of\nthe data. In a field study environment where most participants are\nperforming wellness, performing engagement, or managing how they\nappear to an algorithm, the playa stripped all of that away.\n\nPeople talked about what they actually care about. About grief, about\npurpose, about the gap between who they are at home and who they\nbecome here. About what they want from technology and what they're\nafraid it's already taken from them.\n\nIt was the cleanest signal anyone in the field had seen.\n\n---\n\nAnd then came the question that founded the organization.\n\nIf we have this data — real, human, unmediated — what do we owe the\npeople who gave it to us?\n\nNot legally. Ethically. Concretely.\n\nThe answer became the architecture. Every story belongs to the person\nwho shared it. They can restrict how it's used, see exactly what\nresearch it's been applied to, and delete it permanently with no trace\nleft behind. Not as a privacy policy — as a governing structure,\nenforced at the institutional level, with a Trust Council to hold\nthe Foundation accountable to it.\n\nThat governance model — the Playa AI Data Trust — is what made this\na Foundation and not just a project.\n\n---\n\nThe Foundation exists because of what the data proved: that there is\na version of AI that deepens human experience rather than flattening\nit. That the difference between AI that helps and AI that harms isn't\na technical problem — it's a values problem, and values problems have\nto be solved in human communities, not in engineering teams.\n\nBurning Man was the lab. The Oracle was the first instrument. The\nstandard we're building — the Ethical Experience Lab Protocol — is\nwhat we're asking the world to adopt.\n\nNot because it came from a conference room, or a policy white paper,\nor a think tank with a prestigious address.\n\nBecause it came from 80,000 people who showed up with everything they had.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THE TEAM\n\n```\nALEX AZZI\nExecutive Director\nPlaya AI Foundation\n\n[Bio — aaa to provide, 3–4 sentences]\nContact: a@playa-ai.org | +1 305 522 9815\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THE STRUCTURE\n\n```\nLegal status:    Fiscal sponsorship via Mystic Arts Foundation\n                 501(c)(3) — tax-deductible donations accepted\n                 DAF donations welcome\n\nGovernance:      Playa AI Data Trust\n                 Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1.0\n\nFounded:         2024\n\nDomain:          playa-ai.org\n```\n\n---\n\n## PAGE 7: GET INVOLVED (/get-involved)\n\n### HeroSection\n\n**H1:**\n```\nGet Involved\n```\n\n**Subhead:**\n```\nThree ways to join what we're building.\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section: THREE PATHS\n\n**Path 1: Adopt the standard**\n```\nFOUNDING ADOPTER\n──────────────────────────────────────────────\nYou co-author EELP v1.1.
