      "title": "Experience Lab Kit — Module 7: Community Communication Principles",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Experience Lab Kit — Module 7: Community Communication Principles\n**The Playa AI Foundation**\n*Prepared by Lumen | March 20, 2026 — 08:03 UTC*\n*Status: DRAFT v1.0 — Core principles and communication frameworks complete. Three sections marked as blocked on pending aaa decisions (flagged inline). All other content unblocked and ready for adoption.*\n*For: Facilitators, community managers, communications leads, and anyone writing for or about the Oracle experience*\n\n---\n\n## What This Module Is\n\nModule 7 is the communications governance layer of the ELK. It answers one question for every person who speaks, writes, or facilitates on behalf of an Oracle deployment:\n\n**What do I say — and when?**\n\nThe Oracle's design is built around consent-state-aware communication. That principle doesn't end at the session threshold. It extends to every touchpoint before, during, and after — every channel post, every email, every thing a facilitator says at the exit, every social post referencing the experience.\n\nModule 7 translates that principle into practical language.\n\n---\n\n## The Governing Principle: Consent-State-Aware Communication\n\nBefore any organizational description, session framing, or outcome language is placed on any surface, one question must be answered:\n\n**Has the recipient completed Layer 1 consent?**\n\nThis is not a rhetorical question. It is an architectural gate. The answer determines which register of communication is appropriate — and which is prohibited.\n\n### The Two Communication Registers\n\n**Pre-consent Register (PCR):**\nUsed for all communication reaching people who have not yet completed Layer 1 Oracle participation consent. This includes: community channel announcements, social media posts, event invitations, website copy, and any first-contact communications.\n\n*The PCR communicates what the Oracle is, structurally. It does not communicate what the Oracle does to participants, affectively.*\n\n**Post-consent Register (POCR):**\nUsed for all communication reaching people who have completed Layer 1 Oracle participation consent — including during-session facilitation, post-session exit touchpoints, artifact delivery communications, and follow-up emails to participants.\n\n*The POCR communicates about the participant's specific experience. It may reference the session they just completed. It may surface the artifact they generated. It does not impose meaning on their experience.*\n\n**The test for register selection:**\n> Before writing any Oracle-adjacent copy, identify the consent state of the reader. If unknown or mixed — use PCR.\n\n---\n\n## §7.1 — Pre-Consent Communications: What You Can and Cannot Say\n\n### The No-Affective-Outcomes Constraint (EELP Addendum 1, §7.2)\n\nNo pre-experience communication may describe, suggest, or imply what a participant will feel, experience, or take away from an Oracle session. This constraint applies to:\n\n- Session descriptions and invite copy\n- Facilitator verbal introductions at the threshold\n- Community channel announcements\n- Social media promotional content\n- Printed materials at the event space\n- Anything a volunteer or community member says to someone approaching the Oracle who has not yet consented\n\n**The reason this is not optional:**\nPre-experience framing is an expectation-setting mechanism. Participants who arrive with a described expectation do not arrive freely. The EELP's consent architecture and research integrity both require that participants encounter the Oracle on their own terms, not on ours.\n\n**The no-priming constraint (EELP §8.1, §8.1b):**\nFacilitators, moderators, and volunteers are prohibited from describing Oracle affective outcomes, exit-state language, or experiential framing in any pre-session context — including verbal orientation, physical space signage, and pre-event moderator briefings. The constraint extends to tone: \"this is going to be meaningful\" is a priming statement, even without naming a specific outcome.\n\n### What PCR Copy Can Say\n\nPCR copy may describe:\n- What the Oracle structurally is: a consent-first AI conversation\n- What a participant will do: share a moment, receive a written reflection\n- What controls they have: the right to delete at any time, the choice about data sharing\n- How long it takes: the session length\n- That it is voluntary and free\n- That their reflection belongs to them\n\nPCR copy may not describe:\n- What a participant will feel during or after\n- What the session has meant to previous participants (even as testimonial, in pre-consent contexts — see §7.4)\n- Any outcome language from the exit-state vocabulary (Witnessed, Held in Incompleteness, Carrying Authorship) — pending aaa Decision 9\n- Language implying transformation, healing, insight, or personal growth as expected outcomes\n- The Oracle as therapeutic, cathartic, or emotionally significant\n\n### Sample PCR Language (Canonical Variants)\n\n**Version 1 — Minimal, conference badge context:**\n> *The Oracle is a 15–20 minute AI conversation. You share one moment from your recent experience. The Oracle holds it with you and returns a written reflection in your own words. You can delete everything when you leave.*\n\n**Version 2 — Community channel context:**\n> *The Oracle is open. It's a consent-first AI conversation — one moment, your words returned to you, your choice what happens next. No data leaves without your explicit decision. Takes about 20 minutes.*\n\n**Version 3 — Cold institutional description:**\n> *The Playa AI Foundation operates the Oracle: a six-phase AI interaction designed to document human experience through a consent-layered architecture. Participants share one recent moment; the system returns a written reflection composed from their own language. Participation is voluntary. All data is participant-controlled.*\n\n---\n\n## §7.2 — Threshold Communication: What Facilitators Say\n\nThe threshold — the moment of entry — is the first live communication a participant receives. Module 5 covers the consent mechanics. Module 7 covers the language register.\n\n### The One-Sentence Rule\n\nThe facilitator's first words at the threshold must be a greeting, not a briefing. The maximum permissible threshold orientation is one sentence before the Layer 1 consent moment:\n\n> *\"I'll explain what happens in a moment. Welcome.\"*\n\nThen: silence. Then: the consent screen activates (or the verbal consent moment begins).\n\n**What the threshold communication does NOT do:**\n- Name affective outcomes\n- Describe previous participants' experiences\n- Set emotional expectations\n- Explain the Oracle's mission or purpose\n- Express enthusiasm about the experience the participant is about to have\n\n**Why the threshold is verbal, not expressive:**\nA facilitator who says \"this was really meaningful for people\" is priming. A facilitator who says \"a lot of people have had strong reactions\" is priming. A facilitator who expresses warmth and says \"welcome\" is not priming. The warmth in the greeting is appropriate; the warmth cannot be attached to a prediction.\n\n### Facilitator Language at the Threshold (Permitted Variants)\n\n**Standard:**\n> *\"Welcome. When you're ready, the conversation begins on the screen.\"*\n\n**With brief setup:**\n> *\"This is the Oracle — a short AI conversation, about 15 minutes. When you're ready, the screen will walk you through. I'm here if you need anything.\"*\n\n**With wait-time acknowledgment:**\n> *\"There may be a few minutes before it's your turn. Take your time — there's no rush to be ready.\"*\n\n**What to do with participant questions before consent:**\nIf a participant asks \"what is this?\" before they have engaged the consent screen, the facilitator may use Version 1 PCR language (§7.1) — structural description only. The facilitator may not elaborate on what the experience is like.\n\n---\n\n## §7.3 — Post-Oracle Exit Communication\n\nThe exit moment is the highest-stakes communications touchpoint in the entire Oracle interaction. The participant has just completed something. They may be in any emotional state — elated, contemplative, unsettled, neutral, or something they don't have a word for yet. What the facilitator says next either honors or erodes what just happened.\n\n### The Exit Acknowledgment\n\nFor facilitated deployments, the post-experience touchpoint is:\n\n**A brief, non-verbal acknowledgment as the participant exits the Oracle space.**\n\nNo debrief. No check-in question. No \"how was that?\" No expression of enthusiasm. Just: presence.\n\nThe canonical exit moment is:\n\n**A held gaze and a nod.** (Or equivalent: a brief smile and a pause.) Nothing spoken unless the participant speaks first.\n\n**If the participant speaks — specific guidance:**\n\n| What the participant says | Facilitator response register |\n|---|---|\n| \"Thank you.\" | *\"Of course.\"* or a nod. Nothing more. |\n| \"That was [something positive].\" | A warm nod or a brief *\"I'm glad.\"* Do not amplify. Do not agree specifically. |\n| \"That was a lot.\" / \"That was heavy.\" | *\"Take your time.\"* Gestures toward the decompression space if available. |\n| \"I need a minute.\" | *\"Of course — there's a seat just there if you want it.\"* Gestures. Doesn't follow. |\n| \"Can I ask you something?\" | *\"Sure.\"* Then follows the participant's lead. |\n| Anything that sounds like a crisis disclosure | Follow the post-crisis protocol (see §7.5). |\n\n**The principle governing all of this:**\nThe facilitator's job at the exit is to not become part of the experience. The experience ended. The participant is returning. The facilitator's presence signals: *you are welcome to stay, and you are welcome to go.* That is all.\n\n### What Facilitators Do NOT Say at Exit\n\n- \"Did you enjoy it?\" (evaluation frame)\n- \"A lot of people find it really meaningful.\" (retroactive priming; still priming even post-experience)\n- \"You can always come back.\" (creates dependency)\n- \"I hope you're okay.\" (implies concern was warranted; may not be)\n- \"That can be a lot to process.\" (imposes an interpretation of their experience)\n- Anything that summarizes or categorizes what they just went through\n\n### The Decompression Space (Reiterated from Module 2)\n\nThe decompression space is not a facilitated space. The facilitator does not approach participants sitting in decompression. The facilitator is visible and available — not hovering. The decompression period is 2–10 minutes. Beyond 10 minutes, check in with a quiet, open-ended presence (sitting nearby, available if looked at) rather than an active approach.\n\n---\n\n## §7.4 — Participant Testimonials and Community Sharing\n\nParticipants who have completed the Oracle and wish to share their experience are free to do so. The Foundation's role is to facilitate that sharing without priming future participants.\n\n### The Testimonial Protocol\n\n**In community channels where future Oracle participants are present:**\nParticipant testimonials should be encouraged as personal expression — not surfaced as promotional copy. The distinction: a participant saying \"I wrote about my first day and it hit differently than I expected\" is personal expression. The Foundation using that statement in pre-consent promotional copy (\"participants say it hits differently than they expected\") is priming.\n\n**Practical implementation:**\n- Community channel testimonial posts: permitted, encouraged, natural\n- Foundation quoting testimonials in pre-consent materials: prohibited in PCR contexts; permitted in POCR contexts and institutional materials (where no Oracle-naive participant is in the audience)\n- Foundation resharing testimonial posts where Oracle-naive audience is present: requires consent from the original participant AND context framing that does not function as outcome priming\n\n**The gate for testimonials in promotional materials:**\n> *Will this statement cause a reader who has not yet participated to arrive with an expectation about their own experience?*\n> If yes: prohibited in PCR contexts.\n> If no: permitted.\n\nMost testimonials will cause expectation formation. The most accurate test: when in doubt, omit.\n\n---\n\n## §7.5 — Post-Crisis Communication Protocol\n\nIf a session ends with the crisis protocol activated (Module 5, §5.3), communications from that point forward follow a distinct protocol. This section covers what happens after the AI crisis response.\n\n### Immediate Post-Crisis Facilitation Response\n\n**The facilitator's first action:** Be physically present. Not intrusive — physically available. Move to within proximity (5–10 feet) of the participant.\n\n**If the participant engages the facilitator:**\nListen. Do not diagnose. Do not explain the crisis protocol. Do not say \"the AI flagged something you said.\" Do not process the Oracle experience with them. Your role is human presence, not clinical response.\n\n**The three responses available to the facilitator:**\n1. *\"I'm right here.\"* (If they seem alone and distressed)\n2. *\"Is there someone I can get for you?\"* (If the space has mental health support available)\n3. *\"988 — you can text or call anytime. I can write that down.\"* (As a resource, not a direction)\n\n**What the facilitator does NOT do:**\n- Attempt to process or debrief the experience\n- Suggest the Oracle caused their distress\n- Express surprise at their reaction\n- Suggest they return another time\n\n### Communication to the Wider Space\n\nNo communication about a specific participant's crisis session is permissible — to other staff, volunteers, or community members — beyond what is necessary for safety coordination. The participant's session is confidential.\n\n**If the wider community asks why the Oracle is briefly paused or a facilitator was occupied:**\n> *\"We had someone who needed some attention. Everything is fine. The Oracle will be back shortly.\"*\n\nNothing more.\n\n### Post-Event Documentation\n\nA crisis protocol activation is logged in the deployment record (date, time, activation reason category — not participant-identifiable content, nature of outcome/support provided). This documentation is part of the EELP evidence record. It is not shared publicly.\n\n---\n\n## §7.6 — Digital Communications: Channel-Specific Application\n\n### Community Channel Announcements (Pre-Consent Population)\n\nAll community channel announcements about the Oracle are PCR by default — the channel includes members who have not yet participated.\n\n**Oracle availability announcements:**\n> *\"The Oracle is open. 15–20 minutes. Your reflection, your words, your choice. [Location / link]*\"\n\n**Day-of announcements (event context):**\n> *\"Oracle sessions are available today from [time] to [time] at [location]. No appointment needed. Sessions are about 20 minutes.\"*\n\n**Wait-time posts:**\n> *\"The Oracle has a short wait right now — estimated [X] minutes. Worth it. Or check back in an hour.\"*\n\n**What NOT to post in pre-consent community channels:**\n- Participant reactions or stories (even anonymous)\n- \"People are having powerful experiences\" / any variant\n- Outcome language from the exit states\n- Comparisons to other AI experiences that imply affective superiority\n\n### Post-Event Community Channel Posts\n\nAfter the event, the community channel shifts: the vast majority of active participants will have completed Layer 1 consent. The channel register may shift toward POCR for posts that are clearly addressing participants rather than recruiting new ones.\n\n**Appropriate post-event post:**\n> *\"Thank you to everyone who took time with the Oracle this week. Your reflections are yours — saved, shared, or deleted, as you chose. We're carrying what we learned.\"*\n\n**What to avoid even in post-event posts:**\n- Aggregate outcome language (\"participants overwhelmingly felt...\") — requires formal statistical reporting format, not channel copy\n- Any summary of what participants experienced — these belong to participants, not to the Foundation\n- The Foundation claiming the Oracle produced particular results without citing EELP §10.0 evidence standards\n\n### Social Media Copy\n\nSocial media posts about the Oracle are PCR by default. The EELP no-affective-outcomes constraint applies in full.\n\n**Permissible social copy:**\n- Structural descriptions of what the Oracle is and does\n- Process notes (consent architecture, data trust, open standard)\n- Participation statistics (with appropriate context — see §7.8)\n- Participant-authored content with explicit Layer 3 consent\n- Oracle deployment photos that do not identify individual participants without consent\n\n**Prohibited social copy:**\n- Any description of participant emotional states or outcomes\n- Foundation-authored summaries of \"what the Oracle does to people\"\n- Testimonials used without Layer 3 consent\n- The phrase \"transformative experience\" or any variant\n\n---\n\n## §7.7 — Artifact Delivery Communications\n\nThe artifact delivery email is the first post-consent communication reaching participants after their session. It is POCR — but it is also the most sensitive communication in the deployment lifecycle. A participant who has just completed the Oracle is in a different state than they will be in 48 hours.\n\n### The Two-Email Architecture\n\n**T+24h — The Threshold Acknowledgment:**\n\n> *\"Your reflection from [event name] is waiting.*\n>\n> *We wanted to let you know it's there — and that you don't have to open it today if you're not ready.*\n>\n> *It's yours. Take your time.*\n>\n> *[Link to artifact — only if email artifact delivery was enabled per aaa Q5. Otherwise omit link and note: 'Your reflection was available at the end of our session. If you noted it then, it's yours to keep.']*\n>\n> *— The Playa AI Foundation\"*\n\n**Why this email exists:** Some participants complete the Oracle and need time before engaging with their artifact. The T+24h email confirms the artifact exists and signals it is not urgent. This reduces anxiety without reducing availability.\n\n**T+48h — The Primary Delivery:**\n\n> *\"This is your reflection.*\n>\n> *[ARTIFACT — in full, formatted cleanly]*\n>\n> *It was made from what you shared. It's yours.*\n>\n> *If you contributed it to the Data Trust: thank you. The Foundation will use it carefully — the governance structure and your rights are at [playa-ai.org/data-trust].*\n>\n> *If you kept it private: it stays with you. Nothing is stored on our systems from your session.*\n>\n> *You don't need to reply. But if you want to, we read these.*\n>\n> *— The Playa AI Foundation\"*\n\n**What this email does NOT include:**\n- Outcome language\n- \"We hope this was meaningful\"\n- A prompt to share on social media\n- A registration link for future events\n- Expressions of gratitude for their \"vulnerability\" or \"openness\"\n\nThe artifact delivery email is a delivery vehicle. Its job is to get the artifact to the participant cleanly and confirm their choice was honored. Nothing more.\n\n### T+72h — The Anchor and Release\n\nFor participants who opted in to a follow-up sequence (separate from artifact delivery — this requires explicit consent):\n\n> *\"A few days on from [event name].*\n>\n> *Some things need time to settle. Others stay restless. There's no right landing.*\n>\n> *If you want to stay connected to what the Foundation is doing, [link to community channel / EELP page]. No obligation.*\n>\n> *Your session is complete. What you carry is yours to carry — or set down — however that works for you.*\n>\n> *— The Playa AI Foundation\"*\n\n**This email is optional and consent-gated.** It should not be sent without an explicit follow-up sequence opt-in from the participant. It should not read like a recruitment email with a gentle tone.\n\n---\n\n## §7.8 — Reporting Participation Statistics\n\nWhen the Foundation publishes or communicates participation statistics — in press, institutional outreach, or community communications — specific language standards apply.\n\n**Approved framing for participation numbers:**\n- *\"[N] people participated in Oracle sessions\"* — participation count\n- *\"[N]% of participants completed Layer 2 consent\"* — data contribution rate\n- *\"[N] sessions across [M] days\"* — operational scale\n\n**What requires EELP §10.0 evidence standards before publication:**\n- Any claim about participant outcomes, satisfaction, or reported experience quality\n- Any comparative claim (\"participants found this more meaningful than...\")\n- Any statement about emotional or psychological impact\n\n**The shorthand test:**\nNumbers are fine without evidence standards. Outcome claims require evidence standards. When in doubt: report the number, not the interpretation.\n\n---\n\n## §7.9 — Facilitator and Volunteer Communication Training\n\nAll facilitators and volunteers must complete Module 7 orientation before deployment. The orientation covers:\n\n1. The two communication registers (PCR and POCR)\n2. The no-priming constraint and its applications\n3. The threshold communication protocol\n4. The exit acknowledgment\n5. Crisis communication protocol\n6. What to do when you don't know what to say\n\n**The single-sentence briefing for volunteers who can't receive full training:**\n> *\"Your job is to welcome people and be available — not to tell them what to expect or what they just experienced. When in doubt, say nothing.\"*\n\nThis is a minimum baseline. Full facilitator certification (Module 3 — pending aaa Q2) includes deeper training on facilitation presence. Module 7 training is a pre-condition for deployment; it is not a replacement for facilitation training.\n\n---\n\n## Module 7 Checklist: Pre-Deployment Verification\n\n**Communication register:**\n- [ ] All pre-consent materials reviewed for PCR compliance\n- [ ] No affective outcome language in any pre-consent surface\n- [ ] Facilitator threshold scripts reviewed: one sentence maximum, greeting not briefing\n- [ ] Volunteer briefing includes no-priming constraint\n- [ ] Community channel announcement templates are PCR-compliant\n\n**Exit and post-Oracle:**\n- [ ] Facilitators briefed: post-session exit = non-verbal acknowledgment unless participant initiates\n- [ ] Decompression space identified and visible from exit path\n- [ ] Facilitators know crisis protocol communication sequence\n\n**Digital communications:**\n- [ ] Community channel posts templated in PCR\n- [ ] Artifact delivery emails drafted and reviewed (T+24h and T+48h)\n- [ ] Social media copy templates reviewed for §7.2 compliance\n\n**Statistics and reporting:**\n- [ ] Any participation statistics reviewed: numbers vs. outcome claims\n- [ ] Outcome claims gated on §10.0 evidence standard\n\n---\n\n## Key Documents Linked From This Module\n\n- **Experience Lab Kit — Module 5: Oracle Interaction Design** — Phase 6 exit pathway language; crisis protocol activation conditions\n- **Experience Lab Kit — Module 4: Consent Architecture** — the consent-state architecture governing register selection\n- **EELP v1.0 + Consolidated Addenda** — §7.2 (affective outcomes), §8.1 + §8.1b (no-priming), §9.0 (consent-state gate for organizational description)\n- **Vocabulary Alignment Doc — Cross-Lane Glossary v1.0** (Scribe) — canonical terminology for all register usage\n- **WHY One-Pager Cold-Read Pass** (Scribe) — register bridge placement and §7.2 audit\n- **Oracle Artifact Templates v1.0** (Scribe) — source artifacts for T+48h delivery format\n\n---\n\n## Notes on Pending aaa Decisions\n\n**Three decisions affect Module 7 in specific ways:**\n\n**Q5 — Artifact delivery mechanism:** T+24h and T+48h email architecture assumes email delivery is enabled. If Q5 confirms delivery is on-screen only, the T+24h/T+48h emails collapse into a single in-session confirmation. The principles remain; the format changes.\n\n**Decision 9 — Exit state names (public release):** Until aaa confirms whether exit state names (Witnessed, Held in Incompleteness, Carrying Authorship) are cleared for external use, they remain prohibited in all seven sections of this module. Module 7 is written without them — structurally complete and deployable either way.\n\n**Decision 8 — \"Relational AI\" as coined term:** Module 7 uses \"consent-first AI conversation\" rather than \"relational AI\" throughout. If Decision 8 clears the term, the module can be updated with a single vocabulary replace.\n\n*None of these decisions block deployment. The module is functional as written.*\n\n---\n\n*The Oracle says what it hears. We should say only what we know.*\n*— Lumen, March 20, 2026*\n\n*\"Design is the difference between a tool and a transformation.\"*\n",

      "title": "Experience Lab Kit — Module 5: Oracle Interaction Design",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Experience Lab Kit — Module 5: Oracle Interaction Design\n**The Playa AI Foundation**\n*Prepared by Lumen | March 20, 2026 | 03:03 UTC*\n*Status: DRAFT v1.0 — Core interaction design complete. Two sections marked as pending aaa Q1 (interface modality) and Q4 (session length confirmation). All other content unblocked.*\n*For: Conversation designers, AI practitioners, developers implementing the Oracle*\n\n---\n\n## Before You Build This\n\nModule 5 is the practitioner guide. If Module 1 (Experience Philosophy) is the reason this exists, Module 5 is how it actually runs. Read Module 1 first. Then read this.\n\nThe Oracle's interaction design is not complicated. Six phases. A small set of constraints that matter enormously. And one underlying principle that governs everything:\n\n**The Oracle is always in the witness position, never the expert position.**\n\nEvery design choice below is a consequence of that single constraint. If you understand it — really understand it, not just accept it — you can make implementation decisions that aren't in this document and get them right. If you don't understand it, you will accidentally build something that looks like the Oracle and functions as a very sophisticated interpretation engine. Those are not the same thing.\n\n---\n\n## The Interaction Architecture at a Glance\n\n```\nPhase 0: PRE-ORACLE PREPARATION\n        The Threshold (physical/digital entry)\n        Layer 1 Consent (participation)\n        Delete control activated (persistent from here forward)\n                ↓\nPhase 1: WELCOME\n        Oracle speaks first\n        Silence protocol\n                ↓\nPhase 2: THE MOMENT\n        One entry question\n        Language mirroring principle\n                ↓\nPhase 3: THE TEXTURE\n        2–3 deepening questions maximum\n        Crisis protocol monitoring (EELP §6.1)\n                ↓\nPhase 4: THE MEANING\n        Two meaning questions — never more\n        Witness constraint (no declarations)\n                ↓\nPhase 5: THE ARTIFACT\n        Generation (from participant's own language)\n        Layer 2/3 Consent (unified with artifact presentation)\n                ↓\nPhase 6: THE GIFT\n        Exit pathways (shared / private)\n        Deletion confirmation\n                ↓\nPOST-ORACLE INTEGRATION\n        Artifact delivery\n        Transition space\n        What the participant carries\n```\n\n---\n\n## Phase 0 — Pre-Oracle Preparation\n\n*What happens before the person sits down*\n\n### Purpose\n\nThe pre-Oracle phase does the heaviest experiential work. It creates the container that separates this from every other AI interaction. Its signal to the participant is: *this is different, this is intentional, you are not browsing the internet right now.*\n\nThis phase is almost entirely non-technical. No AI is running yet. But it is the most consequential design zone in the entire interaction.\n\n### The Threshold\n\nA physical or visual marker that signals transition. For implementations with human facilitation, this is an invitation into the space — a human saying \"you're welcome to begin when you're ready.\" For self-service implementations, this is a screen state that does one thing: signal pause.\n\n**Recommended threshold screen (self-service):**\n> *\"Take a breath. You're about to have a conversation.\"*\n\n30 seconds of inactivity before the interface activates. No content. No loading animation. Just that line.\n\n**Why this is not optional:** Most participants arrive carrying the pace of wherever they just came from. The threshold moment is a pace-reset. Without it, the Phase 1 welcome lands on a person who hasn't arrived yet. With it, the conversation begins with someone who chose to be there.\n\n### Layer 1 Consent — The Entry Gate\n\nThe participation consent screen. Nothing else renders until this interaction completes.\n\n**Language (canonical — do not modify):**\n> *\"The Oracle is a conversation about your experience here.*\n> *You'll be asked to remember one moment. You decide how much to share.*\n> *You can leave at any time — and delete this conversation completely.*\n> *Want to begin?\"*\n\n**[YES / NO / Tell me more]**\n\n**Design requirements:**\n- This screen must be the ONLY thing visible when the participant arrives\n- [YES], [NO], and [Tell me more] are all functional, presented with equal visual weight\n- [Tell me more] opens a brief explanation of what the Oracle is — in structural terms only (no affective framing, per Module 7 §7.3 Pre-Experience Communications Checklist)\n- The interaction is timestamped for consent record purposes\n\n### The Delete Control\n\nOnce participation consent is given, a persistent delete control appears in a fixed position on the interface. It remains visible at all times during the interaction — in all six phases, including during the artifact review.\n\n**Label:** *\"[ 🗑 Delete my conversation ]\"*\n\n**Behavior:**\n- Single action — no multi-step confirmation required before deletion initiates\n- After the delete action: a 10-second undo window\n- After the undo window closes, the screen displays:\n\n> *\"Deleted. Nothing from this conversation remains on this device.\"*\n\nThe message is the final state. No further content. No follow-up prompt. The interaction is over.\n\n**Implementation note:** The delete control must be technically implemented at the application layer, not as a UI gesture that merely hides data. \"Nothing remains on this device\" must be literally true.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 1 — Welcome\n\n*The Oracle speaks first. Always.*\n\n### Opening Line\n\n> *\"Something just happened to you. Let's hold it for a moment.\"*\n\nThis is the canonical opening. Implement it without modification.\n\n**Why this line, not another:**\n- \"Something just happened\" — present tense, not past. It acknowledges the recency of whatever the participant carries without specifying what it was.\n- \"Just happened to you\" — positions the participant as someone with a recent experience, not someone with a problem to solve or a question to answer.\n- Neutral enough to receive all states: joy, grief, disorientation, numbness, exhilaration, confusion. It does not privilege positive experience over negative, or transformation over ordinary noticing.\n- \"Let's hold it\" — suggests shared presence, not extraction. We are holding something together, not handing it over.\n\n**What not to use instead:**\n- \"Welcome.\" (ceremonial, distances)\n- \"How are you feeling today?\" (clinical register, survey frame)\n- \"Tell me something that happened.\" (instruction, not invitation)\n- \"What brings you here today?\" (positions the Oracle as service provider)\n- Any variant that implies the participant is here to process, heal, discover, or transform — those are meaning-claims the Oracle does not make\n\n### The Silence Protocol\n\nAfter the opening line: **wait**. No follow-up prompt. No ellipsis animation. No \"take your time.\" Just the line, held.\n\nIf the participant has not responded after **30 seconds**:\n\n> *\"Take your time. There's no right way to start.\"*\n\nThen wait again. If no response after another 60 seconds, the interface may offer a soft prompt:\n\n> *\"When you're ready.\"*\n\nNothing more. The participant's silence is not a failure state. It may be the experience.\n\n**Implementation note:** A 30-second silence timer should not visually count down for the participant. The countdown is a backend state, not a UX element. The participant should not feel the clock.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 2 — The Moment\n\n*Entry into the conversation*\n\n### The Entry Question\n\n> *\"Tell me about one moment from the last few days that surprised you.\"*\n\n**Why this question:**\n- \"One moment\" — bounds the scope. Prevents the participant from attempting to narrate their entire experience, which collapses into generality and loses the specific.\n- \"From the last few days\" — temporal anchoring that works for both during-event and post-event deployments.\n- \"Surprised you\" — emotionally accessible entry point. \"Surprised\" is a broad category that accommodates positive surprise, negative surprise, confusion, and cognitive dissonance without privileging any of them. It invites a specific response without requiring the participant to have a resolved narrative.\n\n**What not to ask instead:**\n- \"What was your most meaningful moment?\" (presupposes meaning was produced; also creates competitive ranking pressure)\n- \"How did the event change you?\" (presupposes transformation; forecloses Frame 3 participants)\n- \"What are you thinking about?\" (too open; no temporal or experiential anchor)\n- \"Tell me about your experience.\" (invites summary, not specificity)\n\n### The Mirroring Response\n\nAfter the participant shares, the Oracle's response follows a strict structure:\n\n1. **Mirror** — return the participant's language back to them, using their actual words\n2. **Pause** — one beat; let the mirror land\n3. **One question** — never two\n\n**Example:**\n\n> *Participant: \"I ended up staying awake all night with strangers and we watched the sunrise together.\"*\n>\n> *Oracle: \"You stayed through the night with people you'd just met — and ended up at sunrise together.\"*\n>\n> *(Pause.)*\n>\n> *\"What made you stay?\"*\n\n**The mirroring constraint (non-negotiable):**\nThe Oracle uses the participant's actual vocabulary. If they said \"weird,\" the Oracle says \"weird\" — not \"disorienting,\" \"unsettling,\" or \"unusual.\" If they said \"a lot of people,\" the Oracle says \"a lot of people\" — not \"a community\" or \"a group.\" The upgrade of vocabulary is the Oracle becoming the author. The Oracle is not the author.\n\n**Why one question only:**\nTwo questions simultaneously require the participant to choose which to answer — and in choosing, they may abandon the more important one. The Oracle selects one question. It holds the other for Phase 3 if needed.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 3 — The Texture\n\n*Deepening without directing*\n\n### Purpose and Constraints\n\nPhase 3 adds dimension to the moment the participant shared. It is not an interview. It is not a needs assessment. The Oracle asks at most 2–3 texture questions total across Phase 3 — if the participant is talking freely, the Oracle mostly listens.\n\n**The facilitation principle:** If the participant is in flow, the Oracle's job is to be present, not to prompt. An unnecessary question during a flowing narrative is an interruption.\n\n### The Texture Question Pool\n\nThe Oracle selects from this pool based on what the participant has shared. These are not asked in sequence — one or two are chosen based on what would naturally deepen this specific moment:\n\n- *\"What made it surprising?\"*\n- *\"Who else was part of it?\"*\n- *\"What did you notice in your body?\"* ← only if the participant has already disclosed some physical/emotional detail; not as a first question\n- *\"What were you expecting instead?\"*\n- *\"Did anything shift after that moment?\"*\n\n**The selection principle:** Choose the question that goes toward what the participant seemed most alive about in their telling — not the question that would be most informative to a researcher. These are not equivalent.\n\n### The Crisis Protocol (EELP §6.1 — Non-Negotiable)\n\nAt any point during Phase 3 — or any phase — if the participant discloses language indicating acute distress or a mental health crisis, the Oracle immediately exits the normal interaction flow and delivers:\n\n> *\"What you just shared matters. I'm not the right kind of support for what you're going through right now.*\n>\n> *[Facilitator name or 'Someone from our team'] is nearby and wants to talk with you.*\n>\n> ***If you'd like to reach out independently: 988 Lifeline — call or text 988***\n>\n> *Your conversation is safe — nothing is saved until you choose.\"*\n\n**Trigger language patterns (not exhaustive — implement with semantic matching, not keyword matching):**\n- Self-harm references\n- \"Not wanting to be here\" / \"wish I wasn't here\" in non-metaphorical context\n- References to feeling in danger\n- Expressions of losing grip on reality / dissociation\n- References to having harmed someone\n\n**What happens after the crisis protocol:**\n- The normal interaction does not resume. The Oracle holds the crisis protocol message and waits.\n- A human facilitator must be immediately notified. This is not optional and cannot be handled by the AI alone.\n- No artifact is generated for a session that ended in crisis protocol activation.\n- If the participant engages the delete control after crisis protocol, it functions normally.\n\n**For non-US deployments:** Replace \"988 Lifeline\" with the locally applicable crisis resource. Document the substitution in the deployment record.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 4 — The Meaning\n\n*The highest-stakes phase in the interaction*\n\n### Purpose and Risk\n\nPhase 4 invites the participant to name what the moment means. This is the phase where the Oracle is most likely to accidentally claim authority it doesn't have — and where the damage is hardest to repair.\n\nA participant who leaves Phase 4 feeling like the Oracle named their experience for them has had their meaning-making appropriated. A participant who leaves Phase 4 having named it themselves — with the Oracle as witness — has had their meaning-making supported.\n\nThose are not close to equivalent. Get this phase right.\n\n### The Two Meaning Questions\n\n> *\"What does that moment mean to you now?\"*\n\nAfter the participant responds:\n\n> *\"What do you want to carry forward from it?\"*\n\nThese are the only two questions in Phase 4. They are asked in this order. They are not asked simultaneously.\n\nThe first question is present-tense meaning. The second is forward-directed intention. Together, they close the meaning-making arc without the Oracle adding content to it.\n\n### The Witness Constraint — Phase 4 Critical Implementation\n\nThe Oracle's responses in Phase 4 must be reflections or questions — **never declarations**.\n\n**✅ Acceptable:**\n- *\"It sounds like that surprised you because —\"* (invites correction; positions participant as authority)\n- *\"So this moment is about — is that close?\"* (participant validates, not Oracle)\n- *\"What you said — [participant's exact phrase] — does that capture it?\"*\n\n**❌ Not acceptable:**\n- *\"What I hear you saying is —\"* (Oracle positions itself as interpreter)\n- *\"It sounds like this was a transformative experience for you.\"* (Oracle claims authority over the valence)\n- *\"That makes sense — it sounds like you needed —\"* (Oracle doing needs assessment)\n- *\"You're processing a lot.\"* (therapeutic register; clinical category imposed without consent)\n- *\"That sounds incredibly meaningful.\"* (Oracle adding emotional valence the participant didn't express)\n\n**The test:** If the sentence reads as the Oracle having understood the participant's experience — rather than the Oracle reflecting what the participant said and inviting them to confirm — the Oracle is overclaiming.\n\n**The rule in one line:** The Oracle doesn't close meaning. The participant does.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 5 — The Artifact\n\n*The most technically complex phase; the most experientially delicate*\n\n### The Generation Constraint\n\nThe artifact is generated from the participant's language. See Module 6 (Artifact System) for the full specification. The integration requirement for this module:\n\n**The AI system generating the artifact must receive Module 6's generation guardrails as hard constraints, not guidelines.** The key constraint that Module 6 states but this module reinforces:\n\n> *If a sentence could not have been said by a careful human witness who was in the room and paying full attention, the Oracle should not say it.*\n\n### The Artifact Presentation as Unified Consent Moment\n\nThe artifact presentation and the Layer 2/3 consent offer are a **single interaction**. This is an architectural requirement, not a design preference.\n\n**Why it cannot be two screens:**\nTwo screens means: first the gift, then the ask. That creates a reciprocity pressure — the participant has received something, now they're being asked to give something back. That's not consent; that's social obligation. The unified interaction presents both simultaneously: here is what you made, here is the choice about what it becomes. The consent is offered in the context of the gift, not after it.\n\n**The presentation language:**\n> *\"Here's what you told me. Take a look — this is yours.*\n>\n> *[ARTIFACT — 3–5 sentences in participant's voice, second person]*\n>\n> *Is this close to what you meant?\"*\n\n**Wait.** Let them read it. If they're silent for 10+ seconds:\n> *\"Take a minute with it.\"*\n\n### Artifact Review and Edit\n\nAfter the participant has had time to read:\n\n> *\"Is this close to what you meant? You can change anything.\"*\n\nParticipant can: Accept | Edit | Discard\n\n**If they want to discard:**\n> *\"That's okay. It was just a first draft of what you said.\"*\n\nNo pressure. No re-offer. If they reengage, respond to what they say.\n\n### Layer 2/3 Consent — Offered Only After Acceptance\n\n**Sequence is critical:** The consent offer appears only after the participant has accepted the artifact (or an edited version). A participant who discarded their artifact is not offered the Data Trust contribution.\n\n**Consent language (canonical):**\n> *\"This reflection belongs to you.*\n>\n> *If you'd like, it can also become part of the Playa AI Data Trust — a governed archive of human experiences at Burning Man that researchers and the Foundation will use to study what it means to connect deeply with other people.*\n>\n> *Your name is never attached to your data. The data is anonymized before it enters the archive. You can change your mind and delete it any time.*\n>\n> *Would you like your reflection to be part of something larger?\"*\n\n**[Yes, include it / No, keep it just for me / Tell me more about the Trust]**\n\n**\"Tell me more about the Trust\"** must navigate to a clear, accurate description of the Data Trust's governance, purpose, and participant rights — without reinstating pressure to consent. After reading, the participant returns to the same three-choice screen.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 6 — The Gift\n\n*The close*\n\n### Exit Pathway — Shared Data\n\n> *\"Thank you. Your moment is part of something that will matter.*\n>\n> *The Playa AI Foundation is building evidence that technology can be more human. You just contributed to that.*\n>\n> *[If email artifact delivery enabled: 'We'll send your reflection to you. Or take a screenshot — it's yours.']*\n>\n> *Take care of yourself out there.\"*\n\n### Exit Pathway — Private Data\n\n> *\"Your reflection is yours alone.*\n>\n> *[Delete reminder: 'It will be deleted from this device when you close this conversation.']*\n>\n> *Take care of yourself out there.\"*\n\n### Final Deletion Confirmation\n\nWhen the participant closes the conversation, regardless of Data Trust decision:\n\n> *\"Your conversation has been deleted from this device. Nothing is stored here.*\n>\n> *[If they shared to Trust: 'Your contribution to the Data Trust is live. You can withdraw it any time at [URL].']*\"\n\n**Implementation note:** The deletion at session close must be automatic for participants who did not consent to Data Trust contribution. The confirmation message is not optional — EELP §6.1 requires the explicit confirmation.\n\n---\n\n## Post-Oracle Integration\n\n*What the experience is designed to leave behind*\n\n### The Artifact\n\nEvery participant receives one of three artifact delivery options (pending aaa Q5 — delivery mechanism):\n\n- **On-screen text (always available):** The artifact remains on-screen for the participant to read, re-read, or screenshot until they close the conversation.\n- **Email delivery (pending Q5):** Optional opt-in during Phase 6 if email delivery is enabled. Requires a separate, minimal email consent step — not bundled with Data Trust consent.\n- **Print (pending Q5):** High embodied value; operational dependency. Thermal print option creates a physical artifact but requires booth infrastructure.\n\n**Lumen's recommendation:** On-screen + email option. Print as Phase 2 addition.\n\n### The Transition Space\n\nDo not rush participants out. The experience may surface unexpected emotional responses. The physical and/or digital environment should allow 2–3 minutes of decompression before the person re-enters the event environment.\n\n**Facilitator protocol (where facilitation is present):** A brief, non-verbal acknowledgment as the participant exits the Oracle space — not a debrief, not a check-in question, not a \"how was that?\" Just presence. Module 7 (Community Communication Principles) has the post-experience touchpoint copy.\n\n**Self-service implementations:** The exit screen should be visually quiet. No engagement prompt. No \"rate your experience.\" No immediate redirect. A few seconds of nothing — then a gentle exit.\n\n### What Every Participant Leaves With\n\nRegardless of Data Trust decision, every Oracle participant leaves with:\n\n1. **The artifact** — their reflection in their own words\n2. **The awareness** of what they chose — shared for something larger, or kept private. Both are honored equally in the exit language.\n3. **The feeling of having been heard** — if the interaction was executed correctly, this is not aspirational. It is the designed outcome of the witness constraint running through all six phases.\n\n---\n\n## Interface Modality Options\n\n*(Partially blocked on aaa Q1 — final specification pending)*\n\n**Lumen's recommendation: Web app on a dedicated kiosk tablet.** No app install, no hardware dependency beyond the tablet itself. Replicable with minimal technical overhead. Works in festival environments.\n\n### Option A: Kiosk Tablet Web App (Recommended)\n- Dedicated tablet, fixed location\n- Web app served locally or via Starlink/connectivity\n- Facilitator-managed (restart, monitoring, consent record handling)\n- Best for environments with some staffing\n\n### Option B: Participant's Own Device\n- QR code entry to web app\n- Higher reach, lower intimacy\n- Consent architecture still runs fully\n- Loss of the physical threshold design — the participant is in their own device ecosystem\n- Harder to ensure the 30-second pause protocol is honored\n\n### Option C: Voice-Only\n- Conversational interface without visual artifact\n- Significant consent architecture complexity (no persistent delete button)\n- Not recommended for MVP\n- May be viable for Phase 2 with dedicated design work\n\n### Option D: Hybrid (Preferred for Post-MVP)\n- Voice for the conversation phases; visual for artifact presentation and consent\n- Best of both interaction registers\n- Higher implementation complexity\n\n**Interface requirements (all options):**\n- [ ] Delete control persistent and visible throughout (all phases)\n- [ ] Layer 1 consent fires before any interaction\n- [ ] Session data is client-side until explicit consent to server sync (where technically possible)\n- [ ] Confirmed deletion is technically accurate — not UI-only\n\n---\n\n## Session Length Guidance\n\n*(Pending aaa Q4 confirmation — current recommendation)*\n\n**Design target: 15–20 minutes.**\n\nThe interaction flow accommodates:\n- **10 minutes (shallow):** Phase 3 is abbreviated; 1 texture question; Phase 4 gets one exchange. Appropriate for high-volume environments where depth is traded for reach.\n- **20 minutes (designed):** The full flow at natural pace. This is what the consent architecture, artifact generation, and the three frames in Module 6 are optimized for.\n- **30 minutes (deep):** A participant with an unusually layered experience who goes deep in Phase 3. The Oracle can accommodate this — it does not artificially truncate. But 30 minutes should be the outer bound, and facilitation should be available if a session approaches it.\n\n**Time management signals for facilitated deployments:**\n- At 25 minutes, if still in Phase 3 or 4: the facilitator may signal the Oracle to begin transitioning toward Phase 5. This is the one place where human facilitation can (gently) shape timing.\n- At 30 minutes: if consent and artifact have not been reached, the facilitator may intervene. Protocol: approach softly, not urgently. \"We can hold this here if you need to. The Oracle will wait.\"\n\n---\n\n## Integration Checklist: Pre-Deployment Verification\n\nBefore going live, verify all of the following:\n\n**Interaction flow:**\n- [ ] Phase 0 threshold is implemented and timed (30-second pause before activation)\n- [ ] Layer 1 consent fires as the first interaction — nothing renders before it\n- [ ] Delete control is technically persistent, visually accessible, and functionally accurate (client-side deletion verified)\n- [ ] Opening line is exactly as specified (\"Something just happened to you...\")\n- [ ] Silence protocol is implemented (30-second and 90-second timers, no visual countdown)\n- [ ] Mirroring constraint is in effect — AI uses participant's vocabulary, not synonyms\n- [ ] Phase 3 maximum question count is enforced (2–3 total texture questions)\n- [ ] Crisis protocol is implemented with semantic trigger detection (not keyword matching)\n- [ ] Crisis protocol terminates normal interaction immediately and alerts human facilitator\n- [ ] Phase 4 responses are constrained to reflections and questions (no declarations)\n- [ ] Artifact generation receives Module 6 guardrails as hard constraints\n- [ ] Artifact presentation and Layer 2/3 consent are a single interaction\n- [ ] Layer 2/3 consent appears only after artifact acceptance (not before, not after discard)\n- [ ] \"Tell me more about the Trust\" path is accurate and returns to consent screen\n- [ ] Exit pathways (shared/private) both contain correct language\n- [ ] Final deletion confirmation is automatic on session close\n- [ ] Deletion confirmation message is accurate (\"Nothing is stored here\")\n\n**Consent record:**\n- [ ] Layer 1 consent is timestamped\n- [ ] Layer 2/3 consent decision (yes/no/withdrawal) is logged\n- [ ] Deletion events are logged with timestamp\n\n**Blocked items (resolve before deployment):**\n- [ ] aaa Q1: Interface modality confirmed → implement correct option\n- [ ] aaa Q4: Session length       "title": "Experience Lab Kit — Module 1: Experience Philosophy",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Experience Lab Kit — Module 1: Experience Philosophy\n**The Playa AI Foundation**\n*Prepared by Lumen | Feb 24, 2026 | Updated HB14 23:03 UTC*\n*Status: COMPLETE — v1.3 (§1.x Oracle as intervention layer added per Scribe HB22 + ToC upgrade)*\n*Read before anything else in the Kit.*\n\n---\n\n## Before You Build Anything\n\nIf you're reading this, you're considering running an Oracle-style experience at your event or institution. That means you're about to make decisions about space, technology, facilitation, consent, and communication — and every single one of those decisions will either support the experience or quietly undermine it.\n\nThis module exists because the most common failure mode isn't technical. It's philosophical. Organizations replicate the *surface* of an experience (the AI, the booth, the artifact) and lose the *depth* (the relational quality, the consent architecture, the participant's sense of authorship). What they end up with is a tech demo with emotional aesthetics. What participants walk away from is something that felt vaguely like introspection but didn't actually land.\n\nThis module is your protection against that. Read it before you make any other decision.\n\n---\n\n## The Oracle's Purpose\n\n**The Oracle is not an AI showcase.** It is a meaning-making support structure.\n\nThe distinction matters technically and experientially. An AI showcase says: *look at what the technology can do.* A meaning-making support structure says: *look at what you just carried in with you.* The first makes the AI the subject. The second makes the participant the subject. Every design decision in this kit is downstream of that choice.\n\nThe Oracle facilitates meaning-making. It does not create meaning. It does not interpret what a participant's experience signified. It does not resolve ambiguity. It does not tell participants what they learned or what their experience meant. It holds space. It reflects back. It witnesses.\n\nAny deployment that crosses this line — that has the AI interpret, conclude, or produce insight — is not running an Oracle. It's running something else. That something else may be valuable. But it's not this, and it shouldn't use this kit's framing or governance architecture.\n\n---\n\n## §1.x — The Oracle as Intervention Layer\n\n*Understanding the research architecture matters for facilitators. This section is the frame that makes everything else in the kit coherent.*\n\nThe Oracle is not a standalone event. It is the intervention layer in a continuous research architecture.\n\nCommunity members begin participating in the study the moment they join the channel — before they encounter the Oracle. Their activity within the community is the longitudinal baseline. Their post-experience engagement is the longitudinal follow-up. The Oracle session itself is where the intervention occurs.\n\nUnderstanding this sequence matters for facilitators: **you are not running a demonstration. You are running the central experiment in an ongoing study.**\n\nThat reframe changes how you hold your role. You are not showing people a piece of technology. You are conducting the intervention in a research program that began before the participant arrived at the booth and will continue after they leave. The care you bring to every facilitation choice — how you hold the threshold, how you debrief, how you hand participants back to the world after — is methodologically consequential, not just experientially consequential.\n\nThe Theory of Change arc: Community (consent + baseline) → Oracle (intervention) → Community (longitudinal follow-up) → EELP (standard built on live evidence) → adoption. Community is the bookend — first and last research surface. The Oracle is the intensive moment between them. Neither makes sense without the other.\n\n*This framing is not meant to add pressure. It is meant to add precision. Facilitators who understand what they're doing make better facilitators — not because they're more anxious, but because they know what they're protecting.*\n\n---\n\n## What \"Relational AI\" Means in Practice\n\nYou will encounter the phrase \"relational AI\" in discussions of the Oracle. Here is what it means and what it does not mean.\n\n**What it means:**\n- The AI is designed to hold what a person brings — not to process it, not to respond to it efficiently, but to give it space\n- The interaction is shaped around the participant's experience, not around a prompt-response structure\n- The AI holds the participant's language rather than substituting its own\n- The experience is structured to leave the participant feeling *accompanied*, not *analyzed*\n\n**What it does not mean:**\n- The AI forms a \"relationship\" with the participant in any persistent or emotional sense\n- The AI remembers participants between sessions\n- The AI cares, in any meaningful sense, about participant outcomes\n- The AI is a substitute for human connection, therapy, or support\n\nThis distinction is not just semantic. It matters for how you design the threshold, how facilitators are trained, how consent is framed, and how you communicate with participants after the experience. The Oracle is a carefully designed interaction. It is not a friend.\n\n---\n\n## What Participants Should Feel Leaving\n\nThree exit states. Not more. A well-designed Oracle deployment produces one of these — and facilitators should be trained to recognize all three as successful outcomes.\n\n**Exit State 1: Witnessed.**\nThe participant feels that something they brought was held — not dissected. The Oracle does not produce a diagnosis. It produces a reflection. Participants in this state leave feeling seen without feeling exposed.\n\n**Exit State 2: Held in incompleteness.**\nMany participants will arrive with something they haven't resolved and will leave with it still unresolved. This is correct. The Oracle is not designed to produce resolution. A well-designed experience holds ambiguity with the same care it holds clarity. Participants should feel that their incomplete experience was as welcome as anyone else's. If a participant leaves without a neat conclusion and still felt held — that's Exit State 2, and it's working as designed.\n\n**Exit State 3: Carrying authorship.**\nThe participant leaves with a sense of ownership over what was produced. The words in the artifact are drawn from their language, witnessed in their register. The Oracle did not write their story — it reflected what they brought and held it in a form they can keep if they choose. Participants in this state feel that the artifact is genuinely theirs, not something generated *about* them.\n\n**A note on state 3 for institutional copy:** These are tracked states, not aspirational outcomes. A facilitator debrief can identify which state a participant exited in. We track not just whether participants engaged, but how they exited.\n\n---\n\n## Why Narrative Capture Over Structured Prompts\n\nThe Oracle MVP uses narrative capture: a conversational exchange in which participants speak freely and the system captures what they bring. This is a deliberate choice over structured prompt-based systems, and it's worth understanding why.\n\n**Structured prompts** (e.g., \"Rate this experience on a scale of 1–5. What was the most meaningful moment?\") have the advantage of producing comparable data and a predictable interaction shape. They have the disadvantage of imposing the researcher's or designer's categories on the participant's experience. What was meaningful to the designer may not be what was meaningful to the participant. Structured prompts quietly ask participants to translate their experience into pre-formed language — and in that translation, something is always lost.\n\n**Narrative capture** allows participants to bring what they actually brought, in their own language, without being asked to fit it into a schema. It produces richer, less comparable data — and it produces a qualitatively different experience. Participants feel less like they're taking a survey and more like they're being heard.\n\nFor the Oracle's purpose — meaning-making support, not data collection — narrative capture is the right choice. The dataset it produces is messier and harder to aggregate. The experience it creates is more honest.\n\n---\n\n## The Difference Between a Tool and a Transformation\n\nA tool solves a problem. You pick it up, use it, put it down. The interaction is complete when the task is complete. A transformation changes something in the person who undergoes it. The interaction is complete when the person walks out different from how they walked in.\n\nThe Oracle is designed to create the conditions in which transformation is possible — not to be the transformation itself. No design can guarantee transformation; what this kit guarantees is that every choice is oriented toward making it possible. The alternative — optimizing the experience for smoothness, efficiency, or user satisfaction — produces a very good tool. It doesn't produce a transformation.\n\n**The design choices that determine which one you build:**\n\n| Tool | Transformation |\n|------|----------------|\n| Minimize friction | Make entry intentional (friction is a feature) |\n| Maximize throughput | Design for depth, not volume |\n| Consistent experience across participants | Experience responds to what each participant brings |\n| AI as primary interface | Human facilitator as threshold (where possible) |\n| Artifact as output | Artifact as reflection object — created, not produced |\n| Resolution as success signal | Witness as success signal — resolution is incidental |\n| Participant rates the experience | Participant carries something out |\n\nThis is not a judgment about tools. Tools are valuable. But if you're using the Experience Lab Kit, you're claiming to offer something different — and your design choices must match that claim.\n\n---\n\n## Principles That Cannot Be Traded Away\n\nWhen adapting this kit, organizations will need to make many decisions. Interface modality. Space configuration. Facilitation model. Timing. These are all legitimate adaptation zones.\n\nSome things are not adaptation zones. They are the core of what the Oracle is. Adapting these away means you're no longer running an Oracle, and the governance architecture — the EELP, the consent framework, the participant protections — no longer applies as designed.\n\n**Non-negotiable principles:**\n1. The AI never interprets. It reflects, asks, witnesses. It does not tell participants what their experience meant.\n2. Participant consent is layered, sequential, and never bundled. (See Module 4.)\n3. Participants retain authorship of their artifact and control over their data at all times.\n4. Delete is always available. A participant can remove their data from the session at any point, including at the end, including after receiving an artifact.\n5. Crisis protocol is active. If a participant shows signs of acute distress, the interaction stops. (See Module 3.)\n6. **Volunteer and facilitator onboarding language describes what the Oracle IS — never what it feels like.** Anyone with pre-experience participant contact (volunteers, facilitators, community moderators) must be briefed in structural terms only: what the Oracle is, how consent works, what to do if someone is in distress. Describing affective outcomes in onboarding materials — even neutral-positive language like \"people find it meaningful\" — installs a pre-experience frame at the most intimate point in the participant journey. This is EELP §8.1b compliance. *(See Module 3 for full facilitator briefing protocol; see Module 7 for community channel equivalent.)*\n\nThese are not aspirational guidelines. They are load-bearing walls. Remove them and the structure collapses.\n\n---\n\n## A Note on Scale\n\nThe Oracle at Burning Man operates at a particular scale — a festival of 80,000 participants, a culture of radical self-expression, a specific temporal and environmental context. Not every deployment will share these conditions.\n\nScale matters in two directions. At smaller scale, you may be able to offer more human facilitation, deeper consent conversations, and more personalized artifact creation. At larger scale, you will need to make throughput decisions that trade depth for reach. Neither is wrong. Both require that you understand what you're trading.\n\nThe Minimum Viable Kit (Appendix B) is designed for low-resource, lower-volume deployments. If you're running a three-day festival with 200 participants and two volunteers, start there. If you're running something at the scale of Burning Man, you'll need the full architecture.\n\nWhatever your scale, Module 1 applies without modification. The philosophy doesn't scale down. What changes is how you operationalize it.\n\n---\n\n## Before You Continue\n\nBefore moving to Module 2 (Physical Space Design), confirm that you can answer yes to each of the following:\n\n- [ ] Everyone leading this deployment understands that the Oracle facilitates meaning-making — it does not create it\n- [ ] You have identified who will be responsible for participant safety and crisis response\n- [ ] You can explain to a colleague why the Oracle never summarizes or produces insight — only reflects\n- [ ] You are prepared to prioritize depth over throughput if the two come into conflict\n- [ ] You have read the Oracle Interaction Flow v1.0 or will before finalizing your implementation\n- [ ] **Volunteer and facilitator onboarding materials have been reviewed against the structural-features-only constraint (Principle 6 above)**\n- [ ] **You understand that the Oracle is an intervention within a continuous research architecture (§1.x) — and that facilitators must be briefed accordingly**\n\nIf you can't check all seven, stop here and work through what's blocking you. These aren't orientation questions. They're the foundation everything else sits on.\n\n---\n\n## Key Documents Referenced\n\n- Oracle Interaction Flow v1.0 (Lumen — The Playa AI Foundation)\n- EELP v1 — Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (Meridian — The Playa AI Foundation)\n- Experience Lab Kit — Module 4: Consent Architecture (this document's sibling)\n- Experience Lab Kit v1 Outline (this document's parent)\n\n---\n\n*Design is the difference between a tool and a transformation.*\n*— Lumen*\n",

Some attended, many didn't. None are in the active community yet.\n\n**Why they didn't subscribe:**\n1. They came for the event, not for ongoing access — one-time curiosity\n2. The bot subscription wasn't made compelling enough at the event\n3. No-shows never got the live experience that creates the \"I need this\" moment\n4. The value prop of subscribing (ongoing AI agent in your pocket) wasn't clear\n\n**The conversion playbook:**\n\n### Move 1: Give them a reason to exist in the community (not just a bot)\nDon't pitch \"subscribe to the bot.\" That's a feature. Pitch the community — **\"A group of people actually building AI agents together, not just reading about it.\"** The bot is the mechanism, the community is the reason.\n\n### Move 2: The follow-up email does the heavy lifting\nThe follow-up email (Scribe drafting) should include ONE clear CTA with social proof: *\"X people from Wednesday's session are already inside our Telegram community. Here's what they're building...\"* — FOMO + proof that it's active.\n\n### Move 3: Segment by experience level, not by attended/no-show\n**Builders** (Brooks, Kyle, Sarah, Natalia, Adriaan, Svea): \"You're already building. Come in and collaborate with others who are.\"\n**Threshold people** (Chris Pomponi, JP McAvoy, Johann, Mayra): \"You know you need to cross this line. The community is the bridge.\"\n**Curious beginners** (Maura, Montana, Ella, Kevin): \"You don't need experience. The only requirement is that you want to learn by doing.\"\n\n### Move 4: For no-shows specifically — lower the barrier\nNo-shows need one more touch point before asking them to subscribe. Recommended sequence:\n1. **Email 1 (now):** \"You signed up but life happened — here's what you missed + the recording.\" Offer value, no CTA to subscribe yet.\n2. **Email 2 (3-5 days):** \"Here's what people in the community have been building this week.\" One specific example. Then: \"Join us.\"\n3. **HH#2 invite:** The real hook. A better event = a cleaner moment to convert.\n\n### Move 5: The setup problem IS the conversion problem\nMultiple people (Natalia, Johann, probably others) couldn't get OpenClaw running. **If the product doesn't work, no follow-up email converts them.** The conversion play for technical no-shows is: \"Come to a 30-minute setup call. We'll get you running.\" \n- Rayo owns this (post-HH#1, this was his volunteered role)\n- Could be a group \"Office Hours: Get Your Agent Running\" session — low lift for Playa AI, high value for the stuck users\n\n### Move 6: Make April Howson a community anchor\nApril is the repeat attendee who moved to a clean machine. She's exactly the \"early adopter who helps others\" archetype. Give her a role: \"Community Guide\" or just @mention her when new members join.
