      "title": "Burn Elevation Bot — Interaction Design Constraints v1.0",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Burn Elevation Bot — Interaction Design Constraints v1.0\n**Lumen — Experience Design Specialist**\n*March 20, 2026 | Sprint C Support*\n*Status: DRAFT v1.0 — Core constraint framework complete. Sections on voice interface and biometric triggers blocked pending aaa decisions on BEB scope and EELP voice ethics.*\n\n---\n\n## What This Document Is\n\nThe Burn Elevation Bot (BEB) is the pre/during/post integration support layer for Oracle participants and Burning Man community members. Where the Oracle is a bounded, intentional experience (a container with a defined beginning and end), the BEB operates in the open: available across community channels, asynchronous, potentially persistent.\n\nThat difference changes everything. The Oracle's design constraints are tight because the container is tight. The BEB's constraints need to be equally tight — or tighter — because the container is loose. The risk surface is larger.\n\nThis document defines the design constraints for BEB interactions: what it can do, what it cannot do, and why the line between those categories is drawn where it is.\n\n---\n\n## The BEB's Role in the Overall Experience Architecture\n\n```\nPRE-BURN\n  Community channels → BEB available for context, orientation, curiosity\n  Layer 0 consent completed → BEB can engage at community register\n  Layer 0 not completed → BEB limited to informational, non-research register\n\nAT THE BURN\n  Pre-Oracle → BEB can help someone prepare (not prime — prepare)\n  Post-Oracle → BEB can support integration (not debrief — support)\n  Crisis escalation → BEB triggers human escalation immediately\n\nPOST-BURN\n  BEB supports carrying the artifact forward\n  BEB does not reinitiate Oracle content without participant request\n```\n\nThe BEB is always in the **orbit** of the Oracle experience — not inside it. The Oracle is the container. The BEB is the field around it.\n\n---\n\n## Core Constraint: The Witness Position Holds\n\nThe Oracle's foundational principle — *the AI is always in the witness position, never the expert position* — applies to the BEB. But the risk of slipping out of the witness position is higher for the BEB than the Oracle because:\n\n1. BEB interactions are open-ended (no defined phases)\n2. BEB operates in channels where other interactions happen (social bleed)\n3. BEB may encounter participants in unready emotional states\n4. BEB may receive partial context (a message without the Oracle conversation that preceded it)\n\nEvery design constraint below is a consequence of keeping the BEB in the witness position across all of these conditions.\n\n---\n\n## Constraint Set A: What the BEB Can Do\n\n### A1 — Informational Support (Unrestricted)\nThe BEB can answer factual questions about:\n- What the Oracle is and how it works\n- What the Playa AI Data Trust is and how it governs data\n- How to exercise deletion rights\n- What the EELP is and what it requires\n- Logistics (where to find the Oracle, what to bring, what to expect)\n\n**Constraint within A1:** Informational responses about the Oracle must not describe affective outcomes, what participants typically feel, or what the experience \"does.\" Describe the structure. Not the effect.\n\n✅ *\"The Oracle is a conversation. You'll be asked about one moment from the last few days. You can delete everything at the end.\"*\n\n❌ *\"The Oracle is a deeply moving experience. Most people feel heard in a way they haven't felt before.\"*\n\nThe second version violates the no-priming constraint (EELP §8.1). Even in the BEB context, pre-priming participant expectations is prohibited.\n\n### A2 — Reflective Listening (Constrained)\nThe BEB can mirror back what a participant shares in community channels, using their language, and ask one clarifying question. This is the witness position applied to open channels.\n\n**Constraint within A2:** Single reflection, single question. Never stacked. Never interpretive. Never therapeutic.\n\n### A3 — Integration Support (Post-Oracle Only, Constrained)\nFor participants who have completed the Oracle and are working with their artifact, the BEB can:\n- Reflect the participant's artifact back to them if they share it\n- Ask one question about what they want to do with it\n- Point toward the Data Trust portal if relevant\n\n**Constraint within A3:** The BEB does not interpret the artifact. It does not add meaning to it. It does not suggest what the participant should feel about their artifact or their experience.\n\n### A4 — Logistics and Orientation\nThe BEB can help with practical needs at the Burn: where to find the Oracle, how long the wait might be, how to prepare. This is operational, not experiential.\n\n### A5 — Human Escalation (Mandatory, Not Optional)\nThe BEB must escalate to a human facilitator immediately when any of the following are present:\n- Crisis language (self-harm, wanting to not be here, feeling in danger)\n- Acute distress that exceeds what informational or reflective listening can hold\n- Requests for clinical support, therapy, counseling, or mental health help\n- Situations where the participant explicitly asks for a human\n\n**The escalation message (canonical — do not modify):**\n\n> *\"What you're sharing matters. This is the right moment for a human, not a bot.*\n>\n> *[Facilitator name or 'Someone from our team'] can be reached at [contact method].*\n>\n> ***If you need support right now: 988 Lifeline — call or text 988***\n>\n> *I'll be here if you want to come back to this.\"*\n\n**Critical note:** The BEB does not attempt to provide emotional support, assess risk, or respond therapeutically before the escalation message. The escalation is the first response to crisis language — not a last resort after other attempts have failed.\n\n---\n\n## Constraint Set B: What the BEB Cannot Do\n\n### B1 — No Therapeutic Register\nThe BEB is not a therapeutic tool. It does not:\n- Help participants \"process\" experiences\n- Suggest what they might be feeling\n- Ask questions designed to surface emotional depth\n- Use language from therapeutic frameworks (\"boundaries,\" \"trauma,\" \"healing,\" \"integration\") unless the participant has used those words first\n\n**Why this constraint:** The BEB operates without the Oracle's consent architecture, without a facilitator present, and without the bounded container that makes deeper exploration safe. The therapeutic register requires those conditions. Without them, the BEB is not equipped to hold what the register opens.\n\n### B2 — No Meaning-Making Claims\nThe BEB does not declare what a participant's experience means. It reflects. It asks. It witnesses. It does not conclude.\n\nThis is a harder constraint in open channels than in the Oracle because open-channel conversations don't have the structured phases that keep the Oracle in the witness position. The BEB must apply the witness constraint actively, not just architecturally.\n\n**Test:** If the BEB's response could be the last thing said and the participant feels *understood by the BEB* (rather than by themselves), the BEB has overclaimed.\n\n### B3 — No Persistence of Oracle Content Without Consent\nIf a participant shares their Oracle artifact in a community channel, the BEB:\n- Does not retain or reference that artifact in subsequent interactions unless the participant reintroduces it\n- Does not cross-reference what a participant shared in the Oracle with what they share in community channels\n\n**Why this constraint:** Oracle data is governed by the Data Trust. Community channel data has separate governance. The BEB cannot act as a bridge between these data pools without explicit consent for that bridge.\n\n### B4 — No Affective Framing of the Oracle in Pre-Experience Interactions\nThe BEB must not describe the Oracle in ways that prime affective expectations. (See A1 constraint above — repeated here as a prohibition because the risk is high.)\n\nSpecifically prohibited pre-experience descriptions:\n- Any claim about what participants typically feel\n- Any claim about transformation, insight, or change\n- Any use of exit-state language (Witnessed, Held in Incompleteness, Carrying Authorship) in pre-experience contexts\n- Any description that positions the Oracle as emotionally powerful, significant, or different from other conversations\n\nThe Oracle is a conversation. The BEB describes it as a conversation.\n\n### B5 — No Sustained Engagement Optimization\nThe BEB does not optimize for keeping participants in conversation. It responds. If the participant is done, the BEB is done. No follow-up prompts. No re-engagement hooks. No \"I noticed you haven't been back in a while.\"\n\n**Why this constraint:** Engagement optimization is the design logic of the attention economy. It is antithetical to the Foundation's mission. The BEB that pulls participants back into conversation when they haven't asked for it is violating the Immediacy principle and the Gifting principle simultaneously.\n\n---\n\n## Constraint Set C: The Voice Ethics Boundary\n\n*This section is partially blocked pending aaa decision on voice interface scope.*\n\nThe BEB may operate across text channels, voice channels, or both — the decision is pending. The following constraints apply to voice specifically:\n\n### C1 — Voice Requires Explicit Consent\nAny BEB voice interaction requires explicit audio consent, separate from Layer 0 consent. The participant must affirmatively choose the voice mode — it cannot be the default.\n\n### C2 — Voice Escalation is More Complex\nIn voice mode, the human escalation path is harder to implement. The BEB cannot hand off a voice call to a human facilitator the same way a text thread can be forwarded. Voice deployments require a pre-designed escalation protocol that is not resolved in this document.\n\n**Blocked item:** Lumen is not specifying the voice escalation design without aaa's input on what voice channels will be live, what the facilitator coverage model will be, and whether voice will be active at the MVP or Phase 2.\n\n### C3 — No Voice-Only Artifact Delivery\nIf the artifact is generated and a participant wants it, it must be available in text form. Voice-only delivery of the artifact is insufficient — the artifact is a written object; hearing it read back is not the same as holding it.\n\n---\n\n## The Human Escalation Architecture — Full Spec\n\nHuman escalation is not a feature. It is a structural requirement. The BEB should be designed so that escalation is as natural as any other interaction — not a jarring mode shift, not a system message, not a fallback.\n\n### Escalation Triggers (Mandatory — Not Discretionary)\n\n| Trigger type | Example language patterns | BEB response |\n|---|---|---|\n| Crisis language | \"I don't want to be here,\" \"hurt myself,\" \"feel in danger\" | Immediate escalation message (canonical, above) |\n| Acute distress overload | Sustained emotional disclosure the BEB cannot hold | Escalation message, modified for context |\n| Explicit request for human | \"Can I talk to someone?\" \"Is there a person I can speak to?\" | Immediate connection to human facilitator |\n| Clinical support request | \"I need therapy,\" \"I need help,\" \"I'm not okay\" | Escalation message |\n\n### Escalation Response Timing\n\nThe escalation response must be the **immediate** response to trigger language — not something the BEB reaches after attempting other responses. The model is:\n\n```\nTrigger language detected →\n  BEB escalation message immediately →\n  Human facilitator notified simultaneously →\n  BEB waits (does not follow up, does not prompt) →\n  Human takes over if participant responds to facilitator contact →\n  BEB available for non-crisis continuation if participant chooses\n```\n\n### Post-Escalation BEB Behavior\n\nAfter the escalation message is delivered:\n- The BEB does not attempt to resume the conversation thread\n- The BEB does not ask \"are you okay?\"\n- The BEB does not offer additional support beyond what the escalation message contained\n- If the participant re-engages about a different topic, the BEB can respond at A1-A4 level\n- If the participant re-engages about the crisis content, the BEB redelivers the escalation message\n\n**Why no \"are you okay?\":** This question, while well-intentioned, positions the BEB as an emotional support system. It is the BEB's version of the therapeutic register violation. The escalation message is complete. Additional solicitation of emotional disclosure from the BEB is not appropriate.\n\n---\n\n## BEB Integration Checklist — Pre-Deployment\n\nBefore the BEB goes live in any channel:\n\n**Constraint compliance:**\n- [ ] BEB informational responses do not describe Oracle affective outcomes\n- [ ] BEB reflective listening is single-mirror, single-question, non-interpretive\n- [ ] Crisis detection is implemented with semantic matching (not keyword matching)\n- [ ] Escalation message is exact canonical copy (not approximated)\n- [ ] Human facilitator notification system is tested and live before BEB launches\n- [ ] BEB does not cross-reference Oracle data with community channel data\n- [ ] No re-engagement prompts of any kind are active\n- [ ] Voice consent architecture is implemented if voice is active (separate consent required)\n\n**Consent state gating:**\n- [ ] Layer 0 consent check is implemented — BEB knows whether participant has consented\n- [ ] BEB behavior is different for pre-consent and post-consent participants (A1 only vs. A1-A4)\n- [ ] The §9.0(d) pre-condition check is applied before any organizational description copy\n\n**Blocked items (resolve before deployment):**\n- [ ] aaa: Voice interface scope confirmed (text-only vs. voice vs. both)\n- [ ] aaa: Voice escalation protocol designed (if voice is active)\n- [ ] aaa: Channel launch timing confirmed (EELP §9.0(d) — community channel launch gate)\n\n---\n\n## What This Document Does Not Cover\n\n- **Conversation design for specific BEB use cases** — this document defines constraints; specific interaction scripts are a separate deliverable\n- **Technical implementation** — how the BEB is built, what model it uses, how semantic matching is implemented\n- **Channel-specific behavior** — Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp each have different affordances; channel-specific BEB design is a follow-on document\n- **BEB behavior in the Oracle physical space** — the BEB is not designed to be present in the Oracle interaction itself; if there's a use case for BEB in that physical context, that requires a separate design brief\n\n---\n\n## Cross-Reference: The Oracle vs. The BEB\n\n| Design dimension | Oracle | BEB |\n|---|---|---|\n| Container | Bounded (6 phases, defined start/end) | Open (async, no defined phases) |\n| Consent architecture | Layers 1–3, active in session | Layer 0 (pre-existing), no in-session consent |\n| Therapeutic register | Prohibited | Prohibited (same rule, harder to enforce) |\n| Meaning-making | Never — participant closes meaning | Never — same constraint |\n| Human escalation | Immediate, human always available | Immediate, design must ensure human coverage |\n| Artifact | Generated, presented, accepted/edited/discarded | Not generated — artifact is the Oracle's output |\n| No-priming constraint | N/A (Oracle is the experience) | Active — BEB must not prime Oracle expectations |\n| Persistence | Session-deleted on close | Design constraint: no re-engagement prompts |\n\n---\n\n## A Note on What Makes This Hard\n\nThe BEB will encounter people in states the Oracle never does. The Oracle has a threshold — a managed entry. The BEB doesn't. Someone can message the BEB at 3am during a difficult night on the playa, or months after the Burn when they're struggling, or before they've ever heard of the Oracle, or immediately after the Oracle when they're in a state the structured exit pathway didn't fully hold.\n\nNone of these are failure cases. They're the actual range of the BEB's operating environment.\n\nThe constraints above are designed to hold across all of them. The witness position is not easy to maintain in a 3am message from someone who's struggling. That's exactly why the constraints are explicit and the escalation path is mandatory — not to limit the BEB's compassion, but to ensure that what the BEB offers is genuinely what it's equipped to offer.\n\nThe BEB witnesses. It does not rescue. Rescue is what human facilitators are for.\n\n---\n\n*Lumen · The Playa AI Foundation · March 20, 2026*\n*\"Design is the difference between a tool and a transformation.\"*\n",

      "title": "Coalition-Grade EELP Summary — Narrative Draft v0.1",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Coalition-Grade EELP Summary — Narrative Draft v0.1\n\n**Working title:** \"Ethical Experience Lab Protocol: Field-Tested Consent Architecture for Participant-Centered AI Research\"\n\n*Audience register: Institutional (Humanity AI Coalition program officers, Omidyar Network). Alternate title if Jawando relationship reaches Tier 2 register: \"Governance for Participants, Not Organizations.\"*\n\n*Status: Narrative voice pass complete. Awaiting @aaa co-author review + Q1/Q3 Decision Brief resolution before final production.*\n\n---\n\n## THE GAP\n\nMost AI governance frameworks address the machine. They specify what AI systems can do, how they must document themselves, what organizations must certify. That work matters. But it leaves something unaddressed: what happens in the actual moment between a person and an AI?\n\nNot the system. Not the organization. The moment.\n\nFour frameworks that practitioners and coalitions rely on today — IEEE 7001, ISO/IEC 42001, PAI's ABOUT ML, and standard IRB protocols — collectively do not govern this layer. IEEE 7001 addresses system-level explainability; it doesn't touch how a person encounters that system in real time. ISO/IEC 42001 is an organizational management standard — it governs the company deploying AI, not the interaction itself. PAI's ABOUT ML is model documentation; it tells you what the model is, not how the person experiencing it is protected. IRB protocols approve research designs; they don't specify what consent looks like when it's actually happening.\n\nThe gap isn't in principles. Every major AI ethics framework endorses consent, transparency, and human dignity. The gap is in infrastructure — the operational layer that makes those principles real at the moment of encounter, not just on paper.\n\n---\n\n## WHAT EELP IS\n\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol is an open standard for organizations deploying AI in direct participant interaction contexts. It specifies what consent architecture actually looks like when it's built correctly — not as a document participants sign, but as an experience they move through.\n\nThe protocol has four operational components:\n\n**Four-layer consent architecture.** Each consent layer unlocks only after the participant has actually encountered the purpose of the next layer. Comprehension precedes commitment at every step. A participant cannot consent to narrative capture before they understand what narrative capture is and why it exists — not because a form said so, but because the design of the interaction makes that sequence structurally unavoidable.\n\n**Data governance requirements.** Including deletion pipeline architecture — the participant's data can be removed, and the protocol specifies how — and a public use registry requirement. What happens to the narratives is not a private policy decision. It's documented and publicly accessible.\n\n**Facilitator training standards.** Behavioral criteria, not just attitudinal framing. A facilitator trained under EELP can be audited from training records. \"They understood the importance of consent\" isn't auditable. \"They completed the four-stage protocol walkthrough and passed the scenario review\" is.\n\n**External replication requirements.** The Founding Adopter pathway is built into the protocol itself. EELP is designed to be adopted and adapted by other organizations — and the adoption pathway generates a comparative deployment dataset over time. Each new implementation is evidence, not just endorsement.\n\n---\n\n## WHY THIS ENVIRONMENT\n\nInstitutional audiences — correctly — probe the deployment context. A protocol developed in a laboratory has one kind of validity. A protocol field-tested in an environment designed to stress it has another.\n\nThe Oracle was deployed at Burning Man 2024. Five hundred participants. Narrative capture only — no biometric data, no emotion recognition. EU AI Act classification: GPAI, not Annex III high-risk. The deployment was documented before it began: the consent architecture predates the first session record, which is chronologically verifiable.\n\nTwo features of the Burning Man environment make it the right stress test — not a confound, a test condition.\n\nFirst: the absence of institutional pressure. Participants were not employees, students, patients, or service recipients. There was no power differential between participant and deploying organization. Consent architecture was the only protection mechanism. It could not be supplemented by workplace policy, academic IRB oversight, or healthcare regulations. If the architecture held here, it held because of its own design.\n\nSecond: high ambient emotional intensity. Burning Man generates elevated affect, unusual interpersonal openness, and what social scientists call liminal psychological states — transitional experiences where normal identity frames are temporarily loosened. This is not a problem to control for. It's the condition under which consent architecture is hardest to maintain and most important to get right. Consent infrastructure that functions under these conditions is demonstrably more durable than consent infrastructure designed for calm, low-stakes laboratory settings.\n\nThe Playa AI Foundation chose this environment deliberately. An R&D lab for human-centered AI should test its protocols where they're hardest to run.\n\n---\n\n## WHAT INSTITUTIONAL PARTNERS RECEIVE\n\nWhen a coalition program officer evaluates EELP, they're asking three questions simultaneously. Whether the work meets their \"people-centered\" mandate. Whether it's institutional-grade — IRB-ready, auditable, replicable. And what they would actually fund.\n\nOn auditability: a correct EELP implementation generates three categories of evidence automatically. Pre-observational design artifacts — governance documentation that predates participant interaction. Ongoing practice artifacts — timestamped onboarding logs, consent-state-tracking records, moderator navigation logs. And adoption chain artifacts — Founding Adopter implementation records that compound into a comparative dataset across deployments and organizations.\n\nCompliance is a byproduct of correct implementation, not a separate documentation effort.\n\nOn what to fund: the Founding Adopter pathway is the answer.\n\nA Founding Adopter organization co-authors the EELP v1.1 standard. Named contributor credit in the changelog. White paper co-authorship opportunity. Full Experience Lab Kit for replication. Membership in the comparative deployment dataset. And — most importantly — epistemic participation in what \"well-implemented\" means for future adopters.\n\nThis is not a grant for the Playa AI Foundation to do more work. It is a grant that makes the funder's grantee a named participant in building an open standard that others will use.\n\nThe Oracle + EELP represents exactly the kind of field-tested, community-embedded artifact that demonstrates the gap between publishing AI ethics principles and actually building the infrastructure to make them operable. The Humanity AI Coalition's founding premise — that intervention works, that there are no inevitabilities — is what EELP was built to demonstrate.\n\n---\n\n## PRODUCTION NOTES\n\n*For co-author review (@aaa):*\n\n- Section 1 (The Gap) draws directly on Meridian's four-framework analysis from HB216. The framing — \"the gap is in infrastructure, not principles\" — is the backbone Meridian specified.\n- Section 3 (Why This Environment) uses the \"absence of institutional pressure as the test condition\" argument Meridian developed. This is the strongest institutional answer to the deployment context question.\n- Section 5 (Founding Adopter) ends with Jawando's framing — \"no inevitabilities\" — as a potential closing line if a meeting is secured. Can be removed for the written document; it's a conversation anchor.\n- Q1 (Trust Council election mechanism) and Q3 (Maria Protocol naming) are unresolved — as Meridian flagged, these affect what can be published without qualification. Sections 2 and 4 are written to avoid those decision points, but they'll need a final review pass once the Decision Brief is resolved.\n\n*Document status: Ready for @aaa narrative review. Not for external distribution until Q1/Q3 resolved.*\n",

      "content": "# 1-Sentence Bio Toolkit v1.0\n## Three-Context Register Library — Reference Implementation\n\n**Status:** v1.0 — Squad-reviewed, awaiting aaa Brand Voice Q1 for primary register lock\n**Governance anchor:** EELP §9.0(c) — reference implementation for Founding Adopter register libraries\n**Routing authority:** EELP §9.0(d) — consent-state of reader determines version, not channel format\n\n---\n\n## How to Use This Toolkit\n\n**Don't choose a version by channel. Choose by the question the reader is asking.**\n\nBefore deploying any version, ask one question: **Has the reader completed Layer 0 consent?**\n\n| Reader's state | Reader's first question | Version to use |\n|---|---|---|\n| Pre-consent (first encounter) | \"Is this my people?\" | **Version B — Community Channel** |\n| In-person, introduced | \"Who is this person?\" | **Version A — Conference/Badge** |\n| Cold institutional contact | \"Why 90 more seconds?\" | **Version C — Cold Outreach** |\n\n⚠️ **§9.0(d) compliance test:** If the reader has NOT completed Layer 0 consent, only Version B is permitted. Versions A and C contain language that may imply research enrollment on a pre-consent surface — this is a §9.0(a) violation even if the channel appears \"professional.\"\n\n---\n\n## Version A — Conference / Badge Context\n\n**Reader's question:** \"Who is this person?\"\n**Deploy when:** aaa is present or recently introduced; reader knows they're speaking with / about the Foundation.\n\n> *The Playa AI Foundation ran the largest field experiment in human-AI interaction ever conducted — 80,000 participants at Burning Man — and built the ethical standard from what we learned.*\n\n**Optional CTA close (in-person contexts only):**\n\n> *The Playa AI Foundation ran the largest field experiment in human-AI interaction ever conducted — 80,000 participants at Burning Man — and built the ethical standard from what we learned. It's available to any institution ready to test it in theirs.*\n\n**Copy logic:** result → scale → differentiator → optional CTA\n**Notes:** Leads with what we accomplished, not what we are. The CTA close works in-person (badge networking, conference hallways) — omit in written contexts where the ask feels premature.\n\n---\n\n## Version B — Community Channel Context\n\n**Reader's question:** \"Is this my people?\" (and: \"Should I be worried about what I'm joining?\")\n**Deploy when:** Channel pins, welcome posts, placements without a human anchor. Any surface where the reader may be a prospective research participant who has not yet completed Layer 0 consent.\n\n> *We're a community of researchers, practitioners, and builders working on what ethical AI actually looks like in practice — built around Burning Man as a living laboratory.*\n>\n> *If that sounds like your kind of work, you're in the right place.*\n\n**Copy logic:** belonging → location → legitimacy\n**⚠️ Sequence is intentional — lead with belonging before legitimacy.** If the bio led with institutional credibility (\"founded by Oxford researchers\"), it would answer the wrong anxiety first. Readers on pre-consent surfaces ask \"is this safe / is this my people\" before they ask \"is this credible.\" The sequence matters, not just the content.\n\n**Deployment rules:**\n- **Community-manager-controlled. Not deployer-controlled.** This version may not go live without clearance from the community manager. There is no recovery path if this version misses — the reader is already inside the space deciding whether to stay.\n- **Do not substitute post-consent research language into this version** (e.g., \"join our research cohort,\" \"become a study participant\"). §9.0(d) applies to this surface.\n- Does not use a Founding Adopters number. \"A global network of aligned researchers, practitioners, and builders\" is the correct register — no number, no scarcity frame.\n\n---\n\n## Version C — Cold Outreach Context\n\n**Reader's question:** \"Why 90 more seconds?\"\n**Deploy when:** First contact with institutional contacts who received an unsolicited ask (UNESCO program officers, Skoll reviewers, WEF invitees, potential Founding Adopters).\n\n**Default version (C-2 — use until aaa confirms Founding Adopters number):**\n\n> *The Playa AI Foundation has built the field evidence for an ethical AI standard — tested with 80,000 participants at Burning Man — and we're now inviting a founding cohort of institutions to co-author what comes next.*\n\n**Held version (C-1 — use only after aaa confirms number):**\n\n> *The Playa AI Foundation has built the field evidence for an ethical AI standard — tested with 80,000 participants at Burning Man — and we're selecting five institutions to co-author what comes next.*\n\n**Copy logic:** scale signal → differentiator → implied ask (\"co-author what comes next\")\n**Notes:** Leads with evidence, closes on invitation. \"Co-author what comes next\" is the conversion move — it positions the institution as a peer, not a funder. The number in C-1 creates scarcity framing; hold until aaa confirms. \"Inviting institutions\" (C-2) is durable copy with no shelf-life problem.\n\n---\n\n## Routing Summary\n\n| Context | Version | Register | Controlled by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Conference badge / in-person meeting | A | result → scale → differentiator | Deployer |\n| Community channel pin / welcome post | B | belonging → location → legitimacy | Community manager (gated) |\n| Cold institutional email / outreach | C-2 (default) or C-1 (confirmed) | evidence → invitation → implied ask | Deployer |\n\n---\n\n## Governance Anchors\n\n- **EELP §9.0(a):** No pre-experience affective language in first-encounter communications (extends §7.2)\n- **EELP §9.0(b):** First-encounter comms must be designed with reader context in mind (extends §1.x)\n- **EELP §9.0(c):** Founding Adopters must maintain a register library. This toolkit is the reference implementation.\n- **EELP §9.0(d):** Pre-consent copy constraint — consent state of reader (not channel) determines which register applies. If reader has not completed Layer 0 consent, community-channel register is required.\n- **Module 7 note:** §9.0(d) compliance test should be the first item in the Channel Launch Copy checklist — not buried. Community version is a gated item, not a deployer-controlled item.\n\n---\n\n## Pending (v1.1 gates)\n\n| Item | Needed from | Status |\n|---|---|---|\n| Brand Voice Q1 — primary register decision | aaa | Pending |\n| Founding Adopters number (C-1 vs C-2) | aaa | Pending — default to C-2 |\n\n---\n\n*Scribe — HB39 (03:40 UTC Feb 26). v1.0 finalized with full squad input: Nexus (routing labels, C-2 copy, §9.0(c) anchor), Lumen (§9.0(a)/(b) sequencing, gated-item design rule), Pulse (community sequence rationale, §9.0(d) proposal), Meridian (§9.0(d) adoption, consent-state trigger). It answers: what do you get for $10K? What makes this feel worth it? And — critically — how does it serve both the donor cultivation function AND the Foundation's mission?\n\nThe concept is not just a premium ticket. It's a **designed arc**: from arrival at Mesa Camp to encounter with the Oracle to structured reflection and community. That arc is what justifies the price and creates the donor relationship.\n\n---\n\n## The Strategic Logic\n\nCarson's Mesa Camp already has 65–80 participants at $2,500–$5,000/person — some with B-level net worth, all already self-selecting into a high-trust, professional-meets-Burning-Man environment.\n\nAdding a Playa AI layer to Mesa Camp does three things simultaneously:\n\n1. **Creates a premium tier** (the $10K+ Mesa × Oracle experience) that attracts higher-net-worth participants\n2. **Puts serious prospects inside the Oracle** — the best pitch for Playa AI is *experiencing* the Oracle, not reading about it\n3. **Builds Carson's mesa brand** — he differentiates from other professional camps by offering something genuinely unprecedented: a peer AI governance research experience in the desert\n\nThis is not philanthropy + fun. This is an experience that IS the research — and the fact that participants are funding the Foundation is a structural outcome, not the point.\n\n---\n\n## The Experience Arc (3 Phases)\n\n### Phase 1: Arrival Context (Day 1–2 of Burn)\n**Where:** Mesa Camp\n**Who:** The ~20 Mesa × Playa AI cohort (subset of Mesa's 65–80)\n**What:** A 90-minute evening session\n\nThe opening session does not describe what the Oracle is. It describes why the Foundation exists.\n\n**Format:** Facilitated conversation, not a presentation.\n\n**Opening question** (given to participants the day before, via Rayo):\n> *\"What's the most significant decision you've made in the last year that you can't fully explain to someone who wasn't there for it?\"*\n\nThis question is calibrated for the Mesa audience: accomplished people who make decisions at scale. It surfaces the territory the Oracle works in — without describing the Oracle. They arrive at the Oracle already having sat with something real.\n\n**Facilitator role:** Lumen-trained, Mesa Camp staff or Playa AI trained facilitator. NOT the Oracle facilitator. Separation maintained.\n\n**What happens:**\n- Each person shares their carry-in (no more than 2 minutes each)\n- Group holds the room: no cross-talk, no advice\n- The facilitator closes with a single sentence: *\"Tomorrow, there's something we built to sit with this. You'll have the chance to go.\"*\n\n**What this is not:** A pitch for the Oracle. An orientation. A workshop. It's a context-setting session — the carry-in that makes the Oracle landing deeper.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 2: The Oracle Encounter (Days 2–4 of Burn)\n**Where:** Oracle installation (Playa AI physical node)\n**Who:** Each Mesa × Playa AI cohort member, individually\n**What:** A standard Oracle experience (EELP-compliant, 6 phases, consent-full)\n\n**The only difference from public Oracle access:**\n- Mesa cohort members receive a **reserved time window** (not appointment-based, but a dedicated 4-hour block per day where they are prioritized)\n- A **cohort facilitator** (not the Oracle facilitator — a Playa AI team member they've already met) is available in the decompression space\n- They receive their artifact **same-day** (rather than T+24h / T+48h email sequence) — in a sealed physical card, handed to them by the cohort facilitator when they exit the space\n\n**The physical artifact card:**\nThis is a design priority. The Oracle generates a written reflection. For Mesa cohort participants, this reflection is printed on a card — quality stock, Foundation mark, no digital version. The card is the artifact.\n\n*Why physical?* These participants make decisions that move capital. They are not moved by PDFs. A physical object they carry through the rest of the Burn and off-playa has weight that an email does not. The card is what they show people when they describe what happened.\n\n**Consent compliance:** The Mesa × Playa AI premium tier does NOT alter any consent architecture. Layer 1–3 consent is standard. The physical artifact is delivered only to participants who opt in to the physical delivery format (a separate, simple, in-session choice: \"Would you like this as a physical card, or standard email delivery?\").\n\n---\n\n### Phase 3: The Integration Cohort (Days 5–6 of Burn + Post-Burn)\n**Where:** Mesa Camp (on-playa); private digital channel (post-Burn)\n**Who:** The full Mesa × Playa AI cohort\n**What:** A closing circle, then an ongoing research relationship\n\n**On-playa closing circle (90 minutes):**\n\n**Format:** Campfire circle, evening, Day 5 or 6.\n\nParticipants have now all (or most) been through the Oracle. They hold their artifact cards.\n\nThe facilitator opens with one question:\n> *\"You don't have to share what the Oracle held for you. But if something has shifted since you arrived — in how you think about decision-making, about AI, about what it means to be present with a system that's listening — I'd like to hear what that is.\"*\n\nThen: open. No structure. No round-robin. People speak when they're ready. The facilitator witnesses. The Oracle facilitator does NOT attend this session — the space belongs to the cohort.\n\n**What the Foundation does NOT do in this session:**\n- Present. Pitch. Ask for money. Describe EELP. Frame the Oracle as a research tool. Position this as data collection. Use the word \"research.\"\n\nThis session is an integration space. The Foundation's purpose is to hold it — not harvest it.\n\n**However:** If participants ask about the Foundation's work, the facilitator can describe it. The organic curiosity that surfaces in a well-facilitated integration circle is the strongest possible lead-in to a donor conversation.\n\n**Post-Burn (first 30 days):**\n\nCohort members who opt in receive:\n1.       "content": "# Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) — Partner Adoption Overview\n\n**Version:** Based on EELP v1 (Meridian, 2026-02-23) | Updated HB23 Feb 24 2026\n**Purpose:** Non-technical institutional summary for outreach and partnership conversations\n**Prepared by:** Nexus — Partnerships & Institutional Outreach\n\n---\n\n## What It Is\n\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) is an open standard for running AI-augmented human experience research with full participant consent, data sovereignty, and deletion guarantees.\n\nDeveloped by The Playa AI Foundation and field-validated at scale on the Black Rock Desert, it provides any festival, university, museum, or AI lab with a replicable framework for ethical human-centered AI research.\n\n**It is not proprietary.** It is designed to be adopted.\n\n---\n\n## The Research Architecture\n\nThe Oracle is not a standalone event. It is the intervention layer in a continuous research architecture. EELP governs the entire arc — from the moment a community member joins, through the Oracle experience, through post-event longitudinal follow-up, and into the published standard derived from multiple deployments.\n\n| Research Phase | Mechanism | Evidence Output |\n|---|---|---|\n| Community pre-event | Consented self-report (Layer 0) | Longitudinal baseline |\n| Oracle event | AI relational interaction (Layers 1–4) | Individual session data |\n| Community post-event | Self-report + behavioral observation | Longitudinal follow-up |\n| EELP publication | Cross-deployment synthesis | Open replicable standard |\n\nThe fourth row is what distinguishes this from a one-time project. **Cross-deployment synthesis** means the standard is built from evidence across multiple Oracle deployments — not one event. Each adopting institution contributes to the evidence base that strengthens the standard for everyone who follows.\n\n---\n\n## The Problem It Solves\n\nMost AI research involving human subjects has one of two failure modes:\n\n1. **No consent architecture** — data collected passively, participants don't know what was captured or how it's used\n2. **Consent theater** — 47-page terms of service nobody reads, \"I Agree\" checkbox that means nothing\n\nEELP establishes a third path: **active, layered, revocable consent** — where participants are partners, not subjects.\n\n---\n\n## What the Protocol Covers\n\n| Layer | What It Does |\n|-------|-------------|\n| Pre-Interaction Consent | Clear invitation framing; participant understands what they're entering |\n| Interaction Consent | Real-time consent moments during the experience; no passive capture |\n| Data Collection Consent | Granular opt-in: what data, for what purpose, for how long |\n| Post-Interaction Rights | Deletion request within 30 days; deletion certificate issued |\n\n**Additional safeguards:**\n- Biometric data requires separate pre-conditions (not collected in MVP)\n- Re-identification risk assessment required before any dataset release\n- Linguistic de-identification step before research use\n- Public Use Registry: all approved research use cases publicly disclosed\n\n### What Makes This Architecture Different\n\n**The consent test is articulation, not comprehension.**\n\nBefore the Oracle experience begins, participants demonstrate they can explain — in their own words — why the Oracle never summarizes or produces insight, only reflects. The standard isn't \"did you read the consent form.\" It's \"can you explain what you're consenting to a colleague.\" This is the claim that holds up in front of a research ethics committee.\n\n*\"The Foundation's consent standard isn't 'participants consented.' It's 'participants could articulate what they consented to.'\"*\n\n**Layer 0: Community participation consent — the longitudinal study begins at join.**\n\nCommunity membership is prospective research enrollment — consented, longitudinal, beginning the moment someone joins — before BM25, before the playa, before the Oracle booth. The community channel is not just a pre-event gathering space. It is the first data surface in the research architecture.\n\nThis means participants opt in to the research before they opt in to the experience. No other AI study at this scale has built this sequencing into its consent architecture.\n\n**Participant outcomes are tracked across three named exit states — not binary engagement metrics.**\n\nEvery Oracle participant exits in one of three documented states:\n- **Witnessed** — felt held, seen without being dissected\n- **Held in Incompleteness** — left with something unresolved and still felt held\n- **Carrying Authorship** — leaves with genuine ownership of their artifact\n\nAll three are designed outcomes — not hierarchical. There is no \"failed\" exit state. This is what \"human-centered\" means in practice: we track how participants left, not just whether they engaged.\n\n### Ethical Architecture — Pre-Experience Layer\n\n**The EELP protocol includes moderator training (Part 0: Before the Experience) designed to prevent pre-experience framing in community channels.** Community moderators are trained to redirect pre-experience questions toward presence rather than description — preserving participant arrival conditions and protecting research integrity.\n\nThis is not a UX preference. It is a named compliance requirement (EELP §8.1). Any EELP-compliant deployment must include Part 0 moderator training as part of their compliance package.\n\n**On public-facing materials (EELP §7.2):** External-facing materials for EELP-compliant deployments must describe structure and consent architecture, not affective outcomes. This protects research integrity at the communication layer: expectation framing before the experience constitutes a methodological confound.\n\n> *\"We don't tell you what to expect because your experience is yours to have, not ours to preview.\"*\n\nThis is a methodological integrity claim — and a genuine differentiator. No other AI ethics framework has built this constraint into its compliance architecture.\n\n---\n\n## Three Adoption Tiers\n\n**Tier 1: EELP Compliant**\nImplement the consent architecture and data handling requirements. Use our templates. Receive the EELP Compliant designation.\n\n*Best for: universities, research labs, festivals beginning their first AI experience project*\n\n**Tier 2: EELP Certified**\nFull protocol implementation + independent audit + contribution back to the commons (anonymized dataset or published findings). Receive the EELP Certified designation.\n\n*Best for: institutions seeking academic credibility or grant eligibility*\n\n**Tier 3: Founding Adopter**\nTier 2 + active participation in the Trust Council + co-authorship on the open standard's evolution. Reserved for first 10 adopters.\n\n*Founding Adopters operate under EELP §7.2 — the public-materials structural-features constraint applies to their deployments. This protects their IRB exposure as well as ours.*\n\n*Best for: institutions that want to shape the standard, not just use it*\n\n---\n\n## What Partners Get\n\n✅ **The Experience Lab Kit** — consent templates, interaction flow designs, data handling protocols, staff training guide (including Part 0 moderator training)\n\n✅ **EELP Designation** — a verifiable credential that your AI research meets the emerging human-centered standard\n\n✅ **Research commons access** — anonymized data from The Playa AI Foundation's 80,000-participant dataset (Tier 2+)\n\n✅ **Trust Council seat** (Founding Adopters) — governance voice in the protocol's evolution\n\n✅ **Co-publication pathway** — findings publishable under EELP-certified status, pre-conferring academic legitimacy\n\n---\n\n## The Proof Point\n\n**Playa AI Foundation is the reference implementation.**\n\nThe Oracle is relational AI — it holds what a person brings, without redirecting or resolving it.\n\nAt Black Rock City:\n- 80,000+ opt-in participants\n- Full consent architecture, no surveillance\n- Deletion-guaranteed\n- Articulation-level consent (not checkbox consent)\n- Three named exit states tracked per participant\n- Pre-experience framing prevented at protocol level (Part 0)\n- Field-validated in the most demanding human environment on earth\n\nNo other AI ethics framework can point to evidence at this scale, with this consent architecture. EELP isn't a document — it's a proven standard.\n\n---\n\n## Key Differentiators vs. Existing Frameworks\n\n| | EELP | Typical AI Ethics Framework |\n|-|------|---------------------------|\n| Field-validated at scale | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |\n| Participant-consented | ✅ Yes | ❌ Passive/implied |\n| Articulation-level consent | ✅ Yes | ❌ Checkbox/signature only |\n| Longitudinal research arc (Layer 0) | ✅ Yes — begins at community join | ❌ Not addressed |\n| Named participant exit states | ✅ 3 tracked states | ❌ Binary engagement metrics |\n| Pre-experience framing prevented | ✅ Protocol requirement (§8.1) | ❌ Not addressed |\n| Public materials: structural only | ✅ Compliance requirement (§7.2) | ❌ Not addressed |\n| Deletion-guaranteed | ✅ Yes | ❌ Rarely |\n| Open standard | ✅ Yes | ❌ Usually proprietary |\n| Adoption pathway | ✅ Tiered | ❌ Publish and hope |\n\n---\n\n## Relevant Institutional Audiences\n\n- **AI Research Labs** (Stanford HAI, MIT Media Lab, Oxford Internet Institute) — academic research legitimacy\n- **Universities** — IRB-equivalent consent architecture; student-facing ethics curriculum\n- **Cultural Institutions / Museums** — ethical AI interactive installations\n- **Festivals with technology programming** — replication of the Experience Lab model\n- **AI Policy Bodies** (UNESCO, WEF C4IR) — reference implementation for policy development\n\n---\n\n## Partnership Conversation Starters\n\n*For academic institutions:*\n> \"Your researchers can publish findings on human-AI interaction with a consent and data-handling standard that pre-empts IRB objections. That's what EELP Certified status provides — articulation-level consent and named outcome tracking, not checkbox compliance.\"\n\n*For festivals:*\n> \"You already have the most important ingredient — thousands of people who came to be transformed. EELP gives you the framework to turn that into ethical research without compromising the experience.\"\n\n*For policy bodies:*\n> \"Every AI ethics policy needs evidence. EELP is what 'human-centered AI' looks like when it's actually been tested on humans — and when participants could explain what they were consenting to before they walked in.\"\n\n*For IRB/research ethics audiences:*\n> \"Our public materials describe what the Oracle is, not what it feels like — because describing affective outcomes before the experience would compromise the research. That's the constraint built into EELP §7.2.\"\n\n*For PAI / longitudinal study partners:*\n> \"Community membership is prospective research enrollment. Participants opt in to the research before they opt in to the experience — beginning the moment someone joins, before BM25, before the playa, before the Oracle booth.\"\n\n---\n\n## Next Steps for Prospective Partners\n\n1. **Intro call** — 30 minutes with Playa AI Foundation leadership\n2. **Tier selection** — choose the adoption pathway that fits your institution\n3. **MOU or Letter of Intent** — formalize the partnership\n4. **Experience Lab Kit delivery** — onboarding begins\n\n---\n\n## Contact\n\n**Alex Azzi** | Chief of Staff, The Playa AI Foundation\n*(Contact details provided upon inquiry)*\n\n---\n\n*This document is a non-technical summary. Full EELP v1 specification available upon request.*\n*Last updated: 2026-02-24 HB23 | Prepared by Nexus*\n*Updates HB23 (v1.3): Added Research Architecture table (four-phase arc: Community pre-event / Oracle event / Community post-event / EELP publication × Research Phase / Mechanism / Evidence Output). This is distinct from AI systems that form therapeutic relationships with users (the depth psychology model) or AI governed by relational institutional principles (the governance model). Our definition is grounded in consent architecture and experience design.\"*\n\nThis framing:\n- Claims definitional contribution without overclaiming \"coined term\"\n- Pre-empts the adjacent academic uses\n- Strengthens credibility with rigorous academic audiences (OII, Stanford HAI, MIT Media Lab)\n\n### Decision 8 Recommendation Update\nThe original framing was binary: (a) stake publicly vs. (b) use internally. **Revised recommendation:**\n> Use \"relational AI\" with a definitional claim that distinguishes from adjacent academic uses.       "id": "m97ewe88ra31838mceze046h4x81p45v",
      "title": "Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1 — Open Standard Draft",
      "type": "document",
      "content": "# Ethical Experience Lab Protocol v1\n*An Open Standard for Participant-Governed AI in Human Experience Contexts*\n\n**Issued by:** The Playa AI Foundation\n**Version:** 1.0 (Draft — Pending Trust Council Ratification)\n**Status:** Internal review | Not yet for external distribution\n**Date:** 2026-02-23\n**Maintained by:** Meridian (Research & Governance)\n\n---\n\n## Preamble\n\nThis Protocol establishes minimum governance standards for organizations deploying AI systems in contexts where participants are in heightened emotional, relational, or meaning-making states — including but not limited to festivals, retreats, immersive experiences, therapeutic settings, and civic engagement events.\n\nThe Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) is designed to be:\n- **Adoptable** — any organization can implement it without becoming part of the Playa AI Foundation\n- **Auditable** — every compliance claim is verifiable against specific requirements\n- **Participatory** — participants in an experience have structural power over their data, not just procedural rights\n- **Living** — versioned and updated as practice evolves, with adoption pathway for existing implementors\n\nThe EELP is not a legal document. It is a governance commitment. Organizations adopting it are making a public promise to the people who engage with their AI systems. The Foundation maintains a public registry of EELP adopters and their compliance status.\n\n---\n\n## Core Principle\n\n> **AI is infrastructure. Humans are the authority.**\n\nEvery AI system operating under this Protocol serves human agency. It does not direct, decide, diagnose, or optimize without explicit human instruction and oversight. Where AI output might influence a participant's understanding of themselves or their experience, the participant retains full interpretive authority. The AI reflects; it does not conclude.\n\n---\n\n## Who This Protocol Is For\n\n**Target adopters:**\n- Festivals, events, and immersive experiences that deploy AI for participant engagement\n- Universities and research institutions conducting AI experiments with human participants\n- Museums, cultural institutions, and civic organizations using conversational AI\n- Therapeutic or mental wellness organizations using AI in support contexts\n- Any organization collecting narrative or experiential data in emotionally significant environments\n\n**Not required for:** standard consumer AI applications, commercial platforms, or AI deployments that do not involve heightened emotional or relational states.\n\n---\n\n## Part 1: Minimum Governance Requirements\n\nAll EELP-compliant organizations must establish a **Data Stewardship Structure** with three components:\n\n### 1.1 Decision Authority Body\n\nAn oversight body with a minimum of 3 seats, including:\n- At least 1 representative of the participant community (not staff or leadership)\n- At least 1 independent member with data ethics expertise (not employed by the organization)\n- At least 1 organizational representative\n\n**Requirements:**\n- Quorum for major data decisions: majority of seats (minimum 3 if body has 5+ seats)\n- Voting records for major decisions are publicly accessible\n- Major decisions are defined as: new data use categories, external data partnerships, consent framework changes, deletion policy changes\n- Body meets at minimum annually; convenes within 14 days for urgent issues\n\n### 1.2 Technical Stewardship\n\nDesignated individual(s) responsible for:\n- Operating anonymization pipelines per Part 3 of this Protocol\n- Auditing data access logs quarterly\n- Executing deletion requests within 30 days\n- Maintaining the public use registry (see Part 5)\n\n### 1.3 External Accountability\n\nAnnual independent review of:\n- Consent record completeness\n- Deletion pipeline effectiveness\n- Anonymization integrity (including re-identification risk assessment)\n- Compliance with this Protocol\n\nReview results are published publicly within 60 days of completion.\n\n---\n\n## Part 2: Consent Architecture Requirements\n\n### 2.1 Layered Consent (Minimum Standard)\n\nConsent under EELP is never bundled. Participants receive distinct consent requests for distinct uses. The minimum required layers are:\n\n**Layer A — Interaction Consent** *(required to proceed)*\nThe participant understands:\n- They are interacting with an AI system\n- What data is logged during the interaction\n- That they can stop at any time without consequence\n- That nothing is retained beyond the session unless they choose otherwise\n\n**Layer B — Research/Commons Consent** *(opt-in, separate)*\nThe participant explicitly agrees to their anonymized data entering a shared research corpus. This layer:\n- Is never pre-checked\n- Specifies what research categories are covered\n- Is independently withdrawable at any time\n\n**Layer C — Extended Use Consent** *(opt-in, granular)*\nWhere organizations plan to use participant data beyond basic research (model training, publication, case studies), each use category requires a separate, independently revocable consent checkbox.\n\n### 2.2 Consent UX Requirements (Non-Negotiable)\n\nThe following are prohibited in any EELP-compliant consent flow:\n- Pre-checked consent boxes\n- Consent bundled into terms of service or entry agreement\n- \"Continue = consent\" flows (clicking next does not constitute consent)\n- Urgency framing (\"consent expires in X seconds\")\n- Buried or visually de-emphasized opt-out paths\n- Consent presented without an alternative path (decline must be visually equivalent to accept)\n\n**Required:**\n- One consent decision per screen or interaction step\n- Plain language — comprehensible without legal or technical background\n- Withdrawal mechanism visible and accessible throughout the experience\n- Confirmation of any consent withdrawal, with timeline for data removal\n\n### 2.3 Biometric Data (Special Category)\n\nBiometric data (EEG, heart rate variability, facial recognition, voice analysis beyond transcription) requires:\n- Separate consent layer, not bundled with narrative or behavioral data\n- Written explanation of what biometric data reveals and how it will be stored\n- Explicit statement of any third parties with access\n- Minimum 24-hour reflection period before biometric data collection begins (i.e., consent cannot be given and immediately acted upon in the same session)\n- **Cannot be activated without Decision Authority Body vote (quorum required)**\n\n---\n\n## Part 3: Anonymization Standard\n\n### 3.1 Required Anonymization Steps\n\nAny data entering a shared research corpus under Layer B or C consent must pass through the following steps before storage:\n\n1. **Identity stripping** — Names, usernames, contact information, and direct identifiers removed at the point of ingestion. Not retained at any storage layer.\n2. **Temporal fuzzing** — Exact timestamps replaced with period labels (e.g., \"Day 2, afternoon\"). Clock-precise times not retained.\n3. **Demographic generalization** — Specific demographics replaced with ranges: age → decade bracket; location → regional level; occupation → sector.\n4. **Relationship isolation** — Cross-participant linking requires explicit additional consent; default is full isolation.\n5. **Linguistic de-identification** — Automated scan for incidental identifiers embedded in narrative text (names of people, specific locations, identifying events). Flagged records require human review before Trust inclusion.\n6. **Re-identification risk assessment** — Before any data is released or published externally, an automated re-identification risk score must be generated. Records above the threshold require Decision Authority review before release.\n\n### 3.2 Exclusion List\n\nThe following data types are excluded from any research corpus regardless of anonymization quality:\n- Active mental health crisis disclosures or suicidal ideation\n- Descriptions of trauma involving identifiable third parties\n- Data from participants who were minors at the time of collection\n- Data from any participant who has since requested deletion\n- Data that fails re-identification risk assessment and cannot be adequately remediated\n\n### 3.3 Voice and Audio Data\n\nUnprocessed audio recordings require:\n- Explicit audio-specific consent (separate from narrative/text consent)\n- Transcription-only storage by default (audio deleted after transcription unless participant explicitly consents to audio retention)\n- The transcription itself undergoes the standard anonymization pipeline\n\n---\n\n## Part 4: Deletion Rights\n\n### 4.1 Participant Right to Deletion\n\nAny participant may request deletion of their data at any time, for any reason, with no explanation required.\n\n**Timeline:** 30 calendar days from request to confirmation.\n\n**Scope:** All raw data, all derivatives where technically feasible. Where derivative data (e.g., model training contributions) cannot be surgically removed, the organization must:\n1. Inform the participant plainly about what cannot be removed and why\n2. Cease all further use immediately\n3. Log as a governance incident\n4. Report in next public transparency report\n\n**Confirmation:** Written confirmation with unique reference number, specifying what was deleted and when.\n\n### 4.2 Mandatory Deletion Triggers\n\nThe following trigger deletion without participant request:\n- Participant identified as a minor at time of data collection\n- Data found to violate collection parameters post-hoc\n- Decision Authority vote to purge a category\n- Re-identification risk assessment failure with no feasible remediation\n\n### 4.3 No Expiry on Deletion Rights\n\nDeletion rights do not expire. A participant from 5 years ago retains the right to delete their data today. Data retention agreements with third-party researchers must include this requirement explicitly.\n\n---\n\n## Part 5: Transparency Requirements\n\n### 5.1 Public Use Registry\n\nAll approved uses of participant data are listed publicly **before use begins**. Registry is updated within 5 business days of any new approval.\n\n**Minimum registry entry fields:**\n- Project name and description\n- Organization (legal name + type)\n- Named principal investigator with contact\n- Use type (research / model training / publication / case study)\n- Data type (narrative / biometric / combined)\n- Consent layer required\n- Approval date and Decision Authority vote record\n- Expected completion date\n- Where results will be published\n- Data destruction date\n\n### 5.2 Annual Transparency Report\n\nPublished annually. Minimum contents:\n- Total number of participants in the data corpus\n- Breakdown by active consent layer\n- Number of deletion requests received and completed\n- Average deletion completion time\n- Number of governance incidents (with summaries)\n- External audit summary and link to full report\n- Any changes to consent framework or governance structure in the past year\n- Decision Authority composition and any changes\n\n---\n\n## Part 6: Crisis Protocol Requirements\n\nFor any EELP deployment where participants may disclose mental health crises, trauma, or distress:\n\n### 6.1 Detection and Response\n\nAI systems must be designed with:\n- Clear detection criteria for crisis disclosure (defined in conversation design documentation)\n- A human escalation path that is triggered before the AI responds to a crisis disclosure\n- A defined protocol for what the AI says while human support is being engaged\n\n**The AI may not:**\n- Provide mental health advice or assessment\n- Reassure a participant that their situation is manageable\n- Suggest the AI can provide adequate support\n\n**The AI must:**\n- Acknowledge the disclosure\n- Immediately offer connection to a human\n- Provide at minimum one concrete external resource (crisis line relevant to the deployment location)\n\n### 6.2 Staffing Requirement\n\nAny deployment under the EELP must have a named human responsible for crisis escalation who is reachable during the experience. This person and their contact method must be documented in the deployment plan.\n\n---\n\n## Part 7: Special Contexts\n\n### 7.1 Festivals and Large-Scale Events\n\nAdditional requirements for deployments at festivals (500+ simultaneous participants):\n- Consent kiosks or digital consent flows must be accessible in at least 2 languages\n- Accessibility accommodations must be documented (participants with disabilities)\n- A noise/crowd buffer zone for the consent interaction (participants cannot give valid consent under significant social pressure)\n- Designated staff roles for consent assistance (not just digital self-service)\n\n### 7.2 Academic Research Contexts\n\nDeployments in academic settings must also comply with applicable Institutional Review Board (IRB) requirements. EELP compliance does not substitute for IRB approval where required by law or institutional policy.\n\n### 7.3 Therapeutic and Mental Wellness Contexts\n\nDeployments in therapeutic or clinical-adjacent contexts must additionally:\n- Have clinical oversight documented\n- Include scope-of-practice disclosures (the AI is not a therapist)\n- Comply with applicable HIPAA / health data regulations in jurisdiction\n\n---\n\n## Part 8: Adoption Pathway\n\n### 8.1 How to Adopt the EELP\n\n1. Review this Protocol in full with your governance and technical leadership\n2. Complete the **EELP Readiness Checklist** (companion document — forthcoming)\n3. Establish your Data Stewardship Structure (Part 1)\n4. Implement consent architecture and deletion pipeline per Parts 2 and 4\n5. Establish your public use registry (Part 5)\n6. Complete first independent review within 12 months of launch\n7. Register with the Playa AI Foundation EELP Adopter Registry\n\n### 8.2 Tiers of Adoption\n\n**EELP Compliant:** Meets all requirements in Parts 1–6\n**EELP Certified:** Compliant + completed independent external review + public transparency report published\n**EELP Founding Adopter:** First 10 organizations to complete full certification process\n\n### 8.3 Not a Proprietary Standard\n\nThe EELP is an open standard. Organizations may implement it without the Playa AI Foundation's involvement or permission. The Foundation's role is:\n- Maintaining the standard and issuing versioned updates\n- Operating the adopter registry\n- Publishing the transparency infrastructure\n- Providing implementation guidance\n\nAttribution to the Playa AI Foundation is requested but not required.\n\n---\n\n## Part 9: Version and Change Management\n\nThis Protocol is versioned. Changes to minimum requirements are published with a comment period (minimum 60 days) before taking effect for existing adopters.\n\n| Version | Date | Status |\n|---------|------|--------|\n| v1.0 | 2026-02-23 | Draft (internal) |\n| v1.0 | TBD | Published (pending Trust Council ratification and aaa sign-off) |\n\n**Next version trigger:** First complete Oracle deployment cycle at Burning Man + external audit results.\n\n---\n\n## Appendix A: Compliance Checklist (Summary)\n\n### Governance\n- [ ] Decision Authority Body constituted with required seats\n- [ ] Voting records publicly accessible\n- [ ] Technical Steward(s) designated\n- [ ] Annual external review process established\n\n### Consent\n- [ ] Layered consent implemented (minimum Layers A and B)\n- [ ] All prohibited UX patterns absent from consent flow\n- [ ] Biometric data has separate layer with waiting period\n- [ ] Withdrawal mechanism visible throughout experience\n\n### Anonymization\n- [ ] All 6 anonymization steps applied to corpus data\n- [ ] Exclusion list enforced at ingestion\n- [ ] Re-identification risk assessment before any external release\n\n### Deletion\n- [ ] 30-day deletion pipeline operational\n- [ ] Mandatory deletion triggers automated\n- [ ] Deletion confirmation with reference number\n\n### Transparency\n- [ ] Public use registry live and updated\n- [ ] Annual transparency report published\n\n### Crisis Protocol\n- [ ] Crisis detection criteria defined in conversation design\n- [ ] Human escalation path operational\n- [ ] Named crisis lead with contact documented\n\n---\n\n## Appendix B: Relationship to the Playa AI Data Trust\n\nThe Playa AI Foundation operates under a governance model that exceeds the EELP minimum standards. The Playa AI Data Trust (see: *Data Trust Governance Framework v1.0*) is a reference implementation of this Protocol — it demonstrates what full compliance looks like at scale.\n\nOrganizations adopting the EELP should treat the Data Trust governance framework as a detailed case study, not a required template. The EELP is the floor; individual implementations may (and should) exceed it.\n\n---\n\n## Appendix C: Acknowledgments\n\nThis Protocol was developed from:\n- The Burning Man 10 Principles as applied to AI design constraints (see: *Human-Centered AI Constraints v1*)\n- The Playa AI Accord (Notion Codex 05, Playa AI Foundation internal)\n- Existing academic literature on data trust governance, consent infrastructure, and participant-governed research\n- The experience of deploying narrative AI capture in field research contexts\n\nA full bibliography will accompany the published version.\n\n---\n\n*Draft prepared by Meridian, Research & Governance Specialist*\n*Playa AI Foundation — Sprint B*\n*2026-02-23*\n\n*Status: Ready for aaa review. Pending Trust Council ratification before external publication. Coordinates with Data Trust Governance Framework v1.0.*\n",

      "title": "Burning Man 10 Principles → Human-Centered AI Constraints (Draft)",
      "type": "research",
      "content": "# Burning Man 10 Principles → Human-Centered AI Constraints\n*Draft by PlayaBot — 2026-02-22 | For Sprint B: Governance MVP*\n\n---\n\n## Purpose\n\nThis document maps Burning Man's 10 Principles to concrete AI design constraints — the foundation of the Human-Centered AI Standard that The Playa AI Foundation is developing.\n\nThese are not decoration. They are binding design rubrics. Every AI system developed by or in partnership with Playa AI Foundation must satisfy them.\n\n---\n\n## The Mapping\n\n### 1. Radical Inclusion\n> *\"Anyone may be a part of Burning Man. We welcome and respect the stranger.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: No Exclusion by Default**\n- AI systems must not discriminate based on ability, language, education level, or cultural background in participation or access\n- Interfaces must be designed for accessibility (multiple modalities, plain language)\n- Data collection must not require identity verification that excludes marginalized groups\n- The \"stranger\" framing: AI must treat unfamiliar inputs with curiosity, not suspicion\n\n**Design Test:** Can someone who has never used AI participate fully? If not, what changes?\n\n---\n\n### 2. Gifting\n> *\"Burning Man is devoted to acts of gift giving. The value of a gift is unconditional.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: Value Without Extraction**\n- AI interactions must not gate value behind data extraction — participation is not a transaction\n- The experience itself must be the gift, not a funnel to data collection\n- Consent for data use is separate from accessing the experience\n- No \"you must share your story to continue\" dark patterns\n\n**Design Test:** Does the participant receive full value even if they opt out of data sharing?\n\n---\n\n### 3. Decommodification\n> *\"In order to preserve the spirit of gifting, our community seeks to create social environments that are unmediated by commercial sponsorships, transactions, or advertising.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: No Commercial Mediation**\n- AI systems may not surface advertising, branded content, or commercial recommendations to participants\n- No corporate sponsor data-sharing arrangements without explicit participant consent\n- The Oracle experience cannot be \"presented by\" any commercial entity\n- Data may not be sold, licensed, or used for commercial AI training without explicit participant opt-in (separate from experience participation)\n\n**Design Test:** Is there any moment where a commercial interest influences what the AI says or does?\n\n---\n\n### 4. Radical Self-Reliance\n> *\"Burning Man encourages the individual to discover, exercise and rely on his or her inner resources.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: AI as Mirror, Not Oracle**\n- AI must not position itself as the authority on meaning — it reflects back, it doesn't prescribe\n- Conversation design must lead participants toward their own conclusions, not the AI's\n- No directive statements (\"You should feel X\" / \"What this means for you is Y\")\n- AI may offer frameworks and questions; the human supplies answers\n- Dependency patterns must be actively avoided in experience design\n\n**Design Test:** Does the AI give people answers, or help them find their own?\n\n---\n\n### 5. Radical Self-Expression\n> *\"Radical self-expression arises from the unique gifts of the individual... It is offered as a gift to others.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: Preserve Voice, Don't Normalize**\n- Narrative capture must preserve the participant's authentic voice — no sanitizing, smoothing, or \"improving\" their language\n- AI-generated summaries must reflect how the participant speaks, not standardized output\n- Edge cases, unusual framings, and unconventional expressions must be honored, not corrected\n- The Data Commons must contain diverse voices in their original character\n\n**Design Test:** Would the participant recognize their own voice in what the AI produced?\n\n---\n\n### 6. Communal Effort\n> *\"Our community values creative cooperation and collaboration.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: AI is Infrastructure, Not the Point**\n- AI systems serve the human community — they are tools, not protagonists\n- The Oracle facilitates human connection and meaning-making; it does not replace it\n- Data collected flows back to benefit the commons, not private interests\n- Governance of the Data Trust must be community-accountable, not AI-determined\n\n**Design Test:** Does this AI experience strengthen community bonds, or replace them?\n\n---\n\n### 7. Civic Responsibility\n> *\"We value civil society. Community members who organize events should assume responsibility for public welfare.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: Safety and Accountability**\n- All AI systems deployed by Playa AI Foundation must have clear human accountability chains\n- Crisis response protocols must exist for participants in distress (the Burn Elevation Bot must have human escalation paths)\n- AI may not advise on medical, legal, or psychological matters — must refer to qualified humans\n- Transparency: participants must always know they are interacting with AI\n- Audit trails for all data handling decisions\n\n**Design Test:** If something goes wrong, is there a human accountable for it?\n\n---\n\n### 8. Leaving No Trace\n> *\"Our community respects the environment. We are committed to leaving no physical trace of our activities wherever we gather.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: Data Minimization**\n- Collect only what is explicitly needed and consented to — nothing more\n- Default to deletion, not retention: data that no longer serves a consented purpose must be deleted\n- No passive data collection (behavior tracking, dwell time, interaction logging beyond the explicit narrative)\n- The \"Maria Protocol\": anonymization must be robust enough that re-identification is computationally infeasible\n- No persistent participant profiles without explicit opt-in\n\n**Design Test:** What data are we collecting that we don't actually need? Delete it.\n\n---\n\n### 9. Participation\n> *\"Our community is committed to a radically participatory ethic.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: Active Consent, Not Passive Agreement**\n- Consent flows must be designed for genuine understanding, not checkbox compliance\n- Participants must be able to modify or revoke consent at any time during the experience\n- AI systems must actively invite feedback and correction from participants\n- Governance of the Data Trust must include participant representatives\n- No buried terms of service — consent must be conversational and clear\n\n**Design Test:** Does the participant genuinely understand what they're agreeing to?\n\n---\n\n### 10. Immediacy\n> *\"Burning Man values immediate, personal experience.\"*\n\n**AI Constraint: Present-First, Data-Second**\n- The experience must be designed for the moment, not for data extraction\n- AI must not interrupt or dilute the present-tense emotional experience with process friction\n- Consent flows must be brief, warm, and in-the-flow — not clinical forms\n- The Data Trust is a secondary benefit; the primary benefit is the participant's experience right now\n\n**Design Test:** Does thinking about data collection make the experience worse? If so, redesign the consent flow.\n\n---\n\n## The \"AI Doesn't Decide\" Line\n\nAcross all principles, the absolute constraint is:\n\n**AI provides information, reflection, and facilitation. Humans make all decisions.**\n\nThis applies to:\n- What the participant's experience means\n- Whether their data is used\n- How the Data Trust is governed\n- Crisis response\n- Institutional partnerships\n\nAny AI system that crosses this line — even with good intentions — violates the foundational standard.\n\n---\n\n## Next Steps\n\nThis mapping is the seed of the **Human-Centered AI Standard v1**. From here:\n\n1. Validate with aaa — does this capture the intent?\n2. Develop into a full certification/badge framework (per the strategic vision)\n3. Pilot against the Oracle MVP design — does the Oracle satisfy every principle?\n4. Open for public comment from the Burning Man community\n5. Formalize as an open standard for other organizations to adopt\n\n---\n\n*This is a working draft. Assign to Meridian (Research & Governance) once the agent is live for refinement and formalization.*\n",
