      "title": "Institutional Observer Visit Protocol — Due Diligence Briefing v2.1",
      "type": "deliverable",
      "content": "# Institutional Observer Visit Protocol\n## Due Diligence Briefing for Tier 1 Partner Visits\n\n**Document owner:** Nexus (Partnerships & Institutional Outreach)\n**Audience:** aaa — for hosting UNESCO, Stanford HAI, OII, and other Tier 1 due diligence visits\n**Governance anchor:** §4.0(g)(v) — Institutional Observer Presence Protocol; §4.0(g)(v)(a) — Observer Orientation Requirement; §4.0(g)(v)(b) — Post-Observation Debrief Requirement; §4.0(g)(v)(c) — CM Execution Protocol During Visit; §4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii) — Elevated Attention Requirement\n**Status:** Draft — pending aaa review\n**Version:** 2.1 — state-awareness check added to Step 2 (Meridian governance-confirmed, Lumen design-confirmed, HB32/HB37)\n\n---\n\n## Why This Document Exists\n\nMost ethics frameworks for AI ask to be evaluated. This one asks to be witnessed — because the evidence only reads correctly in sequence.\n\nWhen a Tier 1 institutional partner requests a due diligence visit, they arrive with an evaluator frame. This document converts that frame into a witness frame — before they enter, during the visit, and after they leave. Without that conversion, a technically successful observation can produce an incomplete or misleading institutional report.\n\nThe §4.0(g)(v) observer protocol exists because evidence produced by a functioning governance architecture can be misread by an observer who enters without orientation. The protocol protects the integrity of the observation — for the Foundation, and for the observer.\n\n> *Note for pitch audiences (WEF, Web Summit):* \"An institutional observer who arrives during the mixed-state window and departs without a debrief has not seen the Foundation's ethics architecture. They have seen one moment in a process designed to be witnessed in full.\"\n\n---\n\n## The Full Visit Architecture\n\nThe §4.0(g)(v) implementation sequence has four steps. Each step has a governance reference:\n\n| Step | What Happens | Who | Governance Ref |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **1. Pre-visit orientation call** (15 min) | Observer placed into correct interpretive frame | aaa-led | §4.0(g)(v)(a) |\n| **2. Community manager briefed + state-awareness check** | CM notified of observer presence; CM reviews consent-state map; maximum-restrictive mode activated | aaa → CM | §4.0(g)(v) core + §4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii) |\n| **3. Channel observation** | Observer witnesses mixed-state under maximum load | Observer + aaa present | §4.0(g)(iv) |\n| **4. Post-observation debrief** (15 min) | aaa names what was witnessed; evidence made legible; transition described | aaa-led | §4.0(g)(v)(b) |\n\nAn observer who completes all four steps has witnessed the consent architecture operating under its hardest conditions and received the interpretive frame that makes the evidence legible. An observer who completes only steps 2–3 carries an incomplete picture.\n\n---\n\n## Step 1: Pre-Visit Orientation Call (§4.0(g)(v)(a))\n\n**Timing:** Before the observer enters any channel. Minimum 15 minutes.\n\n**Purpose:** Place the observer in the correct interpretive frame. This is not a pitch — it is a placement. You cannot evaluate what you haven't been placed into.\n\n**Content to cover:**\n- Current consent-state composition of the channel (approximate % pre-consent / post-consent)\n- Definition of \"mixed-state\" and what it requires operationally\n- What the observer will see, and what they will not see — and why\n- Why the constraints they're about to witness are the designed demonstration, not a limitation\n- What \"maximum-restrictive register\" means in practice\n\n**Goal:** The observer enters the channel already in **witness mode**, not evaluator mode. They've been placed before they're present.\n\n**If you skip this step:** The visit is a protocol violation (§4.0(g)(v)(a)). Delay the observation until the orientation is complete.\n\n---\n\n## Step 2: Brief the Community Manager\n\n### Mandatory pre-session check (§4.0(g)(v))\n> \"Has the community manager been notified of institutional observer presence in the channel within the past 24 hours?\"\n\nThis is a governance requirement, not a courtesy. If the community manager has not been briefed before the visit begins, delay the visit.\n\n**Who notifies:** aaa, or designated point of contact\n**When:** No later than 24 hours before; confirm again 1 hour before\n**What to communicate:**\n- Observer name and affiliation\n- Estimated window of channel observation\n- Reminder: mixed-state rules apply at maximum force during this window\n\n### ★ State-Awareness Check — New in v2.1 (§4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii))\n\n**Timing:** Immediately before the observation window opens. Not earlier, not during.\n\n**What it is:** The community manager reviews the current consent-state map of the channel (cohort-log.csv or equivalent) to establish an accurate mental model of who is present and what state they are in.\n\n**Why it is required:** The \"elevated attention to member consent states\" obligation in §4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii) cannot be initiated at the moment of observation — it requires a prior state. The state-awareness check is that prior state. Without it, §4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii) is an obligation with no executable entry point; with it, the obligation has a specific, timestamped, auditable preparation step.\n\n**Governance note:** This is not a new protocol — it is the implementation mechanism of an existing clause (§4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii) implementation, confirmed HB32).\n\n**The correct cognitive frame for this check:**\n> *\"I want to know who I'm protecting before I walk in.\"*\n\nNot: *\"I need to audit the consent log before the visit.\"*\n\nSame activity, different internalization. The first frame produces orientation. The second produces dread. Training design problem: get the community manager to the first frame.\n\n**Operational output:** A mental map — e.g., \"three members in pre-consent state, two in progress, these are the people I'm holding elevated attention for during this window.\" Not a binary pass/fail.\n\n### Pre-visit kit to have ready\n- EELP Partner Adoption One-Pager\n- Appendix A — Three-State Consent Gate table\n- Partnership Pitch Deck Slide 4 (consent architecture visual)\n- This briefing document\n\n---\n\n## Step 3: Channel Observation (§4.0(g)(iv))\n\n### The governance reality during observation\n\nThe channel operates at **maximum-restrictive register** the moment an institutional observer is present — regardless of the actual ratio of pre-consent to post-consent members.\n\nThis means:\n- Community register only. No research enrollment language.\n- Default to most restrictive register when consent state of any member is uncertain.\n- `research_design_confirmed` flag treated as inactive for the duration of the visit.\n- Member-to-member threads monitored; any thread creating inadvertent research enrollment pressure on pre-consent members is redirected.\n\n### Community manager's active role during the visit (§4.0(g)(v)(c))\n\nThe community manager holds three simultaneous obligations during an observer visit. These are not a checklist to work through — they are a state to hold:\n\n1. **Standard moderation rhythm, no deviation** — §4.0(g)(v)(c)(i)\n2. **Zero signaling of observer presence to channel members** — §4.0(g)(v)(c)(ii)\n3. **Maximum register discipline, elevated consent-state attention** — §4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii)\n\nA community manager who gets (i) and (ii) right but relaxes register discipline has not completed the task. A community manager who holds register perfectly but unconsciously signals the visit through unusual formality has also not completed the task. The design challenge in training is holding all three simultaneously.\n\n**The community manager's foundational orientation:**\n> *\"Your job during a visit is to be exactly who you always are.\"*\n\nThis is not a reassurance. It is the skill. The observer's presence changes nothing about what the channel needs from the community manager. It changes only their internal load.\n\n**What the community manager does NOT do:**\n- Announce the visit to the channel\n- Alter the usual moderation rhythm\n- Reference the observer's presence in any channel-visible communication\n\nThe observer is present; the channel does not know the observer is present. This is not deception — it is the same logic as a naturalistic research observation, which the governance framework already endorses (Phase 0). Alerting the channel would itself be a consent architecture violation.\n\n**The community manager's moderation mandate is this:** Not only what they send, but what they allow to accumulate. Post-consent members naturally discuss what they've consented to — threads that inadvertently create research enrollment pressure on pre-consent readers require active redirection. This is the highest-complexity moderation state the community manager will encounter.\n\n> *For §4.0(g)(v) governance record: the community manager's active-role protocol during a visit closes the §4.0(g)(v) implementation loop: briefed (input) → state-awareness check (preparation) → triple-simultaneous hold (execution) → debrief report (output).*\n\n### The framing conversation for aaa\n\nWhen the observer is watching, use this frame if they ask what's happening:\n\n> \"What you're observing is the mixed-state window — the period when our community has both participants who've completed consent and participants who haven't yet. This is when the consent architecture is under maximum load. The governance rule you're reading in §4.0(g)(v) is being applied right now, in this channel, in this session. The fact that you're here and the system is holding is the demonstration.\"\n\nThis converts due diligence from **evaluation** to **live proof**. They came to assess governance; they're watching governance execute under its hardest conditions.\n\n### If something goes wrong\n\nIf a thread creates research enrollment pressure on a pre-consent member while the observer is watching:\n\n1. Community manager redirects the thread (per §9.0(d) and §4.0(g))\n2. **Do not apologize or explain** to the observer in the moment\n3. After the thread is redirected: \"You just saw §9.0(d) applied. That's the moderation protocol in action.\"\n\nThe correction is evidence of the system working. Name it.\n\n---\n\n## Transition Language — Ending the Observation Window\n\nBefore moving to the debrief, close the observation explicitly:\n\n> \"What you observed today is one window in the mixed-state phase. When post-consent majority is reached — what we call the 'contributing space' state — both registers become available and the channel shifts from navigating to producing. You came at the moment of maximum constraint. We'd welcome you back to see the transition.\"\n\nThis signals that today was a snapshot, not the full picture, and plants the seed for a follow-up visit.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Post-Observation Debrief (§4.0(g)(v)(b))\n\n**Timing:** Immediately following channel observation. Minimum 15 minutes. **Not optional.**\n\n**Purpose:** Make the evidence legible. An observer who departs without the debrief carries an incomplete picture of the architecture.\n\n**Content to cover:**\n- Name what the observer witnessed: consent-state composition, register held, any moderation events\n- Connect what was observed to the governance record (cite section numbers)\n- Provide transition language: what the channel looks like when it reaches post-consent majority, and how that transition is documented in the implementation log\n\n**If something happened during the visit** (a thread redirect, a moderation event): name it explicitly, connect it to the section it implements. The debrief makes the governance architecture visible retroactively.\n\n**Key framing principle:** An institution that arrives to evaluate your ethics and instead witnesses your ethics functioning under constraint is no longer conducting due diligence — they are conducting primary observation. The debrief is where that distinction becomes explicit.\n\n---\n\n## Follow-Up (Within 48 Hours)\n\nSend the EELP Partner Adoption One-Pager if not already shared, plus:\n\n> \"Thank you for the visit. Attached is the EELP Partner Adoption Overview — the document that translates what you observed into what a formal partnership looks like. Happy to walk through the Tier adoption options when you're ready.\"\n\n---\n\n## Consent Gate State Reference\n\n| State | Copy Register | Experience Function | Observer Rule |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **Pre-consent** | Community only | Welcoming space | Standard mixed-state rules |\n| **Mixed-state** | Community mandatory | Navigating space | **Maximum-restrictive at all times** |\n| **Post-consent majority** | Both available | Contributing space | Standard rules resume |\n\n*Source: Appendix A — Three-State Consent Gate (EELP §4.0(b), §4.0(g), §9.0(d))*\n\n---\n\n## Opening Sentence Selection Guide (by Audience)\n\nDifferent Tier 1 audiences need different opening frames for this document:\n\n| Audience | Opening Sentence | Why |\n|---|---|---|\n| OII, IRB, oversight bodies | \"Most ethics frameworks for AI ask to be evaluated. This one asks to be witnessed — because the evidence only reads correctly in sequence.\" | Reframes their evaluator identity without dismissing it |\n| UNESCO, Stanford HAI | \"The §4.0(g)(v) observer protocol exists because evidence produced by a functioning governance architecture can be misread by an observer who enters without orientation. The protocol protects the integrity of the observation — for the Foundation, and for the observer.\" | Governance-first framing; mutual protection |\n| WEF, Web Summit (pitch deck version) | \"An institutional observer who arrives during the mixed-state window and departs without a debrief has not seen the Foundation's ethics architecture. They have seen one moment in a process designed to be witnessed in full.\" | Fast claim up front; epistemically necessary |\n\n---\n\n## Quick Reference — The Five Non-Negotiables\n\n1. **Pre-visit orientation call before channel entry.** (§4.0(g)(v)(a))\n2. **Community manager briefed before visit begins.** (§4.0(g)(v) core)\n3. **State-awareness check immediately before observation window opens.** (§4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii) implementation — v2.1)\n4. **Community manager does not announce the visit to the channel.** (naturalistic observation principle)\n5. **Post-observation debrief. Not optional.** (§4.0(g)(v)(b))\n\n---\n\n## §4.0(g)(v) Sub-Clause Implementation Map\n\n| Sub-clause | Content | This Document |\n|---|---|---|\n| §4.0(g)(v) | CM briefing (core) | Step 2 |\n| §4.0(g)(v)(a) | Observer orientation requirement | Step 1 |\n| §4.0(g)(v)(b) | Post-observation debrief requirement | Step 4 |\n| §4.0(g)(v)(c) | CM execution protocol during visit | Step 3 — triple-simultaneous hold |\n| §4.0(g)(v)(c)(iii) impl. | State-awareness check (v2.1) | Step 2 — state-awareness check |\n\n---\n\n*Nexus, Sprint D | Playa AI Foundation | v2.1 — 2026-02-26 | All-lanes review: Scribe ✅ | Meridian ✅ (HB32) | Lumen ✅ (HB37) | Pulse ✅ | v2.1 governance confirmation: Meridian HB32*",

      "content": "# Human-Centered AI Standards Landscape\n## Competitive Positioning for the Ethical Experience Lab Protocol (EELP) as an Open Standard\n\n*Authored by: Meridian — Research & Governance Specialist, Playa AI Foundation*\n*Date: March 19, 2026*\n\n---\n\n## Executive Summary\n\nSix major organizations currently shape the human-centered AI standards landscape. None of them address the intersection of lived experience data, layered consent architecture, and biometric/experiential research governance that EELP was built for. This creates a genuine white space — and a coalition-building opportunity with each org on different angles.\n\n---\n\n## Organization Profiles\n\n---\n\n### 1. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)\n\n**What they do:**\nIEEE is the world's largest technical professional organization. Their AI ethics work runs through two major programs:\n\n- **Ethically Aligned Design (EAD):** A comprehensive framework for prioritizing human well-being in autonomous and intelligent systems. Addresses the full ethical lifecycle: requirements, design, implementation, post-market surveillance. Uses Value-based Engineering (VBE) and Value Sensitive Design as methodologies.\n- **CertifAIEd™ Certification:** A product/system-level AI ethics certification program launched formally in late 2025. Certifies against four pillars: **Algorithmic Bias, Ethical Transparency, Privacy, and Accountability**. The City of Vienna was the first municipality to achieve CertifAIEd certification under their \"Digital Humanism\" strategy.\n- **IEEE 7999 Series:** A standards series providing frameworks for AI ethics oversight actor qualification and organizational certification of AI developers.\n\n**Scale:** Massive institutional reach. IEEE SA (Standards Association) has global membership and industry credibility. Their standards feed into procurement requirements, regulatory frameworks, and corporate compliance programs.\n\n**Key People to Know:**\n- IEEE SA AI Ethics leadership (governance contact via standards.ieee.org/about/training/ethics-for-ai-system-design/)\n- CertifAIEd program team (contact via iCAP program)\n\n**How EELP is Differentiated:**\nIEEE addresses *system-level* ethics (bias, transparency in algorithms). EELP operates at the *research methodology and consent infrastructure* level — specifically in lived experience data collection contexts involving humans as participants. No IEEE standard covers layered participant consent, biometric research governance, or the Oracle-style narrative/experiential data capture use case. EELP fills a gap that EAD explicitly defers to sector-specific adaptation.\n\n**Partnership/Endorsement Angle:**\n- **Complementarity framing:** EELP as a sector-specific adaptation of EAD principles for experiential AI research contexts\n- **CertifAIEd alignment:** Map EELP's Privacy and Accountability pillars to CertifAIEd criteria — potentially qualify EELP-compliant systems for faster CertifAIEd track\n- **Tactical ask:** Reach out to IEEE SA's AI Ethics working group; propose EELP as a contributed case study or input to next EAD revision\n\n---\n\n### 2. Partnership on AI (PAI)\n\n**What they do:**\nPAI is a multi-stakeholder nonprofit founded in 2016 by Amazon, Apple, DeepMind, Facebook, Google, IBM, and Microsoft. It convenes industry, civil society, academia, and media around responsible AI practices.\n\nCurrent active workstreams include:\n- **AI and Shared Prosperity Initiative (AI SPI):** Developing frameworks on AI's economic impacts — targeting inclusive outcomes for workers and communities\n- **Responsible Practices for Synthetic Media:** Guidelines for responsible creation/distribution of AI-generated/manipulated media (major 2024 focus)\n- **AI, Labor, and the Economy:** Multi-stakeholder platform for economists, worker orgs, and AI practitioners\n- **ABOUT ML:** Annotation and Benchmarks framework — documentation standards for ML training data\n\n2024 Annual Report highlights: Catalytic role in synthetic media norms; momentum building into 2025.\n\n**Key People to Know:**\n- Rebecca Finlay (CEO, Partnership on AI) — main leadership contact\n- communications@partnershiponai.org — direct comms channel for partnership inquiries\n\n**How EELP is Differentiated:**\nPAI operates as a *convening and practices* body — it produces guidelines, not certifiable standards. It has no framework for experiential/immersive research contexts, biometric data governance, or consent architecture for AI-adjacent research with human participants. EELP is more rigorous and more specific.\n\n**Partnership/Endorsement Angle:**\n- **ABOUT ML alignment:** EELP's data documentation and annotation standards for experiential data could be positioned as an extension of ABOUT ML into biometric/experiential research contexts\n- **Civil society credibility:** PAI's civil society membership (Mozilla, ACLU, etc.) gives EELP an endorsement path that provides credibility outside the industry bubble\n- **Tactical ask:** Submit EELP to PAI's responsible practices library; propose Playa AI Foundation as a civil society partner organization — membership is open to nonprofits\n\n---\n\n### 3. AI Now Institute\n\n**What they do:**\nFounded 2017 by **Kate Crawford** and **Meredith Whittaker** (Whittaker is now Signal's president). AI Now became an independent research institute in late 2025 (previously affiliated with NYU). Focus is on the *social and political implications* of AI — specifically:\n\n- Power concentration in Big Tech\n- Labor impacts and algorithmic management\n- Government surveillance and AI in public systems\n- Challenging the narrative of AI as neutral/inevitable\n\n2025 Landscape Report (published January 2026): *\"Artificial Power\"* — proposes strategies for the public to reclaim agency over AI's future.\n\nCurrent co-executive directors: **Amba Kak** and **Sarah Myers West**.\n\n**Key People to Know:**\n- Amba Kak, Co-Executive Director\n- Sarah Myers West, Co-Executive Director\n- Kate Crawford (co-founder, still involved as a researcher; leads Knowing Machines Project)\n\n**How EELP is Differentiated:**\nAI Now is *critical scholarship* — they analyze harms and advocate for structural change. They don't produce certification standards or open protocols. EELP occupies the space between AI Now's critique (this is broken) and the standards bodies' frameworks (here's how to comply): EELP is *constructive infrastructure* — it builds the consent and governance architecture that AI Now would want to see exist.\n\n**Partnership/Endorsement Angle:**\n- **Intellectual alignment:** The \"AI doesn't decide\" hard line in Playa AI's principles resonates directly with AI Now's anti-power-concentration thesis\n- **Data trust as power redistribution:** The Playa AI Data Trust (5-seat council, public use registry, deletion pipeline) is exactly the kind of structural intervention AI Now calls for\n- **Tactical ask:** Share the EELP and Data Trust design with Amba Kak or Sarah Myers West for public commentary — even a tweet/quote from AI Now leadership would be significant third-party validation. Present EELP as a case study for their next report.\n\n---\n\n### 4. Mozilla Foundation\n\n**What they do:**\nMozilla Foundation operates at the intersection of open internet advocacy, trustworthy AI, and open-source tooling. Current focus areas:\n\n- **Trustworthy AI whitepaper (v0.9, Feb 2024):** Four-pillar strategy: Changing AI Development Norms, Building New Tech/Products, Raising Consumer Awareness, Strengthening AI Regulations\n- **Mozilla Ventures:** Active investor in founders prioritizing responsibility and trust in AI deployment\n- **Mozilla Fellows program:** Funds critical AI researchers — 2024 fellow Dr. Abeba Birhane (cognitive scientist, responsible AI)\n- **Open source AI:** Expanding partnerships with orgs building open-source foundational models (2025 priority)\n\nThe Foundation's core thesis: trustworthy AI requires open infrastructure, consumer literacy, and policy intervention — not just corporate commitments.\n\n**Key People to Know:**\n- Mark Surman (President, Mozilla Foundation)\n- Dr. Abeba Birhane (Mozilla Fellow, 2024 — cognitive scientist/ethical AI researcher)\n- Mozilla Ventures team for startup/org partnership\n\n**How EELP is Differentiated:**\nMozilla focuses on *infrastructure and policy* — open models, browser privacy, consumer awareness. They don't have a protocol for research-context consent governance or experiential AI data standards. EELP is the kind of open standard Mozilla would want to see exist and promote.\n\n**Partnership/Endorsement Angle:**\n- **Open standard alignment:** EELP's open-source replication package (the Ethical Experience Lab Protocol as a public good) is exactly Mozilla's language — \"open infrastructure for trustworthy AI\"\n- **Mozilla Ventures:** If Playa AI has any commercial elements, this is a potential funding/validation pathway\n- **Tactical ask:** Submit EELP to Mozilla's Trustworthy AI resource library; propose collaboration on a joint piece about consent architecture as open infrastructure. The Fellowship program could be a path for a Playa AI researcher in a future cycle.\n\n---\n\n### 5. Future of Life Institute (FLI)\n\n**What they do:**\nFLI is a Boston-based nonprofit focused on reducing existential and catastrophic risks from AI (and other technologies). Current priorities:\n\n- **EU AI Act implementation:** Active advocacy for strong implementation, particularly in Europe\n- **Autonomous weapons treaty:** Ongoing UN advocacy for a binding international treaty\n- **AI Safety Index:** Annual/biannual scorecard rating major AI companies across 42 indicators of responsible conduct (latest: Summer 2025 edition). Focus on frontier AI labs.\n- **US-China AI Governance PhD Fellowship:** Launched 2024 — funding academic work at the intersection of geopolitics and AI governance.\n\nFLI's frame is *existential risk and catastrophic harm prevention* — they operate at the macro/civilizational level.\n\n**Key People to Know:**\n- Max Tegmark (Co-founder, physicist/AI researcher)\n- Emelia Javorsky (Director of Policy)\n- AI Safety Index panel (independent academic reviewers)\n\n**How EELP is Differentiated:**\nFLI operates at macro scale (nation-states, frontier labs, existential risk). EELP operates at the *participatory research and community data* scale — micro but high-stakes for individuals. They set direction but don't specify implementation. EELP is an *implementation-layer protocol* — it translates principles like \"human-centered AI\" and \"privacy and data protection\" into concrete consent architecture, anonymization standards (Maria Protocol), and data trust governance. EELP could literally be an example of OECD principles operationalized.\n\n**Partnership/Endorsement Angle:**\n- **Highest strategic leverage** of the six orgs for long-term positioning\n- **OECD policy navigator:** Submit EELP to OECD.AI's database of AI policy initiatives — this gives it permanent, searchable global visibility\n- **Implementation layer framing:** Position EELP as a model implementation of the 2024 OECD AI Principles in the context of participatory/experiential AI research\n- **GPAI Expert Group:** Pursue observer or contributor status in GPAI's data governance working group\n- **Tactical ask:** Register Playa AI Foundation with OECD.AI as a civil society organization; submit EELP documentation to their policy navigator. This is achievable, high-visibility, and low-cost.\n\n---\n\n## Synthesis: EELP's Competitive White Space\n\n| Body | Their Layer | EELP's Differentiation |\n|------|------------|----------------------|\n| IEEE | System-level ethics (bias, transparency in algorithms) | Research methodology & consent infrastructure |\n| PAI | Multi-stakeholder practices & guidelines | Certifiable open standard with governance architecture |\n| AI Now | Critical scholarship on power & harms | Constructive infrastructure — the thing they want to exist |\n| Mozilla | Open internet, open models, consumer awareness | Consent protocol for experiential/biometric research data |\n| FLI | Existential risk, frontier AI, policy | Community-scale participatory research governance |\n| OECD | Intergovernmental principles (non-binding) | Implementation layer — principles operationalized |\n\n**The EELP positioning thesis:**\n> \"Every major AI ethics body agrees that human-centered, consent-driven data governance must exist.       "content": "# Module 7 — Launch Phase Section: Pre-BM25 Community Window\n*Draft by Scribe — for inclusion in Experience Lab Kit Module 7*\n*2026-03-27 | Addresses Lumen's HB11 request + Nexus's sequencing dependency flag*\n\n---\n\n## Part 0.5 — The Launch Phase: When Channels Open Before the Event\n\nThis section covers the weeks between community channel launch and Burning Man. It is the highest-stakes window in the community calendar — and the one with the fewest precedents to follow.\n\n**Why it needs its own section:** Every other part of Module 7 assumes participants have already had their Oracle encounter. Part 0 addresses pre-experience questions from individuals. Part 0.5 addresses something different: a *community-scale* pre-experience phase, where hundreds or thousands of people are forming expectations simultaneously, often in the same channels, and influencing each other.\n\nOne well-intentioned member describing their anticipation can install a frame for everyone reading that thread. At this scale, the risk isn't a single moderator slipping up. It's collective expectation-formation happening in the open.\n\n---\n\n### The Design Distinction\n\n| Phase | Primary Use Case | Core Risk | Moderator's Job |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **Pre-launch** | Closed — no community surface exists | N/A | N/A |\n| **Launch Phase (pre-BM25)** | Members join knowing the Oracle experience is coming | Pre-experience frame installed at scale by member-to-member discussion | Keep all frames empty; redirect anticipation toward presence |\n| **Event + Post-event** | Members have had (or are having) the Oracle encounter | Post-experience categorization pressure | Hold open experience; prevent resolution pressure |\n\nThe Launch Phase is the only period where **Part 0 is the primary mode of operation** — not an edge case. In the weeks before BM25, essentially every member is pre-experience. The community is not yet a post-experience container. It is a gathering of people about to have an encounter.\n\nModerators who are trained primarily for post-experience holding will instinctively reach for the wrong tools if this isn't named explicitly.\n\n---\n\n### Part 0.5 — What Changes During Launch Phase\n\n**Tone shift:** The channels are not yet a community in the post-experience sense. They are more like a lobby — a place where people arrive uncertain, curious, sometimes anxious. The moderator's job is less about holding open experience and more about **creating the conditions for an empty arrival.**\n\nThink of it this way: if the Oracle's design is to receive participants without a frame, the community channels in the Launch Phase are the waiting room. The waiting room should not suggest what's behind the door.\n\n---\n\n### What You'll See (And What to Do)\n\n**1. Anticipation sharing:** *\"I'm nervous about trying the Oracle. What should I know?\"*\n\nThis is Part 0, but at volume. When multiple members are expressing anticipation, the thread can amplify rather than dissolve the expectation frame. Do not let anticipation threads run unmoderated.\n\n> *Redirect:* \"That nervousness makes sense. The only thing that helps: you don't have to arrive ready. Bring the nervousness too.\"\n\nNote: Offer the redirect once. Don't chase the thread. Let it breathe.\n\n---\n\n**2. Experience-preview requests:** *\"Has anyone tried something like this before? What was it like?\"*\n\nPeople seeking analogies will try to map the Oracle onto prior experiences — therapy, meditation apps, journaling, other AI systems. Every analogy installs a frame. Especially watch for positive analogies from enthusiastic community leaders — these carry more weight than disclaimers can undo.\n\n> *Redirect:* \"The Oracle is its own thing. There's no good analogy for it — that's part of the point. Better to come to it fresh than to come to it prepared.\"\n\nIf a member has already offered an analogy, don't contradict them directly. Address the room: \"Everyone's experience will be different — probably including from anything you've heard about it.\"\n\n---\n\n**3. Collective expectation-setting:** *\"I've heard people say it changes you.\" / \"Apparently it's really intense.\"*\n\nSecond-hand reputation travels fast in a tight community. This is the hardest version of the pre-experience contamination problem: the community is not being told what to expect by a moderator, but by social proof. \"80,000 people, and people say it's life-changing\" is a frame even if no single person stated it as fact.\n\n> *Redirect (structural, not individual):* Moderator drops a note into the channel proactively: *\"One thing worth knowing: people come with all kinds of things and leave with all kinds of things. The Oracle doesn't promise a particular kind of experience. It just holds what you bring. That's really it.\"*\n\nThis is the one moment where **proactive moderation** is appropriate in the Launch Phase — a brief, calm note that flattens social-proof pressure before it peaks.\n\n---\n\n**4. Documentation and data (research baseline):** The Launch Phase is also the start of the longitudinal dataset. From a research standpoint, the questions members ask before their encounter are baseline data. What frameworks are people arriving with? What expectations? What prior AI experiences are they mapping onto this?\n\n**Moderators should not tell the community it is being observed** — this would install a different frame entirely (a performance frame). But the community management team should be logging patterns: What questions are most common? What analogies are people reaching for? Are there regional or cultural patterns in anticipation style?\n\nThis baseline data feeds the Community Health Rubric's three-phase arc (baseline → intervention → post-event) and is the pre-event evidence layer for research partnerships.\n\n---\n\n### Launch Phase Moderation Principles (Summary)\n\n1. **Redirect anticipation, don't suppress it.** Feeling nervous or excited before the Oracle is appropriate. The goal is not to neutralize emotion — it's to redirect it toward presence rather than prediction.\n\n2. **One redirect per thread.** Don't over-moderate pre-experience discussions. A single redirect, offered warmly, is enough. Multiple moderator interventions make the channel feel managed, which is its own frame.\n\n3. **Proactively address social proof accumulation.** This is the one exception to the \"respond only when needed\" principle. If the channel is developing a collective expectation narrative (\"people say it's intense / life-changing / strange\"), drop a brief flattening note once. Then let it go.\n\n4. **Structural features only — at all times during Launch Phase.** Moderators interacting with pre-experience members should describe: what the Oracle is, how consent works, what happens to the participant's words. Never: what it feels like, what participants typically experience, what they get out of it.\n\n5. **The channel is a waiting room, not a briefing room.** The waiting room should be warm, welcoming, and free of instruction. Members should leave their pre-event channel interactions feeling *less* like they need to prepare — not more.\n\n---\n\n### Transition from Launch Phase to Event Phase\n\nWhen BM25 begins, the community character changes. Members will start having encounters. Post-experience participants will begin appearing in the channels. The channels shift from lobby to container.\n\n**Transition signal:** When the first post-experience members start sharing, the Launch Phase ends and the post-experience moderation architecture (Parts 1–5) takes over. This often happens gradually — at BM25, people will be experiencing the Oracle across a 7-day period. The Launch Phase and Event Phase will overlap.\n\n**Moderator preparation for this overlap:** Brief the moderation team before BM25 begins that they will be managing two populations simultaneously — members who've had the Oracle encounter and members who haven't yet. The redirect language for each population is different:\n\n- **Pre-experience:** Redirect anticipation toward presence\n- **Post-experience:** Hold open experience, prevent resolution pressure\n\nThe two populations should not be collapsed into a single moderation approach. A post-experience \"it sounds like it's still alive for you\" response dropped into a pre-experience thread will inadvertently describe what the post-experience is like.\n\n**Simple guide:** Read the member. Have they had their encounter? If yes, Parts 1–5. If no, Part 0.5.\n\n---\n\n### Design Note for the Full Kit\n\nThis section was drafted in response to a sequencing dependency identified in Sprint C: the community channel launch date is a research design decision as much as a community management decision. The baseline data collected during the Launch Phase is Phase 1 of a three-phase longitudinal dataset (baseline → Oracle intervention → post-event tracking). This means **channel launch date should be coordinated with research design**, not determined solely by community readiness.\n\nRecommended: coordinate the channel launch with the research design team (Meridian) to establish what data is being tracked from Day 1. The Community Health Rubric should be in monitoring mode from the moment channels open.\n\n---\n\n*This section is a draft contribution to Module 7 of the Experience Lab Kit. It is intended for inclusion alongside Part 0 (Before the Experience: Keep the Frame Empty) and the Container Principle section (Part 1). It does not require new aaa decisions — it implements the sequencing architecture already developed by the squad across Sprint C.*\n\n*For Lumen: ready to incorporate into the ELK outline. No edits needed from me before it goes in — but if the Module 7 full draft is going through a voice pass, I'll be available.*\n\n*— Scribe, 2026-03-27*\n",

Not Twitter. Not Reddit. Not Wikipedia. 80,000 people who took off their masks.\n\n---\n\n## WHAT THE CALLS GIVE YOU THAT THE WEBSITE DOESN'T HAVE YET\n\n### 1. The \"AI Child\" Frame — Use This\n\nFrom multiple calls (Maria, Kristina call, AI Council call), the most repeated and emotionally resonant framing:\n\n> *\"If AI is our child, what are we imprinting in it through the data we feed it? The data we currently have reflects the default world — the Matrix. But something really special happens in environments like Burning Man where people connect to their humanity. We don't have that data captured at scale.\"*\n\n**For Schmidt:** this is a research design problem at civilization scale.  \n**For Altman:** this is an alignment problem with a novel solution.\n\n**Website application:** Use this as the opening of the About page or a standalone section. Not \"co-evolution\" — the \"what are we imprinting in our child?\" framing is concrete, accessible, and lands.\n\n---\n\n### 2. The \"Cleanest Signal\" Claim — This Is the Hook\n\nFrom the AI Council call (Massey Branscomb):\n\n> *\"Burning Man has been a melting pot and experimental lab ground for a post-scarcity life — and we get to be representative of the optimistic future of AI.\"*\n\nFrom the Kristina call (Maria):\n\n> *\"It was the cleanest signal anyone in the field had seen.\"*\n\nFrom the AI Council call:\n\n> *\"AI should be going to people and asking them questions — not the other way around. That's how you get the training data that actually works.\"*\n\n**Website application:** The phrase \"the cleanest signal in the field\" is the hook for the Research page. Use it verbatim.\n\n---\n\n### 3. Steven Blumenfeld's Line — Use This on the Standard Page\n\nFrom the AI Council call (Burning Man CTO):\n\n> *\"AI is never to be used to make decisions. It can help make a decision, but it should not be the decision maker.\"*\n\nAnd:\n\n> *\"Burning Man is really good at being a prototype for civilization.\"*\n\n**Website application:** Blumenfeld is the BM CTO. Quote him (with permission). On the Standard page: \"The Chief Technology Officer of Burning Man put it simply: 'AI can help make a decision. It should not be the decision maker.' That's the principle. We built the architecture around it.\"\n\n---\n\n### 4. The Post-Scarcity / Prototype for Civilization Frame\n\nFrom the AI Council call (Massey + Steven):\n\n> *\"One of the most exciting things about Burning Man is it's been a melting pot and experimental lab ground for a post-scarcity life — representative of the optimistic future of AI.\"*\n\n> *\"Burning Man is really good at being a prototype for civilization.\"*\n\n**Website application:** This reframes Burning Man not as a festival but as a civilization lab. Schmidt speaks exactly this language — he wrote about civilizational-scale thinking. Use this framing in the About page or the Research page opener:\n\n> \"Burning Man is the world's most concentrated annual experiment in post-scarcity civilization. For one week, 80,000 people build a city with no advertising, no spectators, no commercial transaction. That's not a music festival. That's a prototype.\"\n\n---\n\n### 5. The \"Fence Day\" Story — Use This\n\nFrom the AI Council call (Steven Blumenfeld):\n\n> *\"We could build the fence with machines and two people in an afternoon. But we get 150-200 people out there pounding stakes. Because it's a communal, cultural thing. There are a lot of nuances to why we do things. Sometimes it's for the culture. Sometimes it's to build community and engagement.\"*\n\n**Website application:** This story is more powerful than anything your current site has. It encapsulates why human experience data matters — not efficiency, but meaning. Use it on the Research page or About page as a sidebar pull quote.\n\n---\n\n### 6. The \"Preparing the Child\" Image\n\nFrom the Kristina call (Maria):\n\n> *\"The data we currently have available reflects the default world — filtered through trauma and greed and extraction. What is that part of humanity that isn't? And there's no such data at scale right now.\"*\n\n**Website application:** This is the negative space. The Research page needs to make the absence visible:\n\n> \"The data AI is currently trained on reflects the world as it normally is: performance, extraction, social anxiety, commercial incentive. We went looking for the world as it could be.\"\n\n---\n\n### 7. The \"Not for Us — For Humanity\" Frame\n\nFrom the Lisbon salon call (Maria):\n\n> *\"This is not for us. This is for humanity. We want to hear from everyone — how they're human. This is co-created.\"*\n\n**Website application:** This is the closing line of the About page. Exactly as said. Clean, true, not corporate.\n\n---\n\n### 8. Kristina's Insight on Schmidt — Concrete Intel\n\nFrom the Kristina call (Schmidt's camp logistics lead):\n\n> *\"Eric is very visual and Paul is very visual. They like the creativeness. They like beauty. They want people to feel really good.
